articles.title: Mars n’est pas morte, une sonde européenne détecte les signes d’un magma endormi sous ses volcans
articles.text:
Au-dessus de fissures volcaniques sur Mars, la sonde européenne ExoMars TGO a détecté du chlorure d'hydrogène, un gaz que rejettent souvent les volcans terrestres. Un indice que la planète rouge garde de la chaleur sous sa croûte, voire des refuges pour la vie.
Mars pourrait abriter une activité volcanique en sommeil, selon une étude internationale fondée sur les données de la sonde européenne ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO). À contre-saison, l'orbiteur de l'ESA a repéré du chlorure d'hydrogène au-dessus des mêmes fissures du volcan Alba Mons, un signal qui pourrait trahir un magma endormi sous la surface. La découverte relance l'éternel débat sur l'activité de la planète rouge, et pourrait bien indiquer aux scientifiques où chercher la vie.
Sur Mars, un gaz volcanique qui n'en fait qu'à sa tête
Le chlorure d'hydrogène (HCl), TGO l'a signalé pour la première fois dans l'atmosphère martienne dès 2021. Comme ce gaz s'échappe couramment des évents volcaniques sur Terre, donc par des fissures et des fumerolles, les chercheurs se demandaient s'il en allait de même là-haut. Mais pour l'essentiel, il suit un calendrier bien réglé, car il culmine pendant l'hiver de l'hémisphère nord puis disparaît presque entièrement l'été, un va-et-vient qui semble surtout lié aux cycles de la poussière et de l'eau. Presque, car une exception revient avec une régularité d'horloge.
Au début de l'été, dans l'hémisphère nord de Mars, des pics de chlorure d'hydrogène apparaissent au-dessus des fissures qui zèbrent les flancs d'Alba Mons. Ils ont été repérés par l'ACS (Atmospheric Chemistry Suite), un ensemble de spectromètres infrarouges embarqué sur TGO. Ces instruments analysent la lumière du Soleil qui traverse l'atmosphère martienne, où chaque gaz laisse sa propre empreinte, un peu comme une signature. Daniel Mège, co-auteur principal de l'étude publiée dans Science Advances, compare l'exercice à la recherche d'une aiguille dans une botte de foin. La sonde a détecté une poignée de molécules, venues d'une source qui ne s'active peut-être que par intermittence, alors qu'elle tourne sans cesse autour de Mars pour surveiller l'atmosphère de toute la planète.
Il fallait comprendre comprendre d'où venait ce gaz. La caméra CaSSIS, elle aussi à bord de TGO, a révélé à cet endroit des fissures fraîches et étroites, parfois longues de plusieurs centaines de mètres, associées à des changements de couleur du sol. L'hypothèse des chercheurs ? En hiver, quand le thermomètre descend jusqu'à −120 °C, la glace bouche ces fissures. Aux premiers beaux jours, elle se sublime (elle passe directement de l'état solide à l'état gazeux) et libère le gaz piégé.
Un volcanisme martien en sommeil… et peut-être des niches pour la vie
Pour l'équipe internationale menée par le chercheur Alexander Trokhimovskiy, ces émanations proviendraient d'un magma chaud en profondeur. Les fissures joueraient le rôle de fumerolles, ces évents dont nous parlions plus haut, par lesquels un volcan terrestre « respire », et les décolorations alentour pourraient être des dépôts laissés par les gaz. Selon Daniel Mège, la répartition du gaz évoquait d'emblée un volcan, mais il a fallu examiner toutes les réactions chimiques possibles de l'atmosphère pour le démontrer. Dans l'étude, les auteurs avancent l'idée d'une chambre magmatique en sommeil, une sorte de plomberie volcanique enfouie.
C'est tout le paradoxe martien. La planète abrite les plus grands volcans du Système solaire, sans qu'on sache à quel point ils sont encore actifs. D'après les images prises en orbite, certains semblent l'avoir été au cours des derniers millions d'années, et des sismomètres y ont enregistré des séismes. Pourtant, aucune éruption ni nouvelle coulée de lave n'a jamais été observée. « Nos résultats suggèrent que Mars a conservé assez de chaleur interne pour entretenir une activité volcanique jusqu'à récemment, et peut-être encore aujourd'hui », avance Daniel Mège, professeur au Centre de recherches spatiales de l'Académie polonaise des sciences.
Quant à la question de la vie… Par le passé, ces gaz venus du magma ont pu être bien plus abondants. Ils auraient alors contribué à épaissir l'atmosphère, qui retenait mieux la chaleur, à adoucir le climat et à permettre à l'eau liquide de couvrir une bonne partie de la surface. Et si de la lave remontant dans la croûte rencontre de l'eau souterraine, elle pourrait la réchauffer et créer des poches chaudes, propices à la vie. C'est ce qu'on appelle des systèmes hydrothermaux : sur Terre, des micro-organismes prospèrent dans ce type d'environnement. Pour Daniel Mège, chercher la vie dans les fissures d'Alba Mons aurait donc tout son sens. Si de tels systèmes y sont actifs, ils fourniraient aux micro-organismes les ingrédients et l'énergie nécessaires, tout en les protégeant d'une surface hostile et changeante. Colin Wilson, responsable scientifique de TGO à l'ESA, estime que ces résultats pourraient être le plus grand succès de la sonde à ce jour.

articles.title: ‘The fun for creators lies in the creative process itself’: Hideo Kojima says AI can’t replace human creativity in video games — and admits he’s worried for the future
articles.text:
Hideo Kojima says AI can't replace human creativity in video games — as he warns that craft is irreplaceable and 'I don’t want a future where that’s lost'
‘It’s the trial and error that gets the adrenaline pumping’, he says
- Famed game creator Hideo Kojima has voiced his opinions on AI
- He said human creativity is a vital part of the game-development process
- And he’s worried about a future where AI dominates the industry
Legendary games maker Hideo Kojima is known for the creativity of his output, from the Metal Gear Solid series to Death Stranding, so it’s unsurprising to hear that he has strong opinions on the use of AI in video games. And in a fresh interview, he told readers exactly where he feels AI falls flat compared to human-made artistic expression.
Speaking to Japanese site Game*Spark, Kojima said that while it’s good that AI has improved efficiency, “the fun isn’t in finishing the picture. It’s in the process … While it’s fine to tell a computer to create this or that, and then say, ‘That’s wrong, change it,’ I don’t find that very interesting in terms of craftsmanship.”
“I’m worried about what will happen to that aspect of the enjoyment of craftsmanship in the future,” he added.
Kojima said he feels that there’s a distinction between using AI for creative output and employing it to form a finished product: “If you’re just making a ‘product,’ that’s fine, but I think the fun for creators lies in the creative process itself. I think ‘creativity’ and ‘products’ are different things.”
In other words, AI doesn’t offer creators the kind of spark they get from crafting something themselves. And it’s that kind of magic that so often resonates with consumers of Kojima’s media.
His comments reflect those of Jason Graves, the composer of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s soundtrack, who spoke out against AI music generation, saying that “Music is not just a bunch of notes strung together.” Instead, the process is essential as it is based on “creative instincts forged by emotion and all the little decisions that give a piece of art its own unique personality.”
The effort itself is key
Kojima didn’t just muse on what AI means for video games and other creative outlets in the present — he also had thoughts on how it could impact the future.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
For instance, the game director said: “It’s not about telling someone to make a song like this and then being satisfied with the result; it’s the trial and error in between that gets the adrenaline pumping, and it’s incredibly exciting. I don’t want a future where that’s lost.”
He then reflected that, “I think it will be fine for five or 10 years, but if AI continues unchecked, perhaps a future where AI plays a vital role in creative fields will come someday. Well, I won’t be around by then. It’s up to the younger generation to decide, so I want to pass the baton to them.”
If the goal is purely to improve efficiency, AI could help to build a “good future,” Kojima noted. But for someone like him, there’s evidently much more to crafting something than just making it quickly with minimal effort.
Indeed, the effort itself is a key part of creative development. As Kojima put it, “Even with plastic models, the shape is the same no matter who builds it, but the process of assembling it is what’s interesting, isn’t it?”

articles.title: Cosmic at SEMICON Europa 2026: Advancing High-Complexity Semiconductor Test Solutions - EE Times
articles.text:
ALTOPASCIO, Italy — Nov. 9, 2026 — Cosmic Group will participate in SEMICON Europa 2026 in Munich, held concurrently with electronica from Nov. 10 to 13, 2026. Cosmic will be located at booth C1255.
Rooted in the tradition of technological innovation “Made in Europe,” the group aligns perfectly with this year’s event focus: “Europe’s Next Era: Navigating the Perfect Storm.”
Headquartered in Altopascio, in the Italian province of Lucca, Cosmic combines long-established leaders in the development of automated test equipment (ATE) and semiconductor testing services.
The brand brings together the skills, technologies and experience of the companies integrated through an acquisition strategy launched in 2022, following Xenon Private Equity’s investment in Microtest. Today, Cosmic operates through two complementary and independent divisions: Cosmic Equipment and Cosmic Services. The company has a presence in Europe, the U.S. and Asia, with 15 direct locations and a team of more than 400 professionals.
At SEMICON Europa 2026, Cosmic will welcome visitors to a space designed to showcase the engineering excellence of its two divisions, which synergistically combine technologies, expertise and services for semiconductor testing.
The Cosmic Equipment division designs and manufactures semiconductor test solutions—high-performance platforms for the automotive, industrial, power and high-reliability sectors. Its portfolio includes ATE for mixed-signal and high-power applications, as well as handlers and burn-in solutions.
At the center of the exhibition area dedicated to the Equipment division, the new range of ATE systems will be presented. The centerpiece of the booth is MISTRAL, the next-generation ATE platform designed to accelerate time to market—from development through volume production—while optimizing the cost of test (CoT).
Designed for mixed-signal, smart-power and digital device applications, MISTRAL combines high-density instrumentation, a modular and scalable architecture and an AI-native test development environment (Polaris, Testing Operating System), radically simplifying the way test solutions are created, implemented and scaled.
Particularly worth mentioning are the wide-bandgap semiconductor test solutions for silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN), engineered to ensure the highest quality and reliability as well as to detect defects already at the silicon device stage, while the device is still on the wafer.
With the growing adoption of 3.3-kV SiC devices, test architectures must evolve to ensure the highest standards of efficiency and reliability.
Cosmic addresses this industrial challenge with VIP Ultra and the M2 platform, a complete suite of high-performance modular ATE systems dedicated to the testing of semiconductors, wafers and power devices.
At SEMICON Europa 2026, Cosmic experts will be available to support customers in developing their projects across the entire supply chain—from design through qualification to production—combining local expertise with a global vision.
In this context, the Services division positions itself as a strategic outsourcing partner for services and operational support, working alongside customers at every stage of the device lifecycle. Its specialized know-how ranges from design-for-testability (DFT) support and the development of customized tests to wafer sort, final test, characterization, qualification, burn-in and failure analysis.
Thanks to a technologically independent approach, Cosmic Services works with the leading ATE platforms available on the market, integrating the ideal solutions for the specific requirements of each project.
At this special turning point in history, genuine European supply chain resilience requires well-established partners. Through the combination of advanced test solutions and specialized services, Cosmic supports the development of a stronger, safer and less dependent European semiconductor supply chain, thus contributing to the goals of European supply chain resilience in terms of supply security, strategic autonomy and industrial resilience for the sector.
About Cosmic
Cosmic is a global player in advanced competitive semiconductor test solutions built on a growth and integration strategy since 2022. With more than 400 professionals across 15 direct locations in Europe, the U.S. and Asia, Cosmic operates through two distinct and complementary divisions.
The Equipment division designs and manufactures automated test equipment (ATE) systems for mixed-signal and high-power applications, as well as handlers and burn-in systems, delivering advanced technological platforms for the automotive, industrial and power markets.
The Services division provides a full range of test services, from wafer sort and final production testing to characterization, qualification, reliability testing and advanced failure and technology analysis, as well as ASIC design and design-for-testability (DFT) support to optimize device performance, testability and time to market.
Together, the units enable customers to select optimal solutions from a comprehensive portfolio, underpinned by deep technological expertise and international operational excellence, thereby contributing to improved quality, efficiency and time to market in advanced electronics and high-reliability applications.

articles.title: Apple explique comment désactiver le nouveau logo lumineux des MacBook Pro PROLED XDR
articles.text:
Abandonné depuis des années, le logo luminescent d’Apple a marqué son grand retour, fin octobre, en trônant fièrement sur le capot du nouveau MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. Une nouveauté cosmétique globalement saluée mais qui n’est pas pour autant du goût de tout le monde. Apple explique donc cette semaine comment désactiver cet effet.
Dévoilé fin octobre à l’occasion d’une courte keynote organisée rien que pour lui, le nouveau MacBook Pro PROLED XDR est le premier MacBook à disposer d’un écran OLED tactile : une révolution copernicienne pour Apple qui s’était jusqu’à présent interdit d’exploiter des commandes tactiles et gestuelles sur macOS.
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
Le grand retour de la pomme luminescente…
Derrière cette nouveauté majeure (pas sur le marché, certes, mais dans la galaxie Apple) se cache un autre changement totalement cosmétique cette fois : le retour de la pomme luminescente, plaquée sur le capot de l’appareil.
Délaissée depuis 2016, cette particularité esthétique a donc fait son grand retour sur le MacBook Pro PROLED XDR. Le logo d’Apple reste en métal poli et réfléchissant lorsque le Mac est éteint ou que son capot est fermé, mais dès qu’on met le contact ou qu'on déploie l’écran, la pomme s’illumine en tirant parti du système de la lumière émise par la dalle OLED de ce nouveau MacBook.
Sa luminosité dépend donc principalement de l’intensité lumineuse choisie par l’utilisateur côté écran, mais aussi des conditions de lumière ambiante et de la couleur choisie pour le châssis, rapporte 9to5Mac.
« Le logo Apple situé derrière l’écran intégré s’allume dès que le Mac est en veille active. Sa luminosité s’ajuste automatiquement en fonction du niveau de luminosité de l’écran intégré et des conditions d’éclairage détectées par le capteur de lumière ambiante de l’ordinateur. Quel que soit le niveau de luminosité de l’écran, le logo Apple sera moins lumineux dans une pièce sombre et plus lumineux dans une pièce claire », explique pour sa part Apple à propos de cette « nouveauté ».
… et comment la désactiver
À l’occasion du début des livraisons de son MacBook Pro PROLED XDR, Apple explique néanmoins comment désactiver complètement ce rétroéclairage de la pomme… Si vous préférez la voir éteinte. Pour ce faire, un rapide détour par le Terminal de macOS est par contre nécessaire. On apprend par ailleurs que l’utilisateur doit disposer des droits d’administrateur pour procéder à cette désactivation.
Voici les commandes à entrer dans le Terminal pour désactiver le rétroéclairage de la pomme, et le réactiver par la suite si vous changez d’avis :
- Désactivation : « sudo defaults write com.Apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0 ».
- Réactivation : « sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode ».
Apple explique enfin que toute réinstallation de macOS a pour effet de réactiver cette sympathique luminescence de son logo sur le capot de l'appareil..
Source : Guilherme Rambo sur X / 9to5Mac

articles.title: Pour le Black Friday 2026, cette brosse Philips notée 4,5/5 passe sous les 190 €
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 – La brosse à dents électrique Philips Sonicare 9900 Prestige à 189,99 € (-31%)
La brosse à dents électrique Philips Sonicare 9900 Prestige passe sous les 200 € chez Amazon soit une baisse d'environ 31% sur le prix habituellement constaté.
Lancée à l'occasion de l'édition 2021 du CES, la brosse à dents électrique Philips 9000 Prestige est enfin commercialisée en France. Ce nouveau modèle est censé apprendre des habitudes de l'utilisateur et s'adapter à chaque besoin.

Points forts
- Une application très riche en conseils et informations.
- Trois niveaux d'intensité.

Points faibles
- Brosse à dents à bruyante.

articles.title: Los directores financieros asumen la gestión de la inteligencia artificial como nueva responsabilidad corporativa
articles.text:
Los directores financieros (CFO) están ante una transformación sin precedentes: a las responsabilidades tradicionales de supervisión contable y control presupuestario se suma ahora la gestión de la inteligencia artificial como herramienta de trabajo y como área de rendición de cuentas corporativa. Un nuevo informe de Salesforce, elaborado a partir de una encuesta doble ciego a 865 líderes financieros de tres continentes, documenta cómo la función del CFO se ha ampliado en el último año y cómo la IA —incluyendo los agentes autónomos— está en el centro de ese cambio.
Casi tres cuartas partes de los responsables financieros reconocen que el alcance de su rol creció durante 2026. La gestión del uso y la expansión de la inteligencia artificial es la razón más mencionada, por encima de cualquier otro factor consultado en la encuesta, incluida la propia complejidad de los ingresos. Al mismo tiempo, el 65 % de los equipos financieros gestiona ahora múltiples modelos de ingresos, y el 71 % vende a través de más canales que hace un año.
“A los responsables financieros se les pide que hagan más: no solo informar sobre los resultados financieros, sino también ampliar hacia nuevos modelos de negocio, habilitar más canales de distribución y desarrollar una estrategia de IA para su empresa. Lo que llama la atención es que muchos están recurriendo a la IA, no porque sea la última tecnología de moda, sino porque necesitan una forma de gestionar la complejidad sin tener que aumentar la plantilla. La oportunidad es significativa, pero también lo es el riesgo. Los responsables financieros necesitan una IA en la que puedan confiar, gestionar y que se vincule directamente a los resultados empresariales de los que son responsables”, afirmó Sam Chung, Chief Customer Officer de Agentforce Revenue Management.
La mitad de los líderes financieros encuestados afirma ser el principal responsable de las decisiones en materia de estrategia de IA dentro de su empresa. Esto representa un nuevo tipo de competencia: el departamento de finanzas ya no se limita a informar sobre el negocio. Cada vez más, ayuda a determinar cómo la empresa adopta la IA, dónde genera valor y cómo se debe medir ese retorno.
Para los CFO, esto implica que la gobernanza de la IA dejó de ser una cuestión exclusivamente tecnológica para convertirse en una financiera. Las decisiones que antes recaían principalmente en el área de tecnología —dónde implementar la IA, a qué datos puede acceder, qué controles aplicar y cómo medir el impacto— ahora también involucran al departamento financiero, dado que tienen implicaciones directas sobre el control y la auditoría.
El 71% de los CFO ya vende a través de más canales que hace un año
La ampliación del rol del director financiero ocurre en un entorno empresarial cada vez más difícil de analizar y proyectar. El 71 % de los líderes financieros afirma que su empresa vende a través de más canales que hace 12 meses. Si bien las ventas directas siguen representando la mayor parte de los ingresos, el autoservicio en línea, las ventas indirectas o a través de socios, las redes sociales y las aplicaciones móviles contribuyen de manera creciente a la combinación de canales.
Los modelos de ingresos también se diversifican. Aunque los equipos financieros se centraban tradicionalmente en las ventas únicas, el 65 % ya realiza un seguimiento de transacciones en más de un modelo: suscripciones, servicios profesionales, modelos basados en consumo e híbridos conviven dentro de un mismo balance. En otras palabras, los equipos financieros no solo dan seguimiento a más transacciones, sino que gestionan más formas de generar, fijar el precio, facturar, cobrar y reconocer esos ingresos.
Más canales de venta fragmentan los datos y complican la conciliación financiera
Contar con más canales y formas de venta puede significar más formas en que los datos de ingresos se fragmentan. Una transacción puede comenzar en un canal, involucrar a un socio u otra acción de venta y, finalmente, requerir una conciliación entre múltiples sistemas antes de que el departamento financiero tenga una visión completa del negocio. Esa fragmentación operativa es uno de los principales desafíos que los CFO identifican en la encuesta.
Los modelos basados en consumo añaden otra capa de complejidad. Casi 9 de cada 10 líderes financieros afirman que su empresa planea incorporar más productos de este tipo en el futuro. A diferencia de una transacción única —en la que el evento financiero es relativamente sencillo—, los ingresos basados en consumo dependen de lo que el cliente utilice realmente a lo largo del tiempo. Esto exige que los equipos financieros concilien datos de uso con contratos, reglas de precios, registros de facturación y reconocimiento de ingresos, a menudo en sistemas que no fueron diseñados para funcionar juntos de manera fluida.
El trabajo manual todavía representa al menos el 20% de los flujos de trabajo financieros
Cuanto más complejo se vuelve el ciclo de vida de los ingresos, más costoso resulta el trabajo manual. Aproximadamente 7 de cada 10 líderes financieros (67 %) afirman que su equipo aún ejecuta al menos uno de cada cinco flujos de trabajo de forma manual, con frecuencia mediante hojas de cálculo —un trabajo que consume horas significativas cada semana y genera riesgos operacionales—. Frente a ese diagnóstico, los propios líderes estiman que existe margen para automatizar hasta el 40 % del trabajo de sus equipos, siempre que cuenten con la infraestructura adecuada y el apoyo necesario.
La oportunidad que abre esa brecha es precisamente la que está impulsando la adopción de herramientas de inteligencia artificial en el área financiera. El trabajo manual no solo es ineficiente: también es una fuente de error en contextos donde la precisión de los datos afecta directamente la toma de decisiones estratégicas y la información reportada a directorios e inversores.
El 90% de los CFO que usa IA reporta un retorno de inversión positivo
Entre los líderes financieros que ya utilizan inteligencia artificial, el 90 % reporta un retorno de inversión (ROI) positivo. Entre quienes emplean específicamente agentes de inteligencia artificial, más del 90 % reporta beneficios en ahorro de tiempo, productividad, reducción de costos y precisión en las proyecciones, y aproximadamente la mitad califica esos beneficios como significativos.
Muchos de estos resultados se observan en tareas de alto volumen basadas en reglas que, históricamente, han requerido intervención manual. PwC informa que la IA agéntica ya está reduciendo hasta en un 80 % el tiempo que tarda una factura en pasar de recibida a liquidada, entre otras tareas del ciclo financiero. Además de permitir que los equipos aborden el trabajo existente con mayor rapidez, la IA también amplía su capacidad analítica: simular rápidamente cómo un cambio en los precios o en la combinación de canales afectaría las proyecciones es una tarea que antes demandaba días y ahora puede completarse en minutos.
La seguridad y la gobernanza frenan una adopción más amplia de la IA
Los beneficios documentados no han eliminado los obstáculos. Casi la mitad de los líderes financieros (46 %) señala la seguridad como el principal freno para ampliar el uso de la IA, seguida por las preocupaciones sobre gobernanza e integración con los sistemas existentes, con un 42 %. Para los CFO, estos no son conceptos abstractos: se trata de controles concretos, auditabilidad, acceso a los datos y rendición de cuentas ante accionistas y reguladores.
Del mismo modo, muchos líderes identifican la limitada experiencia interna en la materia como una barrera relevante —una brecha notable para una función a la que, al mismo tiempo, se le pide que encabece la estrategia de IA de toda la compañía—. El costo de implementación también figura entre los obstáculos mencionados, aunque en menor proporción que los factores de seguridad y gobernanza.
Los CFO gestionan la IA de la empresa mientras la usan para mantenerse al día
“Las decisiones sobre IA ya no llegan al departamento de finanzas como solicitudes de presupuesto, sino como preguntas sobre riesgo, control y rendición de cuentas. El director financiero ha pasado de simplemente aprobar la IA a ser responsable de ella”, señaló Chung. Esa doble responsabilidad resume el nuevo rol que documenta el informe de Salesforce: los líderes financieros deben gestionar la implementación de la IA en toda la empresa y, al mismo tiempo, apoyarse en ella para manejar una complejidad operativa para la que sus propios equipos aún no se han modernizado por completo.
Los datos recogidos entre el 4 y el 15 de mayo de 2026 —mediante una encuesta doble ciego a 865 directores financieros, directores de contabilidad, vicepresidentes ejecutivos de finanzas y vicepresidentes de finanzas de Francia, Alemania, Japón, el Reino Unido y los Estados Unidos— sugieren que los CFO están abordando ambas tareas con una visión clara del valor para el negocio. La IA ya genera beneficios para la mayoría de los líderes financieros que la utilizan, con margen para ampliar su impacto. El informe completo sobre las prioridades de los directores financieros está disponible en el sitio de Salesforce.

articles.title: AWS' Colleen Aubrey: Stop inventing new AI metrics — it’s your business metrics that matter - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AWS’ Colleen Aubrey: Stop inventing new AI metrics — it’s your business metrics that matter
There isn’t a business or information technology leader today who doesn’t have artificial intelligence at the top of their priority list. The challenge for most organizations is deciding what to measure and how to determine whether an AI initiative was successful.
To better understand how customers should approach AI metrics, I spoke with Colleen Aubrey from Amazon Web Services Inc,, who has some deep experience in this area.
As senior vice president of Applied AI Solutions at AWS and a member of Amazon’s S-team, she builds on that foundation with lessons from 20-plus years at Amazon, where she built customer-facing products for millions of sellers and advertisers. The playbook she drew from that experience gives enterprises a practical path to move out of AI pilot purgatory, and it starts with throwing out the AI return-on-investment slide.
She argues that understanding AI ROI requires thinking in terms of business metrics. “I worry that people start trying to come up with new metrics to measure the impact of AI, but it’s the same metrics,” she explained. “It’s your business metrics that matter.” AWS has spent 20 years building cloud infrastructure. AI business applications are a much newer opportunity.
When Aubrey joined AWS, she inherited 35 application-layer programs. “I would say Connect for the contact center was probably our most successful example,” she told me in a recent interview ahead of AWS re:Invent Nov. 30-Dec. 4.
She studied what made it work: The team had deep operational experience running Amazon’s customer service function; it chose a sharp wedge (outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone rather than chasing feature parity; and the team knew its customers. The lessons from that success are now the blueprint for the expanded Amazon Connect family: Connect Customer, Connect Talent, Connect Health and Connect Decisions.
The playbook Aubrey built for the Connect family closely mirrors what IT leaders need to move their own AI programs out of pilot mode. Here are my five takeaways that should matter to IT leaders:
Feature parity is a trap
The first lesson Aubrey drew from her assessment was about where to start. Nobody runs a better supply chain than Amazon, which is exactly why the early version of AWS Supply Chain was such a useful learning experience. When Aubrey got close to the product, she saw a team working to catch up rather than lead. They had been building five modules that “largely were about getting to feature parity” with entrenched enterprise resource planning vendors that had a decades-long head start.
Connect had taken the opposite path, and it’s instructive. “They understood they weren’t going to achieve feature parity,” Aubrey said of the Connect team. Instead, they led with outstanding voice quality on the AWS backbone, started narrow and built from there.
Aubrey applied that same lesson to the supply chain. She rebooted it as Connect Decisions by asking a different question: where is the pain most acute, and where is the current tooling weakest? The answer was planners. “They’re firefighting the whole time,” she said. “They’re overwhelmed by a whole bunch of signals. By the time they get to decide, the moment has passed.”
The same applies to enterprises. AI projects that stall often try to replicate an entire workflow. The ones that succeed identify a painful decision point and make it dramatically better.
The business metrics haven’t changed
Aubrey’s point about measurement deserves unpacking. “Companies are stuck on what’s the ROI of AI, and they’re looking at return on tokens and this sort of stuff,” she said. “The question is, can you move your business metrics by working in a different way?”
Her proof point is Wells Vehicle Electronics, which, according to AWS, cut inventory by 7% in three months while expanding the SKUs they actively monitor from 20 to 2,000. Nobody at Wells is talking about tokens. They’re talking about working capital. If a project can’t be tied to a metric the chief financial officer already tracks, it’s an experiment, not an investment.
AI doesn’t remove bottlenecks; it moves them
Amazon started where most companies start: with software development, making AI tools available across the company. Aubrey admits there’s a bit of chaos at first. “Everyone’s just experimenting with a bunch of things,” Aubrey said.
She sees that as a feature, not a bug, because that’s where the real learning happens. “You go through this learning period of, you know what, our test coverage sucks,” she said. Fix test coverage, and you find “our pipelines suck,” so you fix pipeline health, eliminate manual intervention and deploy faster. The result in her group this year: a twofold improvement in the velocity of pushes to production.
The lesson is that the velocity didn’t come from the coding assistant. It came from fixing everything downstream that the assistant exposed. Enterprises that buy the tool and skip the plumbing will see activity rise while output stays flat.
Own the outcome, not the task
I asked Aubrey whether Amazon has adjusted its goals to reflect what employees can now do with AI. Her answer was an honest “yes and no.” In her user experience team, roles have collapsed: designers are being pushed to ship code to an alpha environment, and Amazon has created a new “UX tech” role.
The “no” is that org design and goal-setting are still catching up. Her message to her team is blunt: “The only choice you can’t make is to own the task. You have to choose to own the outcome.” Every IT leader should borrow that line. Task-based job descriptions will age poorly.
Good AI with bad UX will fail
AWS’s design philosophy for the Connect family is what she calls “humorphism,” the idea that AI should fit the way people already work, not the other way around. Her biggest concern is the lag between internal prototypes and production.
“Shipping good AI with a bad user experience will fail, in my opinion,” she said. Her team has invested heavily in closing that gap, moving beyond traditional command-based interfaces toward AI that picks up cues, remembers decisions, and carries work forward. The goal, she said, is to make AI so usable that people change how they work, not because they’re told to, but because it makes sense.
She was equally candid about maturity. TE Connectivity has scaled Connect Decisions to 2,000 planners, but Connect Talent reached general availability only in September and has early customers in deployment. Aubrey said the team is focused on getting the product right before aggressively scaling, reflecting the same “pick a wedge” discipline she applied across the Connect solutions.
What this means for IT leaders
- Pick a wedge, not a platform. The temptation with AI is to reimagine an entire function at once. Instead, identify the decision point where people are drowning in signals and acting too late, such as a planner buried in exceptions or an agent handling a surge of rebookings. A narrow, painful problem delivers a quick win, clear metrics and a credible foundation to build on.
- Kill the “AI ROI” slide. Return on tokens, prompts per user, and adoption dashboards measure activity, not value. Before any project is funded, tie it to a business metric the company already tracks, such as inventory, resolution rate, time to hire, or cycle time, and set a baseline. If the metric doesn’t move within a defined window, the project shouldn’t scale, no matter how impressive the demo was.
- Budget for the downstream fix. AI rarely removes a bottleneck; it relocates it. Amazon’s twofold gain in shipping velocity came from fixing test coverage and pipelines, not from the coding assistant. Assume your deployment will expose the next constraint, whether that’s data quality, integration, approvals, or testing. Earmark budget and people for that work up front rather than discovering it six months later.
- Rewrite roles around outcomes. Job descriptions built around tasks will age poorly as AI takes on more of those tasks. Work with HR now to redefine roles and goals around the outcomes people own, and update performance expectations to reflect the tools they have. Be honest with employees that some teams will shrink while others will have new gaps to fill; ambiguity breeds more anxiety than candor.
- Make usability a buying criterion. As Aubrey put it, good AI with a poor user experience will fail. In vendor evaluations, weigh setup, configuration, testing, analytics and day-to-day experience as heavily as model capability, because those factors determine whether business users adopt the product. Ask vendors how business users, not just technical teams, interact with the product day to day.
Final thoughts
What made this conversation valuable was Aubrey’s willingness to share how she thinks about building AI products that work in production, from studying what made Connect successful to applying those lessons across supply chain, hiring, health care, and customer engagement. That candor is a useful model for IT leaders, because most enterprise AI programs are stuck for the same reasons AWS’s applications once were: too much breadth, too little focus and success measured by the wrong yardstick.
The AI era won’t reward companies with the most pilots. It will reward those that pick a sharp problem, fix the plumbing it exposes, redesign work around outcomes and move the metrics they already have.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

articles.title: 'The progress is real': Deloitte report claims some firms are finally seeing return on AI investment — but still lack insight into what actually works
articles.text:
'The progress is real': Deloitte report claims some firms are finally seeing return on AI investment — but still lack insight into what actually works
Companies are finally seeing an ROI, from AI
- Deloitte finds 28% of businesses report current revenue growth, up from 20% earlier this year
- Productivity and improved decision-making are still performing better
- Sovereignty has become an integral part of AI strategies
New Deloitte data has claimed that when it comes to business AI, we're finally at the stage of ROI, with more organizations than before now reaping the rewards of their costly deployments.
As many as 28% now report current revenue growth as a result of their AI strategies, up from 20% compared with earlier in 2026, the firm's report found.
Realizing higher revenue is largely seen as one of the most important returns from AI – with companies spending so much on services and infrastructure, they need to make that money back.
AI adopters are finally seeing increased productivity translate into higher revenue
While other areas like efficiency and productivity (up 74%), decision-making and data insight (up 60%), cost reductions (up 45%) and better client relationships (up 44%) are all moving in the right direction, Deloitte says increasing revenue is still one of the slowest to deliver tangible results.
Deloitte's research also indirectly implies that businesses could be getting carried away with these early signs, because the majority (86%) of businesses surveyed plan to increase AI investments over the next financial year.
Additionally, while early ROI markers are now heading in the right direction, Deloitte worries that many businesses still don't have the right visibility into AI's financial impacts. While three in four (71%) are tracking total spend across token consumption, many can only see the total bill and not the breakdown of which activities lead to which spend.
Jobs are changing because of AI
It's becoming an increasingly familiar concept that employers need to redefine roles as AI becomes more engrained – developers are already seeing a shift from writing code to managing AI agents, for example.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Deloitte says there's a long way to go on this front, because while three in five companies have already redesigned jobs 'moderate[ly]', only 15% of them have done so 'extensive[ly]' and 1% 'completely.'
"Many are still just scratching the surface," the report claims.
The future of AI investments looks different
Looking ahead, Deloitte expects sovereign AI to become even more of an important consideration. Nearly half of Americas (46%) and EMEA (47%) businesses are building in-house to regain control over their workloads, with three in four (74%) global respondents reporting at least 'moderate' importance of sovereign AI.
But the paper does acknowledge the benefits of using centralized hyperscalers, noting that going sovereign or building in-house comes with certain trade-offs – usually "capability, speed or cost."
At the same time, we're hearing more and more about enterprises like Revolut picking up the infrastructure bills themselves, choosing to self-host open-weight models for greater cost predictability, usually at the expense of model performance in scenarios where they can achieve their desired outcomes without leading frontier models.
The report sets out six key considerations for the next stages of AI: adopters must respond by redesigning work as a whole, not just the workflow; costs need to be traceable to the token degree, not just the full bill; AI strategies must align with actions that produce revenue; governance needs to keep up as systems become more autonomous; early adopters are now starting to look at physical AI like robots, and so should you; and sovereignty should be seen as an ongoing effort consideration over a one-time fix.

articles.title: Le Rassemblement national avoue avoir subi une cyberattaque, les données des adhérents récupérées
articles.text:
Le Rassemblement national confirme avoir subi une cyberattaque contre l’outil qui gère ses adhésions, avec à la clé une fuite de données personnelles. Un pirate avait diffusé quelques jours plus tôt 150 000 fiches présentées comme celles de ses membres.
Le Rassemblement national a reconnu, le 4 novembre, qu'une cyberattaque visant son outil de gestion des adhésions avait entraîné une fuite de données personnelles touchant une partie de ses adhérents. L'annonce intervient après la diffusion, le 31 octobre, de 150 000 fiches attribuées au parti par un pirate, que FrenchBreaches a analysées et signalées au RN. Le parti a saisi la CNIL et porté plainte, sans préciser combien de personnes exactement sont concernées.
Le RN confirme la cyberattaque, sans donner le moindre chiffre
Le RN s'est exprimé dans un communiqué de quelques lignes, signé Bruno Bilde et publié le mercredi 4 novembre. Le parti de Marine Le Pen explique que l'outil qui sert à gérer les adhésions a été visé par une attaque informatique, et qu'une partie des informations de certains adhérents a été divulguée sans autorisation. Le Rassemblement national dit avoir vite contenu l'intrusion et mis fin à l'accès non autorisé. Il assure aussi que son fichier n'est pas touché en entier. Le nombre de personnes concernées, lui, n'apparaît nulle part.
Le parti se montre en revanche plus précis sur la nature des données. Il cite le nom, le prénom, l'e-mail, le téléphone, l'adresse postale et la profession, ainsi que l'année d'adhésion, le montant de la cotisation et la fédération de rattachement.
Le communiqué n'évoque pas de pièces d'identité ni de numéros de sécurité sociale dérobés. Il signale lui-même un risque sérieux, celui forcément attendu de l'utilisation abusive de l'appartenance politique de ses adhérents, une information que le RGPD classe parmi les données sensibles.
Notons que le gendarme des données, la CNIL, a été saisie et qu'une plainte a été déposée auprès du parquet de Paris, précise le RN. Ce dernier renvoie les adhérents inquiets vers son délégué à la protection des données et leur demande surtout de se méfier des appels et des messages inhabituels. Un escroc qui connaît votre nom, votre fédération et le montant de votre cotisation peut facilement se faire passer pour le parti, puis vous réclamer un paiement ou d'autres informations.
150 000 fiches publiées par un pirate, et autant de questions
L'affaire a éclaté au grand jour quelques heures avant Halloween, le 31 octobre, sur un forum de pirates. Un certain « shin0bi » affirme y détenir 432 597 enregistrements liés au RN et en publie 150 000 pour appuyer ses dires. Les champs qu'il annonce comprennent même des dates de naissance, absentes du communiqué. FrenchBreaches, qui avait alerté le parti avant ce communiqué, a fait le tri dans l'archive. Une fois les 28 420 doublons retirés, il reste 121 580 lignes distinctes, sans garantie qu'elles correspondent à autant de personnes.
Ce tri fait aussi apparaître quelques incohérences. Par exemple, des fiches dont les adresses sont situées dans divers départements sont rattachées à des cantons toulousains, et d'autres regroupent plusieurs cantons dans un seul champ. S'agit-il d'une extraction authentique, de bases différentes fusionnées, ou d'erreurs de croisement ou de données retouchées ? Pour le moment, aucune piste n'est écartée, et l'authenticité de l'ensemble des 150 000 fiches reste à démontrer.
Une cyberattaque a bien eu lieu, et un fichier circule bel et bien. Mais rien ne prouve encore que l'un soit la copie de l'autre. Le RN n'a pas dit si les données publiées par le pirate étaient celles qui lui ont été dérobées, et le fichier contient des informations, comme les dates de naissance, qui ne figurent pas dans la liste du parti. Une partie des fiches pourrait donc venir de cette attaque, et une autre d’ailleurs. Ce n'est pas la première alerte, puisqu'en juillet, le site du parti avait été piraté et le compte X de Marine Le Pen détourné. Le RN assurait alors que les données de ses adhérents n'avaient pas été exposées. Le parti d'extrême droite n'est pas le seul parti visé. Fin octobre, outre le site des Républicains, à l'autre bout de l'échiquier politique, le PCF avait lui aussi confirmé une fuite touchant ses adhérents. À quelques mois de la présidentielle, les fichiers de militants attirent plus que jamais les pirates.

articles.title: IBM, AMD Mix Quantum and AI at U.S. National Lab - EE Times
articles.text:
Alliance aims to accelerate the creation of scientifically relevant quantum computers by 2028 as part of the Department of Energy’s Quantum Genesis Mission. Leading quantum companies see error correction as a key step toward that goal.
IBM, AMD, and the U.S. Department of Energy (DoE)-funded Quantum Science Center (QSC) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) announced on Nov. 5 a new quantum/AI platform aimed at improving quantum error correction, an emerging focus for the industry.
Researchers are making advances in error correction, including early demonstrations that protect quantum information from noise. IBM claims quantum advantage using techniques with guaranteed correctness, showing that quantum computers integrated with classical computers can solve relevant problems better than classical systems alone. The partners aim to amp up progress by bringing more classical computing into the mix.
The project at the Oak Ridge laboratory co-locates IBM’s quantum computers, including the company’s most powerful quantum processor, the 120-qubit IBM Quantum Nighthawk, with ORNL’s Umbra HPC system, running AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs. AMD provides the classical computing foundation for research into error correction, decoding optimization, and software orchestration.
A quantum error is caused by disruptions to the delicate quantum state of a qubit, which operates near absolute zero. Qubits typically need temperatures between 10 and 20 millikelvin (–273.15°C or –459.67°F).
The co-designed platform under development at Oak Ridge in the U.S. state of Tennessee will let researchers evaluate how to knit together classical and quantum computing to advance quantum error correction. The effort supports the DOE’s Quantum Genesis Mission, which targets 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. IBM said it has demonstrated experiments with up to 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations. For the partners to reach the DoE target, they will need to achieve a roughly 230-fold increase in hard-operation count.
“Today, the question is how to accelerate and optimize error correction to build systems that scientists can use to tackle meaningful problems,” Jay Gambetta, IBM Research director, said in a press statement. “This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software, and workflows that will scale.”
Hard operations
In quantum computing, resource theory divides operations into easy (Clifford) and hard (non-Clifford) sets.
Non-Clifford operations are particularly resource-intensive in fault-tolerant quantum computing because they cannot generally be implemented as cheaply as Clifford operations and require additional error-correction resources, Seetharami Seelam, chief architect of Classical System Co-Design for Quantum-Centric Supercomputing at IBM, told EE Times.
All error-correcting codes admit instructions that are cheap to implement and others that are expensive. So, what is “hard” is a result of the choice of code on any given platform, Seelam noted.
Next era
The next era of computing will combine quantum computing with decades of innovation across the classical hardware and software ecosystem, AMD EVP Mark Papermaster said.
“We are advancing a holistic approach that integrates quantum processors, HPC, and AI,” Papermaster noted. “This co-design platform is an important step toward building the scalable, efficient computing infrastructure needed to make fault-tolerant quantum computing a reality.”
Solving quantum error correction challenges is essential to making quantum computing a practical tool for scientific discovery, and that’s a priority for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, according to Travis Humble, director of the Quantum Science Center at ORNL.
Oak Ridge and AMD are partners in what was possibly the world’s first “exascale” computer.
Europe has led the concept of hybrid classical/quantum computing, as Czechia, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg are working to deploy on-site quantum computers that are integrated with classical supercomputing under the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking, the Center for Strategic & International Studies, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, noted in a March 2026 report.
IBM had a less geopolitical view.
“IBM has been leading the way in developing quantum-centric supercomputing for several years, including a reference architecture for integrating quantum processors with CPUs and GPUs into HPC environments that has been used in deployments in both Europe and Japan,” Seelam said. “The ORNL collaboration represents an important next step in applying that approach in the U.S., bringing IBM quantum computers together with ORNL’s high-performance computing infrastructure and AMD CPUs and GPUs.”
Focus on error correction
Leading quantum computing companies see error correction as a critical step toward the first quantum applications that are scientifically and commercially relevant.
Through 2029, Quantinuum expects its Nexus quantum system to automate and simplify error correction, resource management, orchestration, and deployment, enabling developers to build and integrate increasingly capable applications at the logical level.
$2 billion
IBM and Quantinuum are among nine U.S. companies that got $2 billion from the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump to secure the nation’s quantum leadership.
Quantinuum’s Nexus system supports more than 200 organizations, a 45% increase this year, while total job submissions increased tenfold in the 12 months through August 2026 compared with the preceding 12-month period, the company said in a press release.
“Quantum computers are on the brink of achieving fault tolerance at scale,” José Ignacio Latorre, director of Singapore’s Centre for Quantum Technologies, said in the press release. “It’s exciting: we are entering terra incognita for what we can compute. The new challenge is putting our high-level quantum algorithms into the right form to successfully run on error-corrected hardware. Developer platforms like Nexus help us bridge that gap between quantum algorithm design and deployment.”
IBM said Nighthawk’s high maximum circuit throughput and real-time pulse control enable researchers to test error-correction techniques. Researchers will compare what each technique requires in qubits, time, samples, and classical resources to learn where GPU accelerators, such as AMD’s nodes in the Umbra system, can help the most.
IBM said researchers can use the company’s quantum hardware to measure qubits mid-calculation and act on the results in real time, set the exact timing of the signals that protect qubits from noise, see exactly what the hardware ran, and work directly with raw measurement signals.
Solid partners
The new co-design platform for quantum error correction builds on IBM’s existing collaborations with ORNL and AMD.
Earlier this year, IBM and ORNL demonstrated how workloads running on quantum computers and ORNL’s Frontier supercomputer can simulate magnetic materials and calculate molecular configurations of promising materials for the production of fusion fuel.
IBM has been using AMD GPUs to accelerate the classical diagonalization step in sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), a key quantum-centric supercomputing workflow. Last year, the two companies demonstrated an algorithm that efficiently decodes quantum errors on AMD chips. IBM said the partners’ effort with error correction and HPC workflows may support IBM’s path to its Quantum Starling system, the company’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer.

articles.title: Europe’s Chip Industry: Perfect Storm or Perfect Timing? - EE Times
articles.text:
On the afternoon of Oct. 28, 1991, a low-pressure system began forming east of Nova Scotia, Canada, as Hurricane Grace gathered strength just west of Bermuda. Over New England, a cool, dry air mass settled in, and a high-pressure system built over the Great Lakes. As American journalist and author Sebastian Junger recounts in “The Perfect Storm,” none of these were exceptional on their own. Yet their convergence produced one of the fiercest storms on record.
SEMICON Europa 2026, co-located with electronica 2026 in Munich from Nov. 10 to 13, takes the meteorological event as its central metaphor: “Europe’s Next Era: Navigating the Perfect Storm.” The theme reflects the semiconductor industry’s mounting geopolitical, technological, and competitive pressures.
The warning is not new. At the CxO Summit during SEMICON Europa 2025, Laith Altimime, president of SEMI Europe, described the continent as caught “in a perfect storm.” He said, “As we face a combination of internal challenges and intensifying external competition, collaboration is not optional; it is mission-critical.”
Overdependence and a structural competitiveness gap form the low-pressure system, or Nor’easter. According to a European Commission analysis published in June 2026, total fab production costs in EU fabs are 40% to 50% higher than in Taiwan, South Korea, and China. Europe’s reliance on overseas suppliers is equally stark. In 2024, the EU consumed €55 billion worth of semiconductors and imported €43.6 billion from outside the bloc. Its vulnerability is greatest in leading-edge chips for AI and high-performance computing.
Geopolitical turbulence is the high-pressure system. The European Commission’s 2026 Annual Single Market and Competitiveness Report describes how major powers use tariffs, export controls, and supply chain dependencies as instruments of economic leverage. Russia’s war against Ukraine, military tensions in the Taiwan Strait, conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. technology restrictions, and China’s expanding manufacturing capacity expose Europe’s semiconductor ecosystem to external risks. Europe must navigate between U.S. investment, China’s industrial ambitions, and its own pursuit of technological sovereignty.
The fallout from the first Chips Act represents the lingering effects of Hurricane Grace. In 2025, the European Court of Auditors concluded that “the strategy is very unlikely to be sufficient to achieve by 2030 the very ambitious Digital Decade target of a 20% EU share in the global market value chain by revenue.” The EU’s share is now projected to reach just 11.7% by 2030.
Whether the metaphor holds is the question the conference sets out to test: Is Europe the Andrea Gail, or can it read the forecast and chart a different course?
The proposed Chips Act 2.0, published in June 2026 and targeted for adoption in the second quarter of 2027, does not abandon advanced manufacturing but recalibrates the strategy around a wider set of industrial and policy priorities.
The European Commission’s proposal broadens the focus beyond the race for advanced fabs to the entire semiconductor value chain, from chip design and manufacturing equipment to materials and advanced packaging. It also aims to bridge Europe’s lab-to-fab gap by scaling up pilot lines and bringing research closer to commercial production. Rather than pursuing market share alone, the strategy seeks to secure critical capabilities in both leading-edge and mature-node chips and connect chipmakers more closely with customers in automotive, industrial systems, and data centers. Better access to patient capital could help startups scale up and “create the conditions required for high-potential technology businesses to emerge.”
“Europe’s semiconductor competitiveness depends on the strength of the entire ecosystem, from design and materials to equipment, manufacturing, and advanced packaging,” Altimime said. “The Chips Act 2.0 provides an important opportunity to build on Europe’s existing strengths. Our recommendations aim to ensure that the new framework delivers the speed, investment, and policy certainty needed to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness and resilience.”
Europe does not need to do everything. It needs to be pragmatic about where it can compete, clear-eyed about where demand is growing, and ready to build on its synergies and act together. Navigating the perfect storm will require a common course.
The EU’s motto offers a fitting conclusion: in varietate concordia—united in diversity.

articles.title: NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti Climbs $160 in Eight Days, Now 79% Over MSRP
articles.text:
Friday, November 6th 2026
NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti Climbs $160 in Eight Days, Now 79% Over MSRP
NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 5070 Ti is now close to double its $749 MSRP in the US. According to price tracking by VideoCardz, the cheapest RTX 5070 Ti at major US retailers was $1,339.99 on November 6, about 79% above MSRP, up from $1,179.99 on October 29. That's a $160 jump in just eight days. Some models have already crossed the 2x mark, like the ASUS TUF Gaming OC at $1,499.99 on B&H. Prices are also moving fast. At the time of writing, the cheapest RTX 5070 Ti sold by Newegg itself is an MSI SHADOW RTX 5070 Ti at $1,409.99. Things aren't much better in Germany, where the cheapest listing on Geizhals sits at €1,300 for a PNY model, roughly 48% above the €879 MSRP. 
Things are probably going to get worse, too. NVIDIA's board partners in China are reportedly raising RTX 5070 Ti prices by around 1,000 RMB (about $150) this week, with retail prices expected to follow within a week or two. Unlike the RTX 5090 and 5080 16 GB, which have reportedly been discontinued, the RTX 5070 Ti is still officially in production. After reports of an end of production in January early this year, NVIDIA said it was still shipping all GeForce SKUs, and ASUS denied the card was end-of-life, while admitting that memory supply was hurting production and restocking. The card is still listed at major retailers, unlike the RTX 5080, which vanished from NVIDIA's US Marketplace two weeks after the RTX 5090 did the same. Anyone shopping for an RTX 5070 Ti should probably expect these prices to keep rising for a while.

articles.title: Cómo recuperar fotos eliminadas del celular: paso a paso para rescatar las imágenes en Android, iPhone y Google Fotos
articles.text:
Eliminar una fotografía por error puede convertirse en un problema cuando se trata de un recuerdo importante o de una imagen que no está guardada en otro dispositivo. Sin embargo, antes de recurrir a aplicaciones de recuperación o pagar por programas especializados, existe una alternativa gratuita: revisar la papelera del celular o del servicio de almacenamiento donde estaba guardado el archivo.
Tanto Android como iPhone cuentan con herramientas para recuperar fotografías eliminadas recientemente. Google Fotos, por ejemplo, conserva temporalmente las imágenes borradas y permite restaurarlas desde el teléfono o una computadora. Apple también ofrece una función similar dentro de su aplicación Fotos.
El tiempo disponible para recuperar los archivos depende del servicio utilizado. En Google Fotos, los elementos respaldados permanecen en la papelera durante 60 días, mientras que aquellos que no tienen copia de seguridad se conservan durante 30 días. En el iPhone, las fotografías eliminadas permanecen disponibles durante 30 días antes de borrarse definitivamente.
Por eso, si una imagen desapareció de la galería, conviene revisar estas opciones cuanto antes.
Cómo recuperar fotos borradas en Android con Google Fotos
Google Fotos es una de las herramientas más utilizadas para almacenar imágenes y vídeos en teléfonos Android. La aplicación incorpora una papelera que permite recuperar archivos eliminados mientras permanezcan dentro del periodo de conservación.
Para restaurar una fotografía, sigue estos pasos:
- Abre la aplicación Google Fotos en el celular.
- Pulsa la opción Colecciones, ubicada en la parte inferior de la pantalla.
- Ingresa en el apartado Papelera.
- Busca la fotografía o el vídeo que deseas recuperar.
- Mantén presionado el archivo seleccionado.
- Pulsa Restaurar.
Una vez completado el procedimiento, la imagen volverá a aparecer en la biblioteca de Google Fotos y, cuando corresponda, en los álbumes donde estaba guardada.
Es importante comprobar si la fotografía tiene una copia de seguridad, ya que el tiempo de permanencia en la papelera cambia según esta condición. Si el archivo fue eliminado definitivamente o la papelera fue vaciada, no será posible recuperarlo mediante esta herramienta.
Cómo recuperar fotos eliminadas en un iPhone
Los teléfonos de Apple también cuentan con una función para rescatar imágenes borradas por accidente. La aplicación Fotos incorpora un álbum llamado Eliminado recientemente, donde permanecen las fotografías y los vídeos durante 30 días.
Para utilizar esta opción:
- Abre la aplicación Fotos del iPhone.
- Ingresa en Colecciones.
- Desplázate hasta el apartado Utilidades.
- Selecciona Eliminado recientemente o Eliminados, según la versión de iOS.
- Desbloquea el álbum mediante Face ID, Touch ID o el código del dispositivo.
- Selecciona la fotografía que deseas recuperar.
- Pulsa Recuperar.
También es posible seleccionar varias imágenes para restaurarlas al mismo tiempo. Después de confirmar la operación, los archivos volverán a aparecer en la fototeca.
Si la fotografía ya superó los 30 días o fue eliminada manualmente de este álbum, Apple no ofrece una opción para restaurarla desde la aplicación Fotos.
Cómo recuperar fotos borradas de Google Fotos desde una computadora
Otra alternativa consiste en utilizar una computadora para acceder a la papelera de Google Fotos. Este procedimiento puede ser útil cuando el usuario perdió su teléfono, cambió de dispositivo o no puede ingresar a la aplicación móvil.
Para hacerlo, es necesario seguir estos pasos:
- Ingresa a la página web de Google Fotos.
- Inicia sesión con la misma cuenta de Google utilizada en el celular.
- Abre el apartado Papelera.
- Localiza la fotografía que deseas recuperar.
- Selecciona el archivo y pulsa Restaurar.
La imagen volverá a estar disponible en la biblioteca de esa cuenta. Si el usuario tiene varias direcciones de correo electrónico, también conviene revisar cada una, porque algunas fotografías pueden estar almacenadas en una cuenta diferente.
¿Es posible recuperar fotos eliminadas definitivamente?
No existe una herramienta gratuita que garantice recuperar cualquier fotografía borrada de manera permanente. Cuando un archivo desaparece de la papelera de Google Fotos o del álbum de eliminados del iPhone, las opciones de restauración de esos servicios dejan de estar disponibles.
En estos casos, todavía es posible comprobar si existe una copia en otros lugares, como una computadora, un disco externo, una tarjeta de memoria o algún servicio de almacenamiento en la nube.
También hay aplicaciones de terceros que prometen recuperar imágenes eliminadas, pero sus resultados dependen del dispositivo, del tipo de almacenamiento y de las condiciones en las que se borró el archivo. Algunas, además, solicitan permisos para acceder a información personal o exigen un pago antes de mostrar los resultados.
Por eso, conviene desconfiar de los programas que aseguran recuperar el 100 % de las fotografías. La alternativa más segura es revisar primero las papeleras de Android, iPhone y Google Fotos, y mantener copias de seguridad para evitar perder imágenes importantes en el futuro.

articles.title: Belkin BoostCharge 240 W : cette batterie capable de recharger un PC portable perd 60 €
articles.text:
La batterie externe Belkin BoostCharge 240 W de 27 000 mAh est à 89,99 € (-40 %)
Avec ses 27 000 mAh, son câble USB-C intégré et jusqu'à 240 W en Power Delivery, la batterie Belkin BoostCharge passe à 89,99 € chez Boulanger, 60 € sous son prix de référence.
Vendue et expédiée par Boulanger, cette batterie externe affiche 89,99 € contre un prix de référence de 149,99 €. La livraison à domicile est annoncée dès demain, et le retrait en magasin est offert.
Assez puissante pour un ordinateur portable
Avec une puissance annoncée jusqu'à 240 W en Power Delivery, cette batterie ne se limite pas aux smartphones : elle peut aussi alimenter un ordinateur portable compatible USB-C, y compris des modèles exigeants. Sa capacité de 27 000 mAh permet, selon Boulanger, de recharger cinq à six fois un téléphone.
Le câble USB-C intégré évite d'en chercher un au moment de recharger, et un écran indique la charge restante en temps réel. Des ports USB-A et USB-C supplémentaires permettent de brancher plusieurs appareils.
Pour qui ?
Elle s'adresse surtout à ceux qui travaillent en déplacement avec un ordinateur portable USB-C et veulent une seule batterie pour tous leurs appareils. Pour un simple smartphone, un modèle plus compact et plus léger suffira largement.
Aucun avis client n'est encore publié chez Boulanger pour cette référence.

articles.title: Midterm elections will put AI and data centers on trial, but Big Tech may end up winning anyway - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Midterm elections will put AI and data centers on trial, but Big Tech may end up winning anyway
It may be a little soon to determine the ultimate winners and losers among enterprise suppliers after the midterm elections, but the early line is: Big Tech wins and data center suppliers operators such as chipmakers and neoclouds lose. Or will everybody lose?
The day after the elections, stocks of many tech companies shot up, a bit paradoxically because investors apparently believe potential limits on AI and data centers could tamp down spending on compute and thus improve tech company margins that have made investors nervous. But then on Thursday, tech stocks almost across the board plunged back down even more for a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap — the Nasdaq fell more than 5.5% — on more generalized worries that, well, the AI boom could slow. Suffice to say, investors are still sorting things out.
Marvell Semiconductor this week made a surprisingly huge acquisition with Lumentum, a bet on the AI boom continuing. That is, if it comes off: The drop in Lumentum’s stock price has some speculating it could hunt around for another offer.
And the AI boom indeed continues apace, judging from strong tech earnings, though even pre-election, they reflected investor wariness. AMD, Supermicro and Arista all beat easily, as well as Palantir and Kyndryl, whose stock rocketed 30%. But chipmakers Qualcomm, Arm and Globalfoundries didn’t get the love despite good quarters — especially in Thursday’s bloodbath.
All of which raises the question that Dave Vellante posed in his Breaking Analysis last weekend: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Dave and analyst Crawford Del Prete discussed the prospects.
Next week’s earnings reports include Cisco, CoreWeave, Applied Materials, Cerebras and Nebius, any or all of which could move markets.
Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:
Analysis, opinion and food for thought
Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep No, data centers won’t get shut down, and AI will continue apace — just regulated as it needs to be, and we can hope it’s in the right way to protect people and communities and innovation all at the same time. We can walk and chew gum at the same time if we put our mind to it. Hard to imagine the Dems could do worse than Trump and the GOP have been doing for years now.

articles.title: Invraisemblable : SpaceX veut bâtir en 18 mois la même capacité de data centers que Google en toute une vie
articles.text:
Elon Musk promet de construire des data centers à une vitesse encore jamais vue. S’il tient parole, l’entreprise construirait en 19 mois autant de capacités que Google en 27 ans.
Depuis la fusion de xAI avec SpaceX, Elon Musk a fait de l’intelligence artificielle (IA) l’un des moteurs de son empire. Le groupe a racheté l’outil de programmation par IA Cursor pour 60 milliards de dollars et conçu des satellites dédiés à l’IA.
Récemment, son entreprise s’est aussi endettée de 40 milliards de dollars pour mettre la main sur des puces NVIDIA supplémentaires, preuve de son ambition démesurée pour augmenter drastiquement ses capacités d’infrastructures.
SpaceX avance à vitesse grand V
Car l’homme le plus riche du monde se dit » très confiant « : SpaceX pourra construire 10 gigawatts (GW) de data centers rien qu’en 2027, en plus des 3 GW dont l’entreprise dispose déjà avec ses Colossus 1 et 2. Et selon SemiAnalysis, cabinet d’analyse spécialisé dans les puces et l’IA, le géant spatial égalerait ainsi toute la capacité installée par Google depuis ses débuts, en 1999, mais en un an et demi seulement. Un record absolu.
Pour l’instant, les chiffres vont dans le sens de SpaceX. Les experts affirment que 3,6 GW sont déjà en chantier sur plusieurs sites, tandis que les terrains et bâtiments repérés sur différents sites de l’entreprise pourraient en accueillir plus de 9 au total.
Mais ce sont surtout les délais qui impressionnent les analystes : le premier data center Colossus à Memphis a par exemple été aménagé en 122 jours pour 150 mégawatts (MW). Le second bâtiment, lui, a atteint 210 MW en 91 jours. Le prochain site, dans le Mississippi, devrait être prêt en 4 mois environ, alors que la plupart des constructeurs en mettent entre 8 et 12 mois pour de tels projets.
- Accès aux données X en temps réel
- Bon outil de veille médiatique
- Moins biaisé politiquement que sa concurrence
Une croissance menacée
Une grande partie des équipements viendrait de Tesla, qui les fabriquerait en modules prêts à installer. SpaceX ne dépend donc pas de fournisseurs tiers. L’entreprise lance même certains chantiers avant d’avoir décidé comment les alimenter, et a reconverti son site de Starbase, au Texas, jusque-là réservé aux fusées : deux data centers y sortent de terre.
Malgré tout, de nombreux obstacles subsistent, notamment les niveaux colossaux d’énergie et d’eau que requièrent ces installations. L’entreprise se tourne même vers le gaz naturel pour les alimenter, alors que son patron a longtemps promu la transition énergétique au nom de Tesla.
Mais ce sont surtout les résultats des élections de mi-mandat qui jettent un froid sur ces projections. Car de nombreux candidats démocrates élus, notamment au Texas, plaident pour freiner le développement de ces infrastructures. Il faut dire que la colère règne face à ces ogres énergétiques qui, en plus de nécessiter extrêmement d’électricité, émettent des nuisances sonores phénoménales.
« Les centres de données dans l’espace sont très attrayants en ce moment », a d’ailleurs réagi Elon Musk après les résultats du scrutin. L’entrepreneur est clairement conscient qu’on risque de lui mettre des bâtons dans les roues, alors que l’administration Trump a tout mis en œuvre pour lui permettre d’accélérer ses activités.
Exprimer un data center en gigawatts décrit surtout sa puissance électrique consommée à pleine charge, pas sa surface ni son nombre exact de machines. 1 GW correspond à 1 000 MW, soit un ordre de grandeur comparable à la puissance d’une grande centrale électrique. Cette métrique est pratique car la capacité IA moderne est souvent limitée par l’alimentation électrique, le refroidissement et l’accès au réseau, avant même la disponibilité des bâtiments. Deux sites affichant la même puissance peuvent pourtant fournir des performances très différentes selon la densité de GPU, l’efficacité énergétique et l’architecture réseau. C’est donc un indicateur “infrastructure” plus qu’un indicateur direct de puissance de calcul.
La construction modulaire consiste à préfabriquer des blocs (racks, modules électriques, containers, systèmes de refroidissement) en usine, puis à les assembler rapidement sur site. Cette approche réduit les aléas de chantier, raccourcit les cycles de déploiement et facilite la réplication de sites quasi identiques. Elle impose toutefois une forte standardisation : le design doit être figé tôt, et les adaptations locales (normes, réseau électrique, contraintes climatiques) peuvent ralentir l’intégration. Le module “prêt à poser” ne règle pas non plus le point le plus dur : obtenir à temps les raccordements haute tension, l’autorisation d’exploiter, et une capacité d’eau/refroidissement suffisante. Sur des campus IA très denses, la gestion thermique et la qualité de l’alimentation électrique restent des facteurs limitants.

articles.title: Omarchy 4.5 Arrives with Support Beyond x86-64 and New Desktop Features
articles.text:
Friday, November 6th 2026
Omarchy 4.5 Arrives with Support Beyond x86-64 and New Desktop Features
The Arch Linux-based distribution Omarchy 4.5 has been released, the project's first expansion beyond x86-64. It adds Apple Silicon support, a new floating desktop mode, and a few other updates. Omarchy now runs on Apple M1, M2, M3, and Neo MacBooks. The Apple Silicon support builds on work by the Asahi Linux project and other contributors. It also adds preliminary support for NVIDIA's Arm-based N1X laptops and the DGX Spark systems. However, support for newer Apple M4, M5, and M6 models and Qualcomm Snapdragon X-based laptops is still in development. According to project creator David Heinemeier Hansson, the release includes more than 740 merged pull requests from over 180 contributors during a 12-week development cycle.
The desktop experience remains based on the Hyprland compositor. Users can now switch individual workspaces between tiling, scrolling, and floating layouts using the Super + L shortcut. Floating workspaces have conventional window title bars and a dock with pinned applications, running programs, and an application launcher. Windows can be minimized to the dock with Super + M. Also, applications can be pinned or rearranged via drag and drop to the dock. Users can mix different layouts across workspaces.Omarchy 4.5 also adds several applications, including tools for creating presentations from Markdown files, managing paperwork, analyzing disk usage, recording webcam video, remote desktop access over SSH, and displaying world clocks. Other changes include improved Microsoft 365 web integration, Superwhisper dictation engine, and faster installation. Anush Elangovan from AMD made a full Omarchy install in 7 seconds on his AMD laptop.

articles.title: ‘Instead of inventing completely new abilities for units, it makes sense to see what they have in the tabletop’ — Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director shares how it adapted features from the tabletop experience into the RTS game
articles.text:
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director explains how core 40K tabletop features like ‘Armor of Contempt’ were adapted to the RTS — ‘It’s not the same mechanic, but it does kind of the same thing’
King Art didn't want to completely reinvent the wheel
- Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director Jan Theysen explains how King Art introduced ideas from the Warhammer 40K TTRPG
- Theysen says it took "basic ideas" from the tabletop game that were familiar to fans
- Features like Armor of Contempt were also adapted to make sense for the real-time strategy experience
King Art Games co-founder and Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 creative director Jan Theysen has explained how the studio implemented ideas from the Warhammer 40K tabletop game to make sense for long-time fans and newcomers.
In a lengthy interview with TechRadar Gaming, where Theysen described how the game manifests the classic RTS experience of the 2004 game and which hero mechanics and UI features it borrowed from Dawn of War 2 and 3, the creative director said that it was always King Art's intention to take inspiration from the beloved tabletop game.
"When it comes to basic ideas for factions, or also for units, for abilities, and so on, that's basically the first place we look," Theysen said. "Because instead of inventing completely new abilities for units, it makes sense to see what they have in the tabletop; is this something that we can adapt or change so it works in an RTS?"
Among those features was Armor of Contempt, a combat bonus for the Space Marine faction, which King Art decided to adapt to make sense in the context of the RTS.
"The tabletop is something different, but it's kind of the same idea, which basically means it makes Space Marines harder to kill, right?" the creative director explained.
"In the RTS, we now have Armor of Contempt, which basically works when Space Marines kill enemies, but also if one of them gets killed, there is more contempt [the attribute], and then basically the next damage you receive goes away from the contempt instead of the HP pool, which makes the Space Marine harder to kill, right?"
He added, "It's not the same mechanic, but it does kind of the same thing. And by naming it Armor of Contempt, someone who knows the tabletop already gets a good impression of what it probably does."
