articles.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.
As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.
For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice, which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot, which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

articles.title: Could potential AI clones of GTA VI force a quicker official port?
articles.text:
Yesterday, when reporting on emerging efforts to pipe the console version of GTA VI through a PC’s DLSS-powered Nvidia GPU, we mentioned in passing that PC players could instead just wait for the AI-assisted decompilation port that will no doubt be coming in short order. Now, a former Rockstar tech director says he thinks that exact threat could cause the developer to work faster on the official PC version of its soon-to-release crime/lifestyle simulator.
Obbe Vermeij hasn’t worked at Rockstar since 2009, but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun, he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game’s 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release.
“So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console,” Vermeij said. “So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn’t really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better.”
Those sales caused Rockstar to pivot hard toward the console side of the business, with oft-delayed PC ports of its major games only hitting many months or even many years after their console counterparts. It’s a trend that Rockstar has stuck with even as many formerly console-focused game publishers have started treating the PC as an equally relevant platform and as the line between PCs and consoles itself has gotten much fuzzier in recent years.

articles.title: MakeMyTrip enters shared mobility space with majority stake in Quick Ride
articles.text:
MakeMyTrip enters shared mobility space with majority stake in Quick Ride
MakeMyTrip has acquired the Quick Ride brand and its ride pooling business with a majority stake in this entity.
MakeMyTrip on Friday announced it has acquired a majority stake in 'Quick Ride', a technology-led shared mobility platform, for an undisclosed sum.
The investment provides an opportunity for MakeMyTrip to establish its presence in the shared mobility/ride pooling segment, complementary to the group's existing ground transportation portfolio, the company stated.
Bengaluru-headquartered Quick Ride is a technology-led, asset-light shared mobility platform that connects people travelling along similar routes, enabling affordable ride pooling for everyday commutes.
The 'Quick Ride' brand and its ride pooling business underwent an internal restructuring and are now housed under a new entity, Co Ride Mobility Private Limited. MakeMyTrip has acquired the Quick Ride brand and its ride pooling business with a majority stake in this entity.
Quick Ride's promoters will continue to lead the business. Its erstwhile EV taxi business will remain with the predecessor entity, iDisha Info Labs Private Limited, MakeMyTrip stated.
Rajesh Magow, Co-Founder & Group Chief Executive Officer, MakeMyTrip, said, "As part of our expansion strategy, we have pursued selective strategic partnerships, investments and acquisitions that complement and strengthen our existing business and expand the breadth and depth of our offerings. Ride pooling gives us a presence in high-frequency daily commutes within cities, as well as intercity travel".
Quick Ride will be housed under our ground transport business, and we will bring the learnings from building redBus in India and overseas markets to grow and scale the business, he added.
KNM Rao, Founder and CEO, Quick Ride, said, "Becoming part of the MakeMyTrip group is an important milestone for our team and for the community of users who have placed their trust in us. We look forward to drawing on MakeMyTrip's reach and experience in travel to further scale the business".
In recent years, MakeMyTrip has made acquisitions across travel segments, including Savaari in car rental services, Happay in corporate travel and expense management, Flamingo Transworld in regional group holiday packages and through strategic minority investment in Atlys in visa processing.

articles.title: Adobe-Alternative per KI: Kann Artcraft die Creative Cloud stürzen?
articles.text:
Photoshop-Killer aus der KI? Was das Open-Source-Projekt Artcraft kann
Für Illustrator:innen, Fotograf:innen und Grafikdesigner:innen gibt es kaum eine Alternative zur Creative Cloud von Adobe. Allerdings ist sie nicht gerade günstig: Für das Pro-Abo mit Tools wie Photoshop, Premiere und Adobe Firefly zahlen Einzelpersonen rund 78 Euro pro Monat. Der Software-Entwickler Brandon Thomas will jetzt eine Alternative bieten. Auf Hacker News schaltete er sich kürzlich in eine Diskussion ein und behauptete, er habe Photoshop mithilfe von KI in nur einer Sitzung nachgebaut.
Artcraft befindet sich aktuell in einer frühen Entwicklungsphase
Zusammen mit seinem vierköpfigen Team hat der Entwickler eine kostenlose Open-Source-Software-Suite für Kreative vorgestellt. Das Tool trägt den Namen Artcraft. Die darin enthaltenen Anwendungen weisen eine große Ähnlichkeit zu den altbewährten Bearbeitungsprogrammen von Adobe auf: So wird Photoshop durch Photocraft ersetzt. An die Stelle von Lightroom tritt Lightcraft und so weiter. Wie Futurism berichtet, bestehe das Ziel von Artcraft darin, Adobes Software zurückzuentwickeln und ein gleichwertiges Produkt ohne Nachteile wie Cloud-Anbindung und hohe monatliche Kosten zu schaffen.
Es gibt allerdings einige Einschränkungen. Die aktuelle Version befindet sich laut dem Entwicklungsteam noch in einem frühen Stadium, entwickele sich aber rasant weiter. Tatsächlich verweisen erste Tester:innen auf diverse Defizite und Thomas selbst betont, dass es noch einige Monate dauern werde, bis 99 Prozent der Features abgedeckt werden können. Möglich macht das KI: Bei der Entwicklung der Open-Source-Lösung nutzten Thomas und sein Team eigenen Angaben zufolge Anthropics Claude Opus 5.5 als KI-Tool und Rust als Programmiersprache. Die Programme laufen nicht nur mit Windows und MacOS, sondern auch mit Linux.
Rechtliche Herausforderungen: Wird Adobe sich den Nachbau gefallen lassen?
Thomas betont, dass es sich nicht um ein reines Vibe-Coding-Projekt handele. Er verfüge über 15 Jahre Erfahrung in der Software-Entwicklung und im Umgang mit großen Rust-Projekten. Er wolle mit Artcraft zeigen, was aktuelle KI-Tools leisten können. Aber auch seine Abneigung gegen Adobe dürfte eine Rolle spielen. In einem Reddit-Beitrag schreibt er, dass ihm das Unternehmen mehrfach eine Stornogebühr berechnet habe und er es „seitdem hasse“. Zahlreiche Nutzer:innen der Plattform befürworten die Entwicklung einer Adobe-Alternative. „Ich habe es kurz ausprobiert. Absolut fantastisch“, heißt es in einem Kommentar. Ein:e andere Reddit-Nutzer:in schrieb: „Wird auch Zeit, dass wir Adobe endgültig den Rücken kehren.“
Die Tools von Artcraft sind ein guter Beleg dafür, wie gut KI mittlerweile darin geworden ist, anhand von Vorgaben komplexere Programme zu erstellen. Laut einem Bericht des Standard sieht Thomas das als den Beginn eines neuen Zeitalters, in dem jede:r eigene Alternativen zu kommerzieller Software erstellen und anpassen kann. Ob er seine ambitionierten Versprechen einhalten kann, bleibt abzuwarten. Von einem fertigen Produkt ist Artcraft derzeit nämlich noch weit entfernt. Die Entwicklung der Open-Source-Lösung wirft außerdem auch rechtliche Fragen auf. Wird Adobe den Nachbau dulden – insbesondere, weil Artcraft der Creative Cloud sehr ähnlich ist?
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 09.10.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Adobe ist selbst schuld. Ich hoffe sie verschwinden endlich vom Markt. Ihre Software ist überladen und mit Features vollgestopft, nach denen niemand gefragt hat. KI ist bei ihnen genau so ein Fetisch wie Cloud-Schnickschnack.

articles.title: « Être une femme, ça aide » : Sophie Adenot raconte comment son corps a vécu l'espace (en vidéo)
articles.text:
Lors d’une conférence de presse organisée par l’Agence spatiale européenne (ESA) ce lundi 2 novembre 2026, à laquelle Numerama assistait, l’astronaute française Sophie Adenot est revenue sur les effets de la microgravité sur son organisme.
L’astronaute de l’ESA a amerri le 8 octobre 2026 au large de la Californie, avec le reste de l’équipage Crew-12, au terme de sa mission à bord de la Station spatiale internationale (ISS). Au total, elle a vécu 237 jours dans l’espace (un record européen pour un vol unique). Elle a ensuite passé 3 semaines en réadaptation au Centre des astronautes européens de Cologne, en Allemagne, avant cette conférence de presse au siège parisien de l’ESA.
Elle a surtout décrit un corps qui s’est bien adapté à la vie en orbite, loin de l’image d’un organisme uniquement malmené par l’apesanteur. Pour en savoir plus sur son témoignage, vous pouvez regarder notre vidéo complète sur YouTube.
« Être dans l’espace pour le corps féminin, c’est quand même la panacée », selon Sophie Adenot
Sophie Adenot livre un témoignage qu’on entend rarement, le métier d’astronaute étant encore majoritairement exercé par des hommes : selon elle, le corps féminin se sent particulièrement bien dans l’ISS. Elle explique que les variations hormonales et biologiques régulières préparent en quelque sorte les femmes aux changements profonds d’environnement. Le cycle menstruel ou les grossesses habitueraient peut-être le corps à réagir à des stress extérieurs, avance-t-elle prudemment.
L’astronaute dresse un bilan enthousiaste de son séjour en orbite, où elle dit n’avoir ressenti ni jambes lourdes ni ballonnements. Selon elle, cette capacité d’adaptation du corps féminin rend l’arrivée en microgravité beaucoup plus douce. « Le corps féminin, il a l’habitude de s’adapter et de réagir à des stress extérieurs. »
Sophie Adenot compare volontiers ce voyage en orbite à son expérience de la maternité, deux moments qu’elle qualifie d’intimement « transformateurs ». Devenir mère lui a permis d’aborder sa mission spatiale avec un grand apaisement et une authenticité renforcée. Cette sérénité l’accompagne aujourd’hui, alors que sa mission court officiellement jusqu’en avril 2027 : même de retour sur Terre, Sophie Adenot a tout un protocole à respecter.
Le défi physique des scaphandres inadaptés
Tout n’est pas simple pour autant. Les sorties extravéhiculaires, notamment, sont physiquement très éprouvantes. Sophie Adenot le sait bien, elle qui s’est aventurée trois fois hors de l’ISS en 14 jours, pour un total de 19 heures et 42 minutes passées dans le vide. La Française n’a pas caché l’exigence extrême de ces opérations, confiant récemment que rien que de tenir un stylo est douloureux après cet effort.
Pour tenir le choc, l’entraînement physique est indispensable, d’autant que le scaphandre actuel est, de son propre aveu, mal adapté à la morphologie féminine. « Pour l’instant, on a un scaphandre qui est pas vraiment adapté à la morphologie féminine, mais ce n’est pas grave, c’est pas impossible d’y arriver non plus. » Pour compenser l’ergonomie rigide des combinaisons spatiales actuelles, l’astronaute a dû redoubler d’efforts en amont : « C’est aussi pour ça que j’ai fait autant de sport, pour avoir des gros biceps ! »
Au-delà de la performance physique et scientifique, Sophie Adenot revendique une approche décomplexée et globale de son identité, refusant de s’enfermer dans un rôle unique : « Ce qui compte, c’est d’être authentique. Je suis une femme, je suis une maman, je suis une astronaute, je suis une pilote, je suis une machine quand je suis sur la machine de muscu… C’est important de pouvoir honorer toutes ces facettes et de les accepter. »
Alors que les futurs scaphandres sont déjà en développement pour les missions lunaires du programme Artemis, le témoignage de l’astronaute française rappelle que ces combinaisons devront aussi convenir aux femmes. La question reste sensible pour la Nasa, qui n’a retenu aucune femme dans l’équipage d’Artemis III, mission prévue en 2027, tout en promettant d’envoyer la première femme sur la Lune dans le cadre du programme.

articles.title: Braun Series 9 AIO9540 : la tondeuse barbe, cheveux et corps perd 70 € chez Boulanger
articles.text:
La tondeuse multi-usages Braun Series 9 AIO9540 est à 89,99 € (-43 %)
Barbe, cheveux, corps et nez avec un seul appareil étanche : la tondeuse Braun Series 9 AIO9540 passe à 89,99 € chez Boulanger, 70 € sous son prix de référence.
Vendue et expédiée par Boulanger, la référence AIO9540F1 affiche 89,99 € contre un prix de référence de 159,99 €. La livraison à domicile est annoncée dès demain et le retrait en magasin est offert.
Un seul appareil pour toute la toilette
Ce kit multi-usages se charge de la barbe, des cheveux, du corps et du nez. Avec ses 11 sabots, il propose 14 hauteurs de coupe, de 0,5 à 21 mm, de quoi passer d'une barbe de trois jours à une coupe courte sans changer d'appareil.
La technologie AutoSense adapte la coupe à la densité de la barbe pour un résultat régulier. Braun annonce jusqu'à 120 minutes d'autonomie, et le mode BodyGentle est prévu pour protéger les zones sensibles lors de la tonte du corps.
Étanche et simple à entretenir
La tondeuse est étanche : elle s'utilise sous la douche et se rince directement à l'eau. Une brossette de nettoyage est également fournie pour entretenir les lames.
Ce modèle n'affiche encore aucun avis client chez Boulanger. Il s'adresse surtout à ceux qui veulent remplacer plusieurs appareils par un kit complet, pour moins de 100 €.

articles.title: TSLA, NVDA, META, MSFT: ações de big techs derretem nas bolsas • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
TSLA, NVDA, META, MSFT: ações de big techs derretem nas bolsas
Nasdaq recuou 5,52% nos Estados Unidos, maior desvalorização diária desde abril de 2025. Bolsa da Coreia do Sul interrompeu negociações por 20 minutos após tombo.
A conta da inteligência artificial parece ter chegado a Wall Street. As ações das sete maiores empresas de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos fecharam em queda nas principais bolsas de valores do mundo. A Tesla (TSLA) liderou as perdas, com recuo de 10,8%. A Nvidia (NVDA) perdeu 9,3%, enquanto a Meta (META) e a Microsoft (MSFT) também registraram desvalorização.
O Nasdaq, índice que reúne principalmente empresas de tecnologia nos EUA, recuou 5,52% na quinta-feira (05/11), a maior desvalorização diária desde abril de 2025. A onda de vendas chegou à Ásia hoje (06/11): o Nikkei, do Japão, fechou em baixa de 5,96%. Na Coreia do Sul, o Kospi perdeu 6,02%, depois de chegar a cair 8,55% durante o pregão. A intensidade da queda levou a bolsa sul-coreana a suspender as negociações por 20 minutos.
A Apple (AAPL) foi a empresa que menos perdeu valor entre as gigantes de tecnologia e viu seus papéis recuaram 1,53%. Um dos fatores para a queda mais moderada é a menor exposição da fabricante à atual corrida por infraestrutura de IA.
As fabricantes de semicondutores também sofreram perdas expressivas. A AMD recuou 17,3%, enquanto o índice de empresas de chips da Filadélfia caiu 12,2%. Na Ásia, a fabricante sul-coreana SK Hynix perdeu 10,4%, e a Samsung Electronics recuou 6,4%.
Por trás da desvalorização está uma dúvida sobre o tamanho dos investimentos necessários para sustentar a expansão da IA. Os investidores querem saber quando os bilhões de dólares destinados à tecnologia vão começar a gerar lucro — tanto para as empresas que desenvolvem os sistemas quanto para os fornecedores de equipamentos e componentes.
Segundo levantamento da Reuters, Amazon (AMZN), Meta (META), Microsoft (MSFT) e Alphabet (GOOGL), controladora do Google, elevaram juntas seus investimentos em infraestrutura de US$ 113 bilhões para US$ 207 bilhões em um ano (cerca de R$ 1,1 trilhão).
A previsão é de que as quatro empresas desembolsem outros US$ 232 bilhões (R$ 1,2 trilhão) no trimestre seguinte. Os gastos de capital do grupo podem chegar a US$ 740 bilhões (R$ 4 trilhões).
A maior parte dos investimentos é destinada à construção de data centers, à compra de processadores e à ampliação da capacidade de armazenamento e processamento de dados. Essas instalações reúnem milhares de computadores que permitem treinar e executar sistemas de inteligência artificial.
A expansão do setor, porém, enfrenta um novo fator de incerteza nos Estados Unidos: a possibilidade de regras mais rígidas para a construção dessas estruturas. As eleições de meio de mandato, realizadas na terça-feira (03/11), deram ao Partido Democrata maioria no Congresso americano e aumentaram a preocupação dos investidores com eventuais mudanças na legislação, o que reduziria a demanda por chips.

Democrats’ historic victories in this week’s U.S. midterm elections could also transform the tech industry.
The public voted on 41 data center-related ballot measures on Tuesday — in all but one, the majority voted to impose more restrictions on data center development. And even when data centers weren’t on the ballot directly, they were a major talking point, with newly-elected Democratic governors and congressmembers likely to support additional regulation.

articles.title: Climate protestors storm Microsoft AI data center construction site — Amsterdam reportedly first of many targeted actions across Europe
articles.text:
Protesters storm Microsoft AI data center construction site — Amsterdam reportedly first of 85 targeted actions across Europe
'Screw your data center.'
A Microsoft data center under construction in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, has been overrun by about a hundred protesters, with some carrying placards saying, “Screw your data center.” According to Reuters, the “Stop Dirty Data Centers” coalition is planning actions across 16 countries on November 6 and 7, 2026, including Amsterdam, Dublin, Warsaw, and another Microsoft site in Denmark.
Pure Data Centers, which owns the Amsterdam data center, said, “We respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have.” The report also quoted Microsoft saying that it understood the strong feeling that people have and respected their right to peaceful expression but says that it does not condone any unlawful action.
"On 6-7 November 2026 we are taking action across Europe to say Stop Dirty Data Centres," the group's website reads. "Local communities are rising up to stop dirty data centres where they live. We will unite and exercise our democratic rights to speak out, assemble, and protest to hold elected officials to account. We’re calling for an immediate moratorium on large data centres in Europe!" A map on the site shows actions planned at 85 locations across Europe over the coming days.
The group cited a list of concerns about "the explosion of AI data centres across our towns and cities," and claims to be joining to prevent "the irreparable harms data centres pose to the wellbeing of people and planet." They cite local communities, jobs, housing shortages and rising energy bills, the climate crisis, heatwaves and water shortages, big tech undermining democracies, the mental health crisis, increased surveillance and the erosion of privacy, securitization and militarization, and a toxic supply chain as motivations.
Data center opposition is one of the issues that has taken center stage in the U.S. midterm elections, with Americans overwhelmingly voting against them. It seems that resistance isn’t limited to the United States, though, as European countries take measures to limit their unlimited development. For example, Google has been hit with a criminal probe after its Finnish subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, allegedly destroyed 816 acres of forest without a permit. Denmark has also hit the brakes on data center grid connection requests as total applications exceed 60GW, more than eight times the country’s current peak power consumption. One Italian council also a 200% tax on data center development in agricultural land to encourage developers to reuse old industrial areas instead.
The Stop Data Center coalition claims that it isn’t against progress or that it wants to close down existing projects. Instead, it wants AI data center construction to be held until governments have established clearer rules on their development so that they do not have leave a negative impact on the environment and the people living around them. “AI, of course, is a super important technology and we need to have our own capacity,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told the publication. But she also added that “it's very important for citizens that they can trust that their energy bills are not skyrocketing and there are not electricity blackouts because of data centers, or they are not destroying the environment with these projects.”

articles.title: Russian private data center facilities face strict new rules following Putin orders
articles.text:
Russian data centers ordered to save 10% of capacity for state use following new Putin orders
Russian private data center facilities face strict new rules
- Putin orders private data centres to reserve 10% of their capacity for state use
- State authorities can request reserved computing resources with 24 hours' notice
- Private operators retain ownership while the government gains access to reserved capacity
Russian President Vladimir Putin has directed privately operated data centres to make part of their computing resources available for government information systems.
The measure requires affected facilities to set aside 10% of their capacity, giving authorities access when state digital services require additional computing resources.
According to Russian media outlet Astra, the directive appeared on the country's official legal information website on November 2 2026, introducing a strict implementation deadline.
Moscow tightens controls
Operators have been given 10 days to meet the new requirement, although they can continue using the reserved resources during ordinary business operations.
A special government subcommission will determine when the state can demand access, with facilities required to provide the requested resources within 24 hours.
The arrangement does not amount to an outright transfer of ownership, since companies retain control over their facilities and continue operating their businesses.
However, the government gains authority to requisition part of their available computing resources when designated Russian information services require additional infrastructure.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The decree specifies that companies will receive payment for providing access, with the government body responsible for establishing a ceiling on applicable charges.
Officials must also establish procedures governing allocation decisions, including the creation of the subcommission responsible for administering access requests.
The government has assigned the Ministry of Digital Development responsibility for overseeing the country's data centre capacity.
The ministry will assess available floor space and computing resources across domestic facilities and establish operational standards to ensure reliable and uninterrupted services.
The directive arrives amid continuing pressure on Russian digital infrastructure, including Ukrainian attacks against facilities supporting important domestic internet services.
In October 2026, Ukrainian strikes hit three Yandex data centres inside Russia, disrupting cloud platforms, stored information, database services and other online operations.
The attacks followed Russian assaults against essential Ukrainian infrastructure, forming part of the continuing conflict between the two countries.
Foreign infrastructure remains possible under security restrictions
Despite requiring greater domestic capacity for government systems, the decree allows Russian information services to temporarily operate using computing resources located abroad.
Such arrangements require approval from the Federal Security Service, commonly known as the FSB, giving security officials authority over exceptions.
This provision means the new requirement does not completely exclude foreign facilities, although their use remains subject to government security approval.
Russia has separately explored cooperation with American interests involving large computing facilities, including discussions about potential infrastructure projects between the countries.
On October 16, Kremlin representative Kirill Dmitriev said Moscow and Washington were discussing joint data infrastructure proposals involving possible Russian nuclear energy supplies.
The discussions reportedly include using electricity generated by Russian nuclear facilities to support computing infrastructure.

articles.title: Nvidia tightens tracking of AI GPUs in Southeast Asia as Chinese chip smuggling draws scrutiny, report claims — cloud providers must join monitoring program to qualify for official partner status
articles.text:
Nvidia tightens tracking of AI GPUs in Southeast Asia as Chinese chip smuggling draws scrutiny, report claims — cloud providers must join monitoring program to qualify for official partner status
Nvidia mandates GPU tracking for Southeast Asian cloud partners seeking official status
Southeast Asia computing providers are now reportedly required to register with Nvidia's Fleet Intelligence tracking system if they want to become official Nvidia Cloud Partners (NCPs). The move, according to Bloomberg, is aimed at giving the chipmaker another way to monitor where its AI accelerators are deployed, as Washington grows increasingly frustrated with restricted hardware finding its way into China through regional smuggling networks. Nvidia was not immediately available for comment.
The NCP designation is worth pursuing as it gives cloud providers Nvidia's public endorsement and preferred access to its sought-after AI chips, putting the company in a position to use those benefits as leverage. Customers seeking the status must now enroll in Fleet Intelligence, according to people familiar with the new requirements. Fleet Management was introduced last December primarily as a data centre management tool. It gathers information about NVIDIA hardware deployed across participating companies' infrastructure, including the locations of individual accelerators. That information could give Nvidia a better picture of whether its chips are operating after they leave the supply chain.
The system is, however, a universal tracking mandate. Participation has remained voluntary outside the NCP requirement, and Nvidia does not automatically receive location data from every customer using the software. The company has also not clarified whether existing Cloud Partners will have to enroll to retain their designation or whether the requirement will eventually extend beyond Southeast Asia.
Notably, Nvidia has been developing a way to locate AI for some time now. Last December, we reported that the company had developed software-based GPU tracking, using GPU telemetry and network latency measurements to estimate where processors are operating. Nvidia described the software as a customer-installed agent for monitoring hardware health, integrity and inventory.
The technology has an obvious use beyond data maintenance. The U.S. restricts Chinese companies from purchasing advanced AI accelerators without a license, yet authorities believe billions of dollars worth of the hardware have reached Chinese buyers through third-party networks, with Southeast Asia becoming an important transit point for those transactions.
A C4ADS investigation has previously identified several routes used to move restricted processors into China, including purchases through research initiatives, shell companies and shipments routed through other Southeast Asian countries. The nonprofit examined transactions between 2022 and 2025 and identified $13.4 million worth of Nvidia A100, H100, and AD102-series GPUs moving through regional trade routes. Its report also linked $4.6 billion in hardware purchases to Singapore-based Megaspeed International.
Megaspeed has become a particularly awkward case for Nvidia, with the company being under U.S. and Singaporean investigation for more than a year over suspected chip diversion. Last week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang defended his dealings with the firm, describing them as “completely normal,” adding, “we’ve studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one.” Megaspeed denied any wrongdoing. In April, Megaspeed’s Malysisan data centre landlord terminated its contract, reallocating 68.4 megawatts of capacity to another cloud provider
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Moreover, Megaspeed is not the only example of how difficult it can be to police the movement of AI hardware. Earlier this year, U.S. prosecutors accused people associated with Super Micro of helping divert around $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia-powered servers to China through Southeast Asian intermediaries. The alleged scheme involved falsified paperwork and dummy server shells, with genuine hardware shipped onward after inspections. More recently, the company has faced additional scrutiny over its export compliance after inspections. Nvidia has also reportedly removed half of the Asian companies on its pre-approved buyer list and told cloud providers to keep at least 51% of their computing services with customers outside China.

articles.title: Bonne nouvelle, Nintendo assure que le prix de la Switch 2 ne devrait plus augmenter
articles.text:
Le 8 mai, Nintendo annonçait une hausse du prix de la Switch 2 dans plusieurs régions, en invoquant « l’évolution des conditions du marché ». En France, la console est passée de 469,99 à 499,99 euros le 1er septembre, quand les Américains la paient désormais 499,99 dollars au lieu de 449,99. À l’occasion de ses résultats semestriels publiés le 5 novembre, le constructeur affirme n’avoir aucun projet de nouvelle hausse.
À lire aussi : Il piratait des jeux Switch, Nintendo lui fait payer 4,5 millions de dollars de dommages et intérêts
Nintendo dit avoir mis sa mémoire à l’abri
L’annonce de mai était intervenue en pleine flambée des prix de la mémoire vive, tirée par la demande des centres de données dédiés à l’intelligence artificielle. Les coûts de transport et ceux des plastiques grimpaient eux aussi. Comme un smartphone ou un PC, une console embarque de la mémoire vive, et sa facture suit les cours de ces puces. Le Japon avait encaissé la plus forte augmentation, de l’ordre de 20 % sur certains modèles dès le 25 mai. La France s’en tirait avec 30 euros de plus, soit environ 6,4 %, et les États-Unis avec 50 dollars, soit environ 11 %.
Six mois plus tard, Nintendo déclare n’avoir « aucun projet d’augmenter à nouveau le prix de la Nintendo Switch 2 ». Le constructeur explique avoir pris les mesures nécessaires pour disposer de quantités suffisantes de mémoire, et se dit en position de sécuriser ses approvisionnements. Il ne précise ni jusqu’à quand ces réserves le protègent, ni à quel prix elles ont été constituées.
Des ventes en net recul, face à un été 2025 hors norme
D’avril à septembre, premier semestre de son exercice, Nintendo a livré 6,49 millions de Switch 2, un recul de 37,4 % sur un an, dont 2,67 millions sur le seul été, en baisse de 41 %. La période de référence englobe toutefois le lancement de la console, le 5 juin 2025, quand 3,5 millions d’exemplaires s’étaient écoulés en quatre jours. La hausse française n’est par ailleurs entrée en vigueur que le 1er septembre, au dernier mois du trimestre, ce qui rend hasardeux tout lien direct avec ce ralentissement.
En mai 2025, avant même la sortie, Shuntaro Furukawa, le président de Nintendo, reconnaissait déjà que la console était relativement chère comparée à la première Switch, et en tenait compte dans ses prévisions. Il tablait alors sur 15 millions d’unités pour le premier exercice.Sur la durée, la machine garde une avance confortable sur sa devancière : 26,35 millions de Switch 2 ont été livrées, contre 19,67 millions pour la première Switch au même stade. Nintendo maintient son objectif de 16,5 millions d’unités sur l’exercice, ce qui suppose d’en écouler une dizaine de millions d’ici fin mars, contre 6,49 millions sur les six mois précédents. Les jeux Switch 2, eux, ont atteint 15,03 millions d’exemplaires sur l’été, en hausse de 26 %.
Pour les acheteurs, la Switch 2 reste à 499,99 euros, sans nouvelle hausse annoncée ni baisse évoquée. Ceux qui la visent pour Noël savent au moins à quoi s’attendre, et Nintendo joue son objectif annuel sur ces quelques semaines de fêtes. Rappelons aussi que le prix n’est pas le seul changement que la Switch 2 a connu à la rentrée, puisqu’une révision est apparue sur les étales, avec la promesse d’un remplacement de batterie facilité.

articles.title: It's a weird time to buy a laptop, but the new MacBook Pro doesn't skimp on quality
articles.text:
Let’s get that out there right away, because for a lot of people, it will be the only thing that matters. As with so many things in life, though, you get what you pay for. There’s no questioning the quality of the laptop’s display or most of its other hardware components.
But should you buy it? Well, that’s a complicated question in 2026.
We’re in a time of great uncertainty when it comes to buying a computer. Prices are at levels we’ve not seen in recent history, and they may well keep climbing. Meanwhile, users paying close attention to the early developments in both local and agentic artificial intelligence are asking an important question: “What will computing even look like in a few years, and what does that mean for the computer I should buy today?”
Apple’s new MacBook Pro sits at the intersection of all of this uncertainty. In multiple ways, it’s also straddling different worlds.
It arrives amid a changing of the guard in Apple’s leadership, potentially raising questions about the future direction of Apple’s ecosystem. It’s a mass-market consumer product, but configuring it with enough RAM and storage to make it feel future-proof pushes its price into territory mostly only well-funded businesses can afford. It’s firmly rooted in the computing paradigms of the past 20 years, but it shows early signs of flirtation with new AI workflows. It’s a conventional Apple laptop in most ways, but it also has a touchscreen—something that would never have happened in a prior Apple era.
It’s an outstanding, high-quality product, but whether it’s something you should buy depends on you—what you’re doing right now, what you’ll be doing in the future, and what you value.
Specifications and performance
For most of the specs we look at, Apple isn’t claiming any difference here. The new MacBook Pro promises 24 hours of battery life (though you’d have to use it in a conservative way to achieve that), it has the same ports (three Thunderbolt, one HDMI, one SDXC, and MagSafe), and it has the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity.
And like its immediate predecessor, it offers the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options. Running synthetic benchmarks, we found no meaningful difference at all compared to when we ran the same tests on the previous model, so we won’t spend time discussing their performance today. We’ve covered both thoroughly in prior reviews, and you can read up there if you’d like.
The chips are more than fast enough for normal workflows for the foreseeable future, including most 3D work. AI inference is the main area where they may be less future-proof. To be clear, they’re strong enough for now, but the field is evolving rapidly, and there’s reason to expect significant improvements in future chips on this front.
According to Bloomberg, Apple is skipping Pro and Max versions of the M6 chip that was introduced earlier this year to focus its attention on a significant rework for the M7 due in 2027. “The M7 line is designed primarily around major advancements to on-device AI processing,” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote. The line would emphasize memory bandwidth, which matters for fast, efficient AI inference.
Even without Bloomberg’s report, I’d expect Apple to prioritize those areas in its next high-end chip refresh. That’s partly because there’s another tea leaf to read here: Apple made just such an update with the A20 Pro, which debuted in its latest iPhones several weeks ago. That update brought a substantially improved Neural Engine and a significant increase in memory bandwidth. We also found that the A20 Pro delivered improved 3D graphics performance in some cases.
Similar improvements could come to Macs, meaning it might be worth waiting another year if you’re focused on AI workflows or even 3D applications—especially given the high cost of these machines. That’s part of what makes this such an uncertain time to buy a laptop. We’re in a moment when these companies are revisiting the architecture of these chips because of these new workflows, and we don’t know what the end result is yet.
A monster of a display
Here’s one thing that’s not at all uncertain: The display on the MacBook Pro is the best I have ever used in a laptop. If the display is your primary concern, this is a big moment.
Apple calls it a “tandem OLED display,” meaning a panel with two emissive layers. This approach helps achieve a higher peak brightness, but perhaps more importantly, it can reduce the risk of burn-in. Most of the time, the display won’t need both layers running at full power. Instead, they can share the load and run at a reduced current, helping extend the panel’s lifespan.
The new display can achieve up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness on HDR highlights, but it’s rated for 1,000 nits of sustained brightness. In general, I like the way Apple handles HDR for this at the OS level, too.
This photo doesn’t do the screen justice, but at least you can see the proportions and design here. (It’s the 16-inch model.)
Credit:
Samuel Aoxn
This photo doesn’t do the screen justice, but at least you can see the proportions and design here. (It’s the 16-inch model.)
Credit:
Samuel Aoxn
The brightness matters for HDR content, sure, but what really makes OLED stand out is per-pixel illumination—meaning each pixel can turn on or off independently. That allows for absolute black levels and very strong contrast. The MiniLED display in the previous MacBook Pro offered good contrast for an LCD display, but OLED has a fundamental advantage here, and it shows.
As you’d expect, the screen offers native support for both P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts. It also has a variable refresh rate from 10 to 120 Hz, just like many of Apple’s other products. As before, the MacBook Pro comes in roughly 14-inch (3,024×1,986 pixels) and 16-inch (3,472×2,226 pixels) variants. There’s also a nano-texture glass option to fight glare, though that will set you back another $150.
It’s one of the most impressive displays I’ve used in any device, and it’s certainly the best I’ve ever used on a laptop. The colors are vibrant, the contrast is outstanding, the blacks are inky, and it can get very bright when it needs to—not just with highlights but full-screen brightness as well. And on the whole, it’s extremely precise. Uniformity appears basically flawless. It’s what you’d expect from an ultra-high-end TV or reference monitor, not a laptop or computer screen, and it’s genuinely striking.
We’ll see about longevity, but OLED has come a long way in recent years, and my first impressions are that Apple has made all the right choices here.
I find myself trying to find something negative to say about the MacBook Pro’s screen to avoid sounding too effusive, but I can’t think of anything substantive. The best I can do is complain that Apple’s proprietary “PROLED XDR” label is silly and eye-roll-inducing.
Branding aside, the screen is the main reason to pay extra for this model.
Design
With its lid closed, the new MacBook Pro looks identical to its predecessor. The dimensions are largely the same. It’s slightly thinner, but you’d have to check the spec sheet or handle them side by side to notice.
Pick it up, though, and you’ll find that it’s noticeably lighter than the last model, by about half a pound. It’s not in a totally different weight class, but you can notice the change, and it’s a nice improvement. The reduction is partly due to the display technology switch; it’s easier to make a light OLED screen than a light MiniLED one.
Open the MacBook Pro and turn it on, and you’ll see one of a few other notable differences, depending on whether you’re behind or in front of it. From behind, you’ll see the Apple logo on the lid now lights up, as it did on MacBooks of yore. It’s arguably a little tacky, but it’s also neat and nostalgic. I don’t hate it.
The glow returns!
Credit:
Samuel Axon
The glow returns!
Credit:
Samuel Axon
From the front, you might notice that the already barely there bezels are even more barely there, though that’s subtle. More likely, you’ll see that the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by a cutout just like the Dynamic Island Apple introduced on the iPhone.
A comparatively sensible camera cutout
When I reviewed the first iPhone with a Dynamic Island, I was largely positive about it. No, it’s not ideal to have a cutout on the screen, but Apple has handled it as intelligently as possible, and I would even go so far as to say it has turned what should be an albatross into an attractive feature.
Thanks to the OLED display, it’s possible to make any of the pixels around the camera cutout just as black as it is. Apple has designed live activities, the volume bar, and more to appear as if they are expanding out of and around, and contracting back into, this little dot. It remains ingenious.
When the Dynamic Island first arrived on the iPhone, it helped unify several previously disparate approaches to displaying notifications in iOS, making it especially useful. This time, it doesn’t solve as many problems, but it’s an improvement over the dead weight of the notch. It also helps that the MacBook Pro’s much larger screen means the cutout takes up a small share of the screen’s real estate.
The Dynamic Island on the MacBook Pro.
Samuel Axon
The Dynamic Island on the MacBook Pro.
Samuel Axon
Full-screen apps cut off just below the Dynamic Island by default, just like with the notch before.
Samuel Axon
Full-screen apps cut off just below the Dynamic Island by default, just like with the notch before.
Samuel Axon
The Dynamic Island on the MacBook Pro.
Samuel Axon
Full-screen apps cut off just below the Dynamic Island by default, just like with the notch before.
Samuel Axon
The Dynamic Island works the same with full-screen apps as the notch did. By default, the top of the viewport ends just below the Dynamic Island, so it just looks like there’s a taller top bezel, and it doesn’t cut into the application interface. The menu bar, clock, and other system elements still occupy the space above the application (set against a totally black background) when you move the cursor up there.
I tested a few fullscreen games with it, like World of Warcraft and Cyberpunk 2077. Some behaved by default like the default fullscreen app behavior I just described, but others tried to occupy the whole thing, making the cutout visible. Vitally, every video app I tried avoided the cutout in fullscreen.
This isn’t something to upgrade for, of course. But on the whole, I think it’s an improvement over what we had before.
The most touchable MacBook Pro ever
Apple has finally added a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. I say “finally” because the possibility has floated around for about two decades. Steve Jobs was famously opposed to the idea; there’s even video of him explaining why he thought it would make for a poor user experience.
A couple of years ago, reliable reports emerged that Apple was moving forward with the idea regardless. When I first heard about it, I imagined what could be a really exciting implementation: a convertible laptop that would let you use it in a tablet-like mode, with Apple Pencil support for drawing and writing.
As a game developer, I imagined quickly sketching 2D game maps with an Apple Pencil, using a local AI model to convert them into 3D geometry, and then switching to a laptop configuration to start testing and coding. I also imagined using it like an iPad to more comfortably watch movies on a flight.
That’s not what we got, though. The laptop has the same form factor as the previous MacBook Pro model—no tablet mode or Pencil support. Instead, it just lets you reach up from the keyboard and trackpad to touch the screen. That feels like a missed opportunity.
Some creative apps have implemented touch features that might justify the touchscreen functionality if you use them a lot. For example, you can play the on-screen virtual piano keys on Logic Pro with multiple fingers, which could be nicer than clicking on them. I imagine many people already have workflows built around other approaches, though.
If you were specifically waiting for a touchscreen on your MacBook Pro, this seems like as good an implementation as you could hope for without turning the laptop into a convertible. Apple has put real care into it. For example, it has re-engineered the hinge so the screen is not particularly wobbly when you touch it. It’s fast, accurate, and responsive. It supports multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom or swiping with three fingers to switch desktop spaces.
There’s one use case I find compelling as a developer. Testing iPhone and iPad apps in the Simulator has always been a minor hassle because of the difference in input methods. You either have to approximate only a subset of the interactions available to users with a trackpad and mouse or connect an iPhone or iPad to test them that way. A touchscreen could provide a more elegant way to test such apps in Xcode, Unity, or whatever else you might use.
Unfortunately, some of the UI elements in macOS are too small for my large fingers, so I have to tap very carefully. I also keep forgetting the touchscreen is even there for hours at a time and go back to my normal habits, partly because there’s nothing you can do at the OS level that you can’t do just as easily with trackpad gestures. And as Jobs predicted all those years ago, my arm got tired while I was using it.
For me, it feels faster, easier, more comfortable, and more natural to use the keyboard and trackpad 100 percent of the time, but I admittedly have decades of muscle memory and habits built around them. There’s apparently a generation coming up with the same kind of familiarity with touch interfaces, so this feature may appeal to them. Plus, touchscreen laptops have been a thing on Windows forever, and some people seem to want to buy them, though I never quite got why without an added tablet configuration.
It’s unlikely to account for a big portion of the device’s cost compared with the rest of the OLED panel, memory, storage, and so on. So, my own bafflement aside, I’m not unhappy it’s here. I imagine it will serve those who want it well enough.
The same excellent workstation—if you can afford it
As noted earlier, whether this laptop is worthy of a recommendation depends on you and how you use your machine. That’s always been the case, but it seems more so here.
If you’re a creative professional or a display enthusiast who wants the best laptop screen you’ve likely ever seen, you won’t be disappointed if you shell out for it. And hey, maybe you can show me your workflow and prove me wrong about the touchscreen!
If you’re just looking for a great laptop with strong performance for everyday use, consider the non-OLED, non-touchscreen model that’s still in Apple’s lineup—or even a MacBook Air, which compromises relatively little for most users. And there is, of course, the entire world of Windows and Linux laptops.
If you’re a developer—especially one working at the frontier of AI workflows—well, that’s where things get tricky. Will waiting be worthwhile? So much about how those workflows will evolve and what they’ll demand from your hardware is still so up in the air that I can’t make a confident recommendation. (For what it’s worth, I fit best in this category, and I’m still holding onto my M1 Max machine, though my resolve is wavering.)
All that said, in most ways, this is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve reviewed again and again for the past few years. Touch adds a feature aimed at a particular niche, or perhaps it’s there to roll out the welcome mat for a newer generation. The display is a more substantial update and makes a compelling case for upgrading, especially if you’re coming from an older, pre-MiniLED laptop.
But this is an expensive machine. The configuration I reviewed here (16-inch, M5 Max, 128 GB of RAM, 2 TB SSD) retails for a whopping $7,399, though you could at least shave $1,600 off that by going to a more typical-for-most-people 64 GB. (The cheapest configuration starts at $2,899.)
For the vast majority of buyers, the pre-OLED version that’s still in Apple’s lineup or another MacBook altogether will offer more bang for your buck. If you’re the kind of person who wants OLED or a touchscreen, though, you probably know that already. Based on my time with the new MacBook Pro, both features deliver on their promises, even if the latter isn’t as ambitious as some of us had hoped.
The good
Outstanding display that offers notably better and more accurate image quality while modestly reducing the weight of the device
The M5 Pro and M5 Max are still plenty fast for the majority of users
Strong build quality, solid port selection, and everything else we had positive to say about the last MacBook Pro, too
The bad
For certain workflows, the M5 Pro and M5 Max are already a few months old in an environment where things are moving very quickly
The RAM and SSD price crunch is real, and these prices are a formidable barrier for most people
Samuel Axon is the editorial lead for tech and gaming coverage at Ars Technica. He covers physical and generative AI, large language models, software development, gaming, entertainment, and mixed reality. He has been writing about gaming and technology for nearly two decades at Engadget, PC World, Mashable, Vice, Polygon, Wired, and others. He previously ran a marketing and PR agency in the gaming industry, led editorial for the TV network CBS, and worked on social media marketing strategy for Samsung Mobile at the creative agency SPCSHP. He also is an independent software and game developer for iOS, Windows, and other platforms, and he is a graduate of DePaul University, where he studied interactive media and software development.
Hollywood video engineer here. What's important for the displays we use is that they are reference displays; they meet the intended spec (normally within <1 CIE ΔE2000), and are calibrated to both make sure they do, and to know that they do.
You could say the same about music recording studios: Why bother working with massively expensive, "perfect" speakers in a pristine acoustic environment, where nobody will be listening to the music this way?
It comes down to, there is no "representative" mediocre consumer display that would be worth working on: What's out there in the world varies massively by the monitor's technology, age, price level, and viewing (or listening) environment.
A few mastering studios that could afford it, have put together rooms full of various consumer displays to do what you said: Look at the same content (in an identical environment!) to gauge what do contemporary TV's do to it. It's expensive (yes, even for Hollywood facilities), it's a moving target, and eventually it doesn't tell you a ton. There is a spec of what color on TV's should look like (ITU Rec.709, SMPTE ST 2084, etc.), and it's the TV companies' job to work off it.
And a colorist who's in a room with a director setting the look of a show, can't sit every day staring at 10 screens and playing guessing games. Similarly, audio monitor have a "flat" reference response curve that doesn't represent any common, bass-loving consumer headphones.
That said, the colorist or audio mixer's job includes understanding what consumer tech is like out there, and for example, they may absolutely consider that not everyone has an OLED TV when dialing in the dark shadows. And yes, colorists and producers watch the shows at home on their consumer TV, and they better be happy with the results!
FYI High-end consumer TV's can be very close to the pro monitors. For TV / streaming content, what's often in the room is a reference monitor (e.g. Sony BVM-HX310) and a consumer "client monitor", which may be an off-the-shelf consumer TV like an LG G5 (albeit professionally and carefully calibrated).

articles.title: EUA vão finalmente deixar de usar disquetes no controle de tráfego aéreo • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
EUA vão finalmente deixar de usar disquetes no controle de tráfego aéreo
Disquetes são usados em mais de 400 centros de controle de tráfego aéreo. Sistemas serão modernizados pela FAA até o fim de 2028.
Em clima de “antes tarde do que mais tarde ainda”, a Administração Federal de Aviação dos Estados Unidos (FAA, na sigla em inglês) anunciou que, finalmente, substituirá os disquetes que até hoje estão em uso em numerosos centros de controle de tráfego aéreo do país.
Não é exagero falar em “numerosos”. A FAA utiliza disquetes em pelo menos quatro sistemas do setor aéreo que são acessados em mais de 400 centros de controle de tráfego aéreo. Esses sistemas foram implementados entre as décadas de 1980 e 1990.
Bom, se esses sistemas funcionam até hoje, não há razão para trocá-los, certo? Não é bem assim. A malha aérea atual é muito diferente da que existia há 30 ou 40 anos, tendo muito mais voos. Sistemas obsoletos podem simplesmente não oferecer o suporte necessário a essa demanda, bem como estão mais suscetíveis a falhas.
Não por acaso, o uso de disquetes e sistemas obsoletos pela FAA foi discutido pelo Congresso dos Estados Unidos em junho de 2025. Semanas antes, pelo menos três falhas em sistemas de comunicação e radar foram registradas no Aeroporto Internacional Newark Liberty, em Nova Jersey, causando atrasos e cancelamento de voos.
Como se vê, a modernização dos sistemas é mandatória e, finalmente, ganhará forma.
O plano principal da FAA consiste em substituir os quatro sistemas obsoletos por uma solução moderna de nome Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS), capaz de fornecer diversos tipos de informações aos centros de controle de tráfego, como medições meteorológicas, horários de restrição do espaço aéreo e falhas em equipamentos ou sistemas.
Faz sentido, pois os sistemas obsoletos servem principalmente para fornecimento de informações operacionais. Veja, os disquetes não são usados para o controle do tráfego aéreo em si ou para operar radares, por exemplo. Eles servem, essencialmente, para a transferência de dados entre sistemas acessados pelos controladores de tráfego.
Esse é um trabalho de longo prazo. A FAA pretende concluir a instalação do E-IDS em 435 centros de controle de tráfego aéreo até o fim de 2028. Cinco localidades já passaram pela mudança, incluindo o Aeroporto Internacional de Atlantic City e o Aeroporto Internacional de Nashville.
Para tanto, a FAA contará principalmente com um fundo de US$ 12,5 bilhões que foi aprovado em 2025 pelo Congresso americano como parte da “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”, lei sancionada pelo presidente Donald Trump em julho de 2025 para, entre outros objetos, modernizar sistemas públicos legados.

articles.title: Pentagon offers battery startup 6K $250M loan to build US factory | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity.
The 12-year-old, North Andover, Massachusetts-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. The plant will use a unique microwave-powered process to produce battery materials that don’t rely on Chinese suppliers.
The company previously received a $50 million grant from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, though that 2023 grant was canceled by the Trump administration in a chaotic sweep of Biden-era awards, forcing 6K to reapply.
The factory was originally slated to open in 2024, but the grant cancelation and uncertainties in the EV market forced the company to rejigger its plans.
6K’s manufacturing process uses microwaves to heat metals into a plasma and then deposit them onto a surface, reducing the number of steps required to make cathode material, a key battery component. The company says the process can work on a number of different battery types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

articles.title: The wave of European fridge hacks has reached France's blood supply
articles.text:
What just happened? Refrigeration units operated by Établissement Français du Sang (EFS), France's national blood service, have been hit by a cyberattack. It is the latest in a series of intrusions targeting cold-storage controllers across Europe. No blood products or other biological materials were lost. The attack triggered EFS's alarm system, prompting staff to move the affected stock to functioning storage units before it could spoil.
The French Health Ministry said it is closely monitoring the situation and confirmed that no biological materials were lost. The intrusion appears to have targeted refrigeration equipment at three sites, reportedly including one in Burgundy-Franche-Comté.
The attackers did not breach EFS directly. The agency says the intrusion occurred at one of its service providers, which several outlets have identified as Coolworld, a refrigeration rental company. Coolworld has published a notice attributing the incident to "remote monitoring software" used in its systems. It traced the problem to "a component from a third-party supplier," but has released no further technical details.
Without those details, it is difficult to determine how the attackers gained access. In the earlier supermarket attacks, they targeted refrigeration equipment that was directly exposed to the internet. Coolworld may instead keep its controllers on a private network, which would have required the attackers to breach that network first. One detail stands out either way: EFS's monitoring and alarm system detected the breach, not the vendor's.
Coolworld has not disclosed which brand of controller it uses. The attacks so far appear to have targeted one manufacturer's equipment at a time. Danfoss controllers have featured most prominently, particularly in the attacks at the beginning of November, although they were not the only devices involved.
Copeland's Dixell controllers were also targeted in the attacks in mid-October. During the second wave of supermarket attacks, intruders raised freezer temperatures in Belgium and Sweden to 50 degrees Celsius, destroying food stocks.
The manufacturers' own documentation helps explain how the devices became accessible to attackers. A Danfoss datasheet says its controllers should be installed behind "appropriately configured firewalls and secure LAN" and should not be connected to "any public or non-secure network."
That wording leaves considerable room for interpretation. An installer who opens firewall ports to enable remote access can leave a device almost as exposed as one connected directly to the internet. Danfoss has since issued a support bulletin explicitly instructing customers to install the units behind a VPN. The bulletin appeared only in October 2026, and searches turned up no earlier version of this recommendation.
Copeland's guidance was even less restrictive. Installation manuals for its Dixell XWEB supervisory controllers instruct installers to forward port 80 (the web interface) and port 22 (Secure Shell) to the internet so the units can be accessed remotely. A VPN is mentioned only as an option. Copeland changed its guidance on October 14, following the first wave of attacks, when it published a security advisory stating that the controllers should only be accessible through a VPN.
Two Russia-aligned hacking groups, Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest, have claimed responsibility for the attacks. Several news outlets report having seen the claims in Telegram posts that have since been deleted. Z-Pentest reportedly published 2,500 lines of Danfoss code, although none of that material has been made publicly available. The groups say their goal is to expose poor cybersecurity practices.

articles.title: "Algo extraordinario": el canadiense que fue a la Luna lidera un proyecto urbanístico en Madrid con 12.000 viviendas de lujo
articles.text:
En el episodio de Los Simpsons ‘Marge contra el monorraíl’, un vendedor convence a Springfield de gastarse el dineral en un tren elevado que nadie pidió nunca. Springfield, al menos, llegó a inaugurarlo. Ahora un astronauta que rodeó la Luna en abril asesora un proyecto de 12.000 viviendas de lujo con laguna, paseo elevado y, sí, un monorraíl.
Y aunque el titular lo sitúa en Madrid, los datos lo fijan, de momento, solo en un render. Ya contamos cómo acaban los megaproyectos cuando el dinero no llega y por qué la vivienda amenaza con ser el motor de un nuevo 15-M. Ahí siguen en cola el auditorio del parque Juan Carlos I, el tren Móstoles-Navalcarnero y otras tantas inversiones. Lo de Moon es un diseño muy bonito, habrá que ver si tiene razón de ser.
Quién es. Jeremy Hansen tiene 50 años, fue piloto de caza y en abril viajó como especialista de la misión Artemis II, lo que lo convirtió en la primera persona no estadounidense en llegar hasta la Luna. En septiembre dejó el cuerpo de astronautas de la agencia espacial canadiense, tras 17 años, y pasó a la reserva de la Fuerza Aérea, después de 32.
Lo que nos importa es que hace un par de semanas, el primer ministro, Mark Carney, lo nombró asesor en materia espacial. Compagina ese cargo con el de consejero, miembro del consejo asesor y embajador de Moon World Resorts (estratega espacial, aseveran), al cual apoyan “a título personal”. Sí, cobra por ello.
Su papel. Hansen ayuda a desarrollar la simulación lunar. Admite que aún no sabe cómo funcionará, pero confía en que las soluciones aparecerán “al juntar a los expertos”. Sobre el turismo real a la Luna, no espera verlo pronto: habrá oportunidades para astronautas no gubernamentales, dice, pero no excursiones, por el riesgo de vivir en una nave.
Qué es Moon. Moon World Resorts es una empresa de Toronto que funciona como estudio de diseño y licenciador de propiedad intelectual. No construye nada, pero quiere licenciar hasta 10 proyectos en todo el mundo, cada uno a un único cliente (constructora o fondo soberano) con capital para pagar una obra entera.
Su presidenta, Sandra Matthews, lo compara con la cesión de J.K. Rowling a Universal, aunque insiste en que Moon “no es un parque temático”. La pieza central es una esfera de 312 metros de altura con una réplica de la superficie lunar y una colonia visitable. Un paseo de 90 minutos con traje espacial costaría unos 500 dólares. Los visitantes anuales dependen de a quién se pregunte: 2,5 millones según los fundadores a Gulf News, 10 millones según Matthews a ElPaís. Habría un hotel de 4.000 habitaciones y alrededor se extendería una “ciudad inteligente” de 500 acres (unas 200 hectáreas) con parque, oficinas, residencias de lujo de marca y el mencionado monorraíl.
12.000 viviendas. Las 24 torres suman sobre el papel 12.000 viviendas de lujo, junto a 23 edificios comerciales esféricos y un paseo panorámico. En febrero, los fundadores hablaban de 10.000. El plan descansa sobre capital privado y en la venta de las propias residencias. Es decír, las casas pagarían la atracción que tendrían frente a sus ventanas.
Matthews asegura que ha levantado “millones” de dólares, sin precisar cuántos, y busca más para cerrar el diseño en ocho meses. Después vendría la licencia y unos cinco años de obra. En su web figuran más de 50 empresas de 12 países como socios, de estudios de arquitectura a gimnasios. La lista no dice qué hay firmado.
Escala madrileña. Madrid ya cuenta con un desarrollo mucho mayor que cualquier Luna: Valdecarros, con 51.656 viviendas, el 55% protegidas, y capacidad para unos 150.000 habitantes. Ocupa casi 20 millones de metros cuadrados, unas 10 veces el suelo que pide Moon. Su primera fase, 13.371 viviendas, casi las mismas que promete la Luna, recibió luz verde en octubre y las obras arrancan en breve, a principios de 2027.
Sin suelo. Pero la diferencia clave está en el suelo, en la reparcelación y el calendario. La inversión total de Valcecarros ronda los 7.500 millones de euros. La de Moon se estima en 5.000 millones de dólares. Pero Moon no tiene terreno: sus promotores buscan ubicaciones cerca de grandes aeropuertos. Su programa de preproyecto intenta calcular costes. Henderson, el cofundador, ya explicó que hace falta un Gobierno dispuesto a ceder el suelo y “agilizar los permisos”. En febrero admitía que seguía sin socio de desarrollo y que a muchos promotores locales les interesa más la vivienda de rotación rápida que un activo turístico a largo plazo.
Matthews reconoce ahora que los movimientos en España son solo exploratorios y que no ha habido reuniones con el Gobierno central ni con los autonómicos. Además de Madrid, estudian Sevilla, Valencia y Barcelona. Sí hay equipo: la empresa eligió a la ingeniería Smith + Andersen para los sistemas del proyecto. En Madrid de momento solo hay una cita para la presentación a licenciatarios en primavera y una oficina de venta a inversores con maqueta y recorrido virtual.
Viejo conocido. La realidad es que Moon lleva más de 20 años de gira, si bien España figura entre los candidatos solo desde este febrero. Nació en el año 2000, ya con un diseño y un coste parecidos a los actuales. Después fue a Las Vegas (2002), las Bahamas (2004), el valle de Coachella (2016), Dubái (2022) y hace unos días Abu Dabi. Ahora toca Madrid. Ninguna encontró inversor. En 2022 se anunciaba en Las Vegas, con apertura en 2027, y se esperaba cerrar el primer licenciatario antes de acabar ese año.
Sin embargo, en febrero de 2026, los propios fundadores decían que el rumor de una apertura en Dubái en 2027 les hacía gracia. Su calendario realista pone el primer Moon hacia 2032. Los fundadores presumen de que el proyecto se hizo viral tres veces y admiten que los datos que circulan no siempre son correctos: “En este momento solo se aceptan visionarios”, remata Hansen.
Una pregunta para cerrar: ¿a Madrid le faltan viviendas de lujo? Que la misma semana en que la Policía desalojó la acampada en Sol por una legal protesta por la vivienda llegue este anuncio de 12.000 viviendas de lujo es, como mínimo, algo digno de mención.

articles.title: Les récentes RayNeo GT, qui affichent un écran de 231 pouces devant vos yeux, chutent sous les 200 € pendant le Black Friday chinois — Frandroid
articles.text:
RayNeo, la marque de lunettes connectées AR incubée par TCL, a annoncé en août dernier le lancement de plusieurs modèles. Outre l’iO, une paire de lunettes intelligentes dépourvue de caméra, le fabricant a dévoilé ses GT et GT Max, capables d’afficher un très grand écran virtuel devant les yeux. Pendant l’opération 11.11 d’AliExpress, ce sont les RayNeo GT qui nous intéressent davantage, puisqu’elles permettent de profiter d’un écran virtuel de 231 pouces et d’un suivi spatial 3DoF, le tout pour moins de 200 euros.
Les points essentiels des RayNeo GT
- Un écran virtuel de 231 pouces maximum
- Deux écrans Micro-OLED Full HD
- Un suivi spatial 3DoF
Initialement affichées à 231,42 euros, les lunettes connectées AR RayNeo GT sont aujourd’hui proposées à 191,42 euros sur AliExpress grâce au code promo 11FR40. Ce produit est certifié Marque+.
Un cinéma privé devant les yeux
Avec leurs 68 g sur la balance, les RayNeo GT restent relativement légères pour des lunettes de réalité augmentée. Elles sont évidemment plus lourdes que des binocles classiques, mais vous devriez vite vous y habituer. La marque a par ailleurs opté pour des plaquettes nasales interchangeables et des branches pensées pour le confort, afin de rendre les lunettes agréables à porter lors des sessions de jeu ou de visionnage de films.
Les GT embarquent par ailleurs deux écrans Micro-OLED de 0,6 pouce, offrant chacun une définition de 1 920 x 1 080 pixels. Le taux de rafraîchissement grimpe quant à lui à 120 Hz en 2D, mais se limite à 60 Hz en 3D. Surtout, les lunettes permettent de profiter d’un écran virtuel dont la diagonale peut monter jusqu’à 231 pouces, soit environ 5,87 mètres. D’autres tailles sont proposées, à savoir 136 et 201 pouces. Et le champ de vision atteint 46°. Sans surprise, les GT Max vont encore plus loin avec leur écran ajustable de 227 à 307 pouces et un champ de vision élargi à 59°. La luminosité des GT peut enfin grimper jusqu’à 1 200 nits, mais peut tomber à 336 nits en mode « écran épinglé », que l’on va justement expliquer ci-dessous.
Un écran virtuel stabilisé
Il faut savoir que les RayNeo GT se distinguent de simples lunettes qui affichent une image devant les yeux grâce à leur suivi spatial 3DoF natif, assuré par la puce Zone 360. Associé à la puce d’affichage Vision 4000, le système permet de stabiliser l’écran virtuel en fonction des mouvements de la tête. Trois modes sont disponibles : « épinglé », donc, qui maintient l’écran à une position fixe dans l’espace, « stable », qui stabilise l’image tout en laissant une certaine liberté de mouvement, et « suivi », avec lequel l’écran suit les mouvements de la tête pour qu’il reste centré dans le champ de vision.
Côté audio, les RayNeo GT intègrent un système signé Bang & Olufsen, avec quatre haut-parleurs et la prise en charge de l’audio spatial. Enfin, les lunettes sont compatibles avec une grande variété d’appareils. On peut par exemple les connecter en USB-C à des iPhone (à partir de l’iPhone 15, sauf les iPhone 16e, 17e et Air), à des smartphones Android, à des iPad (dès la 10e gen) ou encore à des PC portables, à condition que leur port USB-C prenne en charge la sortie vidéo DisplayPort. Toutefois, pour lier des consoles, comme la PS5 ou une Xbox, vous devrez passer par un adaptateur HDMI vers USB-C.
Deux autres choses à retenir : pour profiter du Dolby Vision, il faudra vous équiper de l’accessoire Pocket TV Pro de la marque, vendu séparément. De plus, les RayNeo ne sont pas autonomes : elles servent d’écran déporté, et ne permettent pas de lancer directement une application, par exemple.
