articles.title: Deepinder Goyal hits back at doctors, defends wearable device Temple
articles.text:
Deepinder Goyal hits back at doctors, defends wearable device Temple
In a post on X, Goyal said $30 million was invested in building the device, of which he put in $20 million of his personal money.
Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal has posted a series of updates and clarifications on X amid backlash from some Indian doctors who criticised his brain-monitoring wearable Temple. Describing Temple as “an ambitious project”, Goyal gave a detailed explanation on what the team is building.
“The team is delusional enough to think we can build this. And we will,” he wrote on Friday. He also later added that the first 10,000 orders will not have to pay a subscription to use Temple.
Criticising the doctors, he said, "All my emotion last night was directed at a few influencer doctors, who are more influencers than doctors. They did not read our research in detail, and spread twisted facts to call something new a scam. They get views by piling on us."
The open debate started on Thursday when Goyal took to X to defend the device. He said, “First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren't true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple.”
He also said the device features a 14-day no-question return policy. “If the product doesn't work, it fails out of the gate and the company dies before recovering a tenth of its R&D," he said.
Goyal is currently Vice Chairman and Non-Executive Director of Eternal (parent company of Zomato). He is also the founder of healthtech wearable startup Temple and LAT Aerospace.
In the post, Goyal highlighted that $30 million was invested in building the device, including $20 million of his personal money.
Calling this his purpose, he said it's not about the money. “I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck.”
Goyal argued that most wearable companies start with internal studies. He referred to Whoop which shipped its fitness band in 2015 but the first published validation happened a few years later. He also added that Temple had a higher standard. "Pre-prints are a step prior to peer reviewed publications, and they are coming up."
Reposing confidence in the product, he said, “We stand by our science and our methods. Each of our claims is easily verifiable by individuals and institutions alike, and you will see a lot of independent studies come up on their own when the device becomes available to use.”
Moreover, he added that this device is a fitness tracker, and wellness device, not a medical device. “If at some point, we clinically validate any of our metrics, we will let you know.”
However, some doctors were not convinced by Goyal’s response.
Responding to Goyal's claim on showing scientific evidence, an X user, who goes by the handle TheLiverdoc, said the Apple Watch Series 11 and Fitbit Sense had shown clinical evidence before launch. Similarly, Samsung Galaxy Watch8 and Watch9 also passed FDA trials prior to release.
"Meanwhile, the Oura Ring 4 and Whoop 4.0 launched as wellness trackers backed by peer-reviewed sleep studies."
On X, Dr Rishabh Jain responded saying Goyal shared financial and personal sacrifices but no scientific evidence. "Stop calling legitimate scientific scrutiny 'rage'. You have responded to questions about medical accuracy with investment figures, return policies, personal reputation, and promises of future studies. None of these constitutes scientific validation.”
Criticising the return policy he said, "Subjective satisfaction cannot establish medical accuracy.”
Dr Jain further said that doctors are not against innovation. However the evidence needs to show it. "If Temple delivers what it promises, doctors will be among its biggest supporters."
He also said that science is not a popularity contest, and criticism is not “rage".
Dr Jain also asked for data that can be reviewed by independent researchers.
Temple is a wearable device that tracks blood flow and oxygenation inside the brain. Goyal has not disclosed the price of the device.
In May this year, Goyal announced that the first 100 devices were ready to ship to select founding users and was aimed at athletes, scientists, doctors, founders, creators, and others who could provide feedback on the device. Pre-orders for Temple officially opened in India earlier this month.
In February this year, Temple raised $54 million in its first funding round from friends and family investors, at a valuation of about $190 million.
The copy was updated with additional information and quotes.

articles.title: Après Fiat, Opel veut aussi sa petite voiture électrique à moins de 15 000 euros
articles.text:
Le groupe Stellantis a fait une offensive importante au Mondial sous le signe du néo-rétro, notamment avec la 2CV chez Citroën. Si la 2CV a cristallisé toute l’attention, les autres marques du groupe Stellantis pourraient profiter de sa plateforme pour produire un véhicule électrique très abordable. Après Fiat, c’est Opel qui semble être intéressé par la plateforme e-Car.
Opel pourrait avoir sa citadine électrique abordable
Actuellement, la gamme Opel n’a que la vieillissante Corsa en citadine électrique. En revanche, l’Opel Frontera est plus récent et figure parmi les SUV électriques les plus abordables. Toutefois, il reste à plus de 20 000 euros, ce qui n’est pas à la portée de toutes les bourses.
Opel serait alors intéressé par l’utilisation de la plateforme e-Car introduite avec la 2CV pour proposer une citadine électrique abordable dans sa gamme, à moins de 15 000 euros. D’après les informations publiées par le média italien Quattroruote, Opel profiterait de cette plateforme pour faire renaître l’Agila. Une citadine du segment A disparue en 2015, avant d’être remplacée par la Karl jusqu’en 2019 et de voir Opel se retirer du segment A.
Un retour sur le segment A avantageux pour Opel
On dirait que Renault a réussi, avec la Twingo, à relancer une véritable course au segment A avec des motorisations électriques en Europe. Il y a déjà la Dacia Spring et la Nissan Pixo, qui s’appuient sur la base technique de la Twingo, mais c’est maintenant Stellantis qui prépare des voitures du segment A avec la Citroën 2CV, la Fiat Koala, la Leapmotor T03 et certainement l’Opel Agila. Volkswagen a confirmé préparer une citadine du segment A pour la fin 2027 découlant du concept ID.1. Il y a aussi la BYD Dolphin Surf, qui va bientôt être produite en Europe.
Ce segment, qui a failli disparaître, reprend peu à peu de la couleur. La motorisation électrique a remotivé les constructeurs, qui ont pu faire augmenter légèrement les prix de ces voitures au profit d’une meilleure rentabilité du segment A. Mais surtout, pour Stellantis, c’est la catégorie M1E que prépare l’Europe qui intéresse le groupe. Cette catégorie sera avantageuse dans le calcul du bilan CO2. Commercialiser ces petites citadines électriques profitera à toute la gamme, y compris aux voitures hybrides.
Aussi, multiplier les voitures utilisant la plateforme permet de réduire la répartition des coûts de développement et de vendre des voitures moins chères au client. C’est exactement la stratégie qu’adopte Volkswagen avec la plateforme MEB+ utilisée pour l’ID. Polo, l’ID. Cross, le Skoda Epiq et la Cupra Raval.

articles.title: Madrid busca el punto de "no retorno" con la A-5. Le costará 43 días de cierre en su conexión con la M-30
articles.text:
Objetivo: 23 de diciembre.
Esa es la fecha en la que el Ayuntamiento de Madrid quiere tener lista la conexión entre la A-5 y la M-30. Es la última fase de la primera fase de la gran obra que cambiará la fisionomía del suroeste madrileño. Es decir, es el último paso antes de que los coches empiecen a circular bajo tierra y se dé paso a la segunda gran fase de las obras que culminará con la construcción del segundo túnel.
Estas son las fechas y los datos.
43 días. Es el tiempo que estará cortada la entrada a la M-30 y su salida a la A-5 a partir del 10 de noviembre. La obra para soterrar la A-5 en su entrada a la ciudad entra en una fase decisiva porque una vez culminada el tráfico ya circulará bajo tierra. Antes, los operarios tienen que enfrentar uno de los mayores retos de la megaobra.
Está previsto que el corte dure hasta el 23 de diciembre. Hace unos días, el Ayuntamiento ya anunció que esta intervención tenía que llevarse a cabo pero no se puso fecha a la misma ni la duración prevista. Apenas dos semanas después, el corte es casi inmediato. El próximo lunes 10 de noviembre, ningún coche podrá enlazar la A-5 y la M-30 por los actuales túneles de entrada y salida.
"No retorno". Cuando se hizo el anuncio de que se tenía que dar este paso, desde el área de movilidad del Ayuntamiento de Madrid se definió como un punto de "no retorno". Esto es, una vez terminada esta intervención, los coches circularán ya bajo tierra.
Y es que la obra de la A-5 está dividida en dos grandes fases. Primero se ha excavado el túnel que, una vez terminada toda la obra, será el de sentido salida. Terminado este túnel y conectado con la M-30, el tráfico ya pasará a circular siempre bajo tierra. En ese momento comenzarán las obras para excavar el túnel sentido entrada. Una vez terminada esta intervención, el tráfico se regulará a uno u otro lado de la carretera y dejarán de estar enfrentados.
¿Qué se va a hacer? Una vez el túnel de salida se ha excavado hasta la zona cercana a los actuales túneles de la M-30 a la altura del Paseo de Extremadura, queda por igualar ambos espacios. Es decir, hay que derruir la rampa de salida para igualar ambos tramos y que el asfalto quede soterrado.
Esta intervención, según el Ayuntamiento de Madrid, requiere un número de intervenciones de tanta complejidad técnica que no se pueden realizar con el tráfico pasando por uno de los lados. Al mismo tiempo que se realiza esta intervención se va a terminar de rematar el túnel.
Explican desde el área de movilidad que "será necesario el gunitado de los hastiales -una técnica constructiva que consiste en proyectar hormigón a alta presión (gunitado) sobre las paredes laterales o frontales de una estructura (hastiales) para consolidarlas, impermeabilizarlas y reforzarlas-, terminar el drenaje del túnel, las aceras, los bordillos, las canalizaciones, los rellenos y las arquetas que recorren el nuevo tramo. Además, se cerrará el muro divisorio entre túneles de los 40 metros más próximos a Madrid". Igualmente, se instalarán las cámaras, los equipos de supervisión y de comunicación, así como los postes de emergencia o los sistemas contra incendios.
Los datos. En lo que son cifras puras y duras, la obra de demolición de la rampa se extenderá a lo largo de 172 metros. Se calcula que se extraerán 7.000 metros cúbicos de tierra. La cubierta de este tramo estará sustentada sobra 142 vigas prefabricadas de 30 metros de longitud, apoyadas únicamente en los hastiales laterales del túnel. 14 de ellas ya se colocaron durante el cierre de verano. Quedan por montar 128 nuevas vigas.
Además, en el resto del túnel se tendrán que colocar 470 luminarias, con toda sus conexiones y conducciones para el cableado. En las paredes hay que montar 1.400 metros cuadrados de paneles de revestimiento, así como de sellados contra incendios entre la estructura y los cerramientos. Antes de abrir al tráfico se tendrán que hacer las pruebas pertinentes para comprobar que todos los sistemas de comunicación y seguridad funcionan correctamente.
El plan alternativo. Cerrado el tráfico de entrada y salida, los coches que tengan que moverse por la zona lo harán únicamente sobre superficie. Es decir, el tráfico actual se desviará a los barrios aledaños. El Ayuntamiento de Madrid anuncia una "nueva ordenación viaria basada en cruces semaforizados en los entornos de Yébenes, Batán, Villagarcía y Huerta de Castañeda, incorporándose, además, nuevos itinerarios peatonales para garantizar la accesibilidad al entorno urbano y el transporte público".
En el transporte público, se esperan los siguientes refuerzos:
- EMT: las líneas 31, 36, 39, 138 y 158 se reforzarán en un 15,4% del 10 al 26 de noviembre los días laborables. Del 27 de noviembre al 23 de diciembre el refuerzo será del 25% todos los días. La línea 33 tendrá un refuerzo especial para rebajar los tiempos de paso.
- Metro: se mantiene una flota de trenes en reserva en para reforzar la línea 10 si se considera necesario.
- Cercanías: está pendiente la confirmación de si se añadirá algún tren a la línea C-5.
En el caso de que haya que utilizar el coche, se recomiendan los desvíos desde la M-40 si se circula en dirección norte y rodear la entrada a Madrid para hacerla por las carretera M-503 y M-500 por el oeste. Si se quiere acceder a la zona sur de la ciudad, se recomiendan los desvíos desde la M-40 para entrar por la A-42. Lo mismo se recomienda en sentido salida.

articles.title: The Terminal List : Prime Video officialise la suite de la série avec Chris Pratt
articles.text:
The Terminal List : Prime Video officialise la suite de la série avec Chris Pratt
L'univers de The Terminal List continue de s'étendre chez Amazon qui va adapter le troisième roman de la saga de Jack Carr, toujours avec Chris Pratt en tête d'affiche.
Chris Pratt n'en a pas terminé avec The Terminal List sur Prime Video. Nos confrères de Variety nous informe que l'acteur reprendra le rôle de l'ex Navy SEAL James Reece dans Savage Son, un projet dont l'intrigue est basée sur le troisième roman de Jack Carr dans la saga littéraire qui inspire la série The Terminal List.
Une saison 3 ou un spin-off ?
Pour le moment, on ne sait pas encore si cette adaptation de Savage Son sera la troisième saison de The Terminal List ou un nouveau spin-off de la série, même si des sources proches du projet indiquent qu'il s'agira probablement plutôt d'un nouveau show.
Présenté comme un thriller militaire rythmé, Savage Son suivra Reece (Pratt) alors qu'il fait face à sa mission la plus personnelle et dangereuse à ce jour.
Prime Video indique que la série proposera un mélange captivant "d’action, d’espionnage et de survie en milieu sauvage, explorant la frontière ténue entre la civilisation et les instincts sauvages qui surgissent lorsque la survie devient un enjeu personnel."
"L’œuvre de Jack Carr a su toucher le public, témoignant de la puissance de son récit ainsi que de l’incroyable dévouement dont font preuve Chris Pratt et toute l’équipe à chaque épisode," a déclaré Peter Friedlander, responsable de la télévision mondiale chez Amazon MGM Studios. "La franchise 'The Terminal List' continue de trouver un écho auprès du public, et 'Savage Son' propulse l’histoire dans son chapitre le plus intense à ce jour."
La série The Terminal List, basée sur les romans de Carr, est arrivée sur Prime Video en 2022, et sa saison 2 a débarqué sur le service de streaming le mois dernier. En 2025, les fans ont aussi pu découvrir un premier spin-off, The Terminal List: Dark Wolf, porté sur le personnage de Ben Edwards (Taylor Kitsch).
Savage Son sera une production d'Amazon MGM Studios, MRC et Civic Center Media, et arrivera donc prochainement sur Prime Video.

articles.title: Máximo, 26 años: "Me vuelvo a España después de vivir 3 años en Australia, he trabajado en sitios que nunca imaginé"
articles.text:
Cuando Máximo decidió marcharse a Australia con 23 años, pensaba que solo estaría allí unos meses, pero lo que iba a ser una estancia temporal se convirtió en casi tres años lejos de España. Durante ese tiempo, trabajó en lugares que nunca imaginó y conoció a personas que le acompañaron durante una aventura que, tras cumplir 26 años, dejará atrás al volver a casa reconociendo que regresa siendo alguien muy diferente.
El joven compartió su experiencia en su cuenta de TikTok (@maximobilbao). Allí explica cómo ha cambiado su vida durante este tiempo, y asegura que la persona que se fue con 23 años no es la misma que regresa con 26, pero por desgracia no todo han sido buenos momentos. Máximo también habla de las dificultades de vivir tan lejos de casa y de lo que ha supuesto tener que adaptarse a situaciones completamente nuevas. Según explica, la experiencia le enseñó tres conceptos fundamentales: confiar más en sí mismo, cometer errores y empezar de cero en más de una ocasión.
Volver a España después de tres años en Australia ha sido una decisión personal
Aunque muchas personas deciden emigrar para encontrar mejores oportunidades laborales, Máximo defiende que su regreso no responde a ninguna obligación: "No vuelvo porque tenga que volver, vuelvo porque quiero", tal y como explicó en su vídeo. Además, también reconoce que siente que ha llegado el momento de empezar otra etapa y este es uno de sus aprendizajes principales, ya que ahora ha descubierto qué quiere hacer con su vida tras casi un lustro fuera.
Su experiencia coincide con un momento de cambios para quienes buscan trabajar en Australia. En agosto de 2026, el Gobierno australiano suspendió temporalmente nuevas solicitudes del visado Work and Holiday para ciudadanos de varios países, entre ellos España. Sin embargo, las solicitudes para españoles vuelven a estar abiertas, según la información oficial de inmigración, y el programa mantiene un cupo anual de 3.400 primeras visas para España.
Máximo, por su parte, afronta su regreso con ganas de descubrir qué le espera ahora. Como recoge El Español en su publicación sobre el joven, considera que estos tres años le han ayudado a conocerse mejor y a decidir qué quiere hacer a partir de ahora. Para él, regresar a casa no significa dar un paso atrás, sino comenzar otra etapa con todo lo aprendido en Australia.
Foto | maximobilbao (TikTok)

articles.title: IMSI vs IMEI: What Your Phone Broadcasts and Who Can Read It
articles.text:
In April 2026, BleepingComputer reported that Canadian authorities arrested three men for operating an “SMS blaster,” a device that pretends to be a cell tower to send phishing texts to nearby phones.
It’s a close cousin of the IMSI catcher, the fake-tower device used for surveillance. Both work by tricking phones into connecting to the strongest signal and sharing information before anything is authenticated.
One of the main things a fake tower can collect this way is your IMSI, the identifier tied to your SIM, but it’s far from the only thing your phone gives away.
What information does your phone actually broadcast?
Your phone has several radios that connect to different kinds of signals and share different information.
The Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios share hardware addresses, which modern phones randomize or rotate to reduce tracking.
The cellular radio reveals two identifiers that typically never change: the IMSI, which is tied to your SIM card, and the IMEI, which is tied to your device.
IMSI vs IMEI
The IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity) is a unique number assigned by your mobile carrier when you sign up for your service. It lives on your SIM card, and is used by the network to look you up and authenticate you. For the most part, your IMSI never changes.
The IMEI (International Mobile Equipment Identity) is a unique number tied to your physical phone. Unlike the IMSI, the network doesn’t authenticate it, so it names a device without proving anything.
How well each is protected depends on the cellular generation in use. The standards come from 3GPP, the industry body that writes mobile network specifications. Newer generations protect identifiers better, but phones fall back to older ones, which is where fake towers come in.
| Network | IMSI | IMEI | 
| 2G/3G | Sent in plaintext (unencrypted) | Transmitted in plaintext and allowed to be sent without secured channel | 
| 4G (LTE) | Sent in plaintext the first time a phone connects, then replaced by a temporary ID (a GUTI) to reduce the exposure of the IMSI. | Sent only after mutual authentication | 
| 5G standalone | Encrypted (as a Subscription Concealed Identifier, or SUCI). | Sent only after mutual authentication | 
How your IMSI can be leaked
- IMSI catchers/fake base stations: In 4G, a phone will send its IMSI in plaintext to a tower that hasn’t proven who it is, which is what an IMSI catcher exploits. 5G’s SUCI encryption is meant to close that gap, but because 5G coverage isn’t universal, an IMSI catcher can still downgrade your device to 4G or below.
- Paging attacks: An idle phone saves battery by sleeping and waking only at set moments, called paging occasions, to check for incoming calls, texts, or notifications. In 4G, that slot is calculated from the IMSI with a publicly documented formula, so while the IMSI never changes, neither does the slot. (5G calculates it from a temporary ID instead.)
In a 2019 paper, researchers showed how to exploit this.
An attacker who knows your phone number can trigger “silent calls” (calls cut off before your phone rings), texts, or app notifications, and uses a nearby radio receiver to watch which slot sees activity.
After about eight tries on average, the pattern confirms you’re in that area, with no fake tower needed. It worked against all the US carriers tested.
This paging attack is a stepping stone to a more serious one: using a fake tower, an attacker can link your phone number directly to your IMSI. Some carriers, when normal pages to a phone’s temporary ID fail, fall back to broadcasting the raw IMSI in paging messages. Knowing your paging slot, an attacker can trigger that fallback.
A fake tower hijacks your paging channel to block the network’s pages, and a single silent call then makes the carrier send your IMSI over the air where the attacker captures it. The researchers validated this against one major US carrier.
Once an attacker has your IMSI, they can track your location or intercept your calls and texts through signaling attacks, which we covered in an earlier article.
What about the IMEI?
Think of an IMSI catcher as a license plate reader for phones: the IMSI is the plate, which follows your SIM, and the IMEI is the VIN, which stays with the device. In 4G and 5G, a basic fake tower gets the plate but not the VIN, because a phone sends its IMEI only after authenticating with the network.
An attacker generally has to downgrade the phone to an older network first, or use authentication data obtained earlier through SS7 or Diameter attacks, which themselves start with an IMSI. The IMSI rather than the IMEI is used to route a call or look up your location through signaling.
However, if your mobile carrier itself is compromised, whoever has access would be able to track you by your IMEI.
Protect yourself with private cell service.

Most carriers track everything: where you go, who you call, what you do. Cape collects the minimum amount of information required to provide you with service, deletes call and text metadata after 24 hours, rotates your network ID to prevent tracking, defends against SIM- and network-based attacks, and more.

Learn More
Why rotating the IMSI helps
Cape’s Identifier Rotation changes your IMSI every 24 hours, or on demand, cycling through seven IMSIs a week drawn from a shared pool that’s constantly reassigned among customers, so each IMSI carries a tangled history of many people’s activity.
Here’s what that does:
- Harvested IMSIs go stale. Signaling attacks start by harvesting a target’s IMSI, which on a typical carrier stays useful for years. A rotated one stops pointing at you within a day. An attacker can still ask for your current IMSI in real time, which is why rotation is layered on top of Cape’s signaling protections.
- The paging fingerprint moves. In 4G, a new IMSI means a new paging slot, so any pattern an attacker builds no longer matches.
- IMSI catchers lose the thread. A catcher can still grab today’s IMSI, but it can’t match it to yesterday’s, so it can’t build a history of you or confirm you’re nearby using an IMSI it learned earlier. Cape plus GrapheneOS adds LTE-only mode, which blocks downgrades.

articles.title: « C'est fini » : Adam Driver confirme qu'il ne rejouera plus jamais Kylo Ren dans Star Wars
articles.text:
Il l’a incarné trois fois, et il n’y en aura pas d’autre. Voilà, en somme, le bilan d’Adam Driver avec le personnage de Kylo Ren / Ben Solo dans Star Wars. Le 4 novembre 2026, l’intéressé était invité de l’émission américaine The Rich Eisen Show pour présenter Paper Tiger, le nouveau film de James Gray, en salles en France le 25 novembre. Et à cette occasion, Star Wars est revenu sur le tapis.
Il s’agissait de savoir si Adam Driver comptait reprendre encore le rôle de l’une des grandes figures de la troisième trilogie, qui s’est étalée de 2015 à 2019… ou s’il en avait fini pour de bon. L’acteur américain a répondu sans détour : « Oui, c’est fini… Plus de Star Wars ». Et à l’entendre, ce n’est pas faute d’avoir essayé de revenir une dernière fois.
Cette dernière fois aurait pu s’appeler The Hunt for Ben Solo.
Pendant deux ans, l’acteur a préparé ce projet de film avec le réalisateur Steven Soderbergh (Erin Brockovich, la saga Ocean’s, Solaris) et les scénaristes Scott Z. Burns et Rebecca Blunt, jusqu’à obtenir un scénario complet. « On a essayé d’en faire un de plus », a-t-il glissé, avant de résumer la réponse de Disney : « Non, il est mort. »
En clair, les vents contraires étaient bien trop forts pour lancer vraiment la production.
Un refus venu du sommet de Disney
Adam Driver avait révélé l’existence du projet en octobre 2025. Le film devait suivre Ben Solo, le vrai nom de Kylo Ren, et accessoirement le fils de Leia Organa et de Han Solo. L’aventure se serait située après L’Ascension de Skywalker, troisième volet de la postlogie sorti en 2019, où le personnage meurt. Chez Lucasfilm, Kathleen Kennedy, alors présidente du studio, et Dave Filoni avaient soutenu le scénario.
Mais c’est de plus haut que le holà est venu. Bob Iger, alors CEO de Disney, et Alan Bergman, coprésident de Disney Entertainment, ont dit non. Ils ne voyaient pas comment Ben Solo pouvait être encore en vie. Selon Steven Soderbergh, c’est la seule justification que l’équipe a reçue.
Sans doute aurait-il fallu accepter d’inventer une astuce narrative pour justifier sa survie — et peut-être figurait-elle dans le script de travail du film. Mais cela aurait eu pour effet, vraisemblablement, d’amoindrir la force de son sacrifice final.
Depuis, des fans ont fait voler un avion au-dessus des studios Disney et ont payé un panneau publicitaire à Times Square. Adam Driver trouve ça « assez incroyable », mais il n’y croit plus : « S’ils le voulaient, très bien, mais ce n’est pas à nous de décider. Je crois que le train est passé. »
Steven Soderbergh avait déjà annoncé en avril qu’il ne reviendrait pas sur le projet, même avec la nouvelle direction de Lucasfilm, confiée en janvier à Dave Filoni et Lynwen Brennan, et avec Josh D’Amaro, qui a succédé en mars à Bob Iger à la tête de Disney.

articles.title: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate
Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application. Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between. Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control. As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi-day engineering effort.
Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow. To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to address this problem for planning teams in NASC. The server acts as a centralized, agent-agnostic gateway between AI agents and our enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON metadata file that the server discovers automatically on the next pipeline sync.
In this post, we describe the architecture, show how a metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and explain how the serverless infrastructure supports multiple agents and applications in a multi-tenant environment.
Problem statement and design goals
Two interrelated challenges shaped how we designed this system: fragmented data access patterns and an unsustainable onboarding model.
Integration challenge at scale
Our data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain-specific data. Multiple teams wanted AI assistants that could query this data conversationally, but each built its own integration from scratch. Each agent embedded its own SQL generation logic, schema knowledge, and connection handling, so a schema change meant patching every agent individually. Access control was fragmented, with no single audit point for data access decisions. Onboarding a new dataset required custom tool code, query validation, and redeployment, typically a multi-day effort per table.
Design goals
We established four requirements:
- Configuration-driven data lake access. Adding a dataset requires only a metadata file, not code.
- Agent-agnostic tool interfaces. Any MCP-compatible client can invoke the same tools.
- Centralized permission enforcement. Access control is enforced at the MCP server layer.
- Elastic infrastructure. The system scales with bursty AI workload patterns.
Solution overview
The architecture separates concerns into four layers (client, MCP server, tools, and knowledge-base refresh), each independently scalable and deployable. A metadata catalog underpins the tools layer, storing schema descriptions, column-level semantics, and table relationships that the AI agent references when generating SQL. Because the agent derives schema knowledge from the catalog at query time, there is no need to hardcode table structures or redeploy when schemas change. The knowledge-base refresh layer keeps that catalog current, indexing new dataset metadata as it arrives. The following sections describe each layer in detail.
Architecture walkthrough
The following diagram shows the request flow from user query to data layer across all four layers. A user submits a query from a client application (web chat, Slack, an IDE plugin, or an external agent). The request resolves through Amazon Route 53 for DNS and reaches an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet, configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF. The load balancer routes to Amazon Cognito, which authenticates the user and enriches the request. Authenticated traffic then enters the private subnet, where the client layer runs on Amazon ECS Fargate. This layer handles session state in Amazon DynamoDB and forwards requests through an internal Application Load Balancer to the MCP server layer, also on Amazon ECS Fargate. In the MCP server layer, an AI agent powered by Amazon Bedrock orchestrates tools built with FastMCP (a Python framework for building MCP servers). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to every model interaction. On the right, the data layer holds the tool backends. Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift run SQL queries against the data lake, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handles semantic search. Data ingestion into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the knowledge bases is handled by AWS Lambda. Each layer is described in detail in the sections that follow.
MCP client layer: Authentication and session management
A request flows from the client application through Amazon Route 53 for DNS resolution to an Application Load Balancer configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF. The load balancer forwards traffic to the Amazon ECS Fargate client service, which integrates with Amazon Cognito for JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication and Amazon DynamoDB for session storage.
A context mapping configuration drives this enrichment, scoping each query to only the relevant tables. In our testing, this scoping keeps end-to-end interaction latency in the 15–20 second range. The following example shows a context mapping configuration:
When a context specifies tables, the MCP server narrows its search of the metadata catalog to those tables, reducing noise and improving SQL generation accuracy. Adding a new business domain requires only adding an entry to this mapping.
MCP server layer: Stateless execution with conversation state
The MCP server runs on its own ECS Fargate cluster, isolated from the client layer. Requests reach it through Amazon Route 53 and an internal Application Load Balancer in a private subnet. The server handles full orchestration including query analysis, tool selection, execution, and response generation. Through the MCP protocol endpoint (/mcp), a FastMCP-powered JSON-RPC interface, external MCP-compatible clients such as Amazon Q Developer or IDE extensions can discover and invoke tools directly.
Fargate tasks are stateless with conversation state persisted in DynamoDB, so tasks can be replaced or scaled without data loss. When a request arrives, the agent retrieves session history, analyzes user intent using Amazon Bedrock, discovers and invokes appropriate tools, and streams results back to the user.
Tools layer and metadata-driven data lake access
Each tool is registered with FastMCP and discoverable at runtime:
| Sr.no | Tool | Backend | Purpose | 
| 1 | SQL query tools | Amazon Athena Amazon Redshift | SQL queries against any configured dataset in the data lake and Redshift | 
| 2 | Document and metadata search | Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases | Semantic search over internal documentation, table metadata and team wikis | 
| 3 | Policy search | Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases | Search operational policies and standard procedures | 
The Athena query tools are the primary interface to the data lake. The agent first queries the metadata catalog to understand available schemas, generates an optimized SQL query through Amazon Bedrock, validates and auto-corrects the SQL for Athena compatibility, then executes it. Results flow back to the orchestrating agent for natural language synthesis.
Responsible AI controls
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to all LLM interactions and is designed to filter harmful content, enforce grounding checks, and help block prompt injection attempts. These guardrails operate as production controls at the MCP server layer, so every connected agent benefits from the same content safety policies regardless of how it connects. The Athena query tools enforce SELECT-only queries, rejecting write operations at the tool level before they reach the data lake.
Knowledge base refresh layer: Dataset onboarding with a single JSON file
The entire system is built around configuration-driven extensibility. Adding a new dataset requires a metadata JSON file describing the table and an optional context mapping entry. The file captures the table’s schema, business context, and column-level semantics. It serves as the single source of truth that the AI agent uses to understand and query the dataset:
The business_description_for_the_table field carries engine-specific query hints, such as “always use date() to wrap string literals,” that reduce SQL validation failures. The column_details field pairs each column_name [type] with a natural language description and sample values, giving the agent both schema awareness and business semantics. The sample_values field matters for accurate WHERE clause generation because the agent learns real data patterns, for instance that warehouse_id holds codes like FC-EAST-07 rather than spelled-out names like “East region facility.”
The pipeline picks up metadata files, generates vector embeddings with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and indexes them into Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Once indexed, the table is discoverable by all connected agents without manual re-indexing or server restarts.
To improve accuracy for specific applications, an engineer can optionally associate the dataset with a business context. This narrows the search scope, so the agent prioritizes the right tables. The following example shows a context mapping entry:
If no context is specified, the agent searches across all indexed tables. The context mapping reduces latency and improves SQL accuracy by limiting the search space. This scoping is optional and can be added at any time without modifying the metadata files themselves.
Putting it together: A query in action
When a user asks, “What were our top 10 highest-value orders last month?”, the client enriches the request with business context to narrow scope. The agent converts the question into a vector embedding, searches the metadata catalog for matching schemas, and selects the most relevant table via a lightweight LLM call.
Using the selected schema, column descriptions, and engine-specific query hints, the agent generates a SQL statement such as:
The SQL is validated and auto-corrected for engine compatibility, then executed against Amazon Athena. The agent formats the results into a natural language response and streams it back to the user. In our testing, this end-to-end flow completes within 15–20 seconds.
The same orchestration extends beyond pure SQL. Because document search is registered as another tool on the same server, the agent can answer questions that span structured and unstructured sources in a single turn, such as “What was our return rate for Q4, and what does the product team’s analysis say about the root causes?” For that request, the agent runs an Athena query for the return-rate figure and a Knowledge Bases document search for the analysis, then combines both into one response.
Security and multi-tenant access
That single-turn orchestration works only because every tool call passes through the same controlled gateway. The architecture uses layered security rather than a single enforcement point. The MCP server runs in private subnets behind an internal Application Load Balancer and is not reachable from the internet. Only the client layer, which sits behind a public-facing Application Load Balancer with AWS WAF, can route requests to it. Amazon Cognito validates user identity at the client layer, and only authenticated, token-bearing requests are forwarded downstream. At the tool level, the Athena query tools enforce SELECT-only queries, rejecting write operations before they reach the data lake. All tool invocations are logged to Amazon CloudWatch with structured JSON, which gives security teams a single audit point for data access across every agent and application. This architecture is available in the AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases are available.
This centralized design is also what makes the server multi-tenant. Because the standardized /mcp endpoint accepts any MCP-compatible client regardless of which LLM or orchestration framework it uses, multiple agents share the same tools and the same access controls. Adding a new agent requires only pointing it at the server endpoint, so onboarding another team extends the system without weakening or duplicating the security model.
Serverless infrastructure and scaling
Each layer scales through a mechanism suited to its workload pattern:
| Layer | Scaling mechanism | Trigger | 
| Client (ECS Fargate) | ECS Service Auto Scaling | CPU utilization (50% threshold) | 
| MCP Server (ECS Fargate) | ECS Service Auto Scaling | CPU/Memory utilization | 
| Athena | Serverless (automatic) | Query concurrency | 
| Amazon Bedrock | Managed service scaling | Inference requests | 
Amazon ECS Fargate provides serverless compute with no EC2 instances to manage. Downstream services (Athena, Bedrock) scale automatically, so the system handles a single query or hundreds of concurrent queries without configuration changes.
Use cases and extensions
This architecture supports several patterns beyond basic question-answering. Enterprise knowledge assistants can combine data lake queries with document search to answer complex questions spanning both structured data and unstructured knowledge, such as “What’s our return rate for Q4, and what does the product team’s analysis say about the root causes?” Internal analytics copilots let business users query the data lake conversationally without writing SQL, relying on the metadata descriptions and query hints to guide the agent toward accurate, performant query patterns.
The standardized /mcp endpoint also supports multi-agent workflows. Multiple specialized agents for data analysis, document retrieval, and operational alerting can share the same MCP server, each accessing the full tool suite through a common protocol. Onboarding a new team’s data follows the same configuration-driven pattern. They add a metadata JSON file, and within one pipeline sync cycle their dataset is discoverable by every connected agent and application.
Conclusion
A centralized MCP server on Amazon ECS Fargate provides a scalable, secure gateway between AI agents and enterprise data lakes. The metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and the Model Context Protocol standard means any MCP-compatible client can connect without custom adapters.
The key architectural decision is separating the tool layer from the agent layer. Agents evolve rapidly, but data access patterns should outlive any single agent implementation. Treating extensibility as a configuration problem rather than a code problem accelerates onboarding.
To learn more, see Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate, Amazon Bedrock, the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases user guide, Amazon Athena, and the Model Context Protocol specification.
Next steps
We are extending this architecture in two directions. First, finer-grained access control where table owners can mark sensitive columns as restricted per permission group, and the agent automatically excludes those columns from generated SQL without prompt-level changes.
Second, closing the feedback loop so that when queries fail or produce low-confidence results, the system captures the failure pattern and surfaces targeted suggestions for improving column descriptions, adding query hints.

articles.title: Opera passe la barre des 100 millions d'utilisateurs sur bureau
articles.text:
Opera revendique désormais 100 millions d’utilisateurs actifs par mois sur ordinateur, une première pour le navigateur. Selon Statcounter, Chrome et Edge restent pourtant très loin devant sur le desktop.
Opera indique dans un billet que ce cap a été atteint en octobre. Les utilisateurs d’ordinateur représentent désormais un peu plus d’un tiers de son audience totale, proche de 290 millions de personnes.
100 millions d'utilisateurs… et 2,16 % du marché
Opera propose plusieurs navigateurs pour convaincre les internautes de changer. Opera One sert de navigateur principal (productivité et personnalisation), Opera GX s’adresse aux joueurs, Opera Air au bien-être numérique et Opera Neon à la navigation « agentique », où l’IA est en mesure d’accomplir certaines tâches à la place de l’utilisateur. L’éditeur cible surtout l’Europe et l’Amérique du Nord, où beaucoup d’internautes gardent le navigateur installé par défaut sur leur appareil.
Plusieurs fonctions sont arrivées récemment, parmi lesquelles un VPN gratuit qui se connecte tout seul sur un réseau Wi-Fi public ou Paste Protect qui protège contre les attaques ClickFix. Récemment l’entreprise a levé le voile sur WebAI permettant de faire tourner des modèles d’IA en local dans le navigateur.
Sur iPhone et Android, la progression est portée en partie par l’écran de choix du navigateur que le DMA (le règlement européen sur les marchés numériques) impose à Apple. Nous rapportions en juillet qu’Opera One pour iOS avait d’ailleurs gagné 103 % d’utilisateurs actifs mensuels en France sur un an au deuxième trimestre 2026, contre 42 % pour l’ensemble de l’Europe.
Reste à situer ce chiffre sur le marché. Les 100 millions d’Opera sont un nombre d’utilisateurs, alors que Statcounter calcule des parts de marché à partir de plus de 3 milliards de pages vues par mois. Les deux ne se comparent donc pas directement. Sur les douze derniers mois (d’octobre 2025 à octobre 2026), Statcounter donne pour le desktop mondial : Chrome 73,15 %, Edge 10,65 %, Safari 5,78 %, Firefox 4,76 % et Opera 2,16 %. Pris isolément, juin 2026 donnait 1,81 % à Opera, soit un peu moins que sur l’ensemble de la période.

articles.title: The Download: a humanoid cleans house and Samsung builds for the AI boom
articles.text:
The Download: a humanoid cleans house and Samsung builds for the AI boom
Plus: Almost $2.5 trillion has been wiped off tech stocks.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
—Grace Huckins
When I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.
The device that arrived at my building belongs to Tau Robotics, a local startup. Its long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but the technology isn’t quite there yet. For now, humans pilot the robots remotely, watching them work through onboard cameras.
There were some unexpected challenges along the way, but also moments that felt like a glimpse of the future.
A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
Generative AI models depend on stacks of specialized memory chips. To meet soaring demand, Samsung is building a vast new semiconductor manufacturing campus in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.
I visited the sprawling campus south of Seoul, where three fabs already operate around the clock, a fourth is coming online, and thousands of workers are racing to build a fifth.
Step inside the vast chipmaking complex powering the AI boom.
—Michelle Kim
This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Almost $2.5 trillion has been wiped off tech stocks
The Nasdaq suffered its worst day since April 2025 amid fears of an AI slowdown. (CNN)
+ The Magnificent Seven lost over $1 trillion. (WSJ $)
+ Tesla and SpaceX lost over $420 billion combined. (CNBC)
+ Wall Street’s AI sell-off has spread to Asia and Europe. (WP $)
+ The AI stock bubble may finally be bursting. (FT $)
+ What even is the AI bubble? (MIT Technology Review)
2 Emboldened Democrats are lining up to rein in Big Tech
They’re preparing to haul tech CEOs before Congress. (Verge)
+ Bernie Sanders wants a national data center moratorium. (Quartz)
+ Yassamin Ansari plans to pause advanced AI development. (CNBC)
+ The backlash could delay Anthropic’s IPO. (Reuters $)
+ No one wants a data center in their backyard. (MIT Technology Review)
3 The US has warned of an “ongoing cyber threat” to fridges
A spate of hacks has hit commercial freezers. (Reuters $)
+ Russia has denied claims it’s behind the attacks. (Politico)
4 AI is helping Anthropic’s models improve nearly twice as fast
Researchers say Claude is speeding up its successors.(Information $)
+ But recursive self-improvement will take time. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Scientists have new evidence of active volcanoes on Mars
They may boost chances of finding life on the planet. (BBC)
6 Covid vaccines’ economic benefits may be double what we thought
New analysis places their value at up to $64 trillion. (New Scientist $)
7 The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is changing the ocean’s color 
The infamous debris has brightened the water. (Scientific American)
8 NASA has unveiled a mysterious new experimental aircraft
The X-70 is expected to take flight within two years. (Ars Technica)
9 Elon Musk has signaled the end for the Cybertruck
Tesla is winding down production in Texas next year. (FT $)
+ It was one of last year’s biggest tech flops. (MIT Technology Review)
10 Three-hour movies have sent viewers rushing to a pee break app
7,000 RunPee users signed up for You Can See Everything. (WSJ $)
Quote of the day
"The steamroller showed up today."
—Jim Carroll, a senior wealth adviser at Ballast Rock Private Wealth, tells Reuters how investors feel as the AI trade unravels and $2.5 trillion is wiped off tech stocks.
One more thing
How a couple of ski bums built the internet’s best weather app
The best snow-forecasting app for skiers isn’t a federally-funded service or a big-name brand. It’s OpenSnow, a startup that uses government data, its own AI models, and decades of alpine-life experience to deliver the best predictions out there.
The app proved especially vital last winter, one of the weirdest on record. It even made microcelebrities of its forecasters, who sift through reams of data to write “Daily Snow” reports for locations around the world.
—Rachel Levin
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ The US has a new national park: Arizona's otherworldly Chiricahua.
+ Fancy living in a flying saucer? A rare 1960s Futuro house is on the market.
+ Don't Cook That collects real recipes from old cookbooks that you should absolutely not make.
+ Backpack, who rode on his mum's back as a cub, has been crowned Fat Bear Week champion. 
Deep Dive
The Download
The Download: why AI’s latest breakthroughs and fears may be more hype than reality
Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.
The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication
Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.
The Download: weight-loss drugs slowing aging and carbon dioxide batteries
Plus: OpenAI has released 377 new math findings, further rattling the field.

Plus: Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers.
