articles.title: In Other News: Trezor Implant, LLMJacking Bills Hit $1M, SAP Flaws Weaponized Within Days
articles.text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.
This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.
Here are this week’s highlights:
Anthropic adds security center, admin controls to Claude Enterprise
Anthropic has rolled out additional security and administration capabilities for Claude Enterprise, including a security center (in beta) that checks an organization’s Claude configuration for chat, Cowork and Claude Code against settings Anthropic recommends. Inference hooks, now generally available, route prompts and tool calls to an organization’s existing data loss prevention and security tools for inspection, while a centralized console (also in beta) lets companies handle single sign-on, SCIM and other settings across all their Claude organizations from one place.
Fake OpenAI and SpaceX event invites phish Microsoft and Google accounts
Push Security has documented a phishing campaign built around fake registration pages for OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic events, which dangle rewards such as three months of ChatGPT Pro or Grok Heavy to get marketing employees to sign in with their work accounts. The Microsoft option launches a device code phishing flow run through the Kali365 phishing-as-a-service platform. Push links the operator, with medium-high confidence, to earlier fake Zoom event pages and says the campaign relies on Google and Zapier short links, Cloudflare challenges and domains swapped out every few weeks to avoid detection.
Chainalysis breach also exposed password hashes and tokens
Chainalysis has widened its breach disclosure, saying it discovered on November 2 that names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all its users had been exposed, after initially reporting that only non-sensitive data was accessed. The company has since taken several products offline, including its KYT transaction monitoring service after detecting abnormal activity, and is reaching out to customers whose KYT accounts show signs of unauthorized access.
Google hands Agent Substrate, gVisor to CNCF for sandboxing AI agents
Google is donating Agent Substrate, an open source orchestration layer on top of Kubernetes for running large numbers of isolated AI agent sessions, and gVisor, its open source application kernel, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) as Sandbox projects. When an agent goes idle, Agent Substrate saves its state to storage and can bring it back in under 500 milliseconds. gVisor handles system calls in user space so that untrusted, AI-generated code doesn’t interact directly with the host kernel. According to Google, placing both projects under the CNCF gives the community a shared, vendor-neutral base for agent infrastructure that can run on any Kubernetes cluster meeting conformance standards.
‘Hello’ messages hide Chinese-language attack framework targeting Flowise
Era researchers have detailed Greeter, a Chinese-language exploitation framework that bombarded Flowise honeypots with thousands of chat messages reading only “hello” while abusing an old code injection flaw (CVE-2024-58351) to execute commands. The framework mapped the host, queried cloud metadata services, searched for SSH keys and other credentials, tried to set up persistence, and tested whether it could run payloads from memory. Era counted 4,372 Flowise instances exposed online, and of those whose version it could identify, 703 lacked authentication and 46 appeared to share the vulnerable setup used in its honeypots.
LLM Mixers turn hijacked enterprise AI access into underground business
Mandiant says it investigated several LLMJacking cases this year in which attackers took over companies’ access to AI models, generating fraudulent bills of more than $100,000 in a day and as much as $1 million in total at some organizations. Initial access mainly came from stolen or exposed cloud credentials and API keys, and in one intrusion the attackers exploited a LiteLLM vulnerability (CVE-2026-40217) to upgrade ordinary keys to full admin credentials. Google Threat Intelligence Group also found hijacked access being sold through so-called LLM Mixers, including the Jet Night token routing service, which it believes uses stolen keys to offer unlimited plans with claimed frontier model access for around $60 a month.
CryptoBilis-sold Trezor allegedly fitted with seed-stealing implant
Trezor is telling customers who bought its hardware wallets from CryptoBilis since March 2026 to transfer their funds to a freshly created wallet with a new seed, after a buyer reported finding an implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 purchased from the former Southeast Asian reseller, which also sold Ledger devices that were found to have been tampered with. According to the report, which Trezor has not yet verified, an added circuit board fitted with a cellular module and antenna captures the recovery phrase displayed on screen and transmits it over a mobile network whenever the device is connected. No stolen funds have been reported.
Harvard alumni and donor data from 2025 breach added to HIBP
Have I Been Pwned has loaded roughly 851,000 unique email addresses from Harvard University’s November 2025 breach, an incident subsequently tied to a ShinyHunters extortion bid. The records come from Harvard’s alumni and fundraising systems and contain detailed profiles of donors, alumni and parents, as well as some faculty, staff and students, including names, contact details, birth dates and places, employers, ethnicities, marital statuses and donation histories.
SAP exploitation window shrinks to days as ransomware interest grows
Onapsis and Recorded Future report that for SAP vulnerabilities patched in 2025 and 2026, the median gap between a security note’s release and the first verified exploitation or public proof-of-concept was one to three days, down from 489 days for flaws patched in 2021. Ransomware and extortion groups showing up in SAP-related content grew from 8 in 2023 to 26 in 2025, and SAP CVEs with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation or public proof-of-concept code doubled from 9 to 18 between the end of 2023 and mid-2026. The study, drawing on over 1.2 million threat intelligence events, also tracked underground listings for SAP access priced from $500 to $30,000.
Synology flaw patched in 2024 now exploited in ransomware attacks
Synology warns that attackers are abusing a vulnerability fixed in December 2024 to hit devices still running outdated DSM releases, with the goal of encrypting data and extorting victims. The company has not identified the specific flaw beyond pointing to its Synology-SA-24:20 advisory. Synology recommends that anyone on a vulnerable release update DSM right away and turn on automatic updates.
Alleged Nomad Bridge exploiter appears in US court after extradition
Alexander Gurevich, a 49-year-old Israeli national now known as Alexander Block, appeared in a US court for the first time on October 30, a day after Israel extradited him to face charges that he exploited the Nomad Bridge smart contract in August 2022 to take virtual currency worth roughly $2.89 million. According to the indictment, he swapped the stolen WBTC and WETH for other cryptocurrencies and spread them across multiple addresses to obscure their origin. The money laundering charge alone carries a maximum of 20 years in prison.
Related: In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak

articles.title: Identity as an Architectural Concern: Enterprise IAM Beyond Authentication
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Decide how identity will shape your data model during the initial design. A security review at the end can catch a missing check or a bad scope, but it can't restructure a schema that was never built to explain who had access and when.
- Once your access questions are about ownership and validity, a graph fits better than a role table. In our role tables, "who owns this account" required a chain of joins. In Neo4j, it's one traversal.
- About eighty thousand people own our service accounts. Keeping those owners engaged through job changes and departures is most of the governance work, because an account whose owner has moved on is a credential nobody is watching.
- When revocation travels over an event stream, it's eventually consistent. Know your worst-case staleness, cap it with a maximum cache age, and tell your security team what it is.
- Merging attestation, rotation, and vaulting into one workflow cut time-to-revoke from about three days to under one.
After the Login
For a single application, identity is mostly a vendor decision. You pick an identity provider, wire up SSO, validate tokens at the edge, and move on with the features. For one application and one team, that's the right call. It stops being enough as the organization grows. Login keeps working fine. Everything after that gets difficult: who approved a given access and whether it should still exist when an auditor asks about it months later.
This article draws on building and operating an identity and access management platform in regulated financial services, where a wrong entitlement becomes an audit finding. My argument is that at enterprise scale, identity has to be treated as part of the architecture. Teams that add it late tend to find it conflicts with decisions they've already locked in. I'll assume you have experience shipping OAuth 2.0 or SSO. What follows covers the design problems that appear once many services, and many owners, are involved.
Identity as an Architectural Concern
Identity belongs in architecture discussions because it constrains decisions that look unrelated. The data model is where this shows up first. Once you have to explain and audit access, "who can touch this resource" needs to be a relationship you can query with history, because auditors ask what was true six months ago as well as what is true today. Service boundaries and event flows raise their own problems; each gets its own section below.
Regulation adds another constraint. Here's a useful test: Could you answer "Who had access to this system on 14 March?" from your data model alone, without grepping logs across several tools? If not, an audit wasn't part of the design.
A security review can catch a missing check or a misconfigured scope, but it can't retrofit a schema that was never built to answer that question. The cheapest way to pass that test is to record every grant, revocation, and attestation as an event with a timestamp and an actor from the start. Then the auditor's question is one query against the event log.
Where Flat RBAC Breaks Down
The Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) model is used by default and is usually sufficient. It strains when your questions shift from "Does this user have this role?" to how things relate to each other. Our entities are people, the service accounts they own, and the accesses those accounts hold. The questions we kept asking were: "Who owns this account?", "Is this access still valid?", and "What does this person control?"
All three are relationship questions. Ownership is a relationship. An access has a validity window and an attestation history attached to it. A person who leaves or changes roles pulls a set of owned accounts along behind them. In a role table, you rebuild each of those links with joins every time you ask. In a graph, each link is an edge and the query walks them.
That's why our backend models these relationships in Neo4j, queried through GraphQL. GraphQL fits because a query's nesting mirrors the traversal: this account, then its owner, and then its access. A caller asks for exactly the slice of the graph it needs, from an account down to its valid accesses. Nobody handwrites traversal logic or over-fetches a large object and filters it in memory. Figure 1 shows the shape of the underlying model.
Figure 1. Ownership-and-access graph modeled in Neo4j, showing how flat RBAC breaks down when access needs expiration and nuance. (Image source: created by the author.)
Before the query, here is the model it runs against. There are three kinds of nodes: Person, ServiceAccount, and Resource. There are two associations between them. First, a person OWNS a service account, while second, a service account HAS_ACCESS to a resource. The association, HAS_ACCESS, possesses some properties such as expiration, the date for when the access will be no longer valid, and lastAttested, which displays the last date when the access was attested by the owner. Validity is an attribute of the edge rather than of any node since it refers to the particular combination of the account and resource nodes.
This query, as shown below, poses a question we frequently ask ourselves: Who is the owner of this account and which of its accesses are currently valid? Looking through the query from the top, the first MATCH gets the account based on its ID and follows the OWNS relationship until it reaches the owner. The next OPTIONAL MATCH follows the HAS_ACCESS relationship towards each of the resources, and the WHERE clause appended to it filters out any access where the expiry date has expired. Because it is an OPTIONAL MATCH, an account having no accesses left will yield its owner anyway. Finally, the RETURN clause yields the owner’s name along with all the accesses left with their resources, expiry dates, and last attested date in a single array.
Neo4J Cypher Query
// Who owns this account, and which of its accesses are still valid today?
MATCH (p:Person)-[:OWNS]->(a:ServiceAccount {id: $accountId})
OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[g:HAS_ACCESS]->(r:Resource)
WHERE g.expires >= date()
RETURN p.name        AS owner,
       collect({
         resource: r.name,
         expires:  g.expires,
         lastAttested: g.lastAttested
       })              AS validAccesses
Written as SQL against role tables, the same question needs every link lined up by hand:
-- Who owns this account, and which accesses are still valid today?
SELECT owner.name, res.name, g.expires, g.last_attested
FROM service_account acct
JOIN account_owner ao   ON ao.account_id = acct.id
JOIN person owner       ON owner.id = ao.person_id
LEFT JOIN account_grant g
       ON g.account_id = acct.id
      AND g.expires >= CURRENT_DATE
LEFT JOIN resource res  ON res.id = g.resource_id
WHERE acct.id = :accountId;
Even here, it's easy to get it wrong. Put the expiry check in the WHERE clause instead of the join, and accounts with no valid grants vanish from the result, owner and all. The query works, but it still leaves three problems out of view. Ownership is a single join in this example, but ownership can be delegated, and once it can, that join becomes a walk up a chain of unknown length. In the graph, the same chain is a variable-length path in one pattern. The expiry check also has to be repeated in every query that touches grants. Any query that leaves it out returns access that should have been removed. In the graph, the check sits inside the traversal, so a consumer can't skip it by accident. Finally, when a person leaves, the accounts they own aren't in front of you, and you have to go looking for them. In the graph they're one hop away, because "owns" is an edge. Both queries are simplified from what we run in production.
But Neo4j has inherent costs. It's one more datastore to operate, and traversal performance depends heavily on how you model things. A badly shaped graph can be slower than the join it replaced. It was still worth it for us, because ownership and validity are things we traverse constantly. The flat version pushes the hard part onto whoever writes the next query.
Service Accounts: Eighty Thousand Owners, Three Tools
Comparing everything in the platform, the service accounts took the most governance work. Every service account is owned by a real person: Roughly eighty thousand people review, rotate, and vault the accounts they own. An account’s safety depends mostly on that owner: whether they're still engaged and whether they've changed teams or left the company. An account whose owner has moved on is exactly the stale, over-privileged credential that nobody notices until it's misused.
Before the rebuild, the three things an owner had to do (attestation, rotation, and vaulting) lived in three separate tools. An owner had to remember which tool did what. That's a small annoyance for someone who does it daily. For someone who does it twice a year, or who inherited an account when a colleague left, it's a real failure mode.
The rebuild put all three owner requirements into a single workflow, so an owner sees one screen with what they own and what's due. Getting there took more than wiring screens together. Each tool had been built with its own assumptions about schedules and ownership, and once they shared a workflow, those assumptions had to be reconciled. Figure 2 shows the revocation workflow before and after the consolidation: Three separate tools, with revocation taking about three days, became one unified workflow that revokes in under a day.
Figure 2. Revocation workflow before and after tool consolidation. (Image source: created by author.)
Integrating a Vault We Didn't Own
In enterprise identity work, the risky integrations are usually the ones where your system depends on a system you don't govern. For us, that was vaulting. We already handled attestation and rotation well before the rebuild. We had written that code ourselves, so we knew how it failed. Vaulting ran in a separate tool, owned by another team, on infrastructure we couldn't change. Folding it into our workflow meant a critical control now depended on their release schedule and their outages.
The hard part was deciding what our workflow should believe when their API didn't answer, or answered slowly, or answered after our call had already timed out. Those are not edge cases when you're doing this for tens of thousands of owners. They happen every day, somewhere. So we made the integration "fail closed". If the vault was unreachable, the workflow didn't report the step as complete, and an owner was never told a credential was vaulted when it wasn't. That sounds obvious on paper. In practice it meant our side couldn't treat "we sent the request" as success. We had to confirm the vault's own state, reconcile it against ours, and treat any gap between the two as something our side resolves.
Propagating Identity Across Service Boundaries
If every service makes its own access decisions, authorization logic ends up scattered across dozens of codebases, where nobody can audit it. When a rule changes, you hunt for it through every service that has implemented its own version, and you can miss one. What works is letting identity context travel across boundaries while the decision stays in a dedicated policy decision point. Identity propagates through scoped claims using OAuth 2.0 token exchange, so a service acting for a caller gets a narrowed token instead of reusing a broad one.
The controller asks, and the policy decision point decides as shown in the following code snippet:
Java Code
// Authorization delegated to a policy layer, not hard-coded in controllers.
// Illustrative Spring Security style; exact API varies by version.
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http, PolicyDecisionPoint pdp) throws Exception {
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .anyRequest().access((authentication, context) -> {
            AccessRequest req = AccessRequest.from(authentication.get(), context.getRequest());
            return new AuthorizationDecision(pdp.permits(req));
        })
    );
return http.build();
}
The controller never sees the rules, so changing a rule requires changing the PDP and nothing else.
Across a service hop, the incoming token is exchanged for a scoped one before the downstream call:
Java Code
// Narrow the caller's token to just what the downstream call needs,
// via OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693). Illustrative.
TokenExchangeRequest exchange = TokenExchangeRequest.builder()
    .subjectToken(incomingAccessToken)
    .audience("downstream-service")
    .scope("accounts:read")           // scoped down, not the caller's full grant
    .build();
String downstreamToken = tokenExchangeClient.exchange(exchange).accessToken();
The token for each hop records its audience and scope, so the audit log shows what every call was for.
Revocation Over Kafka
Entitlement changes propagate as events using Kafka. A grant, a revocation, or a change of ownership becomes a message that interested services consume. That's a sensible design for a distributed system and it indicates revocation is eventually consistent. Access stops once consumers process the event and invalidate any cached decisions, which happens some time after the revocation is recorded. That gap should be measured and capped before anyone describes revocation to a security stakeholder.
A consumer handling a revocation invalidates the cached decision, so the next check re-resolves from the source of truth:
Java Code
// Kafka consumer: an entitlement revocation invalidates the cached decision.
// Illustrative; run against your own broker and cache.
@KafkaListener(topics = "entitlement-events", groupId = "authz-cache")
public void onEntitlementEvent(EntitlementEvent event) {
    if (event.type() == REVOKED) {
        decisionCache.invalidate(event.accountId(), event.resourceId());
        auditLog.record(event);   // the revocation is itself an audited fact
    }
}
Events can be lost, so the cache also has a time limit. A cached decision is served only while it's younger than a maximum age. After that, it's re-resolved from the source of truth whether or not an event arrived. That maximum age is the worst case scenario for a dropped event. Before we relied on the design, I simulated the consumer and cache to confirm that a missed event never kept access live past it.
Choosing the maximum age involves a real trade-off. A short maximum age causes stale access to expire quickly, which is what security wants, but every expiry sends another check back to the source of truth. At our volume that load isn't free. A long maximum age is easy on the system and worse for revocation, because a dropped event has longer to matter. You pick a number you can live with on both sides, then state it plainly: A lost event leaves access live for at most that long. That's a sentence a security team can plan around.
The cache window was the small part, though. The larger delay was procedural. Before the rebuild, fully revoking access took around three days, most of the time being spent on steps a person had to complete in separate tools. With a single workflow, access revocation takes under a day.
When This Is Overkill
For a single app with a few roles and one team, you can skip all of this. Flat RBAC in your primary database is the right choice, and Neo4j, Kafka, and a policy layer would be over-engineering you'll regret maintaining. The threshold is organizational: many services making access decisions, service accounts that outnumber and outlive the people minding them, ownership that has to be re-verified, and an audit obligation with teeth. Here's how I would weigh each piece:
| Component | Worth It When | Skip It When | 
| Graph database | You traverse ownership and validity constantly | Whether a user holds a role is all you need to ask | 
| Event stream for entitlements | Access changes must reach many services, and you can state the staleness bound | A handful of services read access from one database | 
| Central policy layer | Authorization logic would otherwise spread across many codebases | One app owns all of its own rules | 
What's Next
Authorization is moving out of individual services and into policy engines that can be tested on their own. For service accounts, the zero-trust version of this is continuous verification: an account re-proves its entitlements on a schedule instead of keeping them by default. Our service account rebuild was a manual version of the same idea, because attestation is reverification with a human in the loop. The interesting question is how much of that human step can be made automatic without losing the accountability that a named owner provides.

articles.title: Anthropic no ha puesto freno a la IA y ahora sus modelos avanzan al doble de velocidad que antes, revela estudio
articles.text:
Los modelos de IA de Anthropic mejoran casi al doble de velocidad que antes, y la mayor parte de esa aceleración probablemente se debe al uso de IA en su propio desarrollo. Lo concluyó METR, una organización sin fines de lucro que revisó datos internos de la empresa y publicó su informe el 5 de noviembre.
METR, cuyas siglas en inglés significan Evaluación de Modelos y Amenazas, trabajó en Anthropic desde el 12 de agosto hasta el 29 de octubre. Según su informe, la empresa le dio acceso a datos sobre el entrenamiento, el cómputo, los resultados de modelos todavía no publicados y entrevistas con su personal.
La conclusión central es que, a octubre de 2026, Anthropic mejora las capacidades de sus modelos en tareas bien definidas a un ritmo cercano al doble del que tuvo entre marzo de 2024 y octubre de 2025. METR advierte que la estimación es muy incierta y que la cifra real podría estar entre 1,3 y 3 veces.
Con el índice de pruebas comparativas que usa la propia Anthropic, la aceleración desde octubre de 2025 fue de 1,9 veces, con un intervalo de confianza del 95% de entre 1,5 y 2,8 veces. En la práctica, la empresa avanzó en un año lo que antes le llevaba dos.
Más IA en el desarrollo, no más cómputo
METR afirma estar seguro de que la aceleración no se debe a un mayor crecimiento del cómputo, es decir, de la capacidad de procesamiento usada para entrenar los modelos. Su estimación es que alrededor del 80% de la aceleración actual proviene del uso de IA, aunque aclara que ese número tiene mucha incertidumbre.
Los investigadores de Anthropic usan sus propios modelos sobre todo como asistentes, no como reemplazo. METR indicó que le dijeron que la I+D avanza principalmente con ayuda de IA y no con contribuciones totalmente autónomas, aunque hay señales de que estas últimas tendrán un papel mayor pronto.
Las encuestas internas pintan un cuadro más extremo. En votaciones informales en Slack, los empleados estimaron que el último modelo les permitía trabajar hasta 12 veces más rápido en octubre. METR consideró esas respuestas como evidencia muy débil: se dieron con poco esfuerzo y la mejora individual no equivale a una aceleración de toda la empresa.
La tarjeta técnica del modelo Haiku 5.5 había informado una aceleración de 1,7 veces. METR explicó que su cifra es mayor porque incluyó datos de modelos nuevos que aún no se lanzaron.
Anthropic ocultó la mayoría de las pruebas clave
El informe incluye una salvedad de peso: Anthropic tenía derecho a censurar información no pública, y METR dice que eliminó la mayoría de la evidencia que consideraba más útil para sus conclusiones. La empresa justificó los cambios como una forma de quitar datos confidenciales que podrían acelerar a otros desarrolladores de IA.
Por eso, el público debe confiar en el criterio de METR más de lo ideal. La organización reconoce que el informe no logra transparencia sobre la evidencia, y que sus propios investigadores y los de Anthropic tienen dudas sobre cómo interpretar esos datos.
Anthropic invitó a METR a revisar sus datos mientras se prepara para su debut en Wall Street, en medio del debate sobre el riesgo de que los modelos escapen al control humano, según informó la agencia AP. La conclusión llega después de que el director ejecutivo de la empresa pidiera frenar el ritmo de la tecnología.
METR también señala límites de su propio cálculo: el índice mide tareas fáciles de verificar y podría exagerar la mejora real, y el ritmo de crecimiento de 2023 a 2025 pudo ser inusualmente bajo. Pero también podría subestimarla si la automatización de más tareas de investigación acelera todavía más el progreso.
Sobre el futuro, METR afirma que no vio evidencia de frenos importantes —ni en algoritmos, ni en cómputo, ni en datos— que impidan seguir avanzando en los próximos 12 meses. Aclara que su comprensión de esos posibles obstáculos cambió varias veces durante la evaluación y que no tiene confianza en esa conclusión.

articles.title: Google, Meta, and TikTok sue California over law banning addictive social media features for children
articles.text:
What just happened? Google, Meta, and TikTok are taking California to court over its latest attempt to keep children from getting hooked on social media. The companies have filed separate lawsuits challenging a law that restricts addictive features for children under-16, arguing that the state is interfering with free speech and parents' authority.
The complaints, filed Wednesday, target Assembly Bill 1709. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the measure on September 10 as part of a broader package covering social media and AI chatbot safety. It's scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027.
The restrictions cover personalized feeds, endless scrolling, and autoplay videos, all defined as "psychologically exploitative features." Platforms must also take reasonable steps to verify users' ages. The aim is to stop companies from pushing features designed to keep children scrolling long after they intended to put their phones down, which sounds like a good thing.
According to Reuters, the companies argue that California is dictating how they present content and replacing parents' judgment with its own. Their challenges invoke the First Amendment and the often-used Section 230, which broadly protects platforms from liability for user-generated content.
Meta says the state cannot override its editorial decisions about organizing and displaying posts. Google argues that the restrictions could undermine systems that help children find appropriate videos, while TikTok says they interfere with free expression and parental choice.
Google also says parents are the ones who should decide what is appropriate for their families, pointing to its existing parental controls and protections.
"Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we've built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos," Google spokesman José Castañeda said.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office told The Guardian it was reviewing the lawsuits and would defend the state's child-protection laws.
It's not just the social media giants expressing opposition to the law. The Electronic Frontier Foundation warns that age checks could push everyone to hand over more personal information. It also argues that removing recommendation tools could effectively shut young people out of online communities.
The fight follows Meta's August agreement to pay up to $18 billion and change how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram to settle states' child-safety claims. Those changes include default time limits and mandatory scrolling breaks.
Much of the world is now introducing restrictions or bans on social media use for young people. In Australia, which was the first country to introduce such a law, Reddit challenged its under-16 ban in the High Court, arguing that it restricts political communication and that the platform isn't actually a social media site.

articles.title: Pix pode chegar à Europa após novo avanço nas negociações
articles.text:
O Pix está mais perto de ganhar conexão com o sistema europeu de pagamentos instantâneos. O projeto de integração com o TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS), infraestrutura do Banco Central Europeu (BCE), avançou da fase de pré-investigação para a etapa de investigação. A mudança indica que os primeiros estudos não encontraram obstáculos críticos para a continuidade da iniciativa.
A informação consta em documento apresentado durante uma reunião do TIPS Consultative Group, grupo ligado ao BCE que discute melhorias e testes na plataforma. O encontro ocorreu em 20 de outubro.
Segundo o Banco Central Europeu, a etapa de pré-investigação, realizada em setembro, avaliou aspectos técnicos, jurídicos e operacionais, além da viabilidade comercial de uma eventual conexão entre os sistemas. Não foram identificados impedimentos considerados críticos.
A nova fase vai aprofundar os estudos para determinar se a interligação é técnica e economicamente viável. Ainda não existe prazo definido para sua conclusão.
Conforme informações da Broadcast, a expectativa de fontes próximas às negociações é que o projeto-piloto completo esteja preparado até o fim de 2027.
Na mesma semana em que o documento foi apresentado, o diretor de Regulação e Organização do Sistema Financeiro do Banco Central brasileiro, Gilneu Vivan, viajou a Frankfurt (Alemanha) para discutir a possível integração com representantes do BCE.
Como o Pix poderia funcionar na Europa?
- Uma eventual conexão entre as plataformas permitiria que brasileiros utilizassem suas contas bancárias no país para realizar pagamentos em estabelecimentos europeus;
- Um dos modelos considerados prevê o uso de QR Codes. Nesse cenário, um consumidor poderia abrir o aplicativo de sua instituição financeira brasileira, escanear um código disponibilizado por uma loja na Europa e autorizar o pagamento em reais;
- O sistema faria a conversão cambial e permitiria que o estabelecimento recebesse o valor em euros. A operação poderia ocorrer em poucos segundos, sem que o consumidor precisasse recorrer diretamente a um cartão internacional ou a uma transferência bancária tradicional.
A possibilidade foi explicada à Folha de S.Paulo por Thiago Cavalcanti, presidente da Associação Nacional dos Auditores do Banco Central do Brasil (ANBCB). Ele ressalta que a operação provavelmente envolveria custos, que precisariam ser apresentados de maneira transparente ao consumidor. A taxa de conversão da moeda também seria um fator importante para tornar o serviço competitivo.
O projeto não se limita a compras em lojas. Segundo o Banco Central brasileiro, a conexão entre infraestruturas de pagamentos instantâneos também poderá facilitar remessas internacionais, com recursos disponibilizados na moeda local em poucos segundos.
Leia mais:
- Existem mais de um bilhão de chaves Pix no Brasil: ‘maior caso de sucesso’
- Grupo brasileiro invade sistema bancário em ataque ligado ao Pix
- Em tempos de Master e Ueno, o Brasil tem o Pix
O que é o sistema europeu TIPS?
O TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS) é uma infraestrutura do Eurosistema criada para processar pagamentos instantâneos. Na prática, desempenha função semelhante à do Pix no Brasil.
A plataforma permite que instituições financeiras participantes ofereçam transferências em tempo real, 24 horas por dia, durante todos os dias do ano. Os pagamentos têm liquidação final e irrevogável diretamente em moeda de banco central.
Atualmente, o TIPS opera com euros, coroas suecas e coroas dinamarquesas. O sistema também já permite operações entre essas moedas, possibilitando, por exemplo, que um consumidor sueco pague por uma compra em um país da zona do euro utilizando sua moeda local. Esse mecanismo de conversão entre moedas está disponível desde outubro de 2025.
A possível integração com o Pix faz parte de estratégia mais ampla do BCE para conectar sua infraestrutura a sistemas de pagamentos instantâneos de outras regiões. Entre as iniciativas também estão projetos de interligação com a Índia e a Suíça, além da participação na rede internacional Nexus.
Quando a integração poderá ficar pronta?
Apesar do avanço nas negociações, ainda existem etapas importantes antes de uma eventual implementação.
Segundo informações obtidas pela Folha em setembro, nove áreas do Banco Central brasileiro foram mobilizadas para estabelecer diretrizes de governança e avaliar a compatibilidade entre as plataformas.
Os estudos também precisam considerar os custos de implementação, a sustentabilidade do modelo operacional, os volumes potenciais de transações, a demanda esperada e os impactos sobre o mercado de pagamentos.
Naquele momento, a previsão preliminar dos técnicos era que o corredor de integração pudesse ficar tecnicamente operacional em novembro de 2027, com um projeto-piloto em junho de 2028. Esses prazos, entretanto, dependem das avaliações e de futuras aprovações dos dois bancos centrais.
A conexão também representaria novo passo na internacionalização do Pix. Atualmente, existem iniciativas que permitem transações internacionais envolvendo o sistema brasileiro por meio de acordos entre instituições financeiras de diferentes países, incluindo Argentina, Estados Unidos e Portugal.
A proposta com o TIPS, porém, busca estabelecer conexão entre as próprias infraestruturas de pagamentos, ampliando as possibilidades de operações internacionais.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: TSMC podría comenzar a fabricar RAM, pero no te ilusiones con que baje de precio
articles.text:
Con una crisis de memoria RAM que aún no habría mostrado su peor cara, la industria de los semiconductores busca alternativas para tratar de cubrir la brutal demanda impulsada por la inteligencia artificial. En este contexto, TSMC, el principal fabricante de chips del mundo, podría comenzar a fabricar módulos DRAM.
Según reporta The Information, TSMC analiza ingresar a la producción en masa de memoria 3D RAM por pedido de NVIDIA, su cliente más importante. Todavía no se sabe si la firma taiwanesa realmente dará el paso hacia el citado segmento, pero el solo hecho de que lo estudie es una señal interesante de cara al futuro.
En la actualidad, los principales proveedores de memoria RAM avanzada para servidores de inteligencia artificial son Samsung, SK Hynix y Micron. La demanda de sus clientes es tan grande que las tres están al límite de sus capacidades. Recientemente, Samsung informó que ya tiene vendida toda su producción de memoria de alto ancho de banda para 2027. Micron, en tanto, abandonó la fabricación de memoria para consumidores y se enfocó en el segmento dedicado a los servidores de IA generativa.
Así las cosas, TSMC podría ingresar en el mercado de la RAM para convertirse en otro proveedor de gran escala para las principales tecnológicas del mundo. Hsu Kuo-chin, vicepresidente de empaquetado avanzado de la compañía taiwanesa, estaría liderando esta iniciativa. No obstante, aún se desconoce si realmente se concretará.
TSMC analiza comenzar a fabricar memoria RAM avanzada
Al parecer, las opciones que baraja TSMC en el presunto plan de expandirse al campo de la memoria RAM avanzada son dos. Por un lado, montar sus propias fábricas dedicadas a la producción de este tipo de componentes para NVIDIA y otros de sus clientes más importantes. Por el otro, comprar alguna planta de semiconductores ya existente y adaptarla a la fabricación de 3D RAM.
Es posible que la primera opción sea mucho más lenta y costosa que la segunda, aunque por cómo viene la cosa la crisis de la RAM no se acabará de la noche a la mañana. Samsung espera que la escasez se agrave en 2027 debido a los altísimos niveles de demanda para centros de datos de inteligencia artificial. La empresa coreana incluso vaticina que las consecuencias de la situación actual se extiendan al menos hasta 2028.
Eso sí, si TSMC realmente comienza a producir memoria, no esperes una bajada de precios en la RAM para consumo general. NVIDIA le habría pedido a los taiwaneses que comiencen a fabricar módulos 3D RAM, que tienen celdas de memoria que se apilan en vertical y que se usan principalmente en servidores, superordenadores y centros de datos de IA. Así que esta estrategia no va a cambiar el panorama complejo que hoy afrontan los consumidores.

articles.title: Überraschende Erkenntnis: Das verrät 3I/Atlas über Wassereis in anderen Galaxien
articles.text:
3I/Atlas: Was der interstellare Komet über Wassereis in anderen Galaxien verrät
Als erst drittes bekanntes interstellares Objekt besuchte der Komet 3I/Atlas unser Sonnensystem. Deswegen liefert der 2025 entdeckte Himmelskörper der Wissenschaft einzigartige Einblicke in andere Galaxien und ihre Entstehung.
Studie verglich Wassereis von 3I/Atlas mit anderen Kometen
Zu den zahlreichen Studien, die seitdem über 3I/Atlas publiziert wurden, kam nun eine weitere hinzu. Sie erforscht die Beschaffenheit des Wassereises des interstellaren Kometen.
Die Forschungsergebnisse können Erkenntnisse über Wassereis in anderen Galaxien liefern, indem man 3I/Atlas mit eishaltigen Objekten des Sonnensystems vergleicht. Die von dem Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) im US-Bundesstaat Texas geleitete Studie ist in der Fachzeitschrift The Astrophysical Journal Letters erschienen.
James-Webb-Teleskop analysierte Koma von 3I/Atlas
Das Forschungsteam griff auf Daten des James-Webb-Teleskop zurück. Die Wissenschaftler:innen verglichen drei Beobachtungen, die das Weltraumteleskop zwischen August 2025 und April 2026 gemacht hatte. Die Aufnahmen fanden also vor und nach dem Perihel von 3I/Atlas statt. Der Komet erreichte seine sonnennächste Position am 29. Oktober 2025.
Aufgrund der Erwärmung durch die Sonne setzte der Komet eine Koma aus Gase, Staub und eben Eispartikel frei, die sich mit dem Nahinfrarot-Spektrografen von James Webb analysieren lassen. Diese Spuren geben Aufschluss über die Umstände, unter denen der Komet entstanden ist.
Eispartikel ähnelen bekannten Kometen – und wieder nicht
Die Spektralanalyse der Koma ergab eine starke Absorption von Licht im Bereich einer Wellenlänge von 3,0 Mikrometern. Dies deutete auf die Existenz von Wassereis hin. Bei 1,5 und 2,0 Mikrometern waren die Signale allerdings schwach oder fehlten ganz. Was für Wassereis wiederum untypisch ist.
Die Forschenden verglichen die Messungen mit Modellen für die Lichtstreuung von Partikeln unterschiedlich großer Partikel. Dabei ergaben Eispartikel, die stark mit Staub vermischt sind, die größte Ähnlichkeit mit denen aus der Koma von 3I/Atlas.
Mischung mit Staub charakterisiert Eispartikel von 3I/Atlas
Die Wissenschaftler:innen kamen dadurch zu dem Schluss, dass nicht die Größe der Eispartikel, sondern ihre Durchmischung mit Staub die Charakteristik des Wassereises des interstellaren Kometen bestimmt.
„Die Körner von 3I/ATLAS sind etwa genauso groß wie die in unseren eigenen Kometen“, sagte Studienhauptautorin Silvia Protopapa in einer Mitteilung des SwRI. „Was sie offenbar unterscheidet, ist die Menge an Staub, die in das Eis eingemischt ist.“
Ähnlichkeit mit transneptunischen Objekten
Im Vergleich mit dem Wassereis in der Hülle von Kometen unseres Sonnensystems unterscheidet sich 3I/Atlas damit. Die Eispartikel der bekannten heimischen Kometen sind deutlich reiner.
Doch als die Forschenden die Partikel von 3I/Atlas mit denen von Himmelskörpern verglichen, die jenseits des Eisplaneten Neptun unterwegs sind, ergab sich ein anderes Bild. Hier zeigte sich eine größere Ähnlichkeit zu dem interstellaren Pendant.
„Dies deutet darauf hin, dass die eisigen Bausteine von Planeten – sowohl hier als auch um andere Sterne herum – möglicherweise Eis in Form winziger, mikrometergroßer Körner gemeinsam haben, die von relativ reinem Eis bis hin zu mit Staub vermischtem Eis reichen“, schloss Silvia Protopapa daraus. 3I/Atlas bewege sich am staubigsten Ende dieses Spektrums.
Wassereis formt sich früh bei Entstehung von Himmelskörpern
Die transneptunischen Objekte am Rande des Sonnensystems gelten als Boten aus der Frühzeit unserer Galaxie. Hier haben sich viele frühe Bestandteile erhalten.
Da 3I/Atlas ihnen in Hinsicht auf das Wassereis gleicht, könnte dies laut der Studie darauf hindeuten, „dass die physikalische Form von Wassereis bereits früh in den planetarischen Scheiben festgelegt wird und in den dort entstehenden Eiskörpern zumindest teilweise erhalten bleibt“.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Helium Health gets $2.5m Google.org grant to deploy AI in maternal healthcare - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian e-health startup Helium Health has received a US$2.5 million grant from Google.org to roll out artificial intelligence (AI) solutions that improve maternal healthcare delivery in the country.
Founded in 2016, Helium Health takes hospitals and clinics instantly digital with its flagship Electronic Medical Records/Hospital Management Information System (EMR/HMIS) product, the most widely used such solution in West Africa.
The company is among 15 global recipients of the US$30 million Google.org Impact Challenge: AI for Government Innovation. The initiative backs organisations that work with governments to improve public service delivery.
The funding will support the deployment of clinical AI models through Helium Health’s maternal health initiative, HeliumMum, across the Lagos, Delta, Kano and Oyo states. Lagos will serve as the main launchpad. Helium Health will also join a dedicated Google.org Accelerator programme, where it will receive technical support from Google engineers and AI product experts.
Through HeliumMum, Helium Health will deploy AI tools that help pregnant women identify potential complications early and connect them with appropriate healthcare providers. The platform links women to facilities equipped with electronic medical records and AI-powered clinical decision support systems, so healthcare professionals can make better-informed decisions. It will also give governments actionable data to strengthen maternal health services and identify gaps in care.
The startup aims to reach an additional 1.9 million women over three years and contribute to a 30 per cent reduction in maternal mortality. Helium Health has already reached more than 3.5 million women through its maternal health initiatives over the past decade.
“Nigeria accounts for nearly three in every 10 maternal deaths globally. Behind every maternal death is a woman whose family expected her to come home,” said Dr Shona Oluwatola, head of public health at Helium Health.
“By equipping the 15 selected organisations with funding and pro bono support from Google’s own AI experts, we are empowering the people closest to the problem to show what is truly possible,” said Maggie Johnson, global head of Google.org.

articles.title: If it works in India, it can work anywhere: TDK Ventures’ Nicolas Sauvage on building deeptech for the world
articles.text:
If it works in India, it can work anywhere: TDK Ventures’ Nicolas Sauvage on building deeptech for the world
At TechSparks 2026, the Founder and President of TDK Ventures said Indian deeptech founders should plan for international markets from the start, and use the country’s tough operating conditions to develop capabilities that customers elsewhere would value.
For years, India’s best scientists left for the US. Now they are staying, and more of them are choosing startups over corporate labs. For Nicolas Sauvage, Founder and President of TDK Ventures, those two shifts are the biggest changes in Indian deeptech over the past five to 10 years.
“The best talent starts to go into the startups in deeptech, and they try things that they would not have tried 10 years or even five years ago,” Sauvage said in a fireside chat with Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, at TechSparks 2026.
TDK Ventures is the corporate venture capital arm of Japanese electronics company TDK Corporation. Set up in Silicon Valley in 2019, it opened its Bengaluru innovation hub in 2023, its first office outside the US. India is its second largest market by number of investments, Sauvage said.
The ecosystem he is betting on is growing. India is home to more than 4,200 deeptech startups, which raised $2.3 billion in 2025, up 37% from the year before, according to a Nasscom–Zinnov report.
During the session titled ‘Global by design: What Indian deeptech needs to become globally iconic’, he laid out what Indian founders need to get right to build companies that compete globally, from picking a first customer and the right investors to planning for scale before it becomes expensive to do so.
Where India has the right to win
Speaking on investing in SpaceTech, Sauvage named the US, China, and India as the three countries where he would consider investing as a VC. Space is one area where he believes India has a clear advantage, built on decades of institutional investment through the Indian Space Research Organisation. The government’s space promotion agency, IN-SPACe, projects that India’s space economy will grow from $8.4 billion to $44 billion by 2033, raising its share of the global market from 2% to 8%.
TDK Ventures co-led a $20.5 million Series A in Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Ethereal Exploration Guild (The Guild), which is developing a fully reusable medium-lift launch vehicle.
Sauvage also pointed to a shift in AI. The conversation, he said, has moved from tokens and compute to electrons and gigawatts, which means everything involved in delivering power to chips now matters. TDK Ventures invested in C2i Semiconductors, a Bengaluru startup founded in 2024 by former Texas Instruments engineers that builds power management technology for AI data centres. Germany’s Infineon Technologies announced the acquisition of C2i in August 2026 and completed it in October, about two years after the startup was founded.
Beyond individual sectors, Sauvage credited a cultural trait: jugaad, or resourcefulness under constraint.
“Think about the entrepreneurship journey. It means going from an idea with massive constraints and creating something that’s valuable and does a job. That sounds like jugaad to me,” he said.
That resourcefulness shows up in the numbers, he added. Capital efficiency among Indian portfolio companies is world class. “I’m from Europe, but don’t talk about Europe when we think about capital efficiency,” he said.
Let the first market shape the product
When asked what founders building from India for the world should think about first, Sauvage pointed to Exponent Energy. Founded in 2020 by former Ather Energy executives Arun Vinayak and Sanjay Byalal, the company offers 15-minute fast charging. In June 2026, TDK Ventures co-led a Rs 200 crore ($21.1 million) round in Exponent, taking the company’s total funding since 2020 to $65.7 million.
Exponent’s long-term goal was megawatt-scale fast charging for intercity buses. It could not start there. Instead, it began by supplying battery management systems (BMS) to three-wheeler makers, a fragmented market with more than 70 manufacturers at the time.
“There was no way a German startup would convince BMW to take their solution. No way a US startup would convince General Motors to take their BMS solution,” Sauvage said.
India’s fragmented market let Exponent deploy across many manufacturers in Bengaluru and beyond, giving it a base to build from.
Founders need superpowers, and so do their investors
Sauvage described founders as superheroes. Each needs a superpower: something they know or can do that no one else can. That is what draws investors in. But, like any superhero film, there are many battles before the end, and founders need allies.
“You want to make sure that the investors you pick as an entrepreneur bring the right superpower at the right time,” he said.
Corporate VCs can bring a go-to-market channel, an early anchor customer, a hard-to-access supplier, or help reducing scientific risk, depending on who they are. He urged founders to choose investors based on what they add that the cap table does not already have.
For TDK Ventures, that means drawing on TDK’s work in energy, sensing, passive components, and power supplies. Sauvage said electric motorcycle maker Ultraviolette now gets components typically reserved for TDK’s largest customers, while TDK is working with The Guild on future component requirements and roadmaps.
Alongside seeking venture-capital financial returns, he said, TDK Ventures looks for ways TDK’s capabilities, or “superpowers”, can accelerate and de-risk a founder’s journey towards building a globally significant company.
First principles over trade-offs
Sauvage traced several portfolio wins back to first-principles thinking. TDK Ventures invested in AI chip company Groq in 2020. During an interview with founder Jonathan Ross before investing, Sauvage noticed that every answer, from setting company values to hiring, firing, and designing the compiler, came back to first principles.
That approach produced a chip architecture designed around the compiler, which allowed for fully predictable, low-latency inference. Sauvage said he was convinced inference was the future before the ChatGPT moment, when he estimated the market for inference alone at more than $60 billion. In December 2025, NVIDIA signed a non-exclusive licensing deal for Groq’s technology, reportedly worth about $20 billion, and hired Ross and several members of his team.
He applied the same lens to engineering decisions that look like trade-offs. Ultraviolette, he said, uses first-principles engineering to pursue improvements in performance, weight and cost together. The company now sells its bikes in Germany, France, Switzerland, the UK, and other European markets, bringing its products into markets served by established manufacturers such as BMW. Ultraviolette recently raised $85 million in a round led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures.
Patience and impatience at the same time
Deeptech founders, Sauvage said, need both. “Overnight success takes 10 years,” he said, noting that Groq took 10 years and SpaceX took 17. At the same time, founders need urgency and a sense of contribution to society.
Before investing, he looks for four things: a founder with a superpower, a category-defining product, a large enough market, and evidence the company can win one customer and then the next while staying capital-efficient. Markets worth $1 billion to $2 billion can be too small for the venture returns TDK Ventures seeks, he said, because the firm looks for each investment to have the potential to return the entire fund.
He cited SPAN, a Silicon Valley company led by Indian-origin founder Arch Rao. SPAN began by redesigning the home electrical panel, a product largely unchanged for a century.
As AI infrastructure demand surged, SPAN extended its power-management technology into distributed compute through partnerships, which Sauvage said changed the company’s trajectory.
Longer cycles also explain why India needs more corporate investors now, he argued. Using a roughly four-year journey to success in SaaS and fintech as an illustration, Sauvage described an ecosystem that can recycle entrepreneurial experience about 2.5 times a decade, as founders and employees carry what they have learned into new companies. A ten-year deeptech journey allows only one such cycle over the same period. Networks of repeat founders and alumni-founded businesses, like those associated with PayPal and SpaceX, therefore take longer to develop. Corporate investors can help bridge that gap with technical expertise, suppliers and customer relationships.
“I want global companies, corporates, and their corporate VCs to know this is the time to invest in India for deeptech,” he said.
Build for scale before it gets expensive
Sauvage emphasised thinking about scale and international expansion early, because shortcuts taken to win the first market in India can become expensive to reverse later.
When TDK Ventures met Ultraviolette, the team was already deliberate about Europe while focused on winning in India first, with customers riding its bikes as far as the Himalayas.
His advice to founders: find what is specific to India that a global customer would trust. India’s wide temperature range, for example, could favour energy storage that performs across extremes, such as sodium-ion or thermal batteries.
“Try to think about what makes you being in India a proof point that because you’re successful in India, you will win everywhere,” he said.
For Sauvage, India’s deeptech opportunity rests on more than talent. The founders most likely to build iconic companies are those who treat India as a starting point rather than a boundary, pick investors who fill specific gaps, and design for international markets before shortcuts become costly to undo. It is a long game that demands patience and impatience at once, and in his view, the moment for global capital to back it in India has arrived.

articles.title: Windows 11 27H2 pourrait être la mise à jour majeure que vous attendez tous
articles.text:
La prochaine mise à jour majeure du système d’exploitation de Microsoft ne sera encore pas Windows 12. Si la prochaine version majeure du système d’exploitation de Microsoft fait parler d’elle depuis 2023, son arrivée sur votre PC n’est a priori pas prévue pour tout de suite. Microsoft aurait en effet pour projet de se concentrer encore un peu sur l’amélioration de Windows 11. Et pour la prochaine mise à jour majeure du système d’exploitation, 27H2, dont la sortie devrait être prévue pour l’automne 2027, Microsoft partirait d’une feuille blanche.
Alors que tout le monde s’attendait à voir arriver Windows 12 en 2024, Microsoft a adopté à la place un cycle de publication de mises à jour étalées sur trois ans. Ce cycle arrivant à échéance en 2027, Microsoft prépare l’arrivée de la prochaine mise à jour majeure de son système d’exploitation. Et il ne s’agira visiblement toujours pas de Windows 12. La firme de Redmond semble vouloir tenir sa promesse d’améliorer Windows 11 plutôt que de lancer une nouvelle version de son OS accompagnée de nouvelles fonctionnalités.
Un remplacement complet du système
Contrairement aux mises à jour 25H2 et 26H2 qui n’étaient que de simples paquets d’activation débloquant graduellement les nouvelles fonctionnalités, la mise à jour 27H2 devrait être une mise à niveau complète. La prochaine version de Windows 11 remplacerait visiblement de larges pans du système d’exploitation, comme cela a été le cas avec Windows 11 24H2. C’est en tout cas ce que rapporte The Verge qui cite des sources a priori bien informées sur les plans à venir de Microsoft.
Comme elle l’a déjà fait cette année avec la mise en place de Windows K2, son plan secret pour remettre Windows 11 à flot et regagner la confiance des utilisateurs, Microsoft aurait pour principal objectif de proposer une mise à jour améliorant les performances globales et résolvant surtout les problèmes de lourdeur de son OS.
Les changements à venir avec Windows 11 27H2 seraient d’ailleurs si importants que Microsoft prévoirait de lancer les tests de sa prochaine mise à jour bien plus tôt qu’à l’accoutumée auprès des Insiders.
Pour préparer ce changement, Microsoft aurait prévu de remplacer son emblématique fond d’écran bleu « Bloom » par de nouveaux visuels qui pourraient être dévoilés ce mois-ci lors de la conférence Ignite. Le changement de fond d’écran, qui pourrait par ailleurs varier en fonction des différentes versions de Windows (famille, pro, etc.) reprendrait un design similaire au fond d’écran « Bloom », mais avec une feuille colorée pliée et immergée dans des nuages.

articles.title: Nespresso Vertuo Next : la machine à capsules qui va du ristretto au mug tombe à 49 €
articles.text:
La machine à café Nespresso Vertuo Next De'Longhi est à 49 € (-67 %)
Du ristretto au mug sans aucun réglage, la machine Nespresso Vertuo Next de De'Longhi passe à 49 € chez Boulanger, soit 100,99 € de moins que son ancien prix.
L'offre concerne la version anthracite (ENV120.GY), vendue et expédiée par Boulanger. Le prix de 49 € se compare à l'ancien prix de 149,99 € affiché par l'enseigne. Attention au délai : la livraison à domicile comme le retrait en magasin, offert, sont annoncés à partir du 27 novembre. Boulanger signale aussi 30 € offerts sur une première commande de cafés Nespresso, sous conditions.
Une machine qui s'adapte à chaque capsule
La Vertuo Next repose sur la Centrifusion : la capsule tourne jusqu'à 7 000 tours par minute pendant l'extraction, ce qui forme la crema propre à ce système. La machine reconnaît la capsule insérée et ajuste la préparation, de l'espresso court au grand mug.
Son réservoir de 1,1 litre, placé à l'arrière, limite les remplissages. Le préchauffage annoncé est de 40 secondes, l'écoulement s'arrête automatiquement et un voyant signale le moment de détartrer. Avec 14,2 cm de large, elle se glisse facilement sur un plan de travail.
Un système fermé à connaître avant d'acheter
Cette machine n'accepte que les capsules Vertuo, incompatibles avec les capsules Nespresso Original et leurs nombreuses alternatives. Mieux vaut le savoir si vous avez déjà un stock de capsules classiques.
Sur Boulanger, elle obtient 3,9/5 sur 57 avis, une note qui regroupe plusieurs coloris et versions de la Vertuo Next. Parmi les commentaires publiés, quelques-uns la jugent un peu bruyante pendant l'écoulement. Elle convient surtout à ceux qui alternent cafés courts et longs sans vouloir manipuler de réglages.

articles.title: El sueño de los 2 billones de dólares se evapora: Anthropic afronta con inquietud una salida a bolsa menos potente de lo esperado
articles.text:
Las operaciones de salida a bolsa de las compañías se planifican al detalle durante meses, pero el día D lo determina el calendario. Anthropic había elegido el suyo y quería debutar en Nasdaq antes de Acción de Gracias. Ya había presentado sus cuentas, obtenido todos los permisos y hasta había elegido a los bancos que iban a gestionar la venta de sus acciones. Justo en ese preciso momento, se formó la tormenta perfecta sobre Wall Street.
En pocos días, las elecciones que no han salido como se esperaba han puesto el escenario político de EEUU patas arriba, que ha derivado en un jueves negro para las tecnológicas y los activos más expuestos a la IA a escala mundial. De acuerdo a lo publicado por el Wall Street Journal, ahora, todos miran de otra forma a la empresa de Claude.
El Nasdaq pierde la paciencia…y mucho dinero. El jueves el índice tecnológico cerró con una caída del 5,5% y dejó tras de sí un rastro de pérdidas estimadas en unos 2,5 billones de dólares en una sola jornada. Lo de una mala tarde la tiene cualquier se les quedó corta. El índice se cerró más de un 10% por debajo del anterior récord del 6 de octubre, registrando su peor sesión desde abril de 2025. Tal y como detallaba CNN, Nvidia se dejó un 9,3% y el índice de fabricantes de chips, un 12,3%.
Detrás de este desplome hay una duda creciente entre los inversores sobre cuándo dará beneficios tanto gasto en IA. Los resultados de Alphabet y Meta no lograron calmar a nadie. Sameer Samana, estratega sénior de mercados globales de Wells Fargo Investment Institute, declaraba a Reuters que había "bastante incertidumbre, discontinuidad y un cambio abrupto en las políticas".
Un precio que ya no les cuadra. La idea de Dario Amodei era recaudar hasta 100.000 millones de dólares con una valoración cercana (e incluso superior) a 1,5 billones de dólares. Según las fuentes de Wall Street Journal, tres grandes inversores que planean entrar en la OPV de Anthropic creen que habrá que bajar esa valoración. Algunos la ven más cercana al billón de dólares que a los 1,5 billones que se barajaban en las últimas estimaciones.
Este precio importa más de lo que parece, porque parte del dinero de sus socios llega en forma de acciones. Con una cotización inicial baja, hay que ceder más participación por la misma suma de capital. Haciendo una cuenta rápida, 100.000 millones sobre una valoración de 1,5 billones es un 6,7% de la empresa. Sobre un billón, representaría ceder un 10%. Las salidas alternativas pasan por conformarse con recaudar menos (quizá 80.000 millones de dólares) o tirar por la calle de en medio y retrasar la salida a bolsa hasta que los ánimos se calmen y haya opciones de conseguir una valoración satisfactoria.
OpenAI ya está notando esa rebaja en las expectativas de los inversores y ha reunido "solo" 11.000 millones de dólares de los 30.000 que buscaba recaudar, todo ello con una valoración de 1,25 billones. El refranero español tiene un mensaje para Amodei: "Cuando las barbas de tu vecino veas cortar, pon las tuyas a remojar".
Una factura que no espera. En términos generales, Anthropic goza de "buena salud" financiera y, al menos a corto plazo, la rebaja en su valoración no implica su quiebra financiera. La compañía ingresa 17.000 millones por trimestre pero, según los datos de su documento S-1, la potencia de cómputo se llevó el 58% de esos ingresos en el tercer trimestre, frente al 48% del anterior. La demanda fue mayor de lo previsto y hubo que comprar capacidad de cómputo extra a corto plazo. El crecimiento frena y fue del 47% en el trimestre, tras el 144% del anterior.
Los compromisos de gasto suman unos 895.400 millones, casi todos en la columna de computación e infraestructura. Unos 69.800 millones de dólares vencen en los próximos doce meses. Solo en octubre la empresa añadió 100.000 millones de dólares más, casi lo que podría sacar de la OPV. Eso sí, tenía 146.600 millones de dólares de liquidez a 30 de septiembre. Es decir, obtener una buena valoración le pondría las cosas mucho más fáciles a los de Amodei.
Una nota que encarece la deuda. Blackstone, que financia los chips para Anthropic, ya avisó a los inversores de que espera una calificación BB tras el debut bursátil de la compañía. Es un escalón por debajo del grado de inversión. Esta rebaja en la calificación no cierra la puerta a la financiación, pero sí encarece la deuda, porque quien presta con más riesgo también quiere cobrar más intereses.
Por otro lado, es su folleto S-1 se revela que su línea de crédito tiene garantías. Solo se liberan si dos de las tres grandes agencias (Moody's, S&P y Fitch) le asignan un grado de inversión. Un debut en el Nasdaq flojo no ayuda a conseguir esa buena calificación que necesita.

articles.title: Batteries à 100 000 km : Kia et Hyundai survolent le classement, VW déçoit — Frandroid
articles.text:
Quand on parle de « santé » d’une batterie, on désigne sa capacité utilisable restante, comparée à celle qu’elle avait neuve. On parle de SoH, pour state of health. Une batterie à 90 % de SoH peut encore stocker 90 % de l’énergie d’origine, ce qui se traduit surtout par un peu moins d’autonomie. Elle ne tombe pas en panne pour autant. Cette capacité baisse lentement avec le temps et les cycles de charge, et c’est ce chiffre qui intéresse les acheteurs d’occasion.
Il y a de bonnes raisons de penser que la situation s’améliore avec les générations. Les chimies plus tolérantes, comme le LFP, se répandent. Les systèmes de gestion thermique et les logiciels de pilotage progressent. La réglementation européenne introduit aussi des exigences minimales de durabilité pour les batteries neuves. Le règlement européen Euro 7, adopté en 2024, encadre d’ailleurs ce fameux SoH.
    À lire aussi : 
Voitures électriques : voici les différentes technologies de batteries (sodium, solides, LFP, NMC, NCA…) et leurs avantages
En Europe, la norme Euro 7 impose aux voitures électriques de conserver au moins 80 % de la capacité de leur batterie jusqu’à 5 ans ou 100 000 km, puis 72 % jusqu’à 8 ans ou 160 000 km. Elle s’applique aux nouveaux modèles homologués à partir du 29 novembre 2026, puis à toutes les voitures neuves à partir du 29 novembre 2027. Le règlement européen sur les batteries impose aussi une étiquette à partir de 2026, puis un QR code et un passeport numérique à partir du 18 février 2027, recensant les matériaux de fabrication, l’empreinte carbone, les performances du véhicule, la part du contenu renouvelable, etc. De quoi pousser les constructeurs à soigner la longévité de leurs batteries.
Les « anciennes » voitures électriques s’en sortent plutôt bien
Carla, une plateforme suédoise de voitures d’occasion, a publié le 8 juillet une analyse de 9 954 tests de batterie réalisés entre 2022 et 2026 sur des électriques vendues en Suède. Là-bas, on raisonne en « mil » : 10 000 mil font 100 000 km.
Les mesures ont été faites avec l’outil de diagnostic de batterie Aviloo. Carla ne publie que les modèles qui ont assez de tests, mais sans dire combien de voitures ont été mesurées pour chacun.
L’étude compare donc l’état de santé des batteries à 100 000 km. On retrouve surtout des modèles également vendus en France, mais plus âgés que les nouvelles stars françaises que sont les R5 E-Tech et autres Citroën ë-C3, encore un peu trop récentes pour avoir atteint les 100 000 km.
En tête, nous retrouvons deux cousines coréennes : le Kia e-Niro 64 kWh (97,25 %) et le Hyundai Kona 64 kWh (97,18 %). Suivent la Kia EV6 77,4 kWh (95,95 %), le Volvo XC40 Recharge 69 kWh avec ses cellules de chez CATL (94,70 %) et la Polestar 2 78 kWh, toujours avec ses cellules CATL (94,35 %).
Plus bas dans le top 20, après la BMW i3 (93,77 %), on trouve des Tesla, des Audi e-tron, des Skoda Enyaq et des Volkswagen ID.4, regroupées entre 93,3 et 92,2 %. La Volkswagen ID.3 58 kWh ferme la marche à 91,79 %. En pratique, cela correspond à une perte de 3 à 8 % de capacité.
Sur une voiture annoncée à 400 km, c’est une dizaine à une trentaine de kilomètres en moins, toutes choses égales par ailleurs. Carla y voit une usure nettement plus faible que ce qu’attendent beaucoup d’acheteurs. L’écart entre la première et la vingtième place, environ 5,5 points, n’est pas anodin pour autant : à 100 000 km, deux électriques ne vieillissent pas de la même façon.
Pour situer ces chiffres, Euro 7 fixe un plancher de 80 % de capacité jusqu’à 5 ans ou 100 000 km pour les voitures homologuées à partir du 29 novembre 2026. Les vingt modèles du classement le dépassent de 12 à 17 points, alors qu’aucun n’y était soumis.
Chimie, logiciel, marges : ce qui fait vieillir une batterie
Deux mécanismes se combinent. Le vieillissement calendaire dépend du temps, de la température et du niveau de charge à l’arrêt. Le vieillissement cyclique dépend des charges et des décharges. À l’échelle des cellules, le principal coupable est la SEI (Solid Electrolyte Interphase, soit « interphase solide-électrolyte » en français), une fine couche qui se forme sur l’anode en graphite dès les premières charges. Elle protège l’anode, mais en s’épaississant, elle immobilise du lithium qui ne stocke plus d’énergie.
S’y ajoutent le dépôt de lithium métallique, surtout lors de charges rapides par temps froid, et les microfissures des cathodes, qui gonflent et se contractent à chaque cycle. Ces phénomènes sont bien documentés. On ignore lequel domine dans chaque voiture, et l’étude ne le précise pas. Elle insiste en revanche sur la chimie.
Pour la Tesla Model 3, la version LFP (lithium-fer-phosphate) de CATL affiche 93,3 %, devant les cellules LG Chem (91,5 %) et Panasonic (89,8 % et 88,2 % selon la capacité). Le LFP supporte mieux les recharges à 100 % et les cycles répétés, au prix d’une densité d’énergie plus faible.
Les autres versions reposent sur des chimies au nickel, NMC (nickel-manganèse-cobalt) chez LG et NCA (nickel-cobalt-aluminium) chez Panasonic, plus denses mais plus sensibles. Au sein d’un même modèle, l’écart atteint cinq points, presque autant que les 5,5 points qui séparent le premier et le vingtième du classement. Carla en conclut que la conception de la batterie compte au moins autant que le modèle lui-même. Le logiciel joue aussi, mais son effet est plus difficile à mesurer.
Le système de gestion de la batterie (BMS, pour battery management system) fixe les plafonds de charge, régule la température et garde une réserve de capacité que le conducteur ne voit pas. L’effet des mises à jour ne va pas dans un seul sens. L’Enyaq 77 kWh doté de la version logicielle 3.x.x obtient 92,88 %, contre 92,60 % sans, alors que l’ID.4 passe de 92,77 % à 92,27 %.
Ces écarts sont trop minces pour conclure, d’autant qu’aucune marge d’erreur n’est fournie. Un constructeur qui prévoit une réserve généreuse au départ peut aussi la libérer au fil du temps. Le résultat est alors flatteur sans que les cellules aient mieux vieilli.
Pour un acheteur d’occasion, l’année et le kilométrage ne suffisent donc pas à juger une batterie, puisque deux versions d’un même modèle peuvent afficher cinq points d’écart. Carla, qui fait tester toutes les électriques qu’elle revend, conseille d’ailleurs de demander un test de batterie avant d’acheter.

articles.title: « Ne méprisez pas l’intelligence de vos utilisateurs » : des développeurs accusent Claude Code de divulguer leur adresse email à des sites web
articles.text:
« Je reçois des dizaines d’emails d’arnaque par jour parce que Claude Code a divulgué mon adresse email ».
Voici l’accusation portée le 5 novembre 2026, par taylor-edwards sur le dépôt GitHub de Claude Code, l’agent de programmation d’Anthropic.
Sous la version 2.1.318, sur macOS, l’outil aurait glissé son adresse mail dans l’en-tête User-Agent, la ligne par laquelle un programme s’identifie auprès d’un site web, des requêtes qu’il envoie lors de ses recherches.
Le problème avait déjà été signalé en juillet
Si le ticket est devenu l’un des principaux sujets du jour sur le forum Hacker News, c’est parce qu’il n’est pas le premier et que le défaut était connu depuis des mois. « Ne méprisez pas l’intelligence de vos utilisateurs », prévient un commentateur, phase3dev.
En effet, plusieurs signalements du même type ont été ouverts en juillet, puis en octobre. D’après le ticket #81138, Claude Code lit l’adresse du compte dans un fichier de configuration local et l’ajoute à ce que voit le modèle au début de chaque session.
Face à un site comme Wikipédia, qui demande aux programmes automatisés de s’identifier avec un contact, le modèle a parfois recopié cette adresse dans sa requête.
Un correctif livré, mais qui laisse passer huit cas sur dix-huit
Si Anthropic n’a pas directement reconnu le problème, un contributeur du dépôt a tout de même répondu qu’un module de protection intégré à Claude Code et activé par défaut bloque ce comportement depuis la version 2.1.317.
Insuffisant pour calmer la grogne. Un développeur a testé ce module avec 23 commandes contenant une fausse adresse.
Selon lui, il bloque bien l’envoi dans un User-Agent, mais laisse passer huit autres façons de transmettre l’adresse, par exemple dans un autre en-tête, dans un identifiant de connexion ou lorsque la commande va la chercher elle-même au dernier moment.

articles.title: Chainalysis says breach exposed credentials for all customers
articles.text:
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis says a recent attack on its systems and internal tools has exposed credentials and live tokens for all customers.
Chainalysis provides blockchain analysis tools to trace cryptocurrency transactions and investigate crimes such as fraud, ransomware, and money laundering. Its customer list includes law enforcement, government agencies, financial institutions, insurance companies, and cryptocurrency businesses worldwide.
This follows the company's disclosure last Friday that attackers using AI tools accessed customers' names, email addresses, user IDs, and organizational role labels using what it described as "offensive agentic techniques."
While it initially said the impact was limited and the breach affected only non-sensitive identity metadata, later updates revealed that usernames and password hashes for all customers were exposed in an "on-path attack" (more commonly known as a Man-in-the-Middle or MITM attack).
However, the company found no evidence that the attackers accessed investigative graph data or altered its blockchain attribution repositories.
"On Monday, we discovered certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor," it said in a Wednesday update. "At this time we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated."
While the company locked Chainalysis accounts as a precaution after discovering that some customers' passwords had been exposed and asked users to reset their passwords before signing in again, it has now taken the login portal offline, together with Reactor and Data Solutions, the Know-Your-Transaction (KYT) user interface and API, and address screening products, after discovering further abnormal activity.
To ensure threat actors don't access affected accounts, Chainalysis asked customers to provide trusted IP addresses so they can regain access to the login portal once it is brought back online and reset their credentials.
"Contact support@chainalysis.com or your Chainalysis account team with trusted IP addresses for our allowlist. We will then grant access for users to reset their passwords and rotate API keys to register transactions. We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online. We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate," it added.
"Once access is granted, all users will be required to reset their passwords and rotate API keys, as applicable, before registering transactions," the company noted earlier today.
Chainalysis' disclosure follows several other security incidents affecting cryptocurrency companies in recent weeks. Ledger also asked Asian resellers and distributors last month to remove products from shelves and halt wallet sales while it is investigating multiple hardware implant incidents.
More recently, crypto exchange Binance revealed that North Korean hackers stole roughly $6.34 billion worth of cryptocurrency after compromising its wallet infrastructure by infecting an employee's laptop with malware during a fake job interview.
