articles.title: Le meilleur concurrent à Adobe Creative Cloud va bientôt débarquer sur Linux
articles.text:
Affinity prépare une version Linux, mais n’a pour l’heure annoncé aucune date de sortie. En attendant, il faut passer par des solutions communautaires.
Le compte officiel d’Affinity sur X a récemment répondu à des utilisateurs qui regrettaient l’absence du logiciel sur Linux. L’équipe annonce que la version est « in active development », c’est-à-dire en cours de développement. Le message tombe au moment où Canva lance l’application sur iPad, laquelle vient s’ajouter aux éditions Windows et macOS.
Version native ou Wine : Canva ne dit pas comment il compte s’y prendre
Pour le portage sur Linux, deux options sont possibles. Canva peut développer une version native, pensée pour Linux, ou livrer la version Windows avec la couche de compatibilité Wine. Cette dernière serait alors chargée de traduire les instructions de la version Windows pour que le logiciel tourne sur Linux. Pour l’instant, rien ne dit quelle option sera retenue.
Le 30 octobre 2025, nous rapportions qu’Affinity passait à la gratuité à vie et fusionnait Photo, Designer et Publisher en une seule application, avec un export vers Canva. Elle regroupe aujourd’hui quatre Studios (Vector, Pixel, Layout et Sketch) dans une même fenêtre, avec un format de fichier unique, le .af. L’application est aussi en mesure d’ouvrir les fichiers PSD, AI, IDML, PDF et SVG. Les fonctions d’IA, comme le remplissage génératif ou la suppression d’arrière-plan, passent par un abonnement Canva Pro (12 euros par mois ou 110 euros par an).
En attendant, la communauté a ses solutions, toutes basées sur Wine. Le projet AffinityOnLinux fait tourner le logiciel, avec toutefois des limites sur les mises à jour, l’accélération matérielle et la mise à l’échelle de l’interface. Le script Linux-Affinity-Installer automatise la mise en place. Il se charge de télécharger Wine, puis crée un environnement Windows isolé, récupère l’installateur d’Affinity et ajoute des correctifs graphiques. L’option AppImage regroupe presque tout le nécessaire dans un seul fichier de 2Go ou plus. Les écrans qui s’appuient sur Microsoft WebView2 ne s’affichent pas correctement, et la connexion au compte Canva pose problème après une déconnexion. Des utilisateurs signalent aussi des déchirures d’image, un redimensionnement poussif des fenêtres et des ralentissements au zoom sur les gros projets.
Sur Linux, on trouve déjà Krita, Gimp, Inkscape et Scribus pour le graphisme. Affinity apporterait un outil commercial de niveau professionnel, comme alternative à Adobe. L’idée n’est pas nouvelle, en novembre 2025, Liam Fisher, directeur marketing d’Affinity, laissait entendre à l’ouverture du bureau de Canva à Johannesburg que l’entreprise étudiait sérieusement une version Linux. Mais le logiciel reste propriétaire, ce qui pourrait quand même faire grincer quelques dents.
Source : Affinity (X), heise

articles.title: Nigeria is rewriting its cyber laws, can it stop hackers?
articles.text:
Nigeria is reviewing its cybersecurity laws to counter mounting threats as artificial intelligence (AI) makes fraud, digital deception, and attacks on critical infrastructure harder to detect.
AI was linked to 55% of cybercrime incidents recorded across Africa last year, while deepfake cases increased sevenfold between the second and fourth quarters of 2024. Cybercriminals are using AI to automate scams, create convincing fake identities, and more quickly identify weaknesses in critical systems. This means attackers are adopting the technology faster than institutions can strengthen their defences, leaving existing security systems and laws struggling to keep up.
This growing technology gap is the primary driver behind the current legislative review, as the Nigerian government acknowledges that existing frameworks fail to provide adequate guardrails or align with international best practices.
Nigeria is also considering a national cybersecurity architecture to establish baseline security standards for organisations nationwide. However, unless these reforms improve enforcement, fortify vulnerable infrastructure, and foster local technical expertise, they risk expanding state surveillance powers without making Nigeria’s digital economy any safer.
Nigeria’s cybersecurity reforms are progressing along three distinct tracks. The Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015 was amended in February 2024, while a broader policy review convened lawmakers, government agencies, and industry stakeholders in Lagos. The National Cybersecurity Policy and Strategy, first introduced in 2014 and revised in 2021, is due for its five-year review in 2026. Meanwhile, the proposed National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill 2025, which underwent a public hearing in November 2025, aims to establish a comprehensive legal framework for digital services and e-governance.
Together, these initiatives address cybercrime enforcement, institutional security, and the governance of Nigeria’s expanding digital economy.
What is the government trying to fix?
The government says it has advanced work on a draft executive bill designed to strengthen the nation’s legal protections against cyber threats.
In October 2026, Adedeji Stanley Olajide, Chairman of the House Committee on ICT & Cybersecurity, told TechCabal on the sidelines of the International Cybersecurity Conference in Abuja that “the timeline is immediately after the election…” because not much can happen during political campaign season.
The lawmaker, however, expressed confidence that between January and June 2027, “the cybercrime, cybersecurity, and digital economy bills” would all be enacted into law.
He maintained that, once enacted, these laws would curb cyberbullying and other cyber threats and enforce stricter compliance and security standards across the financial sector.
The urgency for reform is evident: nine in ten Nigerian children face risks of cyberbullying, harassment, and online exploitation.
Financial institutions under siege
Nigeria’s financial sector also faces pressing vulnerabilities. In 2025, Nigeria lost ₦25.85 billion ($19.2 million) to electronic payment fraud. In September 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) cautioned banks, fintechs, and payment service providers that cyber risks and AI-driven vulnerabilities pose direct threats to financial stability.
These warnings align with findings from TC Insights’ report: “The Compliance Reckoning: Regulating Financial Services in the Age of AI.” The study notes that while gross fraud losses decreased in 2025, AI-powered attacks have grown considerably more sophisticated, with escalating regulatory fines underscoring systemic compliance risks.
In 2025 also, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) fined MultiChoice Nigeria ₦766.24 million ($568,630) for data protection breaches and unauthorised cross-border transfers of personal data. Also, the Commission launched investigations into 1,369 organisations across the banking, insurance, pensions, and gaming sectors
In a separate case, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) investigated a ₦3 billion ($2.23 million) fraud scheme that targeted First City Monument Bank customer accounts through unauthorised access.
These incidents demonstrate how systemic cyber vulnerabilities leave consumers exposed, compromise sensitive records, and erode trust in public institutions.
Even the government is not safe
Nigeria’s cybersecurity risks also extend to public institutions as government infrastructure has proven vulnerable. The AI-generated photo controversy involving the Independent National Electoral Commission’s voter register revealed that suspicious voter records entered the commission’s database through authorised registration terminals operated by its own officials, rather than via an external hack. It exposed a weakness in how public institutions control access, monitor staff activity, and verify data before adding it to their systems.
The Corporate Affairs Commission experienced a major breach exposing over 15 million corporate documents and beneficial ownership records. Meanwhile, Remita—the central payment gateway for Nigeria’s Treasury Single Account—suffered a data exposure due to a misconfigured cloud storage bucket that leaked nearly three terabytes of financial data.
Vincent Olatunji, NDPC National Commissioner, at a five-day hands-on cybersecurity training for technical personnel in government ministries, departments and agencies, in June, disclosed that the commission faced over 2,000 cyberattack attempts on its portal in one week.
These incidents highlight the growing threats facing institutions responsible for protecting Nigerians’ personal data, even as e-governance expands.
Across Africa, the case is not different: detecting intrusions is now harder as AI transforms routine cybercrime into automated reconnaissance, synthetic identity fraud, and credential hijacking.
Findings from Esentry and Darktrace—a cybersecurity intelligence partnership focused on enterprise threats—reveal that modern attackers rarely force their way in through software flaws; they enter via compromised credentials and weaponised internal trust that slip cleanly past conventional security alerts. According to the report, West Africa lost over ₦1 billion ($742,104) in fraudulent transactions that slipped past legacy security controls in the first half of 2026 alone.
This dynamic hits Nigeria with disproportionate severity. While South Africa accounted for 45% of Darktrace-observed incidents (20% ransomware), Kenya accounted for 6% (33% ransomware), and Nigeria accounted for only 5% of regional volume. However, ransomware was present in 80% of the investigated Nigerian cases, with data exfiltration in 40%—proving that Nigeria’s cyber risk far outstrips its visibility, masking high-impact extortion behind low detection numbers.
Rather than breaching perimeter walls, threat actors now leverage AI-enabled behavioural evasion to mimic legitimate user actions and quietly hijack authorised workflows—rendering static government firewalls and manual compliance audits obsolete.
Breaches of this magnitude undermine public trust in official registries and jeopardise data essential for corporate verification and anti-money laundering enforcement.
These failures highlight a critical requirement for new cybercrime legislation to establish clear accountability and enforce proper configuration standards for critical data infrastructure.
As legislative frameworks expand, lawmakers must balance state oversight with the protection of privacy and civil liberties. The true efficacy of these reforms will lie in whether they yield higher prosecution rates, fewer systemic breaches, and stronger data protection.
Building local capacity, not foreign dependence
For Nigeria, meaningful investment in cybersecurity sovereignty requires building internal capabilities to secure critical infrastructure, safeguard citizen data, investigate cybercrimes, and maintain vital digital services. Crucially, it also means curbing reliance on external vendors for system maintenance and incident response.
The government’s National Digital Cloud Policy attempts to address these challenges by granting tax and duty waivers on servers and data centre infrastructure to attract private investment. In return, the policy directs federal agencies to migrate legacy systems to the cloud while mandating that sensitive national data—including biometric and healthcare records—remain hosted within Nigerian borders.
Official reports state that over ₦4.5 trillion ($3.34 billion) was allocated to Nigeria’s information technology sector between June 2023 and June 2026.
Additionally, Nigeria aims to attract $250 million in private investment within 12 months and $750 million within 24 months. However, capital targets alone do not guarantee enhanced security capacity. The ultimate test remains whether these capital flows translate into resilient infrastructure, institutional capability, and skilled local talent.
As Abdul-Hakeem B.D. Ajijola, Chair of the African Union Cyber Security Expert Group, noted at the international cybersecurity conference mentioned earlier that the value of security investments must be measured by the capabilities that remain after vendor contracts expire. Procuring third-party software provides temporary protection, but without skilled local engineers to maintain and defend these systems, Nigeria risks trading technological vulnerability for vendor lock-in.
AI is shifting from an advantage for attackers to a standard part of offensive infrastructure. Essentry and Darktrace’s forecasts for the second half of 2026 point to an acceleration in deepfake-driven executive fraud, software supply chain compromises, and automated ransomware targeting cloud assets.
Progress must therefore be measured by operational outcomes: faster threat detection, prompt vulnerability patching, mandatory breach disclosure, rapid service recovery, and strict accountability for non-compliance with minimum standards.
Updating legislative frameworks can clarify agency responsibilities and expand investigative mandates. However, reforms should not be judged merely by the scope of powers granted to the state, but by whether citizens’ data is protected, financial infrastructure remains resilient, and public services can withstand sophisticated attacks.
Ultimately, Nigeria’s success will not depend on passing stricter cybersecurity laws, but on building a digital ecosystem capable of defending itself, recovering from security incidents, and safeguarding the public.

articles.title: Una simple nota de 'gracias' de Angelina Jolie ha llevado a la Generación X y a la Generación Z a debatir si su escritura es legible
articles.text:
Una sencilla nota de agradecimiento de Angelina Jolie terminó convirtiéndose en un pequeño rompecabezas para miles de usuarios en redes sociales. Así, todo empezó en 2023 durante el rodaje de Maria, ya que la intérprete dejó una nota para el personal del hotel Aldemar Olympian Village de Grecia.
Tres años después, la fotografía ha vuelto a circular y la conversación se está centrando en su peculiar caligrafía. Así, mientras algunos aseguran que pueden leerla sin dificultad, otros dicen que solo consiguen distinguir unas pocas palabras. Si quieres saber lo que dice, resulta que el mensaje agradece la estancia en el establecimiento y explica que el equipo de la película disfrutó de su paso por allí, pero descifrarlo fue más complicado de lo esperado.
Como recoge BuzzFeed, algunas personas comparan los trazos con la letra de un médico, pero otras consideran que el problema está en la falta de costumbre de leer textos manuscritos. Por ello, la discusión terminó enfrentando opiniones sobre las habilidades de distintas generaciones.
La escritura cursiva ha ido perdiendo espacio frente a los teclados
El debate tiene un precedente interesante en Estados Unidos, país en el que la enseñanza de la escritura cursiva perdió presencia después de que los estándares educativos Common Core (publicados en 2010) dejaran de incluirla entre sus requisitos. Como ejemplo, la historiadora Drew Gilpin Faust relató en un artículo publicado en The Atlantic que casi dos tercios de los estudiantes de uno de sus seminarios eran incapaces de leer ese tipo de letra.
Una experiencia así no representa a toda una generación, pero sí muestra cómo están cambiando algunas habilidades. La popularización de los ordenadores, las tabletas y los teléfonos móviles han reducido muchas situaciones en las que necesitamos escribir a mano. Por suerte, eso no significa que la caligrafía haya desaparecido de las escuelas y varios estadounidenses han recuperado su enseñanza obligatoria en los últimos años.
Lo que demuestra la nota de Jolie es que algo tan cotidiano como interpretar una carta manuscrita puede variar dependiendo de nuestra educación y nuestras costumbres.

articles.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2
In Part 1, you built a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server.
The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Three things that are fine for one agent and two tools become the work in an enterprise with hundreds of agents and thousands of tools:
| What Part 1 does | Why it stops scaling | What Part 2 does instead | 
| The agent holds each MCP server’s runtime ARN and calls it directly | N agents against M servers is a wiring matrix, and every new tool touches every agent that needs it | Agents reach one Gateway endpoint, and the Gateway holds the target registry | 
| The agent’s role holds the token-exchange permission and reads the provider’s secret | Every agent that acts for users gets a credential path to every resource it might reach | The Gateway redeems the grant, and the agent’s role holds no token-exchange or secret permissions | 
| Each MCP server carries the same groups check in its own code | The same rule, copied into thousands of servers, drifts and can’t be audited or changed in one place | One default-deny Cedar policy set, evaluated at the Gateway before tools run | 
In this post, you make that change on the Part 1 solution. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applications that can’t accept Okta’s grant.
What changes from Part 1
The Okta configuration, the AgentCore Identity credential provider, and the MCP servers from Part 1 stay as they are. Figure 1 shows the architecture with the additions.
- The user signs in, and the backend for frontend (BFF) exchanges the ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) issued to the task agent, agent A, as in Part 1.
- The BFF invokes agent A on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG.
- Agent A forwards the ID-JAG to its Gateway as the bearer token of its MCP session. The Gateway’s inbound authorizer accepts only agent A’s ID-JAGs.
- Policy in AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies for each tool listing and each tool call, before the Gateway invokes a target.
- For calls that Cedar permits, the Gateway has AgentCore Identity redeem the ID-JAG for each target at Okta’s custom authorization server through the Part 1 credential provider. A call that Cedar denies doesn’t redeem the ID-JAG.
- The MCP server checks the user’s groups and scope, as in Part 1, and records each decision as an authz.check span.
- Every hop emits OpenTelemetry spans to AgentCore Observability, which CloudWatch Transaction Search collects, and Okta streams its System Log to CloudWatch through Amazon EventBridge.
The reporting agent, agent B, runs on Amazon EKS and follows the same path through its own Gateway.
Prerequisites
In addition to the Part 1 solution, you need the following:
| Prerequisite | Needed for | 
| eksctl, kubectl, and Docker | The second agent on Amazon EKS | 
| Okta Log Streaming | Okta’s System Log in CloudWatch | 
| AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions | AgentCore Gateways and policy engines, Amazon EKS clusters, CloudWatch log groups, and Amazon EventBridge rules | 
The additions take about 90 minutes. The EKS control plane costs $0.10 per hour, plus nodes and the Amazon EKS Auto Mode management fee, and the AgentCore features charge for what you use. See Amazon EKS pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.
As in Part 1, the base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain on GitHub, and you can build the Part 2 additions on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it.
Create a Gateway that accepts the ID-JAG
The Gateway’s inbound authorizer works like the runtime authorizer from Part 1. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, its audience is the custom authorization server, and allowedClients pins it to one agent:
Figure 2 shows the resulting inbound authorizer.
Each MCP server becomes a Gateway target whose outbound authorization uses TOKEN_EXCHANGE through the Part 1 credential provider, so the Gateway performs the second exchange:
Figure 3 shows a target configured this way.
Three details matter here. First, as in Part 1, the target’s scopes must equal the ID-JAG’s. Second, give each target a static tool schema (listingMode set to DEFAULT with an inline mcpToolSchema), so the tool names your Cedar policies reference are fixed when you write them. In our tests, policies that name tools also couldn’t attach to dynamically listed targets. Third, the Gateway pages tools/list by target, so your client must follow the pagination cursor, or tools from later targets disappear. AgentCore Identity keeps the token from the Gateway’s exchange, so one single-use ID-JAG serves every tool call in a session. In our tests, it also opened a second session within its 5-minute life.
Because a credential provider authenticates as one Okta agent, give each agent its own Gateway and provider. Sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain takes a different route, in which a Gateway interceptor performs both exchanges itself.
Bind tools to agents with Cedar
Attach a Policy in AgentCore engine to the Gateway in ENFORCE mode, and write permit-only policies. Cedar exposes JWT claims as tags. A policy that reads a missing tag errors and is skipped. A skipped permit grants nothing, so default deny holds, but a skipped forbid blocks nothing. Guard each tag with hasTag:
The scope tag holds the ID-JAG’s space-separated scope claim, so the four conditions match xaa:write only as a whole entry. A scope such as xaa:write-admin doesn’t match. A matching policy, written the same way, permits the read tools with xaa:read. Check that every policy is ACTIVE before you attach the engine: an engine whose policies failed to create leaves the Gateway denying every call. Cedar binds tools to the agent and its delegated scope, and the MCP server still decides each user’s authority from the groups claim, as in Part 1.
Point the agent at the Gateway
Agent A now forwards its inbound ID-JAG to the Gateway instead of calling AgentCore Identity itself:
Remove the Part 1 AgentCore Identity statements from the agent’s execution role. That’s the only change to the role, which now holds no token-exchange or secret permissions, because the Gateway’s role holds the permission to exchange tokens. Keep allowedClients on the runtime’s authorizer.
Run a second agent on Amazon EKS
Our second agent, a reporting agent, runs the same code on Amazon EKS with its own Okta registration. Its resource connection allows only xaa:read, and it has its own Gateway and credential provider. EKS Pod Identity gives the pod an IAM role that can invoke models and write its own logs and traces, and nothing else. The AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK exports its traces. The agents-on-eks sample shows the Pod Identity setup.
Outside AgentCore runtime, no authorizer sits in front of the pod, so the agent validates the ID-JAG before a model call. It checks the signature, issuer, audience, token type oauth-id-jag+jwt, expiry, and that client_id is its own. If you kept the Part 1 agent check in the MCP servers, add agent B’s client ID to REGISTERED_AGENTS. Two settings tripped us up. The EKS Auto Mode general-purpose node pool runs only amd64, so build multi-architecture images. And the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, binds to localhost unless you set DOCKER_CONTAINER=true.
Trace every decision with AgentCore Observability
The spans in this section are AgentCore Observability, the component in Figure 1 that sits between the agents and CloudWatch. Runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Policy emit OpenTelemetry spans for each hop without code changes, after you turn on Transaction Search and trace delivery. Your own services add theirs with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT). CloudWatch Transaction Search collects them, the AgentCore console reads them as agent traces, and Amazon CloudWatch Omni reads the same spans as traces.default, which is what lets one query put them beside Okta’s events.
One tool call therefore produces this chain of spans, each naming the control that made a decision:
| Span | Emitted by | What it records | 
| AgentCore.Gateway.InboundAuth | Gateway | Whether the inbound ID-JAG was issued to this agent | 
| AgentCore.Policy.AuthorizeAction | Policy | The Cedar decision for this tool | 
| AgentCore.Identity.GetWorkloadAccessToken | Identity | Binding the agent’s workload identity to the user | 
| AgentCore.Identity.GetResourceOauth2Token | Identity | Redeeming the ID-JAG at Okta for a scoped access token | 
| AgentCore.Gateway.InvokeTool | Gateway | The tool call and its outcome | 
| authz.check | The MCP server (ADOT) | The user’s groups, the agent, the decision, and the reason | 
Okta’s System Log is the one record AWS can’t emit, so you bring it in. Figure 4 shows both paths meeting in Omni.
To set it up:
- Turn on CloudWatch Transaction Search, turn on trace delivery for each Gateway (see this sample script), and add ADOT to the BFF and the MCP servers. The task manager writes each decision, the user, and the agent onto an authz.check span.
- In Okta, add a Log Stream for Amazon EventBridge. Okta delivers each event to a partner event bus in your account, and a rule writes it to a CloudWatch Logs log group. In our tests, events arrived about 1 second after Okta published them. Each ID-JAG grant event names the agent as the actor, the user as a target, and the granted scopes and resource connection.
- Set up an Omni space in the account and AWS Region, add the Okta log group to the CloudWatch Dataset integration, and save a view, view.xaa_authz_decisions, over the authz.check spans.
One query then joins each ID-JAG grant to the decisions it led to:
For Alice, the result shows Okta granting the task agent xaa:read xaa:write for her, then the MCP server denying her create_task 16.7 seconds later and allowing list_tasks after that, as Figure 5 shows.
Each request is also one trace, from the BFF through the agent, the Gateway’s identity and policy checks, and the MCP server’s decision, as Figure 6 shows. Omni marks the trace as a fault because the agent’s create_task call returned the denial.
Two instrumentation details matter. ADOT finds the Region and signs its exports through botocore, so add botocore to services that lack it. Until we did, our MCP servers exported no spans. And ADOT’s agent mode turns off instrumentation for HTTP client libraries such as requests and urllib3 by default, so set OTEL_PYTHON_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS in your BFF to override that default with a list that leaves out the BFF’s HTTP client (requests, in ours), or its trace context won’t reach the agent.
Validate the results
We ran each check through both Gateways with the users from Part 1. Each session listed the tools, then called list_tasks, create_task, and an employee lookup:
| Caller and path | Tools listed | create_task | Reads | 
| Alice, agent A, Gateway A | 6 | Denied by the MCP server: requires xaa-writers | Allowed | 
| Bob, agent A, Gateway A | 6 | Created | Allowed | 
| Carol, agent A, Gateway A | 6 | Denied by the MCP server: no groups claim | Allowed | 
| Bob, agent B, Gateway B | 4: Cedar hid the write tools | Refused by the Gateway: “No policy applies to the request (denied by default)” | Allowed | 
Through the deployed agents, the results matched: agent A denied Alice and Carol and created Bob’s task, and agent B told Bob it had no tool to create tasks. The same user got different authority through different agents, and Okta decided it.
These requests stopped at the front door:
| Request | Response | 
| Agent B’s ID-JAG at Gateway A, or agent A’s at Gateway B | HTTP 403, MCP error -32002 insufficient_scope | 
| An Okta access token instead of an ID-JAG | HTTP 403, the same error | 
| No token | HTTP 401, “Missing Bearer token” | 
| Agent A’s ID-JAG sent to agent B on EKS | Refused in 98 milliseconds, before a model call: “issued to a different agent” | 
The Gateway returns the same generic error for a wrong agent and for the wrong token type, so check your configuration against the token’s client_id and aud when you see it.
The Gateway’s identity and policy work is small next to the tool itself. Medians and 90th percentiles from 24 hours of Gateway A spans in Omni:
| Span | p50 | p90 | 
| Gateway.InboundAuth | 34 ms | 69 ms | 
| Identity.Authorize | 25 ms | 60 ms | 
| Identity.GetWorkloadAccessToken | 48 ms | 94 ms | 
| Identity.GetResourceOauth2Token | 70 ms | 439 ms | 
| Policy.AuthorizeAction (Cedar, per call) | 47 ms | 56 ms | 
| Policy.PartiallyAuthorizeActions (Cedar, per tool listing) | 65 ms | 75 ms | 
| Gateway.TargetInvocation (the MCP server on AgentCore runtime) | 5,565 ms | 6,273 ms | 
The identity and policy spans for one tool call sum to about 0.2 seconds at their medians, and the MCP server’s own authz.check span took under 1 millisecond. Gateway B showed the same pattern, with GetResourceOauth2Token at 408 milliseconds at the median.
Cross App Access or per-user consent
XAA applies where the target application’s authorization server accepts an ID-JAG. There, your Okta administrator decides which agent may act for which users, users see no consent prompt, and Okta evaluates policy each time a token is requested. Applications with their own authorization servers, such as GitHub, rely on each user’s own OAuth consent instead. Figure 7 compares the two, as we measured them.
We deployed the AWS sample 07-consent-portal-auth-code-flow-targets beside our stack, with Okta signing users in to an AgentCore Identity consent portal and a GitHub target on its own Gateway. Alice connected a GitHub test account through the portal, and Bob never connected one. The post Manage end-user OAuth consent for AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore describes this lane in full. Here’s what we observed:
| Action | Next GitHub tool call | 
| Alice consented in the portal | Returned her GitHub identity | 
| Bob, who never consented | MCP error -32042 with an AgentCore authorization URL | 
| Alice suspended in Okta, earlier token reused | Still worked: the Gateway checks the inbound token’s signature and expiry, and that token lived 1 hour | 
| Alice suspended, new sign-in | Refused | 
| Alice unsuspended | Worked with no new consent | 
| Alice’s grant disconnected through the consent portal’s API | Not connected, then -32042 again | 
The two lanes revoke differently. In XAA, Okta’s controls stop the next ID-JAG mint, and issued tokens expire within about 5 minutes. In the consent lane, Okta controls only sign-in: the stored grant outlived the suspension and stayed until we disconnected it. Choose per target application, not once for the enterprise.
Where this pattern applies
In media and entertainment, the fleet arrives quickly. A studio or streaming or games organization has agents for production tracking, title and asset metadata, rights and localization, and viewer or player support, each sitting in front of a different system with its own authorization model and its own auditors. The question isn’t whether one agent can be governed. It’s whether the hundredth one is governed the same way, and whether an administrator can still answer which agents reach which systems for which users.
Nothing here is specific to that industry. The agent is an identity in your IdP, the target is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and the Gateway is where authorization is decided. Teams in financial services, healthcare, and the public sector put different resources behind the same front door and get the same audit trail.
What’s next: observability and evaluations
This post uses AgentCore Observability for one purpose: to prove that each allow and deny traces back to a control. There’s more in it than that, and it’s a body of work in its own right. The spans already carry the model and tool latency behind every governance decision, Transaction Search can alert on a spike in denials, and AgentCore evaluations can score an agent’s behavior against your own criteria, online for live traffic or on demand over a chosen set of spans. A later post takes that up: what to measure on a governed agent, which evaluators catch an agent that reports success after a refused tool call, and how to run both without turning your traces into your largest bill.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the Part 2 resources, then follow the cleanup steps in Part 1:
- Delete the Amazon EKS cluster (eksctl delete cluster) and its Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository.
- Delete the Gateways and their targets, then the Policy in AgentCore engines, and then agent B’s credential provider.
- Delete the CloudWatch Omni space and domain, the Dataset integration, the Amazon EventBridge rule and partner event bus, and the CloudWatch log groups.
- If you deployed sample 07, follow its cleanup steps.
- Delete the IAM roles and policies you created.
- In Okta, delete the log stream, and deactivate and delete agent B and its linked app.
Conclusion
In this post, you moved the Part 1 solution from a topology that suits a few agents and tools to one that holds up across many. The Gateway became the single front door and redeemed Okta’s grant, so the agents held no tool credentials. Cedar policies evaluated by Policy in AgentCore replaced the check copied into each server. A second agent on Amazon EKS joined under its own Okta identity. And AgentCore Observability, with Okta’s System Log beside it in CloudWatch Omni, traced each allow and deny back to the agent, the user, and the control that decided it. The governance mechanism didn’t change, which is the point: only the topology around it did.
To get started, explore the AgentCore samples and Okta’s Cross App Access documentation. For plain token exchange through a Gateway, read Implement on-behalf-of token exchange for multi-tenant agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.

articles.title: Vault Fork OpenBao Adds External Keys and Quantum-Ready TLS
articles.text:
OpenBao has released version 2.7, adding read scaling for PostgreSQL-backed deployments, support for external hardware security module (HSM) and key management service (KMS) keys, and post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. The release also introduces control groups for human review of sensitive operations and new headers intended to keep requests consistent across load-balanced OpenBao nodes.
OpenBao began as a community fork of HashiCorp Vault after HashiCorp changed Vault's licence from the Mozilla Public License to the Business Source License in 2023. The project is now governed under the Linux Foundation's Open Source Security Foundation and is distributed under MPL 2.0, an Open Source Initiative-approved licence. Its stated aim is to provide a secrets manager under open governance rather than control by a single vendor.
The fork was both ideological and commercial. Some users objected to the loss of an OSI-approved licence and to the possibility that a vendor could change the terms governing infrastructure they had already adopted. Others saw a practical opportunity: Vault had placed capabilities such as namespaces, HSM integration and advanced scalability behind enterprise licences, while an open fork could make comparable functionality available without those restrictions. The move followed the wider pattern that produced OpenTofu from Terraform and Valkey from Redis.
OpenBao has developed well beyond a simple continuation of Vault Community Edition. Since the fork, the project has added namespaces for multi-tenant isolation, plugin-based auto-unseal integrations, and read scalability for its integrated Raft storage backend. Version 2.7 extends that scaling work to PostgreSQL, allowing standby OpenBao instances using that backend to serve reads in a similar way to Raft-based deployments.
Alex Scheel announced the release for the OpenBao project, writing that it adds "PostgreSQL horizontal scalability, External HSM and KMS-Backed Keys support, and Post-Quantum Cryptography". He also noted that the release arrived after a shorter development cycle than the previous one and included "many substantial features and several major security patches".
"We are thrilled to announce the availability of OpenBao v2.7, adding PostgreSQL horizontal scalability, External HSM and KMS-Backed Keys support, and Post-Quantum Cryptography!" Alex Scheel
The external keys feature lets the PKI and Transit secrets engines use key material held in an HSM or KMS rather than storing it inside OpenBao. Support is delivered through third-party plugins, building on the auto-unseal plugin work in the previous release. This should appeal to organisations that must keep root certification authority keys or other high-value material under hardware control.
The post-quantum work adds ML-DSA and ML-KEM to TLS listeners, certificate authentication, PKI and Transit. Operators can therefore use post-quantum signatures and key exchange in relevant parts of the platform. The change does not by itself make a deployment quantum-safe: clients, certificate authorities and surrounding systems must also support the chosen algorithms. It does, however, give OpenBao users a route to begin testing hybrid and post-quantum configurations.
"Despite a shorter turnaround than from v2.5.x to v2.6.x, we were excited to see many substantial features and several major security patches land within this release." Alex Scheel
Control groups add an approval workflow to OpenBao. A new control_group stanza in an ACL policy can require a second party to review access to specified paths. This is aimed at high-risk operations where a single authenticated identity should not be able to act alone.
The release also includes breaking changes. The separate HSM distribution has been discontinued because the PKCS#11 plugin is now externalised. Vendor-specific built-in auto-unseal mechanisms for Alibaba Cloud, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud have also moved to plugins. Kerberos, LDAP and RADIUS authentication, along with the LDAP secrets engine, have moved into the openbao-plugins repository. The file storage backend has been removed; the project had never recommended it for production because it lacks high availability and transactions.
Luca Berton, who interviewed Scheel at Open Source Summit Europe, wrote that external keys allow operators to "run your PKI root backed by an HSM" with key material comparable to Vault Enterprise managed keys. He also highlighted the importance of post-quantum support before government transitions expected around 2030, citing the risk that encrypted traffic recorded today could be decrypted in the future.
Commercial support is also becoming part of the OpenBao ecosystem. ControlPlane launched ControlPlane Enterprise for OpenBao in March, offering security hardening, supply-chain assurance, rapid CVE remediation, optional FIPS 140-3 compliance support and 24/7 technical support. That offering illustrates how an open-source project can remain freely licensed while vendors compete on operational assurance. ControlPlane positions the product as a supported path for organisations that want OpenBao's licence and governance model but still need enterprise-style operational commitments. Its materials also contrast OpenBao's MPL 2.0 licence with Vault's BSL 1.1 licence and note that OpenBao retains API compatibility with Vault for many use cases.
Secrets management being a foundational dependency has been covered in InfoQ recently. We previously reported on Vault 2.0 and IBM's support model following its acquisition of HashiCorp, as well as on the broader pattern of community forks preserving open standards after vendor licence changes. OpenBao's progress suggests that the fork is becoming a credible alternative rather than merely a protest project.
OpenBao version 2.8 is expected to focus more on security and stability, with likely improvements to authentication. For teams evaluating a migration, the immediate questions are less about individual features than about operational maturity: plugin lifecycle management, PostgreSQL high-availability configuration, post-quantum client compatibility and the availability of support for production incidents.

articles.title: Paraguay president steps down after digital bank Ueno collapses with 3 million customers inside
articles.text:
Facepalm: Paraguay's central bank has seized Ueno Bank after examiners looking at the digital lender's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending and expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets. Once those errors were corrected, Ueno's capital fell to less than half the legal minimum, and the bank's app, cards and transfers went dark as its branches locked their doors. About 3 million customers, in a country of 6.5 million people, were cut off from the savings, payments and benefits they handled through the bank.
The warning signs went back months. ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper, reported in June that central bank inspectors found a pattern of risky insider lending. Ueno had lent large sums to owner-linked companies beyond legal limits and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.
Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud. They allege that some of the money lent to related companies was diverted to other businesses in the group. On Thursday, a judge ordered six executives jailed pending trial, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, and put two others under house arrest. All eight had turned themselves in after arrest warrants were issued.
Gustale's lawyer, José Fernández Zacur, argued that senior executives relied on staff for lending decisions. "The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan," he told local media.
Ueno grew quickly. It was a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company and won its banking license in 2023. In less than five years, it went from an obscure lender to a household name that claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Generous cash-back offers on groceries brought in users. The bank also opened more than 70 locations, sponsored the national soccer team and put its name on the country's main stadium. That logo has since been removed.
The bank also held a large share of public money. As of last month, Ueno reported about $800 million in public deposits, roughly a quarter of its total. That included money from the state pension and health fund and from the operators of Paraguay's hydroelectric dams.
Those deposits are at the center of the political fight. Peña appointed Carlos Carvallo, the former president of Ueno's predecessor, Financiera Ueno, to run the central bank that supervised the lender. Earlier this week, the central bank chief resigned at Peña's request. Peña also had ties to Grupo Vázquez, which owned Ueno until March 2025. He says he sold his stake in the group that month and had no improper role in the bank's affairs. As recently as last month, he called concerns about Ueno a smear campaign.
 – Santiago Peña (@SantiPenap) November 5, 2026
Opposition lawmakers accuse Peña of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and helping shield the bank from scrutiny. He denies wrongdoing and says the matter is a regulatory issue for the courts. His own Colorado Party turned on him anyway. Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes backed impeachment and said the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money."
In a video posted to X, Peña said he was stepping down for "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions." He also apologized. "I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."
Peña said he would still appear before the Senate to "exercise my right to a defense." Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation, which would let Vice President Pedro Alliana take office without a Senate trial. Opposition senators are still pushing for one. They argue that a resignation would keep Peña eligible to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution. Alliana has distanced himself from Peña and put his own presidential ambitions on hold until the crisis is resolved.
The crisis has hit the economy as well. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the dollar on Thursday, bringing its loss for the week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data. The Labor Ministry estimates about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs at the bank and related businesses have been affected. Outside the Labor Ministry, young employees still in Ueno uniforms burned their credit cards and demanded severance and unpaid wages.
Peña urged a fast fix for the customers still locked out. "Clarifying the facts and resolving the payments are obligations that must advance at the same time," he said.

articles.title: Kubernetes, mark II? Why Google's giving away gVisor, a code sandbox used by Anthropic and OpenAI
articles.text:
Kubernetes, mark II? Why Google’s giving away gVisor, a code sandbox used by Anthropic and OpenAI
Google wants to emulate one of its biggest ever open-source success stories, donating three core AI agent infrastructure projects to a neutral foundation in the hope they become industry standards, just as Kubernetes did for containers.
In a blog post published on Thursday, Drew Bradstock, VP of product management, Kubernetes and orchestration at Google, confirmed that the company is donating gVisor, Agent Substrate, and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF).
The move comes amid growing concerns about the security of autonomous AI agents, particularly their ability to execute code and interact with external systems. In July, models undergoing a cybersecurity evaluation at OpenAI escaped their restricted environment and breached Hugging Face’s production infrastructure, highlighting the challenges of keeping increasingly capable agents contained.
“We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes.”
Bradstock, for his part, argues that addressing such security risks, while making agents more economical to run and train, requires closer cooperation across the various facets of the underlying software and hardware infrastructure. And he believes that putting its technologies under neutral governance could encourage the kind of industry-wide participation that helped Kubernetes become ubiquitous.
“We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes,” Bradstock writes.
Why Google’s giving away gVisor
By way of a brief recap, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018 to improve container security. As The New Stack explained later that year, the technology uses a lightweight kernel running in user space to intercept application system calls, providing an additional layer of isolation between containers and the underlying host operating system. This makes it particularly useful for running untrusted code, including code generated by AI agents.
The technology is used by major AI companies, including Anthropic, which runs code generated by Claude inside gVisor containers on its web platform; and OpenAI, which uses it to isolate code execution. In a security report published just on Wednesday, OpenAI cited sandboxes such as gVisor and Firecracker as important for limiting the damage from exploited Linux kernel vulnerabilities.
The donation itself has been in the works for several weeks. The CNCF accepted gVisor’s application in late September, with Google publicly announcing its plans a few days later. The project’s onboarding process began last week, ahead of Thursday’s broader announcement incorporating all three projects.
In its original October announcement, gVisor contributors and Google software engineers Etienne Perot and Jing Chen sought to reassure users that the company remained committed to the technology. With demand for affordable, secure sandboxes growing, they argued that independent governance could encourage wider participation and adoption, both within Google and beyond.
“We (the gVisor contributors at Google) have been pushing for this move internally with the expectation that this will accelerate gVisor’s growth and adoption both within and outside of Google, in a similar manner as what has happened with Kubernetes,” they wrote at the time.
“We have been pushing for this move internally with the expectation that this will accelerate gVisor’s growth and adoption both within and outside of Google.”
Agent Substrate addresses a different challenge: how to run large numbers of autonomous agents without wasting computing resources while they sit idle. As The New Stack reported in July, the project introduces an additional runtime layer on top of Kubernetes, allowing agents to be suspended when inactive and resumed when needed, without repeatedly creating and destroying Kubernetes Pods. It does this by separating an agent’s persistent state from the computing resources executing it, with gVisor providing one of the available options for securely isolating that execution.
As part of the announcement this week, Google officially released Agent Substrate 1.0 and made it generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).
OpenRL, meanwhile, focuses on reinforcement learning, allowing developers to fine-tune AI models on their own Kubernetes infrastructure. Publicly introduced in June, the project coordinates the training and evaluation processes used to improve models. It also integrates with Agent Substrate, allowing training exercises to run inside isolated environments that can be secured using gVisor.
Collectively, the three projects address the execution, security and training requirements of autonomous AI agents.
Going vendor neutral
The move to CNCF governance should also change how gVisor is developed and maintained. In their October announcement, Perot and Chen outlined plans to move the project’s development and testing infrastructure outside Google, give external maintainers permission to merge code, and introduce a governance model that prevents any single company from exercising unilateral control.
Notably, in the project’s CNCF application submitted through GitHub in September, Perot identified a divide among gVisor’s existing adopters. At one end are major technology companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, which can invest in adapting the technology to their needs; at the other are specialist startups whose businesses depend heavily on secure code execution. The opportunity, Perot suggested, lies in reaching the much broader market between those two camps.
Such companies “don’t have the resources to invest specifically into security but would happily adopt an off-the-shelf, widely-available sandboxing runtime,” Perot wrote in the application.
There’s also the question of why more cloud providers haven’t integrated gVisor into their commercial offerings. In their October announcement, Perot and Chen noted that Google, DigitalOcean and Modal were among the few providers selling general-purpose computing services powered by gVisor, despite evidence that customers were already installing the technology themselves on competing cloud platforms. The engineers suggested that concerns about Google’s control of the project could explain the discrepancy.
“The remaining explanation of the lack of direct integration is likely the project’s (pre-donation) governance risk,” they wrote.
But perhaps the most interesting obstacle concerns the Linux kernel itself. Google and other companies using gVisor maintain their own kernel modifications to improve its performance, particularly for I/O-intensive applications. Those improvements aren’t universally available, potentially leaving other users with slower execution environments.
Bradstock attributes the difficulty in getting those improvements incorporated into the mainline Linux kernel to gVisor’s hitherto Google-centric credentials.
“Upstream Linux maintainers declined to merge them while the project was owned by a single vendor.”
“Upstream Linux maintainers declined to merge them while the project was owned by a single vendor,” Bradstock writes.
There is also documented resistance to at least one earlier gVisor-related kernel proposal on technical grounds. As LWN reported in 2022, Linux kernel maintainers raised security and design concerns about a proposed performance improvement, including questions about its usefulness beyond gVisor.
While such interactions don’t focus on Google’s ownership as a reason for the objections, it’s clear that moving to CNCF governance should go some distance toward addressing concerns about single-vendor control.
And for Google, that effort now extends beyond gVisor. With Agent Substrate and OpenRL also moving to the CNCF, the company is hoping to establish a common foundation for autonomous agents.
“Vendor-neutral ownership lets cloud providers, hardware vendors, and independent software companies participate in the future growth of agentic workloads equally,” Bradstock writes.
Learning Path

articles.title: DigiCert Data Breach Impacts Business Customer Information
articles.text:
DigiCert has disclosed a data breach impacting its business customers’ contact information, including names and email addresses.
The incident involved an internal business system used for archiving customer information, which was moved to a different network segment in February 2025, inadvertently becoming exposed to the internet.
Attackers abused a self-registration feature in the system’s account manager, built for other purposes and not requiring MFA, to create a read-only account that had access to archived data between June 27 and July 2.
DigiCert blocked the unauthorized account on July 2, and determined in October that the account was used to access archived customer contact information, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses.
In some cases, driver’s licenses, passports, utility bills, and other documents containing a name and address that its customers provided were also compromised.
“The access could not write records, act as a validation approver, or issue certificates,” DigiCert says. “The CA systems operate on their own secure network segments and were not affected by this external access.”
According to the company, the incident was initially investigated and remediated as an account-creation event. On October 12, however, it started suspecting that the unauthorized account may have accessed archived data, and launched an investigation.
Since mid-October, the company also implemented additional monitoring and alerting, verified or removed remaining non-DigiCert accounts, reset passwords for all business system users, deactivated the feature that enabled users to self-register, and verified the ownership of the business system and the enforcement of permission policies.
DigiCert did not say how many customers might have been affected. SecurityWeek has emailed the company for information on the matter and will update this article if it responds.

articles.title: Intel’s next-gen Nova Lake needs new motherboards — what we expect from Nova Point and Z990, Z970, and B960 chipsets
articles.text:
Intel’s next-gen Nova Lake needs new motherboards — what we expect from Nova Point and Z990, Z970, and B960 chipsets
More PCIe 5.0 lanes, Thunderbolt 5 support, faster memory speeds, and the potential of active chipset cooling highlight the list of Nova Point chipset features.
Intel’s new Nova Lake-S CPUs are rumored to be on track to start mass production in Q4 2026, with a launch expected in Q1 2027. Unlike previous launches, we’re supposed to see mid-range SKU(s), supposedly an unlocked 28-core product(s), first in Q1, followed later in 2027 by flagship-class models that allegedly use two compute tiles and feature up to 52 cores.
Lip-Bu Tan, Intel CEO, said earlier this year that Nova Lake is “coming at the end of 2026.” Despite the growing number of rumors and statements, we still don’t have a concrete date, but we can expect to see the CPUs soon, and with them, a brand-new socket and motherboard chipsets.
Regardless of how many cores they have or when they arrive, you will need a new motherboard for Nova Lake. The LGA 1851 socket is at the end of its life with the release of Core Ultra Series 2 processors like the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus, released earlier in 2026; that means no more new processors and a dead end. A new socket, LGA 1954, is necessary because Nova Lake CPUs have a significant increase in I/O and power needs. It’s also Intel’s first bLLC (big last-level cache) intended to take on AMD’s X3D CPUs.
We haven’t seen many details about the boards themselves, like pricing, official configurations, or product stacks, and we've only caught glimpses of one or two early models at Computex. Still, we have seen a few interesting platform details and rumors. To that end, we’ve put together a table of what we know so far about the specifications. Some things aren’t official yet and are noted by the tilde (~). We’ve also listed last-gen equivalents for reference.
| 900 Series Chipset, “up to” | B960 (Mainstream) | B860 (Mainstream) | Z990 (Enthusiast) | Z890 (Enthusiast) | Z970 (Enthusiast) | 
| Total PCIe Lanes | 34 | 34 | 48 | 48 | 34 | 
| Processor TB4/USB4 | 1 (TB5, 80Gbps) | 1 | 2 (TB5, 80Gbps) | 2 | 1 (TB5, 80Gbps) | 
| DMI Gen5 Lanes | 2 | 0 (4x G4) | 4 | 0 (8x G4) | 2 | 
| Chipset PCIE 5.0 Lanes | 0 | 0 | 12 | 0 | 0 | 
| Chipset PCIe 4.0 Lanes | 14 | 14 | 12 | 24 | 14 | 
| SATA 3.0 (6G Lanes) | 4 | 4 | 8 | 8 | 4 | 
| USB2 Ports | 12 | 12 | 14 | 14 | 12 | 
| USB3.2 (20G) Ports | ~2 | 2 | ~5 | 5 | ~2 | 
| USB3.2 (10G) Ports | ~2 | 4 | ~10 | 10 | ~4 | 
| USB3.2 (5G) Ports | ~6 | 6 | ~10 | 10 | ~6 | 
| IA OC | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| BCLK OC | No | No (board discretion) | Yes | Yes | No | 
| Memory OC | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Processor PCIE 5.0 Slot Lane Config | 1x16 | 1x16 + 1x4 | 1x16 or 1x8 + 2x4 or 2x8 or 4x4 | 1x16 + 1x4 or 2x8 + 1x4 or 1x8 or 3x4 | 1x16 | 
| Processor PCIE 5.0 Storage Lane Config | 1x4 | 1x4 | 1x8 or 2x4 | 1x4 | 1x4 | 
| ECC | No | No | No | No | No | 
| Simultaneous Displays Supported | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 
| PCIE RAID 0/1/5/10 Support | No | No | Yes | Yes | No | 
| SATA RAID 0/1/5/10 Support | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Intel vPro + Standard Manageability | No | No | No | Yes | No | 
The new lineup consists of five different chipsets. You get Z990 and Z970 for the enthusiast class, B960 for the Mainstream, W980 for workstations, and Q970. You may notice it’s missing the ‘H910’ platform for entry-level PCs, and now we see a second enthusiast-class platform, the Z970, wedged between the B960 and Z990. Z990 is still the flagship, offering more PCIe lanes, a DMI Gen5 x4 link, and 12 Gen5 lanes from the chipset. Z970 is the less expensive enthusiast option and is reportedly built on the same silicon as B960. You get CPU multiplier overclocking, but no BCLK adjustment, and of course fewer ports and lanes than the flagship.
The chipset package itself, internally codenamed “Nova Point,” will also differ slightly and is smaller than Z890 (600 mm² vs 658 mm²). The die-on-package shrinks to 72.5 mm² (11.15 x 6.5mm) compared to 92.9 mm² (11.15 x 8.33 mm), or roughly 22% smaller. Base power increases to 7.9 Watts, up from 6 W on the Z890, with a maximum of 14 W while working.
That power-density increase explains Intel’s rumored active-cooling guidelines for the chipset. When you start connecting components that use the chipset, think some PCIe slots and M.2 drives, the chipset raises its working voltage to maintain signal integrity for all of the bandwidth it now has to provide for the attached devices. Hopefully this is only needed in the high-end Z990/970, where it has a lot more lanes/bandwidth to support, as some of the fans on the chipset (remember early X570?) could get loud.
What to expect from Nova Point motherboards
Beyond the new LGA 1954 socket, not much information has been released about what to expect from motherboard partners. We know the platform's base memory speed is a smoking-fast DDR5-8000, up 800 MT/s over the Arrow Lake refresh chips. And if you don’t have a kit that can run those speeds and want to, it will cost at least $700 from any reputable brand. So the platform's cost of entry will be high unless you’re starting with compatible RAM. That said, you can run slower speeds if you already have DDR5, which would save money, but it could create a performance ceiling.
We’ll also see more abundant PCIe 5.0 connectivity. The upcoming Nova Lake CPUs are said to offer 36 PCIe Gen5 lanes. You get 16 lanes dedicated to graphics, eight lanes to storage, eight lanes to Thunderbolt 5 controllers (4x ea.), and four lanes for the DMI. That said, speeds are the same as the previous generation, since PCIe 4.0 x8 matches PCIe 5.0 x4. The chipset now has 12 dedicated PCIe 5.0 lanes, so motherboard manufacturers can include multiple PCIe 5.0 NVMe slots without sharing bandwidth from the primary PCIe slot or stealing USB4 bandwidth. In theory, you can have five PCIe 5.0 M.2 sockets between the CPU's native lanes and the chipset without sharing bandwidth among PCIe slots or M.2 sockets—a significant upgrade over Z890.
| Lane Category | Lane Count | Type | Functionality | 
| Graphics | 16 Lanes | PCIe 5.0 | Primary GPU Slot (x16) | 
| Storage | 8 Lanes | PCIe 5.0 | Two dedicated M.2 NVMe sockets (4x ea.) | 
| Thunderbolt Reserved | 8 Lanes | PCIe 5.0 | Dual Thunderbolt 5 Controllers (x4 ea.) | 
| DMI Reserved | 4 Lanes | PCIe 5.0 | DMI 5.0 x4 Link to Chipset | 
| Total CPU Native | 36 Lanes | Gen5 | Total Lanes | 
Thunderbolt 5 (TB5) is another feature we’ll see more of on some of these new boards, offering baked-in support via a controller chip, typically the Intel JHL9580. We’ve seen at least one Z890 board (Asus ProArt) already using it, but it should be more prevalent in this generation.
TB5 speeds hit 80 Gbps (bidirectional) or up to a wicked-fast 120 Gbps in single-direction boost mode. TB5 also supports DisplayPort 2.1, USB4, and USB PD 3.1(100-130W depending). So for anyone who needs fast external storage, a board with TB5 plus an appropriately speedy M.2 external drive means transfers will be much faster.
On the networking side, expect another round of 2.5-5GbE on most boards, with the cheapest options opting for the less expensive 1GbE. Premium boards, on the other hand, will work in dual Ethernet connections and 10 GbE. We’ll see a lot of Realtek 8125/8126 (2.5/5GbE) chips, along with some Killer E3100G, and perhaps Killer’s E5000 mixed in, too. 10GbE will still rely on the Marvell AQtion, like the AQC113C.
Integrated Wi-Fi support will vary, with most SKUs opting to use Wi-Fi 7. You’ll see a smattering of the ‘slower’ 160 MHz Wi-Fi 7 which, in reality, is plenty fast and will not be a choke point for most users on less expensive boards. The faster 320 MHz widens the bandwidth highway from four lanes to eight, so you can move twice as much data simultaneously. We expect chips from MediaTek (MT7927), Intel (BE200/202), and Realtek (RTL9822AE) to dominate the Wi-Fi 7 scene for Nova Point boards. Just remember: to take advantage of Wi-Fi 7, you need a Wi-Fi 7-capable router in the first place.
What motherboards can we expect to see?
We’ve seen leaks from the Eurasian Economic Union database Gigabyte (via Videocardz), listing a whopping 24 SKUs. We’ve also seen leaks about several ASRock motherboards via shipping records (via Club386). So far, there's not been a peep from MSI or Asus, but you can bet they’ll have a full complement of new boards of all shapes, sizes, and price points. But remember, just because something is listed in the EEU database doesn’t mean it will be released, or released in the U.S. So until we see an official list from the board partners, take this with a pinch of salt.
For Gigabyte, we see a lot of familiar faces in the list, including the flagship Aorus Xtreme, Aorus Master (now in three different SKUs), Aorus Pro and Elite (six total SKUs), and it even looks like they are planning multiple rear-connect Aorus Stealth options. We’ll also see several Aorus Elite and more affordable Eagle SKUs, along with more Duo X boards (this time from different families), all presumably using a 2-DIMM topology that supports high-density CQDIMMs. Micro ATX and Mini-ITX boards are also listed along with the wood-accent Aero models that made a splash this year.
ASRock is offering six different models, from the flagship-class Taichi (White) and Taichi Creator to the budget Pro RS Wifi and Z990 Challenger SKUs. In between, they have multiple variants of the Steel Legend Wi-Fi. What we don’t see from here are Micro ATX or Mini-ITX form factors, or any Z970 or B960 offerings out of the gate. We'll almost certainly be seeing those before long.
Asus has been tight-lipped, and as of this writing, we haven’t heard a peep about their boards. I’m confident we’ll see the usual ROG Maximus, ROG Strix, ProArt, TUF, and Prime lines (among others), with their typical Asus flair and value-add features like AI-assisted functionality (automating performance, optimizing cooling, managing network traffic, etc.).
MSI has also kept its cards close to the vest, and we haven’t seen much from them yet. But we do expect to see the company's lineup in full force. We expect to see the flagship Godlike board from the MEG series, high-end Ace, and mid-range MPG offerings like the Carbon and Edge, along with the MAG value series like the Tomahawk. I’d also imagine we’ll see some small-form-factor offerings, too, like a Z990 Edge Ti Wifi. In short, motherboard partners won’t miss the boat for a fresh revenue stream, and we’re sure to see a lot of options available come launch day.
Pricing for these future motherboards hasn't been listed. Still, you can imagine, with the increase in PCIe 5.0 bandwidth available and the copper needed to support it, hardware upgrades, and other external factors, it's safe to assume most SKUs will increase in price, or, with some luck, be the same as previous-gen versions. Either way, this is the start of a new platform, and those looking for a long-lasting socket should get in on the ground floor, assuming the performance is good, of course.
Final thoughts
So who are these motherboards for, really? With the cost of video cards, storage, and, of course, RAM through the roof, upgrading to the new platform isn’t going to be cheap, especially if you want to get the most out of it. While RAM speeds tend not to make a significant difference in many cases, it can in others. So reaching the base memory speeds of this new platform will cost an arm and a leg. As mentioned earlier, it will run with existing RAM below that value. Still, performance losses will range from negligible to notable, depending on differences in speed and timings, as well as the work being executed and the application used.
Nova Point-based motherboards are shaping up as a meaningful step for Intel’s new platform: a new LGA 1954 socket, 12 PCIe 5.0 lanes attached to the chipset for Z990, Thunderbolt 5 support, and increased base memory speed to DDR5-8000. We even saw Intel add another enthusiast chipset to bridge the gap between enthusiast and mainstream in these trying times. Most of this information comes from leaks and rumors, and without a firm launch date from Intel, details and lineups could change before the Nova Lake CPUs arrive, supposedly in early 2027. We expect to see a lot of boards at CES 2027, with launches following soon after.
If the new CPUs are competitive with AMD's X3D offering, we can imagine those also costing more than the Arrow Lake refresh chips. If you already have a capable system, waiting to see the official lineups, performance, and pricing is the smarter move. But if you want the most PCIe 5.0 storage and the fastest external connectivity with TB5, this platform is built for you. Otherwise, you can likely make do with what you have for a little while longer, hopefully until inflated prices on at least some major components drop.
Joe Shields is a staff writer at Tom’s Hardware. He reviews motherboards and PC components.

articles.title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
articles.text:
I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning.
I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.
I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.
Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.
But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.
With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.
But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.
The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.
When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.
Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)
You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.
In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.
The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.
Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.
But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.
Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.
