articles.title: 'Other Worlds', la precuela de 'Stranger Things', es oficial: mira el primer teaser
articles.text:
Puede que Stranger Things haya terminado, pero eso no significa que no queden historias por contar dentro del mismo universo. Netflix acaba de oficializar Other Worlds, un spin-off y precuela live-action de su aclamada serie, y el anuncio ha llegado con un primer teaser.
Los detalles sobre Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure son todavía escasos. Lo poco que se sabe es lo que se desprende del breve avance que se ha divulgado este viernes, aunque es lógico pensar que con el correr de los meses iremos conociendo mucho más.
Todavía falta bastante para que Other Worlds se sume al catálogo de Netflix. La nueva precuela de Stranger Things llegará recién en 2028, así que hay tiempo de sobra para conocer datos más finos tanto de la trama como de sus protagonistas.
Los hermanos Duffer, responsables de Stranger Things, son los cocreadores de Other Worlds junto con Kate Trefry. Esta guionista ya tuvo una importante participación en la serie original de Netflix y también ha escrito la obra de teatro Stranger Things: The First Shadow, que explora los orígenes de Henry Creel (Vecna).
Qué se sabe de Other Worlds, la precuela live-action de Stranger Things
En el teaser de Other Worlds se observa una bicicleta tirada contra el cerco de alambre de lo que aparenta ser una base militar de Estados Unidos. Mientras suena la música a través de una radio, se indica que el lugar se emplaza en Marion, Nevada, y que los eventos tienen lugar el 19 de abril de 1955. El clip concluye con una suerte de estampida en las nubes, lo que da la sensación de que algo muy extraño está pasando (o se está probando).
Queda en claro, entonces, que los sucesos de Other Worlds tendrán lugar casi 30 años antes de los de Stranger Things y cuatro años antes de la introducción de Henry Creel en la obra de teatro The First Shadow. Ya se especula con que la nueva serie de Netflix va a explorar en mayor profundidad los experimentos con campos de fuerza y otras tecnologías que luego derivaron en los eventos vistos en los demás títulos de la saga.
De esta manera, los hermanos Duffer van a expandir todavía más el universo de Stranger Things. Recordemos que, además de la serie original y la obra teatral, la franquicia incluye un spin-off animado llamado Relatos del 85. Claro que Other Worlds aparenta ser una producción de gran calibre, más parecida al despliegue de la serie original que los demás títulos.
Por lo pronto, no se sabe quiénes protagonizarán Other Worlds, ni tampoco en qué fecha específica de 2028 debutará en Netflix. Estaremos a la espera de más novedades.

articles.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1 | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end.
In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch.
Solution overview
Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime.
Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this:
- The user signs in to the web front end, a backend for frontend (BFF), with OpenID Connect through the agent’s linked Okta app.
- For each request, the BFF exchanges the user’s ID token for an ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server, authenticated as the agent (RFC 8693 token exchange). Okta checks that the agent is active, that the user is assigned to it, and that an administrator connected it to the target authorization server for the requested scopes. The ID-JAG is single-use and expires in 5 minutes.
- The BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG as its bearer token. The runtime’s JWT authorizer accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent.
- The runtime gets a workload access token from AgentCore Identity that binds the agent’s workload identity to the user, and passes it to the agent code. This workload access token is an AWS-internal binding token: neither Okta nor the resource sees it, so it isn’t one of the three tokens.
- The agent asks AgentCore Identity for an access token. AgentCore Identity redeems the ID-JAG at the resource’s Okta custom authorization server with the JWT authorization grant (RFC 7523), authenticated as the agent. Okta returns a 5-minute access token that names both the user and the agent and carries the user’s groups.
- The agent calls the MCP servers with that token. The task manager checks that a registered agent obtained it, and that the user’s group and scope allow the tool.
Figure 2 shows the same request as a sequence, with the check that each party makes.
Prerequisites
To follow along, you need the following:
| Prerequisite | What we used | 
| An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock | US West (Oregon) | 
| An Okta org with Cross App Access for AI agents and API Access Management (custom authorization servers) | An Okta Integrator Free Plan org | 
| Python, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), boto3, the AgentCore CLI, and the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Python 3.11, AWS CLI version 2, boto3 1.43, AgentCore CLI 0.31.1, and AgentCore Python SDK 1.24.1 | 
| AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions | Permission to create AgentCore resources and IAM roles | 
The walkthrough takes about 1 hour. AgentCore charges for what you use. See Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.
The base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, and you can build the solution in this post on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it.
Register the agent in Okta
Okta needs an authorization server for the resource, the agent, a connection between them, and a policy that admits the agent’s grant. Do all of these steps in the Okta Admin Console: registering the agent creates its linked app, so you don’t need an app integration wizard.
- Create a custom authorization server for the resource application with the audience api://task-manager and the custom scopes xaa:read and xaa:write. Request only the resource’s custom scopes: Okta rejects an ID-JAG request that includes OpenID Connect scopes such as openid or profile (invalid_scope), so a request needs at least one custom scope and no OpenID Connect scopes.
- Add a groups claim to its access tokens, filtered to groups that start with xaa-. This claim carries each user’s authority to the tools.
- In the Admin Console, go to Directory > AI Agents, choose Register AI agent and then Register manually, optionally assign an owner, and create a linked OpenID Connect app. On Client registration, choose Client secret, generate a secret, and then activate the agent. The agent and the app share one client ID, and that app must sign your users in: an ID token from another app fails the exchange with “the client application is not registered for delegation to this agent.”
- On the agent’s Resource connections tab, connect it to the authorization server, limited to the scopes it needs, as Figure 3 shows.
- Add an access policy rule to the custom authorization server that allows the agent’s JWT Bearer grant, with a 5-minute access token lifetime. Without the grant type, the second exchange fails with no_matching_policy, and the lifetime bounds how long a revoked delegation keeps working.
- Assign the users or groups who might act through the agent. They sign in through the linked app, so give it an app sign-in policy that admits them with the authenticators they’ve enrolled. In our sandbox org, the linked app had its own policy with a rule for the test group. For real users, apply your organization’s policy, including multifactor authentication.
Okta’s Cross App Access guide covers the console steps, and the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain scripts the authorization server and its JWT bearer policy. The BFF then requests the ID-JAG, authenticated as the agent:
The AWS sample 06-okta-xaa sends the same request in Python (agent/xaa_client.py). The BFF authenticates as the agent, so store the agent’s client secret in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in code or configuration files.
Set up AgentCore Identity
AgentCore Identity holds three things for this solution, and your agent code doesn’t see the client secret or call Okta’s token endpoint:
| Part of AgentCore Identity | What it holds | Who creates it | 
| Workload identity | The agent’s identity on AWS, bound to the signed-in user for each request | AgentCore runtime, for each agent runtime | 
| OAuth2 credential provider | The agent’s Okta client ID and secret, and the grant to use | You, once per Okta agent | 
| Token vault | The access tokens the provider obtains | AgentCore Identity | 
Create the credential provider
The credential provider performs the second exchange. Point it at the custom authorization server, authenticate it as the AI agent, and set the on-behalf-of grant to JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT, which AgentCore Identity sends as jwt-bearer with the ID-JAG as the assertion:
Okta binds both exchanges to the client named in the ID-JAG, so each Okta agent needs its own provider: when we redeemed one agent’s ID-JAG as another, Okta refused with “The ‘client_id’ in the JWT Bearer Grant must match the ‘client_id’ used to authenticate the client.” AgentCore Identity keeps the secret in a service-managed AWS Secrets Manager secret, which you rotate with update-oauth2-credential-provider. If your team already manages the client secret in Secrets Manager, you can reference that secret’s ARN instead. AgentCore Identity reads the client secret from it, so you can rotate the secret without updating the provider (see Reference your own AWS Secrets Manager secrets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity). To avoid a shared secret, authenticate with a private key instead. See Authenticate with Private Key JWT using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. Figure 4 shows the provider in the AgentCore console.
Use the workload identity that AgentCore runtime manages
AgentCore runtime creates and manages a workload identity for each agent runtime. When a request passes the runtime’s JWT authorizer, the runtime gets a workload access token for that workload identity and the inbound token’s issuer and subject, and passes it to your code. AgentCore Identity then uses the ID-JAG behind it as the assertion for the exchange.
The AgentCore Python SDK keeps the workload access token in BedrockAgentCoreContext, not in the request headers that your entrypoint receives. Our first version looked for it in the headers, found nothing, and fell back to its own GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT call with a second workload identity, on all 21 requests we checked. Read it from the context instead:
AgentCore Identity keeps the access token in its token vault for the rest of the request. Across 10 requests, the agent’s first call redeemed the ID-JAG in about half a second (see the latency table in Validate the results), and the second, for the other MCP server, returned the same token in a median of 58 milliseconds without redeeming the single-use ID-JAG again. A new ID-JAG for the same user got a new token, so each request reflects Okta’s latest decision. The sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain reads the workload access token the same way (agent/agent.py).
Scope the agent’s role to its workload identity and provider
AgentCore Identity doesn’t bind workload identities to credential providers in the same account. The agent’s IAM role does, so scope it to the agent’s own workload identity and provider, and to that provider’s secret:
Take the workload identity’s name from workloadIdentityDetails in GetAgentRuntime, and the provider’s ARN from credentialProviderArn: the segment is oauth2credentialprovider, and with the hyphenated form every call failed with AccessDeniedException. The role needs no GetWorkloadAccessToken permission, because the runtime gets that token, not the agent. Our tests passed with only these two statements.
Deploy the agent on AgentCore runtime
Configure the agent runtime’s inbound authorizer to accept only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, and its audience is the resource’s custom authorization server. In agentcore.json:
allowedClients matches the client_id claim that an ID-JAG carries. Without it, the runtime admitted another agent’s ID-JAG with HTTP 200 and the request failed later, at the exchange. With it, the runtime refused that token with HTTP 401.
Besides the policy from the previous section, the execution role needs bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream. It needs no bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime permission for the MCP servers: each runs on AgentCore runtime behind its own JWT authorizer, with the custom authorization server as issuer and api://task-manager as audience, so the agent calls it with the Okta access token as a bearer token, not with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4).
Enforce each user’s authority in the MCP server
The resource connection sets the scopes for every user of an agent, so all three test users received xaa:read xaa:write, and per-user authority travels in the groups claim instead: Alice’s token carried xaa-readers, Bob’s xaa-writers, and Carol’s had none.
The task manager checks two things: it accepts only tokens a registered agent obtained, and it allows a write only when the group and the scope are both present:
Both checks close gaps we found: a write check that allowed tokens without a groups claim let Carol, who belongs to neither group, create tasks, and before _require_agent a plain token-exchange token, issued to a service app with no act claim, created a task for Bob. The server can read the claims without verifying the token again only because the runtime’s JWT authorizer already verified it. A server without that authorizer in front of it must check the signature, issuer, audience, and expiry itself, as the Part 2 agent on Amazon EKS does.
Validate the results
We ran every check against the deployed solution. Alice, Bob, and Carol each asked the agent to create a task and then list the project’s tasks:
| Caller | create_task | list_tasks | 
| Alice | Denied: requires membership in xaa-writers | Allowed | 
| Bob | Created | Allowed | 
| Carol | Denied: no groups claim | Allowed | 
| Bob, then Alice right after him | Created for Bob, then denied for Alice: no authority carried over | Allowed | 
These requests stopped before tools ran:
| Request | Stopped by | Response | 
| Agent B’s ID-JAG sent to the task agent | The runtime’s JWT authorizer | 401: “Claim ‘client_id’ value mismatch with configuration.” | 
| An ID-JAG held for 245 seconds | The runtime’s JWT authorizer | 401: “Ineffectual token, will expire within the next minute” | 
| A malformed bearer token | The runtime’s JWT authorizer | 403: “Failed to parse token” | 
| One ID-JAG redeemed twice | Okta’s custom authorization server | 400: “The id-jag was already used.” | 
| A narrower scope at the second exchange | Okta’s custom authorization server | 400: “The scope parameter must exactly match the scopes in the id-jag.” | 
| A scope outside the connection | Okta’s org authorization server | 400 invalid_scope | 
| A plain token exchange token at the MCP server | The MCP server | Denied: only tokens that a registered AI agent obtained | 
The token that AgentCore Identity returned matched one we redeemed directly at Okta, claim for claim: sub was the user, cid and act named the agent, scp held the connection’s scopes, groups held the user’s groups, and it lived 300 seconds.
AgentCore Identity adds about 0.6 seconds to a request that takes about 30 seconds end to end, most of it model and tool calls. Medians of five runs from our test client:
| Call | Median | 
| Sign-in, scripted (authorization code flow) | 1,205 ms | 
| ID token to ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server | 216 ms | 
| GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT | 135 ms | 
| GetResourceOauth2Token, including Okta’s JWT bearer grant | 508 ms | 
Govern agents in operation
Okta evaluates the agent, the user, and the connection when it mints an ID-JAG. We measured what each administrator action does to the next request and to issued tokens:
| Admin action in Okta | New requests | Tokens already issued | 
| Delete the agent’s resource connection | Refused immediately ( invalid_target) | Work until they expire, up to 5 minutes | 
| Remove the user’s assignment | Refused within about 1 second, even with an ID token the user already held | Up to 5 minutes | 
| Deactivate the agent | Refused after Okta runs the operation, which our test org queued for 86 minutes | Up to 5 minutes | 
Actions on one agent left the other working. Okta doesn’t re-check the user when an ID-JAG is redeemed: its custom authorization server issued an access token 3 seconds after we removed a user, for an ID-JAG minted before the removal. Okta’s System Log records each grant with the agent as the actor, and Part 2 streams those events into CloudWatch.
Best practices for the delegation chain
Six practices came out of these measurements, each one a property of the chain rather than a preference:
| Practice | What we measured | 
| Mint a fresh ID-JAG for each request | An ID-JAG is single-use and lives 300 seconds. The runtime refuses one with under 60 seconds left, so 225 seconds worked, 245 didn’t | 
| Carry per-user authority in the groups claim, and request one scope set per request | Okta sets scopes from the resource connection, so all three users got the same scopes, and the second exchange must request exactly the ID-JAG’s | 
| Pin the agent at the runtime, and check act and cid in the tool | allowedClients matches the client_id claim an ID-JAG carries. Okta access tokens carry cid instead | 
| Reproduce a failed exchange directly against Okta | Through AgentCore Identity, a scope mismatch and a wrong client both surface as “Token exchange failed with HTTP status 400” | 
| Grant the agent’s role read access to the provider’s secret | GetResourceOauth2Token failed until the role could read it | 
| Keep lifetimes short, and use the resource connection as your kill switch | Deleting the connection took effect immediately. Deactivating the agent sat in Okta’s beta AI agent API queue for 86 minutes, with no cancel | 
Cross App Access compared with plain token exchange
Plain RFC 8693 token exchange also carries the user’s identity downstream. We compared it with XAA against the same Okta authorization server and user:
| Behavior we observed | Plain token exchange | Cross App Access | 
| Agent identity in the token | No act claim | act names the agent | 
| Scopes | Widened: Alice’s own token had xaa:read, and the exchange returned xaa:read xaa:write | The scopes the administrator approved | 
| Exchange rule limited to xaa-writers | Alice still received a token | Alice denied | 
| User unassigned, earlier token reused | Still exchanged | Refused | 
| What administrators see | A service app with a grant type | The agent, its connections, and the agent in each log event | 
These results reflect our Okta configuration. Okta’s guide shows an act claim for exchanged tokens, which we didn’t receive. Plain token exchange carried the user’s identity, but not the user’s authority.
Where this pattern applies
We work with media and entertainment companies, and this is where we met the problem first. A studio or streaming or games organization runs agents against production tracking, title and asset metadata, rights and localization, and viewer or player support. Each system has its own authorization model and its own auditors, and a user’s authority differs by title, territory, or release window, so “which agent might act for which user in which system” has to be answered before an agent ships.
Nothing in the chain is specific to that industry: the agent is an identity in your IdP, the target is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and the user’s authority rides in a claim. Financial services, healthcare, and public sector teams put different resources behind the same controls.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created:
- Delete the AWS CloudFormation stacks that the AgentCore CLI created for the agent and the two MCP servers.
- Delete the credential provider with aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-oauth2-credential-provider --name okta-xaa-obo, and any workload identity you created yourself with delete-workload-identity.
- Delete the IAM policies you added to the execution roles.
- In Okta, deactivate and delete the AI agent and its linked app, and remove the resource connection, the authorization server’s policy rule, scopes, and claim, and the test users and groups.
Conclusion
In this post, you used Okta Cross App Access to decide which agent might act for which user, and AgentCore Identity to carry out each decision. The runtime admitted only the agent’s own ID-JAGs, the credential provider redeemed each one with a secret the agent didn’t hold, the token vault reused the result within a request, and the MCP server enforced each user’s authority from the groups claim.
This design keeps the exchange in the agent’s role and repeats the authorization check in every MCP server. See Part 2 of this series to learn why its design moves both behind one AgentCore Gateway with Cedar policies, adds a second agent on Amazon EKS, and joins the Okta System Log with AgentCore traces in CloudWatch.
To get started, explore the AgentCore samples and Okta’s Cross App Access documentation. For the API details, see On-behalf-of token exchange in the AgentCore Developer Guide.

articles.title: Mass Effect : l’ultime chapitre de la saga annulée aura le droit à un documentaire
articles.text:
La fin d’une époque majeure de l’industrie du jeu vidéo aura bientôt son documentaire. Electronic Arts a brutalement fermé le studio canadien BioWare le 21 octobre, après une série de revers commerciaux. Deux semaines plus tard, Deadline révèle que les sociétés de production Fennessey Films et Score G Productions préparent un documentaire, Massive Effect: The BioWare Story. Commandé par la chaîne canadienne Super Channel, le film retrace l’ascension fulgurante de cette entreprise d’Edmonton devenue une référence mondiale du jeu de rôle, jusqu’à sa fermeture.
Un accès privilégié aux derniers jours du studio BioWare, dans les coulisses de Mass Effect
Le tournage a commencé il y a deux ans, bien avant que l’éditeur annonce la fermeture du studio et l’annulation du prochain Mass Effect. Le plan social qui accompagne cette décision supprime environ 400 postes chez EA, soit 3 % de ses effectifs, dont une cinquantaine chez BioWare. Le film est écrit et réalisé par le Canadien Akash Sherman (Clara). L’équipe de tournage a continué de filmer pendant la fermeture. Elle a pu suivre de l’intérieur les derniers mois du studio d’Edmonton, qui travaillait encore sur les premières phases du prochain Mass Effect.
Fondé en 1995 par trois médecins de formation, Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk et Augustine Yip, BioWare s’était imposé en trois décennies comme une référence du jeu de rôle occidental, avec 100 millions d’exemplaires vendus pour des séries comme Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic ou les premiers Baldur’s Gate.
Les anciens du studio et les fans mis à contribution
Outre les trois fondateurs, Augustine Yip compris, le documentaire donne la parole à des figures du jeu vidéo comme Douglas Reilly (vice-président de Lucasfilm Games), Geoff Keighley (créateur des Game Awards), John Riccitiello (ancien CEO d’EA), Casey Hudson (directeur de Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic et de Mass Effect), la comédienne Jennifer Hale (voix de Shepard au féminin dans Mass Effect), ainsi qu’une pléiade d’auteurs et de développeurs historiques du studio (Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Drew Karpyshyn ou Aaryn Flynn).
Dans une déclaration commune, Ray Muzyka et Greg Zeschuk se disent « honorés et profondément émus » que l’équipe du film leur ait demandé leur bénédiction. « BioWare, ça n’a jamais été seulement un logo ou un bâtiment. C’étaient les histoires que faisaient vivre les gens formidables de nos équipes de développement, et les fans qui ont défendu ces mondes », écrivent-ils. Les fans, qui sont des dizaines de milliers à réclamer le sauvetage de Mass Effect, sont aussi mis à contribution. Le site officiel du documentaire les invite à envoyer photos, vidéos et témoignages, avec une chance d’apparaître dans le film.
Massive Effect: The BioWare Story doit faire la tournée des festivals avant sa première mondiale, prévue en 2027. Il sera diffusé au Canada sur Super Channel, et la société Upstream Flix est chargée de le vendre à l’international. Aucune date ni aucune diffusion en France ne sont annoncées pour l’instant.

articles.title: Why operational excellence will define the next phase of India’s startup growth
articles.text:
Why operational excellence will define the next phase of India’s startup growth
Startups often prioritise funding, sales and expansion while overlooking the operational foundations needed to sustain growth. The article explores why strong processes, reliable data and governance are essential to building scalable businesses.
Growth rarely announces itself. It arrives as a signed term sheet on a Friday evening, a large client wanting to go live in three weeks, or an investor doubling a commitment.
But the win is rarely the hard part. The hard part is the Monday after.
That Monday tells you whether you have built a company or simply had a good quarter.
When operations become a competitive advantage
In most startups, operations sit in the back seat. It is the team that asks for approvals, slows down contracts, and says “not yet” when sales say “yes”. Founders tolerate it the way one tolerates a seatbelt.
I have never accepted that framing. Bain & Company’s long-running research on growth found that 85% of the barriers to profitable growth are internal, with revenue outgrowing talent at the top of the list. Companies rarely lose to the market. They lose to their own machinery, and that machinery is operations.
Build it before you need it
Early on, operations feel optional. A small team, a founder who knows everything, a spreadsheet that works. Why design controls for a business that fits in one room?
Because by the time you feel the need, you are already late. Operations built in the middle of a growth spurt is built under pressure: rushed hires, patched processes, controls bolted on after something breaks. Worse, it takes bandwidth from growth itself. The team that should be closing the next client is busy repairing the last one. You slow down precisely when you meant to accelerate.
Nobody lays the tracks after the train has left the station.
This is not a case for bloat. It is a case for sequencing. Build the backbone one stage ahead of where you are, lean and proportionate, so the organisation absorbs growth instead of buckling under it.
The companies that scale most smoothly are rarely the ones scrambling when growth arrives; the reporting, controls and people for the next stage are already in place. Investors notice the difference.
In due diligence, a clean data room and a well-documented control environment often say more about a company's readiness than its growth curve does.
Run on data, not opinions
Operations is also where a company's data lives, or should. Every onboarding, approval, and report generates information. Most startups treat it as exhaust. The better ones treat it as instrumentation. When operations own clean, consistent data, leadership stops arguing about whose number is right and starts debating what to do about it. You see a bottleneck forming before a client complains. And automation and AI, which nearly every board is now asking about, only work on data you can trust.
Automate a messy process and you simply get the mess faster.
If your founders and your operations team are looking at different numbers, you do not have a data problem. You have an operations problem.
Never pay for the same lesson twice
The same discipline applies to mistakes. A mistake made once is a lesson; made twice, it is a choice.
Every error in a growing firm should leave something behind, whether a changed control, a clearer owner, or a better checklist.
The corollary matters as much. If the same method keeps producing the same disappointing result, the problem is rarely effort. It is the method. Operations should be the function that notices, asks why, and has the licence to change how the work gets done. Processes are not scripture. They are hypotheses, and good operators keep testing them.
Bring operations in before growth is sold, not after
For founders and boards redrawing their organisation charts this year, one test is telling. Do operations hear about a new product, market, or client after it is sold, or while it is being designed? If it is after, operations will always be firefighting, and firefighters rarely get to build anything.
Put operations where growth is planned, not at the end of the line where growth is processed. Give it a seat in strategy reviews, a voice in pricing and launches, and a mandate to say "here is how", not just "not yet".
Three questions are worth asking every quarter:
● If our business doubled next quarter, what would break first?
● Which decisions still need the founder, and should they?
● Would our records survive an investor's due diligence this week?
Will your growth last, or was it just a good quarter?
There is an old military line: amateurs talk strategy, professionals talk logistics.
India's startup story so far has been told in the language of strategy: rounds, valuations, category creation. The next chapter will be about sustaining growth rather than merely achieving it, and it will be told in the language of execution and governance. Momentary growth is an event. Sustained growth is a capability. And capability, in the end, is what operations builds.
(Sandesha Jaitapkar is the COO at Artha Group)

articles.title: "Buscamos a Mister Calvo 2026": el gastrobar de un pueblo de Castellón ha decidido organizar una fiesta de calvos contra la despoblación
articles.text:
Hay quien se deja un dineral intentando recuperar el pelo, otros que directamente se rapan para adelantarse a la naturaleza y luego está Vilafranca del Cid, donde quedarse sin pelo tiene premio. Este pueblo del interior de Castellón busca a su propio Bruce Willis, su Zidane de confianza: el próximo 21 de noviembre, el bar El Forn Gastro celebrará una cena para coronar a Mister Calvo 2026. En Vilafranca, el cabeza de cartel es un pelón.
La propietaria insiste en que es una fiesta abierta a todo el mundo, tenga lo que tenga cada cual sobre los hombros. Todos podrán presumir de azotea con vistas. Si tenemos concursos de belleza y hasta de imitadores de Elvis, está claro que solo faltaba uno para celebrar lo que ocurre cuando el talento capilar se da de baja. Si Julio César tenía problemas de imagen por su coronilla, aquí la corona se la pondrá Mister Calvo.
Cómo se maquinó. La festa dels calvos (i acompanyants) salió de la barra del bar. La propusieron clientes habituales y los dueños, Elia Roig y Rubén Bou, la fueron puliendo hasta convertirla en evento. El local abrió en la primavera de 2025 en un edificio con un horno comunal de piedra del siglo XIII, donde antes había una taberna que cerró. Es un clásico de la zona. De hecho, Su agenda ya incluye jornadas de pintxos, Halloween, Carnaval, Oktoberfest y Navidad. Si funciona, repetirán y coronarán un calvo cada año.
Además, parece una buena iniciativa contra la despoblación (¿capilar?). Vilafranca tiene unos 2.000 habitantes y turismo de motoristas, ciclistas y senderistas. Pero su histórica fábrica de medias Marie Claire anunció el cierre en 2023 con casi 190 despidos y desde entonces no ha levantado cabeza. En este paisaje, un bar que da motivos para salir de casa un sábado de noviembre es un buen punto de encuentro. Y es imposible perderse: el local está en una de las principales arterias del pueblo.
Qué hay en el menú. La cena costará 32 euros. Incluye entrantes, pan, un principal a elegir entre dorada al horno y carne a la brasa, y postre o café. Parece que se puede ser calvo pero no vegetariano; al menos no habrá bocatas de Rodilla. Las plazas son limitadas y se reservan por teléfono. El local ya ha comprado regalos, gorras y pelucas. Los sinpelo podrán probarse la peluca y los melenudos, la gorra. Los criterios del jurado no son públicos, pero se espera relumbre democrático, aerodinámica y dignidad.
No es el primero. En Allo (Navarra) los calvos tienen su propio día dentro de las fiestas patronales. El colectivo local ya va por su decimoséptima concentración internacional y ese programa incluye almuerzo, ronda copera, bautizo de nuevos calvos en el Hoyo de la Fuente y comida de hermandad.
En Sant Boi de Llobregat, municipio perteneciente a Barcelona, una administración de lotería celebra el Calvos Fest. Los participantes pasan el décimo por su cabeza, a sabiendas de que frotar la calva da suerte o, como mínimo, luce. Un peluquero rapaba a quien quisiera sumarse y es el único caso documentado de un negocio que gana dinero con la calvicie por los dos extremos. La tradición, no obstante, es común en toda Iberoamérica.
Calvos del mundo, uníos. He querido contrastar hasta dónde se ha llevado esta ambición planetaria y me he topado con el club de calvos de Tsuruta, el cual se reúne desde 1989 en Japón. Su gran prueba es un tira y afloja con ventosas pegadas a la cabeza. Es alucinante. En Estados Unidos, John T. Capps III fundó en 1972 los Bald-Headed Men of America tras un rechazo laboral por su aspecto. Su convención daba premios a la cabeza más lisa. Prohibido afeitarse, tienes que estar encerado como una sepia.
Como puedes leer, muchas son causas nobles. La fundación St. Baldrick’s organiza actos de rapado a favor de la investigación del cáncer infantil. Suma unos 190.500 cráneos y más de 118 millones de dólares. En Filadelfia, el Bald Fest se hizo viral en 2025 y fue lo que motivó, dicen, a que don Armando Christian Pérez, es decir, el omnisciente Pitbull, reuniera a 22.141 personas con gorro calvo en Hyde Park y se hiciera con un récord Guinness.
Han intentado superarlo: el pasado 18 de julio se intentó el mayor encuentro de calvos en Berlín. Pero no hubo suerte: su organizador explicó que había visto concentraciones de pelirrojos y de pitufos, pero ninguna de calvos.
Cuestión de cabeza. Por fortuna o su contrario, España presume de ser el país con más calvos: un 44,5% de los hombres, según una encuesta de una clínica a 4.284 personas. No es un dato oficial, pero la cola de quienes se reconocen en él ya llena un bar. Porque hoy día todo el mundo sabe un poco de la finasterida (sus efectos duran lo que dura el tratamiento), de minoxidil (en 2024, el 89,1% de los dermatólogos encuestados recetaba minoxidil oral a varones) y la dutasterida. Algún que otro dermatólogo admite que muchos hombres la toman sin supervisión.
El trasplante ha dejado de ser un secreto de vestuario y se ha convertido en un potente negocio: el censo de 2025 de la ISHRS (la sociedad de cirujanos capilares) registró un 20% más de pacientes por cirujano que en 2021. El 95% de quienes se operan por primera vez tiene entre 20 y 35 años y el 90% busca sentirse más atractivo. Insparya, la cadena portuguesa con Cristiano Ronaldo de socio y cara visible, abrió en Madrid en 2019 y sumó 9 millones en ventas y 1.500 pacientes durante sus primeros 9 meses. Hoy presume de 15 clínicas en 5 países y más de 80.000 pacientes, y su clínica de Riad, abierta en octubre de 2025, superó los 550 pacientes en su primer año.
Ya documentamos que alrededor del 80% de los hombres y el 40% de las mujeres sufren alopecia androgénica a lo largo de su vida. La ciencia busca cura en una carrera internacional con un equipo español, un fármaco para la artritis y un laboratorio financiado por Google. Su investigador principal ve el producto en el mercado no antes de 2030. Hasta entonces, Vilafranca ofrece cena y estatuilla para quien no se tape la coronilla. Rindamos honor a Kojak, Yul Brynner, el capitán Picard, Collina o Don Limpio, todos ilustres e inimitables.
Portada de Depositphotos / Zurijeta
En Xataka | La industria del pelo en Turquía tiene un nuevo enemigo: una proteína que nos protege de la calvicie

articles.title: How OPay’s past shows how it will react after pulling IPO
articles.text:
OPay’s rise to one of Nigeria’s largest fintechs came after a series of regulatory hurdles. Now, the latest—an inquiry from Chinese regulators—led it to withdraw its $304 million New York listing on October 30. How the company handled the earlier hurdles best guides what it might do now.
Last week, as OPay’s executives rang the opening bell at the New York Stock Exchange, it was supposed to symbolise the final step in the company’s long journey from a small mobile money operator in Nigeria to a global fintech.
Instead, it was another in a long series of hurdles the fintech has endured as the company suspended the listing after a regulatory inquiry from China, its founder Zhou Yahui’s home country.
Since Opera, the browser company owned by a consortium led by Zhou, acquired a controlling stake in Paycom, a mobile-money operator, in 2018, a mix of luck, almost endless capital, and a willingness to start afresh has created a fintech with 50 million users.
A hyperfocus on payments after it ditched its super app play meant OPay was prepared when Nigeria’s 2023 cash crisis broke commercial banks’ apps, and it emerged alongside other fintechs as a trusted digital payment option. Then it turned profitable in 2025 after rapid growth in its lending business.
External events and policy decisions beyond its control have shaped almost every phase of the company’s journey. To pass this latest hurdle, the company will need to revisit its previous attempts that have brought it success.
How OPay got here
In 2018, a Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) capital rule set a ₦2 billion ($1.4 million) minimum capital for mobile money operators, which made institutions that could not meet the requirements cheap to buy. Paycom was one of those institutions. By July, OPay, with Opera’s backing, launched mobile payments in Nigeria, built on an agent banking model that reached unbanked people. The agent network remains part of its moat.
It also sold OKash, its lending product, to Opera for $9.5 million in December 2018. This sale would be important later, as lending grew to OPay’s largest revenue driver.
By May 2019, it launched ORide, a motorcycle-hailing business in Lagos, that brought visibility and app downloads. Other verticals, like OFood, a food delivery service, and OBus, a bus-sharing service, deepened the company’s relationship with the country’s informal sector.
By July 2019, OPay had raised $50 million from investors like Sequoia China, Source Code Capital, and Meituan-Dianping in the largest Nigerian startup round of 2019, until it raised a $120 million Series B round in November. Most of its investors were Chinese platform builders that helped push the super-app playbook that became successful in Asian markets.
By the end of 2019, OPay claimed to have over 140,000 agents and over $10m in daily transaction volume. Its revenue was $16.7 million for the 2019 financial year—almost 20x growth. It lost $71.5 million that year, with almost half, $36 million, going to scaling ORide.
This was the peak of OPay’s blitzscaling era, where it threw a lot of capital into creating a super app that served Nigerians at different points in their daily lives. This super app approach drew users to its payment service. By launching different verticals that Nigerians interacted with at various points, the idea was that it would create stickiness with OPay, the long-term play.
The super app falls apart
In January 2020, OPay got its first reputational shock when Hindenburg Research, the investigative short-seller publication, published a report that alleged Opera, its parent company, was targeting Nigeria’s poor population with predatory loans as its browser margins disappeared and it pursued revenue growth.
The report showed how Opera launched a series of short-term lending businesses—OKash, OPesa, OPay, and CashBean—in Kenya, Nigeria, and India that violated major Google Play Store short-term lending policies by providing an inaccurate description of its loan businesses.
OPay responded by denying the allegations and taking the lending product off its app.
While it was recovering from the shock of the Hindenburg report, a February ban on commercial motorcycles and tricycles in Lagos State, its biggest state in Nigeria, effectively ended ORide, its most visible product and biggest customer acquirer. It sold some bikes and transferred others to OExpress, a delivery product that was soon shut down. In April 2020, Yahui Zhou, OPay’s founder, officially resigned as Chairman of Beijing Kunlun to become full-time CEO of OPay, a move that showed how OPay’s decision-making power did not reside in its biggest market, Nigeria.
While its super app play was falling apart, OPay told TechCabal at the time that it was having its best year ever, claiming 5 million users and over 60% of mobile money transactions in Nigeria. This would be the moment that birthed today’s OPay, as the company focused on becoming a payments and agent-banking company.
By the end of the year, Opera reported that OPay’s monthly transaction value was over $2 billion, a 4.5x growth.
Unicorn status
When OPay raised $400 million in an August 2021 funding round led by SoftBank Vision Fund, the venture capital arm of Japanese conglomerate SoftBank, it achieved a $2 billion valuation, becoming Africa’s third-largest startup worth over $1 billion. It is still the single-largest investment round secured by an African-based startup.
It also hired Olu Akanmu, a former executive director for retail banking at FCMB, a Nigerian commercial bank, as President and co-CEO of OPay Nigeria. It also acquired a microfinance bank licence from the CBN, allowing it to give out loans, which a mobile money licence does not.
Then, by December 2022, OPay got its single biggest gift when the CBN released redesigned naira notes and set an expiry date for the new ones at the end of January 2023. Cash, the backbone of Nigeria’s economy, became scarce, and the apps of several commercial banks failed.
OPay and other fintechs like PalmPay and Moniepoint benefited from this policy as customers opened accounts and began transacting with them because they worked while banks failed, and their agent networks brought banking to doorsteps.
Akanmu, OPay’s former co-CEO, stepped down in January 2024 after almost two years at the company due to a clash of vision between the former banker and the rest of the company’s leadership based outside Nigeria.
Reckoning
By the second half of 2023, OPay had become a mainstay in the fabric of Nigerian life. By October 2023, OPay was the country’s most-downloaded app. But with scale comes regulatory oversight.
Nigeria’s Data Protection Commission (NDPC) investigated OPay over claims that it opened accounts for people without their consent, which the company denied after an internal investigation. No outcome has been made public after NDPC’s investigation.
OPay’s next interaction with regulators was not that smooth. In April 2024, TechCabal broke the news that the CBN barred OPay from opening accounts for new customers. That ban lasted for six weeks, and the fintech, among other fintechs, had to block P2P crypto transfers, verify physical addresses for all account tiers, and update facial verification.
Then, the CBN fined OPay ₦1 billion ($742,991) in the second quarter of 2024 after a routine CBN audit of the fintech sector revealed compliance issues.
It did not end there. An August 2025 CBN circular ordered every PoS terminal to be geo-tagged within 60 days and locked to within 10 metres of the merchant’s registered address, directly limiting OPay’s agent network business. That same month, the CBN capped PoS agents’ daily cash-outs at ₦1.2 million ($930) and individual customers’ at ₦100,000 ($70), another shock to its agent network.
These policy shocks might have shuttered the growth of most businesses, but OPay weathered these storms and drew 88% of its $536 million revenue from Nigeria.
OPay’s road to the shuttered IPO
On February 12, OPay confidentially submitted a draft registration statement, which became public only in October. In April, Opera, which holds 8.6% of OPay, told investors in a securities filing that it saw an 85% chance of an OPay listing within two years.
Opera was confident because OPay had made a sharp turnaround after losing $50.8 million in 2024. The following year, it made a $72.5 million profit on $536.3 million in revenue, up 161%, as new loans grew 285% to $938.3 million.
On May 1, Bloomberg reported that OPay had hired Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and JPMorgan to prepare a U.S. listing that could value it at about $4 billion, double the $2 billion SoftBank’s Vision Fund 2 set in 2021. With these backers, news about OPay’s IPO picked up pace, and what initially sounded like a pipe dream quickly got credibility.
OPay made its filing public on October 9. It showed first-half 2026 revenue of $467.1 million, up 136.5%, and net income of $90.9 million. Lending, at $236.1 million, had overtaken payments as its biggest business, and Nigeria supplied 89.5% of revenue.
The filing listed the risks that came with OPay’s listing: rising provisions for credit losses as lending grew, heavy dependence on Nigeria, and an Indonesian lending arm that OPay controls through contractual arrangements Indonesia does not expressly recognise.
However, one risk it dismissed in its IPO prospectus came back to prevent its listing. In the prospectus, OPay said it was not required to obtain approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) or complete its filing procedures under China’s 2023 overseas listing rules.
But, according to Bloomberg, a Chinese regulatory inquiry prompted the Nigeria-focused payments company to halt its IPO just hours after setting the price. OPay said it was confident the inquiry would be resolved satisfactorily “in the near future.”
The redemption deadline gives OPay until the end of 2027 to try again, about 14 months. To scale its second IPO attempt, the company will need to revisit how well it bounced back from inquiries by Nigerian policymakers.

articles.title: Sony Bravia Theatre U : l'enceinte qui remplace le casque devant la TV perd 150 €
articles.text:
L'enceinte de cou Sony Bravia Theatre U est à 149 € (-50 %)
Un son de cinéma autour des oreilles sans casque ni voisins réveillés : l'enceinte de cou Sony Bravia Theatre U passe à 149 € chez Amazon, 150 € sous son prix conseillé.
L'offre porte sur le modèle HT-AN7, vendu et expédié par Amazon, avec livraison offerte. Le prix de 149 € se compare au prix conseillé de 299 € affiché sur la fiche, soit 150 € d'économie. Sony pratique le même tarif sur sa boutique en ligne.
Un son immersif sans rien sur les oreilles
Posée sur les épaules, la Theatre U diffuse le son au plus près des oreilles sans les couvrir. On profite d'un film à bon volume tout en restant attentif à ce qui se passe autour, sans déranger le reste du foyer. Sony annonce jusqu'à 12 heures d'autonomie et un poids réduit de 15 % par rapport au modèle précédent.
Avec un téléviseur Bravia compatible (A95L, Bravia 5, 7, 8, 8 II et 9), elle prend en charge le Dolby Atmos et le 360 Spatial Sound Mapping. L'application Sound Connect peut aussi adapter la spatialisation à la forme des oreilles. Deux Theatre U peuvent être associées pour regarder un film à deux.
Polyvalente, mais pensée pour les TV Bravia
Hors du salon, la connexion multipoint la relie à deux appareils à la fois, par exemple un ordinateur et un smartphone, et son micro sert aux appels. Pour le jeu, le câble fourni assure une liaison filaire à faible latence. Elle est certifiée IPX4 contre les éclaboussures.
Ses fonctions les plus immersives restent toutefois réservées aux téléviseurs Bravia compatibles : avec une autre TV, il faut se contenter d'une liaison Bluetooth classique. Sur Amazon, elle affiche 4,1/5 sur 523 évaluations.

articles.title: OpenAI Says New GPT-6 Cyber Model Hunts Flaws Without Crossing the Line
articles.text:
OpenAI on Thursday unveiled GPT-6 Cyber, a security model the company says is far more capable than its predecessor and more disciplined about respecting the limits researchers set for it.
On ExploitGym, which checks whether an AI can exploit a given flaw in a remote target, the new model achieved 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber.
OpenAI rated GPT-6 Cyber as Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, above the High designation given to GPT-5.6 Cyber.
In one alignment test, the model received an exploitation task alongside supporting services that were intentionally easy to hack but off-limits. Without deployment safety prompts, it refrained from exploiting them in 99.93% of cases, compared to 94.49% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. With the safety prompts, it never targeted the decoy services.
“This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately,” OpenAI said.
OpenAI researchers pointed the model at the Linux kernel, where it reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and built functional privilege escalation exploits for 948. GPT-5.6 Sol, tested with the same tooling, produced 166.
OpenAI has reported 304 critical issues to maintainers with proposed fixes.
In Firefox, the model documented 81 new flaws that Mozilla deemed high severity, backing each with evidence and reproducible tests. Mozilla has begun rolling out patches.
New protections include monitoring that checks whether the model’s actions line up with what a user is permitted to do, and safeguards meant to stop OpenAI’s models from aiding efforts to compromise industrial controls and other safety-critical systems.
OpenAI refined these safeguards using feedback from industrial cybersecurity firm Dragos, which tested Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab.
“The skill floor is dropping for the reconnaissance and vulnerability research needed before an attack,” said Dragos chief AI officer Rob T. Lee.
Access is currently limited to select approved customers of Daybreak Red, the part of OpenAI’s Daybreak program aimed at advanced exploit work and authorized testing. They can use GPT-6 Cyber through the API and Codex.
OpenAI plans to gradually open the model to all Daybreak Red customers, who are also getting GPT-5.6 Cyber. A dedicated Daybreak Red group for approved critical infrastructure defenders will permit sanctioned testing of critical systems.
Related: OpenAI Finds GPT-6 Astra Quietly Holding Back on Internal Red-Teaming, Exploit Tasks

articles.title: Ottawa earmarks $176 million to establish online super regulator | BetaKit
articles.text:
An online “super regulator” that was first announced by Ottawa this summer is beginning to take shape after the federal government announced millions in budget spending to support its creation.
The news: Thursday’s federal budget includes $176.3 million over five years to establish the Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada (DSDPCC). The commission will be charged with overseeing private-sector privacy regulation under Bill C-36 and implementing the Safe Social Media Act, which is intended to hold social media and chatbot platforms accountable for online harms.
From the source: The DSDPCC has been described by AI Minister Evan Solomon as “a regulator with teeth.” It would have the ability to impose rules and transparency requirements on companies operating social media or AI chatbots, issue binding orders, compel audits, and fine companies who break those rules up to $10 million, or three percent of their global revenue, whichever is higher.
The context: Initially pitched as the Canadian Digital Safety Commission, the DSDPCC was first unveiled in June when the Government of Canada announced its Safe Social Media Act, and later expanded upon when Ottawa proposed changes to the country’s existing privacy laws. Under Bill C-26, which has yet to be passed into law, the DSDPCC would oversee private-sector privacy regulation, taking those responsibilities away from Canada’s existing Office of the Privacy Commissioner.
The budget was sparse on details as to what the rollout of the commission would look like, or benchmarks for when it might come into effect, but said that funding to establish it would begin being deployed during this year and into next year. Previously, the feds said it could take as long as 18 months to get the commission up and running.
Final thought: The legislation Ottawa’s new super regulator is tasked with overseeing and implementing has drawn criticism from some in the tech community, academia, and elsewhere over its broad mandate, its ability to deliver on goals around age-verification and online safety for youth, and its potential to increase digital surveillance and infringe on privacy rights.
Feature image courtesy Evan Solomon via LinkedIn.

articles.title: It's almost 2027, and the FAA is finally replacing the floppy disks used by US air traffic control
articles.text:
Better late than never It's almost 2027, and the US Federal Aviation Administration has just announced it will replace the floppy disks still used by many US air traffic control systems. The upgrade won't be complete until the end of 2028, almost 20 years after most floppy disk manufacturing ended.
At more than 400 sites, the FAA still uses floppy disks in four systems to upload data to aging information displays that controllers consult for weather conditions, airport status, and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs).
One of these is the Information Display System 4, or IDS-4, which was deployed in the early 1990s and runs on a Microsoft platform that is no longer supported. These systems provide operational information controllers need to manage traffic.
 – Secretary Sean Duffy (@SecDuffy) November 5, 2026
Many US air traffic control facilities still rely on legacy systems tied to infrastructure built in the 1990s. These systems have undergone extensive safety testing and must remain operational around the clock. Replacing that technology is a difficult and expensive undertaking, requiring new systems that meet strict safety and security standards and can be introduced without disrupting operations.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted a message on X yesterday confirming the modernization of the facilities. "Floppy disks from the 1980s: OUT 21st century tech: IN," he wrote.
The new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) will replace the four 1980s-era systems. It consolidates operational information into a shared platform, including weather impacts, equipment disruptions, flight alerts, restricted-airspace schedules, and pilot weather reports. The FAA says it will improve information distribution and reduce repairs and workarounds associated with older equipment.
The FAA wants E-IDS installed at 435 facilities by the end of 2028. Five sites have already replaced their floppy disk-based systems: Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport, Greater Rochester International Airport, and data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City.
In 2023, an FAA assessment found that over a third of the nation's air traffic control systems were unsustainable, and some were starting to fail.
It was reported last year that several FAA sites were still running Windows 95. The FAA also uses decades-old Compaq computers that are so out of date that replacement parts have to be bought from eBay. Another legacy technology still in use is paper flight strips, the pieces of cardstock on which key details of a single flight – such as call sign, aircraft type, and altitude – are printed or handwritten.
"We're moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement.
A lack of funding has long been one of the issues preventing air traffic control modernization. The FAA is now using $12.5 billion in funding provided by President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill to replace the archaic systems.

articles.title: iPhone Duo mit gebrochenen Displays: Ist das Problem größer als gedacht?
articles.text:
Crackgate beim iPhone Duo: Nicht nur gebrochene Displays werden zum Problem
Schon kurz nach dem Verkaufsstart des iPhone Duos meldeten sich erste Käufer:innen mit Problemen. Der innere Bildschirm ist offenbar in einigen Fällen beim Auffalten gebrochen. Die Gründe sind nach wie vor nicht ganz klar. Die Mitarbeiter:innen von iFixit machten, nachdem sie das Gerät auseinandergenommen hatten, eine Stütze, die den Bildschirm eigentlich schützen soll, als vermeintlichen Übeltäter aus. Bloomberg-Reporter Mark Gurman geht davon aus, dass eine „Charge von Duos mit einem defekten Scharnierteil ausgeliefert wurde“, die eben jenes Problem auslöst.
Apple selbst spricht nur von einer „kleinen Anzahl“ betroffener Geräte. Gurman merkt jedoch an, dass „klein“ nach Apple-Standards immer noch tausende Geräte betreffen könnte. Ein Bericht von Macrumors von Anfang November unterstreicht die These. Demnach soll das Unternehmen ein Memo an Store-Mitarbeiter:innen und autorisierte Verkäufer:innen verschickt haben, das Vorgaben enthält, wie mit den Defekten umzugehen ist.
iPhone Duo: Apples Anweisungen an Stores und Reseller
Der Verdacht liegt also nahe, dass das Problem größer ist, als angenommen, wenn Apple so ein Schreiben herumschickt. Allerdings lässt sich das aus der Ferne kaum verlässlich sagen. Wie viele Geräte wirklich von dem Bildschirmproblem betroffen sind, ist nicht bekannt. Sollten Kund:innen mit einem defekten Gerät jedoch einen Store aufsuchen, empfiehlt das Unternehmen Techniker:innen laut Macrumors schlicht, das jeweilige iPhone Duo zu prüfen, und danach nach dem Standardverfahren zu reparieren oder eben auszutauschen. Ob das Schreiben nur an US-Stores und -Händler oder weltweit verschickt wurde, ist unklar.
Der Defekt trat allerdings offenbar schon kurz nach Inbetriebnahme des iPhones auf, wie Macrumors mit Verweis auf Apple schreibt. Einen Rückruf der Geräte durch Apple gibt es nicht, ein Serviceprogramm, wie es der Hersteller etwa bei Kameraproblemen mit dem iPhone 14 Plus angeboten hatte, auch nicht. Bei letzterem hatte Apple den Fehler bei betroffenen Kund:innen kostenlos repariert.
Vorerst gilt damit Apples bislang einzige Aussage zu dem Fehler: Betroffene Kund:innen sollen sich an Apple Care wenden, um ein Austauschgerät zu bekommen. Laut Gurman könne es dabei aber zu Problemen kommen. Weil die Geräte derzeit sehr knapp seien, müssten einige Kund:innen länger auf ihren Ersatz warten. Apple selbst hatte im Rahmen einer Telefonkonferenz mit Investoren angekündigt, dass es schwer vorherzusagen sei, wie schnell man die Nachfrage bedienen könne. Wer jetzt ein iPhone Duo bestellen will, muss sich bis Ende Januar 2027 gedulden. Vorher trifft das Paket nicht ein.
Allerdings sind in den vergangenen Tagen nur sehr wenige Fälle neuer Bildschirmprobleme bekannt geworden. Nach einem holprigen Start droht dem Unternehmen also kein Debakel, wie es zuletzt 2014 beim iPhone 6 („Bendgate“) gab.

articles.title: GitHub Actions Lockfiles Reach GA to Secure Workflow Dependencies
articles.text:
GitHub has made workflow dependency lockfiles for GitHub Actions generally available on October 28, 2026, two weeks after the feature entered public preview. Workflows can maintain clear tag and branch references. The runner executes the specific commits listed in the .github/workflows/actions.lock file, even if those references change later. The feature is available on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. The GA release includes the capabilities from the preview.
The change targets a long-standing weakness in how Actions resolves dependencies. A reference like actions/checkout@v4 or a branch name can change. This means a hacked action can add bad code to a pipeline without altering the repository using it. Teams can pin to full commit SHAs, but this reduces readability. It also leaves transitive dependencies, like those from composite actions, unpinned. Lockfiles address both gaps by recording commits for direct and transitive dependencies.
Tooling comes through the gh actions-lock extension for the GitHub CLI, hosted in the gh-actions-lock repository, which generates and maintains the lockfile. Adoption follows the workflow. Once a workflow is onboarded, every dependency needs a lockfile entry. The Actions runtime then runs the recorded commit, no matter where the tag or branch points. This lets teams migrate incrementally rather than converting an entire organization at once. The extension has a verification mode. It checks if the lockfile is up to date without changing any files. This way, it can act as a CI gate to spot differences between workflow files and the lockfile.
Dependabot integration addresses the usual cost of pinning, which is stale pins. When Dependabot opens a version update for an action in an onboarded workflow, it also updates the matching lockfile entry. Both changes appear in the same pull request, so the workflow reference and locked commit stay in sync. GitHub says this works without additional configuration. For governance, enterprise, organization, and repository admins can enable a "Require lockfile" policy. This policy helps enforce adoption at the relevant scope.
GitHub is explicit about the limits of the mechanism. A lockfile guarantees that runs use the commits you locked, but it does not determine whether those commits are safe, and the announcement advises reviewing dependencies before locking them. The security value therefore depends on the review that happens when an entry is created or updated. In practice, the Dependabot pull request becomes the review point, and teams that auto-merge those updates will carry any malicious change straight into the lockfile.
The release arrives as GitHub tightens other Actions defaults. A November 2 changelog entry announced that pull_request_target will be blocked by default starting December 2, another change aimed at limiting how untrusted code reaches privileged workflow contexts.
For teams evaluating adoption, setup instructions are in the GitHub Docs page on workflow dependency lockfiles. A reasonable starting point is to onboard a few high-privilege workflows, such as release or deployment pipelines, add the staleness check to CI, and confirm that Dependabot's combined pull requests fit existing review practices before enabling the enterprise-wide policy.
Competing platforms have not announced a native equivalent so far. GitLab's pipeline security guidance advises users to manually pin includes and components to commit SHAs. Users should also pin images to digests. After the March 2026 supply chain incidents, GitLab introduced open-source pipeline execution policies. These policies focus on blocking known attack patterns instead of creating a dependency manifest. Microsoft's Zero Trust guidance for Azure Pipelines also suggests using SHA pinning. It advises limiting Marketplace extensions too.
CircleCI orbs use a central semantic-versioning registry instead of commit hashes. This approach keeps the registry immutable. Teams on these platforms often use cross-platform tools. For example, they might use pinner to pin tags to SHAs and add a CI verification step. They may also rely on scanners like ActionSieve to flag unpinned references.
These tools pin the reference written in the pipeline file but do not resolve transitive dependencies, which is the gap GitHub's lockfile design addresses. As with GitHub's feature, none of them judges whether a pinned dependency is trustworthy, so the review step that precedes locking remains the control that matters.

articles.title: Shure’s popular podcasting and streaming mic is almost $50 off
articles.text:
While the Shure Mv7 Plus is popular with streamers and podcasters, it’s equally good at impressing your friends and coworkers on meetings and Discord calls. It’s currently marked down to $255 at various retailers, including Amazon, Guitar Center, and directly from Shure. That’s almost $50 lower than its usual price, and just a few dollars off Amazon’s all-time low. If you don’t already have a stand, both Amazon and Shure are offering a bundle that includes the mic and a desktop stand for $269, and the white model is also discounted at Amazon.
Shure’s popular podcasting and streaming mic is almost $50 off
This Verge-favorite microphone for podcasting is discounted, along with other audio products.
Shure MV7 Plus
Shure’s MV7 Plus is an updated version of its popular USB microphone. The new version features a USB-C port, a customizable LED light panel, and several additional features available in the Motiv Mix app.
When our team shared some of our favorite audio gear in late 2024, we noted that the Mv7 Plus was the mic we send to podcast guests for remote interviews. It’s known for its crisp and clean audio quality, with auto-leveling and denoising, so you can use it without touching an equalizer.
The MV7’s unique shape and sonic profile is inspired by the Shure SM7B (also discounted), a microphone that’s often used in professional recording. This version is meant as a more budget-friendly variant for content creators looking for a simpler setup, with both an XLR output and USB-C, letting you wire into an audio interface or directly to a computer.

articles.title: D-Link warns of multiple zero-days in DGS-3130 Series switches
articles.text:
D-Link shared mitigation measures for multiple unpatched security flaws affecting DGS-3130 series managed Gigabit stackable switches.
These switch models provide multi-gigabit uplinks, allowing enterprise network administrators to eliminate data bottlenecks, and are designed primarily for small-to-medium businesses (SMBs) and metro Ethernet deployments.
While D-Link didn't share details on these flaws and has yet to publicly disclose the CVE IDs for easier tracking, it said Spectrum Community Solutions network engineer Giresh Kumar Enugu found the bugs in the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) authentication, access control, and information handling.
Successful exploitation could allow attackers to obtain sensitive device data, make unauthorized credential/configuration changes, leak SNMP communities, or cause service disruptions and device resets.
The zero-days affect multiple DGS-3130-30TS firmware versions, and the company is still investigating the impact on other D-Link switching platforms and firmware security mechanisms (including SSH service security configuration, safeguards underlying operating-system credentials, and handles firmware encryption/embedded cryptographic keys).
"The reported vulnerabilities involve the D-Link Discovery Protocol (DDP) and certain components of the device's firmware security architecture," D-Link said.
"According to the security researcher, successful exploitation of certain vulnerabilities may allow an attacker with access to the affected network to obtain sensitive device information, perform unauthorized administrative operations, modify device configuration, or disrupt network services."
Until it releases new firmware to address these flaws, D-Link asked admins to disable DDP to remove the primary known attack vector, remove unnecessary or default SNMP community strings, and restrict SSH, web UI, and SNMP accessibility solely to isolated management networks and designated admin hosts.
D-Link also advised admins to maintain offline switch configuration backups and track device logs for unexpected configuration changes, unprompted reboots, or factory resets.
In September, D-Link warned customers of a maximum-severity zero-day (tracked as CVE-2026-86296) with a public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit and no patch, affecting legacy DIR-822A dual-band Wi-Fi routers.
