articles.title: China mantém 600 mil chips da Nvidia parados à espera de autorização
articles.text:
Cerca de 600 mil chips H200 da Nvidia estão armazenados em Hong Kong, aguardando autorização de Pequim para serem enviados à China continental. O governo chinês ainda não liberou importações em grande escala, apesar da demanda de empresas de tecnologia por processadores avançados de inteligência artificial.
A resistência de Pequim reflete a preocupação com a dependência de tecnologia norte-americana. Ao mesmo tempo, empresas chinesas precisam dos chips da Nvidia para atender à crescente demanda por capacidade computacional.
China libera pequenas remessas, mas mantém restrições
Nos últimos meses, Pequim autorizou a entrada de algumas unidades do H200. Grandes empresas chinesas de internet receberam aproximadamente 10 mil chips cada, segundo pessoas ouvidas pela Reuters. Pequenas quantidades também chegaram ao país por meio de intermediários e rotas indiretas.
O H200 não é o processador de IA mais recente da Nvidia, mas oferece capacidades que as alternativas chinesas ainda não conseguiram igualar. O chip é especialmente útil para treinar modelos de IA quando combinado com o software da fabricante.
A oferta limitada está relacionada aos controles de exportação impostos pelos Estados Unidos desde 2022, que restringem o acesso chinês a chips avançados da Nvidia e aos equipamentos necessários para fabricá-los. Com menos unidades disponíveis por canais autorizados, compradores passaram a recorrer ao mercado paralelo, onde os preços subiram.
No fim de outubro, servidores equipados com esses processadores eram oferecidos na China continental pelos seguintes valores:
- Mais de 6 milhões de yuans (aproximadamente R$ 4,94 milhões): servidor com oito placas H200, cerca de três vezes o preço de um ano antes.
- Mais de 20 milhões de yuans (cerca de R$ 16,45 milhões): servidor equipado com os chips Blackwell mais recentes da Nvidia, também sujeitos aos controles de exportação norte-americanos.
Os valores foram informados por uma pessoa familiarizada com o assunto. No caso do H200, o preço correspondia a aproximadamente US$ 900 mil (aproximadamente R$ 4,95 milhões).
Disputa tecnológica entre Washington e Pequim
As restrições aos chips fazem parte de uma disputa comercial mais ampla entre Estados Unidos e China. Washington havia proibido a exportação do H200 para o mercado chinês, mas o governo de Donald Trump mudou a política no ano passado e autorizou a Nvidia a vender os processadores a clientes chineses aprovados, após negociações comerciais entre os dois países.
Em maio, a Reuters informou que os Estados Unidos haviam aprovado vendas a dez empresas chinesas, entre elas Alibaba, Tencent e ByteDance. Pequim, porém, estabeleceu suas próprias limitações às importações.
Em julho, o site The Information informou que autoridades chinesas haviam sinalizado a empresas como Alibaba, ByteDance e DeepSeek a possibilidade de comprar quantidades limitadas de H200 para treinar modelos de IA. Segundo a publicação, o total de aprovações poderia ficar abaixo de 200 mil unidades. O governo também queria que as empresas priorizassem processadores nacionais para a inferência, etapa em que os modelos de IA executam tarefas.
A busca por alternativas não impediu novas encomendas de produtos da Nvidia. Segundo reportagem da Reuters publicada em outubro, ByteDance, Alibaba e Tencent encomendaram mais de 3 milhões de placas gráficas RTX Pro 5500. O modelo é menos potente e está em conformidade com as regras de exportação dos Estados Unidos. O preço de tabela combinado dos pedidos superava US$ 35 bilhões.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Q&A: How hackers turned up the heat on Europe’s fridges | BetaKit
articles.text:
European supermarkets have been targeted by costly cyberattacks to grocery stores, and even blood banks, that tamper with the temperatures of commercial fridges and freezers.
Jeff Shirley is the founder and CEO of Rivercity Innovations, a Saskatoon-based tech company founded in 2017 that uses low-powered sensors to monitor data like temperature, GPS positioning, moisture, and humidity—meaning it will alert a company if its fridges have experienced a drastic temperature change. Rivercity offers its systems in seven countries, and says it’s been receiving calls from European customers since the hacks.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporter Jesse Cole sat down with Shirley to chat about what happened in Europe, and whether Canadian Internet-of-Things devices, from fridges to HVAC systems, should be considered at risk.
The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Why does a fridge need to be connected to the internet in the first place?
Think of a grocery chain with hundreds of stores. You’re not going to send out a technician to every single case at every single store every day to adjust settings and controls. So, experts remote in and simultaneously monitor.
Those pieces of equipment are also not as simple as a house fridge. Sometimes they have different temperature zones. Ice cream is usually -25°C, whereas frozen pizzas might be at -18°C. That all ties into energy management and planning for predictive maintenance.
It’s not just a refrigerator: it’s a very complex, multi-million-dollar coolant system managing its energy to protect the environment and keep your food safe at the right level, and making sure that glass door doesn’t frost up every time you open it. It’s extremely complex.
Can you tell us what happened with these high-profile hacks?
These cooler systems—think your supermarket, your grocery store—they have very big refrigeration freezer systems. These have mechanical rooms that run coolant and power to them. Those coolant systems are monitored by companies and are controlled through a control system. The service companies remote into those systems to check the cooling, the performance, and ensure all of the temperatures are right.
What has happened in Europe is that a vendor had some hardware that required patches. If businesses didn’t patch it, people could see those systems if they were publicly on the internet, through the channels that the remote service companies would use.
Those people attempted to hack the systems and succeeded. They changed the settings, just like if you’re in your house; they increased the thermostat and said, “let’s go to 50°C,” and the system said, “OK, because you’re the service company.”
Freezers, by design, have to run defrost cycles. Sometimes, every eight hours or so, it’ll run up to like -5°C to burn off the frost from the humidity in the store condensing on the glass. Those defrost cycles were leveraged by the hackers to go to 50°C and stay there. Overnight, all the frozen pizzas thawed, all the meat thawed, all the ice cream melted, and you come into the store at 7 a.m. and you have puddles and ruined product.
Which, I imagine, is worth tens of millions of dollars across a chain.
Hundreds of millions of euros were lost in the first wave about three weeks ago, and in the last wave, more countries were hit by similar hacks.
The damage is immediate. The only thing that mitigates it is third-party monitoring, because these coolers are wired to behave like this. They’re not unusual settings for somebody to say, “I want you to be warmer temporarily.”
I don’t believe it was nefarious because there’s no malware that we’re hearing about. Nobody’s saying, “pay me in Bitcoin.” It seems to be across the platform of wired control systems, and I expect it will extend to more countries.
So you need third-party monitoring. Our business—that’s what we do. We’ve been getting calls.
Tell me how that third-party monitoring works.
Think about your local Co-op or IGA. The big grocery stores have wired control systems. They’re physically wired in the building. They’re very expensive and very complex. A smaller company is not going to put a $100,000 wired monitoring system in there. What River City does is monitor the coolers and the freezers. [Editor’s note: It does so using battery power and Long-Range, Wide-Area Network, rather than Wi-Fi.] We alert the staff if the freezer isn’t normal. We send out those alerts as a triage, kind of like a weather warning on your cell phone about tornadoes coming.
Here in Canada, this has been good for our business, but my heart goes out to these companies.
It’s also not just about the hacks. Whether it’s a hack or a forest fire or a flood season, businesses lose their power. So having the ability to get those alerts, to go back and validate that food, is still good.
We have a very awesome client in British Columbia. Do you remember the forest fires in the Okanagan Valley this summer? The power went out; they knew they were going to be down for more than a day. So they decided to donate that food to the first responders in the community, so that client of ours went in, sent the semi-trucks in with permission from the perimeter border guards, and brought that food out to the first responders. Doesn’t that sound better than it’s all melted and on the floor in the morning?
You mentioned these vulnerabilities are stemming from unpatched software. How vulnerable are we in Canada?
There are five or six major players in wired control systems worldwide. In Canada, three or four are very active. They have their own security teams, their own departments. They will advise the grocery chain that this hardware needs to be updated. If the chain has updated it, problem solved.
It’s no different whether it’s a computer or a refrigeration system. You can think of this as a very complex IT nightmare. There will be big chains doing due diligence right now, asking, “are we vulnerable? Have we patched it?” And if they haven’t, just imagine having 1,200 stores with 100 coolers each, and you need to update the control systems in those stores, which might be a complex circuit board and computer and management system. And every store has its latest versions and updates, which might not all be aligned.
Absolutely, it’s going to be our priority for Canadian brands. I think yes, we’re vulnerable, but Canada is a very developed country. We’re on top of things
Do you think this signals anything concerning about the broader Internet-of-Things ecosystem when it comes to cybersecurity risks?
The moral of the story is you can’t run a large enterprise business with IoT-connected devices for the public if you’re not going to put in best practices for security. Use a VPN. Use firewall rules. Use dedicated ports. Use two-factor authentication. Change your passwords to be complex. Change your passwords every 60 days. Who would have thought that the refrigeration control panel needed the default password changed?
It’s a major problem. The Internet of Things is more than just grocery stores.
Commercial properties have a remotely managed central HVAC system. Say somebody hacks a commercial building and turns everybody to 50°C? My advice is to get some safety nets in place.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by JC Gellidon.

articles.title: The Best GPU for Budget PCs: CPU/GPU Scaling Tested
articles.text:
If you're looking to upgrade the graphics card in a budget or older PC, buying a faster GPU doesn't necessarily mean you'll get better gaming performance. In fact, our testing shows that a Radeon RX 9060 XT can actually outperform the more powerful GeForce RTX 5070 when paired with a slower processor. It sounds counterintuitive, but there's a good reason for it.
Recently, we revisited Nvidia's CPU driver overhead issue and found that it can still be a problem for GeForce RTX 50 series GPUs. In that test, we compared the RTX 5070 Ti and Radeon RX 9070 XT using the Ryzen 5 5600, which admittedly is quite a slow CPU to pair with such expensive modern graphics cards.
However, as we've found in previous testing, this is an architectural issue that can affect GeForce GPUs beyond the RTX 5070 Ti. Logically, then, we should see similar behavior with something like the RTX 5060. But as they say, seeing is believing. Perhaps that's why some people dismissed our findings as a complete non-issue that wasn't worth investigating.
So this time, we're looking at more modest hardware configurations, focusing on the GeForce RTX 5060 and Radeon RX 9060 XT. We've also included the RTX 5070 to see how a more powerful GPU scales with slower processors.
It's entirely conceivable that those shopping for an RTX 5060 or RX 9060 XT have an older or lower-end PC, and right now isn't a great time to upgrade to the latest platforms using DDR5 memory.
One of the most popular budget CPUs of the last few years has been the Ryzen 5 5500, much to our frustration. It's a particularly poor choice, but at around $90, it seems buyers just can't resist.
We suspect most buyers see the Ryzen 5 5600 selling for around $150 and assume the $90 Ryzen 5 5500 is almost the same thing, just a bit slower. A 40% saving certainly sounds appealing. Unfortunately, despite the similar names, they're wildly different products.
AMD Ryzen 5 5600 vs. Ryzen 5 5500
|  | Ryzen 5 5600 | Ryzen 5 5500 | 
|---|---|---|
| Price (MSRP) | $200 | $160 | 
| Release Date | Apr 4, 2022 |  | 
| Cores / Threads | 6 / 12 |  | 
| Base Clock | 3.5 GHz | 3.6 GHz | 
| Boost Clock | 4.4 GHz | 4.2 GHz | 
| L3 Cache [Total] | 32 MB | 16 MB | 
| Box Cooler | AMD Wraith Stealth |  | 
| Chiplets | 1 x CCD, 1 x I/OD | N/A (monolithic) | 
| Core Config | 1 x 6 |  | 
| TDP | 65 W |  | 
Whatever the reason, the Ryzen 5 5500 has been selling like hotcakes for years, so there are plenty of them out there. That alone makes it worth including in our testing.
We have a good range of CPUs that should provide some interesting scaling data. The focus here is primarily on CPU performance, so this isn't an exhaustive CPU/GPU scaling benchmark across multiple resolutions. Instead, we're concentrating on 1080p testing to expose CPU limitations.
Then again, you could argue, and some certainly do, that 8GB GPUs like the RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT are 1080p products anyway. We don't want to get too bogged down in the basics of CPU testing (again), so let's jump straight into the benchmark graphs.
Test System Specs
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D AMD Ryzen 7 7600 | MSI MAG X870E Tomahawk Max [BIOS 7E59v5A32] G.Skill Trident Z5 RGB 32GB DDR5-6000 CL30-38-38-96 | 
|  | AMD Ryzen 5 5600 AMD Ryzen 5 5500 | MSI MPG X570S Carbon MAX WiFi [BIOS 7D52v1D1] G.Skill Trident Z Neo RGB 32GB DDR4-3600 CL14-15-15-35 | 
| Graphics Card | GeForce RTX 5070, RTX 5060 & Radeon RX 9060 XT 8GB |  | 
| Power Supply | Kolink Regulator Gold ATX 3.0 1200W |  | 
| Storage | TeamGroup T-Force Cardea A440 M.2 PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD 4TB |  | 
| Operating System | Windows 11 26H2 |  | 
| Display Driver | Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver 621.01, AMD Radeon Adrenalin 26.10.2 WHQL |  | 
Benchmarks
War Thunder
Starting with War Thunder, it's clear that the RTX 5070 is substantially faster than the RX 9060 XT, as you'd expect. When paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, it was 35% faster on average, while even the standard RTX 5060 led the budget Radeon GPU by a 10% margin. Still, using the High Quality preset at 1080p, all three GPUs managed to push over 400 fps with the 9800X3D.
But when we step down to the Ryzen 5 7600, performance becomes much more CPU-limited, with all three GPUs delivering similar results. The RX 9060 XT was slightly faster than the RTX 5060, but Nvidia's additional CPU overhead isn't hurting the GeForce GPUs too much in this example.
Similar results were seen with the Ryzen 5 5600, but once we drop down to the 5500, the RX 9060 XT starts to enjoy a small performance advantage, beating the RTX 5060 by 8% and even the RTX 5070 by 5%.
So when heavily CPU-limited, the Radeon GPU does perform better, though only slightly in this example.
Marvel Rivals
The Marvel Rivals results are far more interesting. First, with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, we see that the RTX 5070 is massively faster than the RX 9060 XT, offering 42% more performance. However, the Radeon GPU manages to edge out the RTX 5060 by a slim 6% margin.
When we retest using the Ryzen 5 7600, not much changes between the RX 9060 XT and RTX 5060. In fact, the margin narrows slightly in favor of the GeForce GPU. However, the much faster RTX 5070 becomes considerably more CPU-limited, shrinking its lead over the Radeon GPU to just 23%.
Then, as we move to AM4 with the Ryzen 5 5600, the RX 9060 XT extends its lead over the RTX 5060 to 7%, while the increasingly CPU-limited RTX 5070 is now just 7% faster than the Radeon.
Up to this point, the data looks like a typical CPU bottleneck, but that starts to change with the Ryzen 5 5500. Using this low-end processor, the RX 9060 XT is now 20% faster than the RTX 5060 and, remarkably, 17% faster than the RTX 5070.
This unusual result highlights the impact of Nvidia's additional CPU overhead. Despite being a much faster GPU under normal circumstances, the RTX 5070 actually falls behind the budget Radeon when paired with a sufficiently slow processor.
Space Marine 2
Nvidia's CPU overhead issue is even more noticeable in Space Marine 2. When testing with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, everything looks pretty normal. The RTX 5070 is by far the fastest GPU tested, rendering 127 fps, making it 21% faster than the RTX 5060 and 31% faster than the RX 9060 XT.
But that all changes with the Ryzen 5 7600. Performance immediately becomes CPU-limited, and the RX 9060 XT is now 6% faster than the RTX 5060 when comparing average frame rates, and 10% faster for the 1% lows. It even manages to beat the RTX 5070.
As we continue to reduce CPU performance, those margins only grow. With the Ryzen 5 5600, the RX 9060 XT is now 15% faster than the RTX 5060, or nearly 20% faster when comparing 1% lows.
But we're not done yet. With the lowly Ryzen 5 5500, the margin balloons to 32%, with a 37% improvement in 1% lows. The RTX 5070 fares slightly better than the 5060, but even so, the RX 9060 XT is still 25% faster.
Hitman World of Assassination
Hitman World of Assassination also proved highly CPU-sensitive. With the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, the RTX 5070 averaged 245 fps, with 1% lows of 128 fps. This represented a 33% advantage over the RX 9060 XT, which averaged 184 fps, while the RTX 5060 managed 181 fps.
Moving to the Ryzen 5 7600 saw the RTX 5070's average frame rate drop by 44% to just 136 fps, with 1% lows falling to 74 fps. Interestingly, the RX 9060 XT pulled slightly ahead at 138 fps, while also delivering stronger 1% lows of 77 fps.
This trend continued with the Ryzen 5 5600 and 5500, where the Radeon averaged 124 and 106 fps, respectively, outperforming the RTX 5070 by approximately 7-8% in both cases.
Battlefield 6
Battlefield 6 also revealed substantial CPU bottlenecks with the Ryzen 5 processors. Starting with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, the RTX 5070 averaged an impressive 251 fps, making it 44% faster than the RTX 5060 and 48% faster than the RX 9060 XT.
However, moving to the Ryzen 5 7600 saw that advantage disappear almost entirely, with all three GPUs averaging between 167 and 169 fps. The 1% lows were noticeably better with the Radeon GPU, though.
Similar results were seen with the Ryzen 5 5600, where the RX 9060 XT edged ahead at 156 fps, compared to 151 fps for the RTX 5070.
Interestingly, with the Ryzen 5 5500, both GeForce GPUs delivered identical results, averaging 126 fps with 1% lows of 97 fps.
The RX 9060 XT, however, was noticeably faster, averaging 143 fps with 1% lows of 111 fps. That made it 13% faster in average frame rates and 14% faster for the 1% lows, another clear example of how Nvidia's additional CPU overhead can become a disadvantage when paired with a slower processor.
Horizon Zero Dawn
Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered gives us some interesting results that don't really highlight Nvidia's CPU overhead issue. Instead, they expose a VRAM-related problem, but only for the RTX 5060, despite both the RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT having just 8GB of VRAM.
The problem for the RTX 5060 is that it features just a PCIe x8 interface, whereas the RX 9060 XT gets the full x16 bandwidth, effectively doubling the available bandwidth for transfers between the GPU and system memory. As a result, the Radeon was 27% faster with the 9800X3D, or a massive 47% faster when comparing 1% lows. That's despite the RTX 5070 beating the Radeon GPU by a 40% margin.
Dropping down to the Ryzen 5 7600 limits the RX 9060 XT more than the RTX 5060, though we're still using the same PCIe 5.0 interface and DDR5 memory.
But when we switch to the Ryzen 5 5600, we're now limited to PCIe 4.0 and DDR4 memory, and this cripples the RTX 5060. The result is particularly poor 1% lows, with the RX 9060 XT delivering up to 61% better performance.
Things get even worse for the budget GeForce GPU with the Ryzen 5 5500, which limits us to PCIe 3.0. Now the RX 9060 XT is more than twice as fast. The RTX 5060 was effectively unusable here, suffering constant stuttering and occasional pauses as data was transferred between video memory and system memory over the severely bandwidth-constrained PCIe connection.
Gears of War: E-Day
Gears of War: E-Day delivered some surprisingly consistent results, particularly with the Radeon RX 9060 XT. Regardless of whether it was paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Ryzen 5 7600, or Ryzen 5 5600, the Radeon averaged exactly 72 fps, dropping only slightly to 70 fps with the Ryzen 5 5500.
The RTX 5070 was considerably faster with the higher-end processors, averaging 97 fps with the 9800X3D and 96 fps with the Ryzen 5 7600.
However, its performance dropped to 79 fps with the Ryzen 5 5600 before falling to just 67 fps with the Ryzen 5 5500. This allowed the RX 9060 XT to pull ahead while also delivering stronger 1% lows of 53 fps compared with 45 fps, an 18% improvement. The Radeon also delivered 36% better 1% lows than the RTX 5060.
The RTX 5060 generally trailed both GPUs, although its results remained relatively consistent. Overall, the Radeon showed very little sensitivity to processor performance, while the RTX 5070 benefited noticeably from faster CPUs, as you'd expect at 1080p.
Hogwarts Legacy
Hogwarts Legacy showed some of the biggest performance differences between the processors, particularly with the RTX 5070. Paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, the 12GB GeForce GPU averaged an impressive 133 fps, comfortably ahead of the RX 9060 XT at 103 fps and RTX 5060 at 99 fps.
However, things changed considerably with the Ryzen 5 7600, where the RTX 5070 dropped to just 76 fps. Interestingly, the RX 9060 XT managed 91 fps, giving it a comfortable 20% performance advantage despite being the slower GPU with the 9800X3D.
The Radeon maintained this lead with the Ryzen 5 5600, averaging 76 fps compared with 68 fps for the RTX 5070. That's a 12% performance advantage over the higher-end RTX 5070 and 17% over the RTX 5060.
Then, with the Ryzen 5 5500, both GeForce cards managed just 60 fps, while the Radeon delivered 73 fps alongside stronger 1% lows of 44 fps, making it up to 26% faster. Again, this strange data is entirely a result of Nvidia CPU overhead issue.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4
Modern Warfare 4 produced some interesting results, particularly for the Radeon RX 9060 XT. With the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, the RTX 5070 comfortably led the pack, averaging 237 fps, followed by the RX 9060 XT at 195 fps and RTX 5060 at 173 fps.
The RTX 5070 maintained its lead with the Ryzen 5 7600, although the gap narrowed to just 16 fps as performance became much more CPU-limited.
Things became more interesting with the Ryzen 5 5600, where the RX 9060 XT actually pulled ahead, averaging 187 fps compared with 175 fps for the RTX 5070. It also delivered noticeably stronger 1% lows at 133 fps, making it up to 16% faster.
This trend continued with the Ryzen 5 5500, where the RX 9060 XT averaged 167 fps, comfortably ahead of both GeForce GPUs. But it was the 1% lows that really stood out, with the Radeon delivering at least 31% better performance.
Overall, the RX 9060 XT proved remarkably consistent across the different processors, while the GeForce GPUs suffered much larger performance losses as CPU performance decreased.
Stalker 2: Heart of Chornobyl
Finally, we have Stalker 2, and once again, the results are quite interesting. The RTX 5070 comfortably led when paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, averaging 120 fps compared with 86 fps for the RTX 5060 and 82 fps for the RX 9060 XT. So we're looking at a massive 46% advantage over the Radeon GPU.
Moving down to the Ryzen 5 7600, the RTX 5070 maintained a reasonable advantage at 102 fps, although the gap between all three graphics cards narrowed considerably with the Ryzen 5 5600. Here, they delivered between 75 and 78 fps, which looks very much like a typical CPU bottleneck.
However, when we reduce CPU performance further, the RX 9060 XT actually manages to pull ahead with the Ryzen 5 5500, averaging 73 fps compared with just 65 fps for the RTX 5070. It also delivers noticeably stronger 1% lows at 61 fps compared with 52 fps.
That's a 17% improvement in 1% lows and a 12% advantage in average frame rates. Once again, we're seeing a situation where Nvidia's additional CPU overhead allows the budget Radeon to outperform a considerably more powerful GeForce GPU.
10-Game Average
Looking at the 10-game average data, the results paint a pretty clear picture. First, as you'd expect, when not CPU-limited, the RTX 5070 is much faster than the RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT, offering 36-39% more performance when paired with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D.
That margin is eroded to 16% over the RTX 5060 when paired with the Ryzen 5 7600, and just 7% when compared with the RX 9060 XT. This is what you'd expect to see, though, and the data is particularly relevant for those trying to maximize frame rates.
In games like Counter-Strike, Apex Legends, Valorant, and Fortnite, your CPU is often more important than your GPU, within reason, of course.
Something we noticed when comparing the Ryzen 5 7600 results with those of the 9800X3D is that the RX 9060 XT went from being just 2% faster than the RTX 5060 with the higher-end CPU to 8% faster with the Ryzen 5 processor. We also saw an even larger improvement in 1% lows.
This trend continued with the Ryzen 5 5600, where the RX 9060 XT was able to match the RTX 5070, making it up to 17% faster than the RTX 5060.
Then, with the Ryzen 5 5500, we run headfirst into Nvidia's CPU overhead issue. As we've said many times in the past, this really is a problem budget gamers need to be aware of.
Using this low-end processor, the RX 9060 XT was 36% faster than the RTX 5060 when comparing 1% lows, and 24% faster in average frame rates. That said, some of these results were skewed by the RTX 5060's limited PCIe bandwidth. However, even when comparing against the RTX 5070, we still find that the RX 9060 XT was 12% faster on average, or 14% faster when comparing 1% lows.
What We Learned: Older CPUs Change the GPU Equation
The main takeaway from all of this is that if you have a lower-end CPU that you're not ready to upgrade, you're generally better off pairing it with a Radeon GPU, such as the RX 9060 XT. It didn't take much of a reduction in CPU performance before the margins started to grow significantly in the Radeon GPU's favor.
For a typical GPU review, we'd normally aim to eliminate as many system limitations as possible, which means testing with a flagship processor such as the Ryzen 7 9800X3D. For the most part, this really is the best way to approach GPU testing, especially when comparing higher-end products like the RTX 5070.
Still, with the 9800X3D, we found the RX 9060 XT to be just 2% faster than the RTX 5060. That margin grew to 8% with the Ryzen 5 7600, which admittedly doesn't change a huge amount, but it does make the Radeon GPU more appealing.
Then, with the Ryzen 5 5600, the margin grew to 12%, a more statistically significant difference. Finally, with the Ryzen 5 5500, we were looking at a complete blowout, with the RX 9060 XT pulling ahead by a massive 24% margin. Again, though, some of that advantage was due to the 5500 being limited to PCIe 3.0.
It's worth noting that the Ryzen 5 5500 is roughly equivalent to the Ryzen 5 3600 in terms of performance, so it's not much slower than something like the Ryzen 7 3700X. This means AM4 owners with processors offering similar or lower performance will likely see better gaming results with a Radeon GPU, especially in scenarios where you're trying to maximize frame rates.
We should also clarify that this has nothing to do with AMD's Smart Access Memory technology, which is essentially Resizable BAR. That PCIe feature is unrelated to the behavior we're seeing here. Similar performance margins can also be observed when testing Intel CPUs of roughly equivalent performance.
We've seen some people claim that Nvidia's CPU overhead issue doesn't affect Intel processors. That's completely untrue, and we demonstrated this years ago. If you have an Intel CPU that delivers gaming performance similar to the Ryzen 5 5500, you're going to see comparable margins between the RTX 5060 and RX 9060 XT.
As for why we didn't include any Intel CPUs in this article, the reasons are simple: AMD has been crushing Intel in the retail CPU market for a while now, with Ryzen processors heavily outselling their Intel counterparts. As a result, a large portion of our audience is using Ryzen processors, so we're focusing on the hardware most relevant to those readers. Ideally, we would include even more data and Intel CPUs, but as it stands, adding more CPU models to the graphs would only clutter the results, making the data harder to digest without providing much additional insight.
Time is also a real factor. Each game required 36 benchmark passes to gather the data, and with 10 games, that's 360 benchmark passes in total. Adding more CPUs would only increase that workload, and as we've explained, without offering much additional value.
Bottom line, if you have an older system and want to upgrade its graphics card, a Radeon GPU is generally the better investment if your goal is to maximize frame rates. In some games, you could be looking at 20-30% better performance.

articles.title: He probado el Lepas L6 PHEV en China: ¿va a reventar el mercado este nuevo SUV?
articles.text:
En el reciente viaje que hice a China para cubrir el Chery User Summit tuve la ocasión de probar muchas de sus novedades. Vimos el Lepas Aura como parte de la Lepas Elegance Week y, también, pudimos conducir el Lepas L6 PHEV. Un vehículo de unos 4,5 metros de longitud que la marca ha confirmado que llegará a España próximamente.
Lepas, para los que aún no la tengan correctamente ubicada, es la nueva marca del grupo Chery (Omoda, Jaecoo y, en cierto porcentaje, también Ebro) en desembarcar en nuestro país. La red de concesionarios está en plena expansión y, en estos momentos, ya comercializan el Lepas L8, un SUV también híbrido enchufable que trata de diferenciarse de sus hermanos, sobre todo, por su diseño y puesta a punto más europea.
El Lepas L6 toma esa misma dirección pero en un formato algo más compacto y, también, más económico. El vehículo llegará tanto en versiones eléctricas como en híbrida enchufable. Nosotros, por el momento, solo hemos podido probar la enchufable por las carreteras de China. Y este es un vehículo interesante porque, en el mercado español, los SUVs de estas dimensiones e híbridos enchufables están ganando mucha cuota de mercado.
La elegancia y refinamiento, el factor diferencial de Lepas L6
Ya cuando probamos el Lepas L8 nos dimos cuenta de ese carácter algo diferente a otros hermanos del grupo Chery. Detalles como la suspensión, algo más europeizada, o las líneas de diseño, que en ciertos aspectos recuerda a lo que vienen haciendo marcas europeas de primer nivel.
En el caso del Lepas L6, esa sensación se repite. Las líneas son más curvas y menos angulosas que en otros modelos de Chery en Europa. También tiene rasgos, como los faros afilados, que tratan de dar ese carácter “felino” que buscan sus diseñadores.
En el interior también se desmarca de otros modelos del grupo Chery, si bien hay elementos claramente comunes. Tenemos una pantalla central de 13,2 pulgadas bastante buena en comportamiento –lleva chip de Qualcomm detrás– que se “fusiona” con la zona del climatizador, los cargadores, el reposabrazos, etc. Frente al conductor, una pantalla de 8,8 pulgadas que actúa como cuadro de mandos. No es inmensa, aunque tampoco lo considero necesario. Muchas marcas chinas se empeñan en poner pantallas inmensas en el cuadro de mandos que no siempre se aprovechan a nivel de software o incluso quedan “tapadas” por partes del volante. Eso sí: en la del Lepas L6 creo que algunos elementos del cuadro deberían ser algo más grandes y otros, en cambio, más pequeños o desaparecer. Pero eso es ir muy al detalle, soy consciente.
Volviendo a la zona central, un par de detalles del Lepas L6 muy bienvenidos son la botonera bajo la pantalla para controlar el climatizador de manera rápida, así como la integración de un cargador inalámbrico con rejilla de ventilación. Esto último para mi es fundamental. De nada sirve tener un cargador de este tipo si el teléfono se termina calentando en exceso y, por consiguiente, se interrumpe la recarga o el funcionamiento de sistemas como Android Auto o Apple CarPlay.
En cuanto a comportamiento dinámico, se repiten las sensaciones que tuvimos con el Lepas L8. Lo principal: la suspensión y dirección son algo más duras y ágiles que en otros vehículos chinos. Eso no significa que sea un coche incómodo o de corte deportivo. No deja de ser un SUV cuyo principal enfoque es la comodidad durante viajes o trayectos diarios. Pero sí responde mejor en una amplia variedad de situaciones.
Una combinación conocida
En cuanto a la unidad de potencia del Lepas L6, encontramos una combinación clásica en Chery. Un motor de combustión interna de 1.5 litros turboalimentado acompañado de un sistema eléctrico que entrega un total de 279 CV, promete una autonomía eléctrica de unos 90 KM y una autonomía total combinada de unos 1.100 KM.
Este sistema puede funcionar en diferentes modos: solo en eléctrico, con la parte eléctrica asistiendo al motor de combustión interna, solo en modo de combustión, con el motor de combustión actuando como generador para recargar la batería... El vehículo, eso sí, alterna de manera automática e inteligente entre todos ellos en función de lo que le estemos pidiendo (velocidad, pendiente, aceleración, etc.) y el modo de conducción seleccionado. Podemos cambiar algunos parámetros, pero el grueso de la gestión la hace de manera autónoma e invisible al usuario.
En cuanto a la respuesta, es más que correcta para el tamaño del vehículo. Ágil en incorporaciones, silencioso en la mayoría de momentos y con una autonomía eléctrica que, a falta de probarlo en profundidad, parece más que suficiente para cubrir los trayectos diarios sin gastar ni un ápice de gasolina.
Respecto a los consumos, poco podemos aportar más allá de las cifras del fabricante sobre el Lepas L6. Si bien tuvimos ocasión de probarlo en ciudad, autovía y carreteras rurales, sería necesario un test más prolongado para poder determinar su rendimiento en este sentido.
Para finalizar, en lo que respecta a espacio interior, se trata de un vehículo amplio en el que pueden viajar cuatro adultos de manera holgada y cinco de manera algo más ajustada. Su maletero es de 435 litros. No es un maletero de referencia en su segmento, pero sí es suficiente para realizar viajes.
Lepas L6: precio y disponibilidad
El Lepas L6 llegará a España en 2027 tanto en versiones híbridas enchufables como en eléctricas. La compañía no ha confirmado aún los precios, pero, considerando que el Lepas L8 se vende por 33.000€ contando todas las ayudas y descuentos posibles, cabe la posibilidad de que este se sitúe justo por debajo de los 30.000 euros contando también con todas las promociones y descuentos posibles.
Un precio parejo al de vehículos del grupo Chery como el Omoda 7, y también a propuestas de Kia, Volkswagen, etc. Eso sí: el Lepas llega bastante bien equipado de serie, sobre todo si se compara con propuestas europeas.

articles.title: Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
articles.text:
A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support. And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.
With data centers demanding more electricity for AI, environmental advocates fear that developers could take advantage of the reforms to evade public scrutiny and rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The bill sacrifices caution for speed, limiting environmental reviews and preventing communities from stopping a project from moving forward by taking it to court.
“Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities,” Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), says in an email to The Verge. “People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision.”
The bill sacrifices caution for speed
The sea change in Congress following the midterm elections could put the bill in an even more precarious position, giving Democrats a better shot at pushing for their priorities in the bill and potentially triggering a fight with President Donald Trump. Should it come up for a vote during the current lame-duck session or get kicked to next year, the bill will test whether Democrats and Republicans can actually get something done to address some of the biggest issues voters carried with them to the polls: rising energy costs and data centers encroaching on their communities.
“They swung big with this bill. It’s a really good bipartisan compromise,” Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells The Verge.
Four senators calling themselves the “four corners” — Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on September 30th. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Whitehouse, a climate hawk, said in the press release.
The announcement simultaneously garnered support from climate and renewable energy groups, as well as fossil fuel interests. “Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” the US Oil & Gas Association said in a statement.
The Senate could vote to move the bill forward as early as next week, teeing it up for potential passage before the end of the year, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman expects President Trump will want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts, adding in an email that the White House has been “very involved” in negotiations. Newly empowered Democrats, however, could decide to drag out debate on the bill until next year in order to make fewer concessions to Republicans.
“Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control.”
If it becomes law, the bill would limit the reach of bedrock laws (stemming back to the 1970s environmental movement) that protect water resources and endangered species and give the public an opportunity to weigh in on large projects that might impact public health. Over the years, however, reviews that once took months at most might take several years or even decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman attributes the delays largely to lengthy legal battles. Now, agencies have to spend more time preparing for lawsuits as they consider permitting applications, Fishman says. That holds up development on all kinds of infrastructure projects, including cleaner energy alternatives to fossil fuels.
Fishman expects BAAJA to be very effective in amending outdated permitting rules that have become burdensome to projects across the board, even those that might ultimately have a net positive impact on the environment. “Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control,” he says. “You want to protect the environment, you want to protect people, but you want to get to a yes or no [on a permit application] in a reasonable amount of time and you don’t want to have this endless litigation cycle.”
The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to issue a decision on a project after completing an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). In many cases, NEPA review is the only opportunity for nearby residents to weigh in on large projects that involve the federal government. And it’s been a key tool for opponents to high-profile projects including the Dakota Access and Keystone XL pipelines. BAAJA narrows the scope of projects subject to NEPA, creating exclusions for transmission upgrades and certain pipeline expansions, to name a couple. Many projects receiving federal loans or grants or that have already been through a similar state environmental assessment would no longer trigger NEPA review.
The bill also sets a strict new 150-day limit for anyone to challenge a project in court over alleged violations of NEPA, the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, or National Historic Preservation Act. And BAAJA strips away a court’s ability to halt a project altogether even if it finds that a federal agency violated NEPA; it would simply force the agency to correct any issues.
The Clean Water Act allows the Army Corps of Engineers to issue general permits to projects that discharge dredged material into US waters as long as they’re deemed as having “minimal adverse environmental effects.” BAAJA could make it easier for large projects including data centers to qualify for those permits.
Some environmental groups are concerned that those general permits would take away public participation requirements for individual projects, especially when it comes to data centers that use a lot of water. The proposals in BAAJA amount to “rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act” and “blocking interference from States and Tribes,” according to the environmental organization Earthjustice Action.
“It will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out.”
They’re also concerned that BAAJA aligns with the Trump administration’s push to deregulate industry and weaken environmental protections in order to swiftly build out more data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them. Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers.
“One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out,” Earthjustice Action President Abigail Dillen said in a Thursday blog. “BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.”
Long pipeline delays slow data center development, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. Permitting reform could benefit data center developers building out their own gas generation rather than relying solely on the grid, so-called “behind-the-meter” projects, by ending regulatory delays when it comes to connecting pipelines. Reforms would also speed grid-connected gas generation, Wood Mackenzie says in a recent news release.
“I don’t think we’re seeing it as this bill helping one type of technology over the other. I think it clears the way for all technologies to get onto the grid a little quicker,” Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American Power for Wood Mackenzie, tells The Verge.
Notably, the bill is supposed to protect bipartisan interests by preventing any single administration from attacking a particular project type — such as the Biden administration attempting to phase down oil and gas in the power sector or the Trump administration issuing stop work orders to wind farms. BAAJA aims to provide “project certainty” by barring federal agencies from canceling or suspending permits they’ve already approved in most cases. It even allows developers to take agencies to court for “disparate treatment” to sue for damages incurred from project delays.
“This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry,” the NRDC warns in its analysis of the bill. It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health.
Despite those concerns, the NRDC and other advocacy groups are optimistic about the bill boosting renewable energy and enabling power grid upgrades needed to meet rising demand while keeping costs down.
BAAJA could shorten the time needed to build a new transmission line nearly in half — from 10 years or more to around five or six years, the NRDC estimates. Transmission lines that carry electricity across long distances — key to getting electrons to urban centers from far-flung solar and wind farms — are particularly tricky to build because of the patchwork of permitting processes they’re subject to across different jurisdictions.
Two separate reports project that the permitting bill would increase renewable energy capacity in the US and cut greenhouse gas emissions as a result. It also points to modest reductions in energy costs as a result of BAAJA passing compared to a baseline reflecting the status quo. The average annual cost of producing electricity would fall by as much as 7 percent by 2041, according to modeling by think tank Resources for the Future. Household electricity bills would lower by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, according to an analysis by research firm Rhodium Group. The White House put out its own analysis in October claiming that the average household could see their electricity bills fall by as much as $251 each year as a result of BAAJA.
One of the ways BAAJA aims to keep utility bills from rising is to force data center developers to pay more for transmission costs. Current law prevents utilities from charging them for costs stemming from both new builds and existing infrastructure, which inadvertently shifts costs to other customers to fill in the gap. The bipartisan bill mandates what’s called “and pricing” so that data centers and other large electricity customers would be on the hook to pay for both added and existing infrastructure.
The bill would also require utilities to disclose electricity sales to data centers. It would force large data center developers to make financial assurances to utilities before they break ground, as well as make them responsible for covering costs of new energy projects even if the data center shutters before the infrastructure is paid off.
Unfortunately, the bill may only solve part of the problem since utility rates reflect more than just transmission costs. Increasing electricity demand from the data center boom can still raise prices for fuel and gas turbines, for example. And the bill doesn’t address other issues that have sparked backlash against data centers, like noise and air pollution from generators on site.
Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even environmental groups concerned about some of the provisions in BAAJA are holding out to see if Congress can amend the bill to strengthen environmental and consumer protections.
The bill has become a sort of Rorschach test for its backers, one expert speaking on background tells The Verge. They’re all optimistic that their energy source of choice, be it oil and gas or solar and wind, will ultimately come out on top — as long as it gets the green light to build.

articles.title: « Aucune interaction n’est nécessaire » : une faille critique met en danger votre smartphone Android, faites vite la mise à jour
articles.text:
Google vient de déployer le correctif de sécurité de novembre pour Android. La mise à jour corrige 216 failles de sécurité, dont 23 jugées critiques. Parmi elles, une brèche particulièrement dangereuse permet de prendre le contrôle d’un smartphone à distance, sans le moindre clic de la part de la victime.
À lire aussi : 1,3 million de boîtiers TV Android piratés – Google démantèle un botnet chinois, installé dès l’usine par un fabricant
Une faille dans le cœur d’Android
La défaillance se trouve dans le Framework, l’un des composants centraux d’Android. Comme l’explique Google dans son bulletin de sécurité, « la plus grave de ces vulnérabilités est une faille de sécurité critique dans le composant Framework qui pourrait conduire à une exécution de code à distance sans qu’aucun privilège d’exécution supplémentaire ne soit nécessaire ». En fait, « aucune interaction de l’utilisateur n’est nécessaire pour l’exploiter », prévient le géant de Mountain View.
La faille se situe plus précisément dans le code chargé de créer les aperçus des photos et des vidéos, comme les miniatures affichées dans une galerie. En exploitant la faille, un pirate pourrait exécuter du code malveillant sur le smartphone sans que son propriétaire n’ouvre un lien ou ne télécharge quoi que ce soit. Toutes les versions d’Android sont concernées, d’Android 14 à Android 17.
Pour l’instant, rien ne prouve que des cybercriminels aient exploité la vulnérabilité pour lancer des attaques. Néanmoins, les cyberattaques reposant sur la faille ne devraient pas tarder à pointer le bout de leur nez. Conformément aux habitudes de Google; le code source des correctifs est rendu public 48 heures après le bulletin. Des pirates pourraient alors l’analyser pour comprendre comment exploiter la brèche. C’est pourquoi il est urgent de mettre à jour votre smartphone.
40 % des smartphones laissés de côté
Malheureusement, tous les smartphones Android ne recevront pas les correctifs adéquats. D’après les données de distribution d’Android, plus de 40 % des appareils actifs tournent encore sous Android 13 ou une version plus ancienne. Ces versions, considérées comme obsolètes, ne reçoivent plus de mises à jour de sécurité de la part de Google. Les smartphones concernés se retrouvent donc à la merci des cybercriminels. Si votre smartphone n’est pas obsolète, l’arrivée de la mise à jour dépend du fabricant, qui doit adapter le correctif à sa surcouche. Certains constructeurs réagissent vite et lancent le déploiement en quelques jours, d’autres en plusieurs semaines.
Pour savoir si votre téléphone est à jour, ouvrez l’application Paramètres, puis rendez-vous dans À propos du téléphone et Version d’Android. Consultez ensuite la date de la mise à jour de sécurité Android. Si elle affiche le 1er novembre 2026 ou une date plus récente, vous êtes bien protégé contre la faille critique. Si une mise à jour est disponible, installez-la sans attendre. Si votre smartphone n’en reçoit plus depuis bien longtemps, on vous encourage à envisager l’achat d’un nouveau smartphone.

articles.title: Bill Gates advierte de la inteligencia artificial sin regular: espera un fuerte aumento de los ciberataques
articles.text:
Bill Gates, cofundador de Microsoft, cree que la inteligencia artificial (IA) sin regulación es una amenaza que no deja de crecer, y es que en una entrevista en octubre anticipó una escalada de ciberataques impulsados por IA en los próximos doce mese.
El riesgo inmediato. Para Gates, que la IA “se descontrole” es un peligro a años vista. Lo urgente es otra cosa: “El frente que probablemente notaremos con más fuerza el próximo año son los ciberataques”.
Sin salvaguardas. Le preocupa la IA sin protecciones: “Pero ahora mismo se permite quitar todas esas salvaguardas. Así que, cuando tienes gente mala, ninguna salvaguarda y los modelos más recientes”, durante el próximo año, “sobre todo en el terreno cibernético, vamos a tener muchas sorpresas negativas”.
Las empresas no bastan. Rechazó además que la autorregulación de las compañías de IA sea suficiente para mantener el mundo a salvo, idea que, según AFP, defiende el presidente estadounidense, Donald Trump.
“La idea de que, para la tecnología más peligrosa que los humanos han inventado jamás, esa sea la última palabra, que las propias empresas sean el único control que tiene la sociedad (…) está claro que no estamos haciendo lo suficiente”, zanjó.
Foto | Wikimedia Commons (Jennifer Jacquemart)
En Xataka | Las empresas de IA tienen tan claro que habrá una gran catástrofe en 2027 que ya preparan el día después

articles.title: Test de la souris KULT Elite M150 : The G-Lab attaque Razer, à un prix tellement plus attractif
articles.text:
La montée en gamme observée sur les claviers signés The G-Lab va de pair avec une évolution similaire dans l’univers des souris. Ainsi, coup sur coup, la marque française a lancé les KULT ELITE M100 et KULT ELITE M150. Nous avons décidé de tester ce second modèle.
- Design et forme agréables
- Sensibilité du PixArt PAW3950
- Qualité des switchs des boutons
- Polling rate 8 kHz en 2,4 GHz aussi
- Souris légère (55 g)
- Endurance (200h avec 2 batteries)
- Dongle à ranger sous la batterie
- Exclusivement pour droitiers
- Grips autocollants : idée perfectible
Un design très inspiré de la Razer Viper V4 Pro
Le renouveau affiché par The G-Lab avec les KEYZ ELITE est donc une nouvelle fois à l’œuvre avec deux souris gaming aux caractéristiques intéressantes, mais aux tarifs savamment étudiés. Au premier coup d’œil posé sur la M150 – et sur la M100 d’ailleurs aussi puisqu’elles sont extérieurement identiques –, on pense immanquablement à un modèle iconique signé d’une marque qui l’est au moins autant, la Viper V4 Pro de Razer.
Testée dans nos colonnes il y a maintenant quelques semaines, la Viper V4 Pro est assurément l’une des meilleures souris gaming actuellement sur le marché. Razer met en avant des caractéristiques techniques affolantes (capteur 55K DPI, polling rate 8 kHz), mais elle est proposée à un tarif tout ce qu’il y a de plus dissuasif : 180 euros. The G-Lab entend donc s’inspirer (très fortement) de la Viper V4 Pro tout en gardant un ticket d’entrée plus raisonnable.
À 125 millimètres de long pour 63 mm de large et 38 mm d’épaisseur, la M150 dispose de dimensions très proches de celles de la Viper V4 Pro (127,1 x 63,9 x 39,9 mm), mais au-delà des mensurations, ce sont les formes et les designs qui interpellent. Jetez un œil à la photo ci-dessous, si ce n’est pour le liseré blanc sur la molette et les boutons de pouce (blancs également) de la M150, il est presque impossible de faire la différence entre les deux souris.
The G-Lab lance deux modèles proches : les M100 et M150. © Nerces pour Clubic
En réalité, les M100 et M150 affichent un léger renfoncement au niveau de la LED placée juste devant la molette, mais c’est à peu près tout. The G-Lab a donc adopté la même forme légèrement allongée avec cette absence de toute excroissance, que ce soit au niveau du pouce ou de l’auriculaire. La souris est légèrement arrondie pour en faire un modèle pour droitier et le dos est plus bombé que sur de nombreux modèles afin de favoriser une « palm grip ».
Sous la souris, notons la présence de deux bandes en PTFE là où Razer opte pour de larges patins. Petit plus de la part de The G-Lab, la batterie dispose d’un compartiment qui accueille aussi le dongle USB : la batterie est donc remplaçable, d’ailleurs deux sont fournies avec la souris. Enfin, précisons que sous la souris se trouvent deux sélecteurs : le premier pour la connexion (filaire, 2,4 GHz ou Bluetooth) et le second pour la sensibilité du capteur.
Sous la souris, les boutons de paramètres et l’accès à la batterie. © Nerces pour Clubic
Capteur 33K et polling rate de 8 kHz
S’il est un terrain sur lequel The G-Lab pouvait difficilement concurrencer un fabricant expert comme Razer, c’est bien celui du capteur optique. Razer conçoit ses propres solutions et son Focus Pro de 3ᵉ génération avec ses 50K points par pouce de sensibilité est en quelque sorte une référence. Pour autant, le Pixart PAW3950 retenu par la firme affiche des caractéristiques déjà remarquables avec, notamment, une sensibilité jusqu’à 30K ppp.
Encore une fois sensiblement derrière le capteur de Razer, le PAW3950 est également donné pour une accélération maximale de 50 G à comparer aux 90 G du Focus Pro. Pas de quoi rougir de honte. Il est par ailleurs intéressant de noter que – tous les fabricants de souris haut de gamme y sont passés – le taux d’interrogation est capable de grimper jusqu’à 8 000 Hz pour plus de réactivité. Là, Razer ne peut faire mieux que The G-Lab.
Hélas, la marque ne donne guère de précision sur les contacteurs employés pour les boutons, et ce, que l’on parle des deux boutons principaux ou de ceux situés au niveau du pouce. Précision utile, ces derniers achèvent de faire de la KULT Elite M150 une souris pour droitier. Nous savons tout de même qu’il s’agit de contacteurs TTC Optical et qu’ils sont donnés pour une longévité de 100 millions de clics. Ça doit laisser le temps de voir venir !
Notons enfin que la M150 est une souris sans fil et que, ce faisant, elle se connecte aussi bien en USB (un câble tressé de 1,6 m est livré) qu’en Bluetooth ou en 2,4 GHz. Le choix du mode se fait via un bouton sous la souris et le 2,4 GHz est assuré au moyen d’un dongle USB. Hélas, si ce dernier dispose bien d’un petit logement pour être rangé, ce compartiment est sous la souris, masqué par la batterie. On aurait aimé plus accessible, mais cela reste gérable.
Et à l’usage, ça donne quoi ?
Cette batterie justement est l’un des premiers atouts de la M150, une fois que l’on utilise la souris. Elle autorise environ 100 heures d’autonomie – un score déjà très appréciable – et se recharge à 100 % en plus ou moins trois heures. Autre point intéressant, The G-Lab ne livre pas une, mais deux batteries avec sa souris de sorte que l’on ne soit jamais démuni. C’est déjà une attention rare dans le monde des souris, c’est d’autant plus vrai à moins de 80 euros.
Mieux, The G-Lab a pensé à un détail intéressant : les deux batteries disposent d’un connecteur USB-C qui permet donc de les recharger sans qu’elles soient à l’intérieur de la souris. Pratique. Au total, on peut donc – comme ne manque pas de le faire la marque – parler d’un maximum de 200 heures d’autonomie. Là encore, rares sont les souris à faire aussi bien. On regrette en revanche la longueur, un peu faible, du câble USB-C livré.
La M150 « nue » est presque identique à une Viper V4 Pro. © Nerces pour Clubic
Du côté de la souris en revanche, l’usage confirme l’excellent travail des ingénieurs de la marque. La prise en main – identique donc à celle de la Viper V4 Pro – est un modèle du genre qui destine la souris plutôt aux grandes mains avec ergonomie en palm grip (prise avec la paume) ou claw grip (prise façon griffe). Des mains moyennes pourront s’adapter, mais il faut reconnaître que les petites mains – d’enfants notamment – seront moins à leur aise.
En revanche, on peut lui ajouter des grips autocollants pour éviter toute glissade potentielle. Franchement, c’est un peu gadget. © Nerces pour Clubic
Rien à redire sur le poids de la souris, même si nous sommes loin des modèles les plus légers. À 55 grammes, la M150 se tient très bien, ne fatigue jamais le poignet, même lors des sessions de jeu les plus intenses. Le repositionnement au centre du tapis de souris ne pose pas non plus le moindre problème alors que la sensibilité du capteur optique est appréciable. Avouons-le, nous n’avons pas le niveau pour exploiter au mieux les 30K ppp du composant Pixart.
Il en va un peu de même pour le taux d’interrogation de 8 000 Hz, même si nous avons été davantage sensibles à cet argument sur les sessions de jeu les plus nerveuses. En revanche, nous avons pu mesurer une baisse très importante de l’autonomie quand le 8 000 Hz est activé en permanence : on peut l’estimer à environ 60 %. Bien sûr, ces 8 000 Hz ne sont activables qu’en mode filaire ou en 2,4 GHz. Le Bluetooth est incapable d’une telle prouesse.
Nous apprécions aussi la qualité et la réactivité des boutons alors que la molette est souple, mais bien crantée malgré tout. Attention, elle n’est pas débrayable. Enfin, rien à redire non plus sur la glisse d’un produit qui bénéficie de patins en PTFE : c’est du très bon travail et à aucun moment nous n’avons eu l’impression de devoir lutter pour parvenir à nos fins. The G-Lab accompagne sa souris d’une planche de grips autocollants. Nous ne les avons pas jugés utiles, mais sachez qu’ils sont là.
Pour assurer la configuration de la KULT Elite M150, The G-Lab reconduit son logiciel, un classique que nous avons déjà testé sur les claviers de la marque. Le programme est très léger, mais il n’est pas (encore ?) question d’une interface exclusivement web. L’avantage, c’est qu’on ne dépend pas ici de la connexion Internet pour ajuster les paramètres. Le défaut étant qu’il faut donc installer un soft de plus sur sa machine.
Le logiciel compagnon s’installe « à l’ancienne » : il est complet, très léger et toutes les options sont plutôt bien lisibles. © Nerces pour Clubic
Il permet de gérer à peu près tous les éléments de la souris, affiche toutes les informations utiles et se montre plutôt agréable à utiliser. Par exemple, la sensibilité du capteur s’ajuste par pas de 50 ppp entre 800 et 30 000 ppp avec cinq paliers configurables que l’on appelle avec un bouton placé sous la souris. Le polling rate est à choisir entre 500, 1 000, 2 000, 4 000 ou 8 000 Hz. Enfin, d’autres options sont là pour la distance de levée de la souris, la réactivité des clics ou le temps avant mise en veille. Propre et complet, on aime.
The G-Lab KULT ELITE M150 : l’avis de Clubic
Tout en adoptant un design vraiment très proche de l’excellente Viper V4 Pro signée Razer, la KULT ELITE M150 en réduit les caractéristiques sur à peu près tous les niveaux : la souris est (un peu) plus lourde et son capteur est (un peu) moins sensible, mais son autonomie est légèrement supérieure.
De plus, si The G-Lab monte en gamme, il n’a pas la prétention de venir « taper » des marques aussi installées que Razer. En revanche, en faisant nettement progresser les caractéristiques de ses mulots, en adoptant un design réussi et des matériaux de qualité, la firme française fait un impressionnant bond en avant. La M150 n’est peut-être pas la toute meilleure souris gaming que vous pouvez trouver sur le marché, mais elle inscrit assurément des points.
Enfin, et c’est sans doute le plus important pour The G-Lab, la marque parvient à garder un tarif relativement accessible. Il faut encore débourser près de 80 euros pour la M150, mais ça reste 2,5 fois moins cher que la Viper V4 Pro dont elle s’inspire. Pour de nombreux joueurs, le choix sera vite fait et si vraiment c’est encore trop cher, la M100 réduit un peu plus la voilure pour 20 euros de moins. Clairement des produits très bien positionnés.
- Design et forme agréables
- Sensibilité du PixArt PAW3950
- Qualité des switchs des boutons
- Polling rate 8 kHz en 2,4 GHz aussi
- Souris légère (55 g)

articles.title: Optasia is betting bigger on microfinance a year after listing
articles.text:
One year after its R23.5 billion ($1.4 billion) debut on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), Africa’s biggest securities market, Optasia is growing faster than expected. But its biggest opportunity may lie beyond the airtime advances that built its business.
The pan-African-listed fintech generated $270 million in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up 45% year on year, as it accelerated its shift towards microfinance. The business uses artificial intelligence (AI) and alternative data to extend credit to underserved consumers. It now wants more than 80% of its revenue to come from microfinance solutions.
Across the continent, millions earn money through informal businesses and gig work but remain excluded from conventional lending because they lack payslips, formal credit histories or assets to serve as collateral. Fintechs use mobile transaction histories, behavioural patterns and machine learning to assess these customers.
Optasia’s ambitions extend beyond consumer loans to merchant financing and working capital for small businesses. But widening access to credit also raises questions about affordability, responsible lending and over-indebtedness.
“The company started with airtime credit, and we did a fantastic job in that space. However, airtime credit is essentially a convenience product,” Salvador Anglada, its chief executive, told TechCabal in an interview on Thursday.
He said the company has shifted focus towards meeting the broader borrowing needs of consumers and small businesses overlooked by traditional lenders. Only 7% of adults in sub-Saharan Africa borrowed from mobile money providers in 2024, yet these providers accounted for nearly 60% of all formal borrowing in the region, according to the World Bank’s Global Findex Database 2025.
“Microfinance services represent a much broader opportunity. They reveal the extent of the demand among people who have never had access to financial services,” said Anglada.
Optasia built its business by allowing mobile subscribers to access airtime advances when they did not have enough money to top up their phones. Its platform has since evolved into a digital financial services business that enables telecommunications companies, banks and other partners to distribute credit.
Microfinance is now central to its growth strategy. In the first nine months of 2026, the segment contributed $194 million, about 72% of group revenue. Airtime credit contributed $75 million.
Anglada said demand came from consumers who need short-term financing and small businesses that struggle to secure conventional bank loans.
“Many small businesses cannot access financial services or loans because they lack the formal structures and documentation traditional lenders require,” he said. “We are building products to address these gaps.”
Anglada points to Pakistan as one of its strongest markets outside the continent, while Ghana, Uganda, Zambia and other West African markets are also recording increased demand.
Traditional lenders typically rely on payslips, credit histories, property ownership and other formal indicators to determine whether someone qualifies for a loan. These requirements can exclude people with irregular incomes who may still repay.
Optasia uses alternative data and machine learning to identify behavioural patterns to establish creditworthiness.
“What we do is identify what we call the signals of the market. These are signals that exist but are not necessarily formalised. We capture them through data and use them to develop features and identify patterns relating to individuals,” Anglada said.
He says the company has developed more than 100,000 features per person, selecting relevant combinations to build a picture of each customer’s behaviour and risk profile.
The objective, he explained, is not simply to determine whether someone qualifies for credit, but to establish how much they can borrow without defaulting and what they can realistically afford to repay.
Optasia’s expansion is taking place under public-market scrutiny. The company listed on the JSE in November 2025, in an initial public offering (IPO) that valued it at R23.5 billion ($1.4 billion).
Reflecting on its first year as a listed business, Anglada says its financial performance has exceeded expectations set at listing.
“Our first-half results in September showed growth of close to 60%. We have also issued a trading update this week covering the first nine months of the year, with revenue growth of approximately 45%,” he said.
He added that both growth and profitability were performing above the guidance provided at the time of the IPO.
Operating as a public company has also changed how Optasia manages its business. Anglada said it has strengthened its regulatory and compliance functions, introduced board committees, and expanded its investor relations capabilities.

articles.title: MetaMask says recent attack didn't affect wallet infrastructure
articles.text:
Cryptocurrency wallet provider MetaMask said a recent security incident has not affected MetaMask wallets or its wallet infrastructure.
The MetaMask non-custodial crypto wallet (developed by blockchain software company Consensys) lets users store and manage assets on the Ethereum network and compatible blockchains.
MetaMask revealed on September 30 that it was investigating an "ongoing infrastructure security incident" and exited affected validators (Ethereum network nodes responsible for proposing blocks, verifying crypto transactions, and maintaining Ethereum blockchain security) within non-custodial staking operations.
While the company shared almost no details at the time and redirected BleepingComputer to the public statement when asked what part of its infrastructure was affected, in a Thursday update it said that a threat actor gained access to systems used to store recipient addresses and diverted some execution-layer staking rewards.
"The issue was identified and addressed on the same day, and approximately 0.385 ETH in rewards was diverted. These rewards are separate from customers' staked ETH," MetaMask said. "We have found no evidence that customers' staked principal or withdrawal keys were compromised, and the affected systems have been secured."
It also added that the attack did not compromise MetaMask users' Secret Recovery Phrases or private keys and that it was working with affected customers to refund the lost rewards.
"Some customers have experienced temporary withdrawal delays as a result of the precautionary validator exits. The process may also have resulted in missed staking rewards while validators were exiting or awaiting reactivation. We are working directly with affected customers and partners to address any outstanding impact," MetaMask noted.
"MetaMask wallet users do not need to take any action as a result of this incident. Customers whose staking arrangements were affected should follow any guidance provided directly by MetaMask or their staking provider."
Last month, Ledger also asked Asian resellers and distributors to halt wallet sales and remove products from shelves while it was investigating multiple hardware implant incidents.
More recently, crypto exchange Binance confirmed that North Korean hackers stole $6.34 billion after compromising its wallet infrastructure by tricking an employee into installing malware in a fake job interview.

articles.title: Opinion: Canada needs a better definition of what makes a company Canadian | BetaKit
articles.text:
On Wednesday, non-partisan public policy institute The Canadian Shield Institute published a policy paper titled “Canadian Dupes: A Better Definition for Real Canadian Companies.” With the Institute’s permission, an edited excerpt from that paper appears below.
“We will be our own best customer,” Prime Minister Mark Carney declared in November 2025, when he announced plans to implement a Buy Canadian Policy as part of the federal budget. But how do you define a Canadian company?
Canada already has a heap of different definitions, and in the past year the government introduced two new policies that each include their own definition of a Canadian company.
“Only a few years ago, the idea of implementing a national Buy Canadian policy was seen as distasteful and parochial. Today, it seems like a natural response to rising trade tensions.”
However, these new procurement policies are among the weakest in terms of defining a Canadian company. The Buy Canadian Policy primarily concerns itself with Canadian supplier materials and whether a company is incorporated in Canada and paying taxes here. By this definition, Walmart Canada or Microsoft Canada would count as Canadian. The Defence Investment Agency relies on the Strategic Partnership Framework definition, which is 161 words long and broadly defines a Canadian company as any company operating in Canada.
The situation is a bit of a mess.
The solution is actually quite simple: For the purposes of public funding, procurement, and strategic industrial policy, the cleanest way to define a Canadian company is simply to start by defining what is clearly not a Canadian company.
We suggest a simple definition: A Canadian company is a Canadian-headquartered firm that is not majority-controlled by a foreign parent or foreign government.
The problem
Inevitably, any time we’re trying to establish a definition of which companies count as authentically Canadian, the government is engaging in a policy project motivated by some kind of economic nationalism.
The economic strategy of Canada’s governments over the past 50 years or more has generally been to prioritize trade, foreign investment, and economic integration. The Buy Canadian Policy, for example, gives a company’s bid a 10-percent discount if it is incorporated in Canada with business operations here—but, of course, that includes local subsidiaries of foreign multinationals.
What we see in this is a policy aiming to encourage as much economic activity as possible without imposing a binary “Canadian vs. foreign” distinction. This light-touch approach may have been fine for the 20th century, but it does not address the most important aspect of the 21st-century economy.
Consulting firm Ocean Tomo estimates that 92 percent of the value of the S&P 500 was derived from intangible assets in 2025, whereas in 1975, only 17 percent of the value of the S&P 500 came from intangibles. These intangible assets move frictionlessly across borders. Patented innovations developed through research and development in one place can be commercialized globally. Wealth creation in the digital economy comes more from ownership and rents that are extracted from intangible assets.
Canada’s fixation on jobs as a primary qualifier for Canadian-ness misses the real engine of economic growth in the 21st century. This decades-long trend has only been supercharged by the recent explosion of AI.
Canada’s light-touch approach is also rooted in a geopolitical time when deeper integration with global supply chains was seen as reciprocal and positive. Put simply: The old definitions are rooted in an economy that no longer exists, and Canada urgently needs a different approach.
The solution
We initially sought to develop some kind of “gold standard” definition for what makes an authentically Canadian firm. Ultimately, there are good arguments to be made that an expansive definition of a Canadian firm should account for multiple factors:
- ownership;
- control;
- headquarters; and
- intellectual property and intangible assets.
Each of these factors captures something real about where value resides. But taken together they create a definition that is harder to administer, easier to contest, and more vulnerable to edge cases. A company can maintain a substantive headquarters in Canada while still being ultimately directed from elsewhere; It can hold important intellectual property here while remaining accountable to a foreign parent.
On the other hand, a Canadian company may take on foreign capital without ceasing to be meaningfully Canadian in every practical sense. In fact, the majority of a venture-backed company’s equity may be owned by foreign investors, but if none of those investors is the majority owner, the company is still functionally Canadian.
That is why we recommend a narrower and more operational rule: foreign subsidiaries should not be treated as “Canadian” firms for preferential access to procurement, public funding, or industrial support when the policy goal is to scale homegrown firms.
A Canadian company is a Canadian-headquartered firm that is not majority-controlled by a foreign parent or foreign government. Paying taxes here should not be enough to establish that a firm should receive preferential treatment intended to build Canadian capacity.
How Canada can implement a fix
Over time, the federal and provincial governments should exclude Canadian subsidiaries of foreign multinationals in all areas of law and policy where we have an existing definition of a Canadian company.
There are some immediate priority areas that the government can get to work on right away. The clearest place to elevate the bar for a Canadian firm is the Defence Industrial Strategy. This strategy is explicitly focused on strengthening Canada; moreover, Canada’s trade agreements have specific carve-outs for national security matters. The same logic should extend to the Buy Canadian procurement policy. When firms are assessed for Canadian-ness, we should not rely only on address and incorporation.
“When firms are assessed for Canadian-ness, we should not rely only on address and incorporation.”
The same definition should govern access to major business supports and economic development tools. Programs explicitly meant to build Canadian capacity should be designed to ensure that public money doesn’t unintentionally subsidize branch plant activity or help foreign parents capture Canadian talent, IP, or tax-supported commercialization. That same principle is especially relevant for innovation supports such as the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax credit.
The provinces and territories should mirror this approach. A common operating definition would ensure firms do not face one test federally and another test provincially.
The world is rapidly changing, and Canada’s national economic and geopolitical strategies need to adjust. Only a few years ago, the idea of implementing a national “Buy Canadian” policy was seen as distasteful and parochial. Today, it seems like a natural response to rising trade tensions. In the realm of digital sovereignty, we are more vividly aware than ever before of the importance of engaging strategically in global trade.
Our proposed standard will not resolve every edge case. But it would end the more serious error Canada makes today: treating foreign subsidiaries as domestic firms for the purposes of building Canadian capacity. If Buy Canadian is meant to mean anything, it has to start there.
