articles.title: Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
articles.text:
Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within its Muse AI assistant. The new feature, called “spaces,” allows Muse to build things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker, trivia game, and more, which you can interact with directly in the app.
Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
You can create things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, or music tracker directly within Muse.
If you connect your space to a relevant app, Muse will update pricing, dates, and other information in the background. Meta says you can create a new space by describing it, and continue to tweak it by asking Muse. You can also interact with your spaces by checking things off, adding notes, and making edits.
You can add spaces to the sidebar in the Muse app, move them into your main tab, as well as schedule when you see them. “For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday,” Meta says.
Meta is rolling out spaces to all Muse users, along with a “specialized” version of its Muse Wonder AI model. The company is also looking into ways to share your spaces with other users and collaborate with them.

articles.title: On a testé l'écran OLED de l'iPad mini 2026 : voici le verdict du 01lab
articles.text:
Après cinq ans d’attente, l’iPad mini est enfin passé sur une meilleure technologie d’écran. Adieu le LCD, bienvenu à l’écran OLED. Sur le papier, il n’y a pas photo a priori. Mais est-ce que les performances de ce nouvel écran sont vraiment meilleures ? Le meilleur moyen d’en avoir le cœur net est encore de le vérifier nous-mêmes.
Nous avons donc sorti notre traditionnelle sonde colorimétrique et le logiciel Calman Ultimate de Portrait Displays pour tester l’écran comme il se doit.
Luminosité : le HDR enfin
Déjà, la taille de la dalle est intéressante, puisqu’on gagne 0,2 pouce dans le passage de génération. Cela permet surtout de réduire la taille des bordures autour de l’iPad. L’iPad mini 2026 obtient en effet un ratio affichage/taille de 81,9 %, contre 77,7 % auparavant.
Ensuite, pour la partie luminosité, le principal apport d’après nos mesures se situe sur le pic lumineux HDR. En effet, l’ancien iPad en était complètement dépourvu, culminant à 509 cd/m² de moyenne, une performance correcte, mais un peu basse. Le nouvel écran OLED de l’iPad mini monte pour sa part à 1153 cd/m² en boost et à 1146 cd/m² en pic HDR. Une bien belle performance.
Colorimétrie : du très bon
Passons maintenant à la colorimétrie. Sur ce terrain, l’écran de l’iPad mini nous fait une démonstration.
La balance des blancs dérive légèrement vers les tons froids comme d’habitude chez Apple, avec 6877 K, lorsqu’on voudrait plutôt viser 6500 K. En revanche, la dérive colorimétrique est très faible, quel que soit le type de contenus que vous regardez. Sur le spectre sRGB, plébiscité pour les contenus web, le delta E 2000 moyen ne monte qu’à 0,9 (plus la valeur est basse, meilleure elle est). L’ancien iPad mini 2024 montait à 1,6 en sRGB pour sa part, il y a donc une petite amélioration sur ce point.
L’évolution la plus importante porte sur l’espace P3, celui des contenus vidéo typiquement, où l’iPad mini monte à un excellent 1,1. Même si nous n’avons pas de mesure pour l’iPad mini 2024, les écrans LCD de tablettes ne sont généralement pas très bons sur cet exercice. La performance affichée ici est donc très satisfaisante.
En conclusion, un bien meilleur écran
À l’arrivée, le passage à la technologie OLED de l’iPad mini va donc bien plus loin qu’une simple amélioration du contraste. La dalle est plus lumineuse, mieux calibrée, mais aussi vraiment compatible avec le P3, tout en étant légèrement plus grande avec un meilleur ratio corps-écran. L’amélioration d’une génération sur l’autre est donc indéniable. Un bel upgrade pour l’iPad mini.

articles.title: Si vous voulez découvrir GTA 6 sur grand écran, ce TV Xiaomi Mini LED 144 Hz tombe au bon moment
articles.text:
Rockstar sort enfin GTA 6 le jeudi 19 novembre 2026 sur PS5 et Xbox Series. Les précommandes numériques pourront être préchargées dès le mardi 10 novembre, deux jours plus tôt que prévu. Vice City sous ses néons mérite sans doute mieux que le vieux téléviseur Full HD du salon.
Si vous comptez changer d’écran avant la date, AliExpress affiche le Xiaomi TV S Mini LED 55 2025 à 378,29 €, au lieu de 478,29 €. Le prix s’obtient avec le code promo 11FR80, à saisir au moment du paiement. La livraison est prévue avant le 19 novembre.
Xiaomi a lancé ce téléviseur en France à l’automne 2024 au prix de 599 €. Par rapport à ce tarif de lancement, la remise dépasse 220 €.
Que vaut le Xiaomi TV S Mini LED 55 ?
Le TV S Mini LED 55 est un téléviseur 4K (3 840 × 2 160 pixels) de 55 pouces. Son rétroéclairage Mini LED repose sur de très petites LED regroupées en 308 zones, que le téléviseur allume ou atténue séparément selon l’image. Les noirs sont donc plus profonds qu’avec un éclairage LED classique, qui éclaire toute la dalle d’un bloc. La couche « QD », pour Quantum Dot, sert à enrichir les couleurs. Xiaomi annonce un pic de luminosité de 1 200 nits.
Côté jeu, Xiaomi vise les consoles. Le téléviseur a trois ports HDMI 2.1 compatibles VRR et ALLM, et deux d’entre eux acceptent la 4K à 144 Hz. Les PS5 et Xbox Series plafonnent toutefois à 120 Hz, les 144 Hz profiteront donc surtout à un PC branché sur la télé. Le VRR cale la fréquence de l’écran sur celle de la console, ce qui évite les déchirures d’image quand le jeu ralentit. L’ALLM bascule automatiquement le téléviseur en mode jeu, à latence réduite, dès qu’il détecte la PS5 ou la Xbox.
Pour le reste, le téléviseur gère le Dolby Vision IQ et le Dolby Atmos, se connecte en Wi-Fi 6 et tourne sous Google TV pour les applications de streaming.
À ce prix, le Xiaomi TV S Mini LED 55 est-il une bonne affaire ?
Sous les 400 €, la plupart des 55 pouces se contentent d’un rétroéclairage LED classique et de ports HDMI sans VRR. À 378,29 €, le modèle de Xiaomi apporte la gestion par zones et la connectique attendue par les consoles actuelles. C’est un très bon prix pour cette fiche technique. Attention à l’année du modèle. Xiaomi vend aussi un TV S Mini LED 55 2026, au même prix de lancement de 599 €. Cette version se limite à 60 Hz en natif, et à 120 Hz seulement en 1080p ou 1440p avec le mode Game Boost. Les 144 Hz en 4K sont réservés à l’édition 2025.
GTA 6 arrive le 19 novembre. Si vous attendez le Jour-J du Black Friday, vous découvrirez Leonida, l’État fictif du jeu, sur votre ancien écran. Pour moins de 380 €, vous pourrez jouer à GTA 6 en 4K avec le VRR et le mode jeu automatique, puis regarder vos films en Dolby Vision.
Singles Day 2026 : tout ce qu’il faut savoir
Le Singles Day, surnommé « Black Friday chinois », tombe le mercredi 11 novembre 2026. Mais il est aussi précoce que son cousin américain : chez AliExpress, les promotions s’étendent du 1er au 18 novembre.
Quels sites participent au Singles Day ?
AliExpress reste le principal rendez-vous de cette opération. D’autres marques organisent leurs propres promotions, comme Lenovo, qui annonce une édition 2026 sur ses ordinateurs et accessoires. Les dates et les conditions varient selon les enseignes.
Les codes promo AliExpress du Singles Day 2026
Ces codes sont annoncés du 1er au 18 novembre, sur une sélection de produits livrés en France :
| Remise | Minimum d’achat | Code | 
|---|---|---|
| 3 € | 18 € | 11FR03 |

| 24 € | 139 € | 11FR24 |

Un seul code peut être appliqué par commande. Leur utilisation peut être limitée en nombre : vérifiez que la réduction apparaît bien dans le récapitulatif avant de payer.
Y a-t-il des frais de douane ?
Pour un produit déjà stocké et dédouané dans l’Union européenne, il n’y a en principe pas de frais d’importation à régler à la livraison. En revanche, les règles ont changé en 2026 pour les commandes expédiées directement depuis la Chine :
- Depuis le 1er juillet, un droit de douane forfaitaire de 3 € par catégorie d’articles s’applique aux envois d’une valeur inférieure ou égale à 150 €.
- Depuis le 1er novembre, des frais de traitement de 2 € par catégorie d’articles s’ajoutent, sans seuil de valeur.
Pour les envois jusqu’à 150 €, ces deux prélèvements représentent donc 5 € par catégorie d’articles, hors TVA et éventuels frais du transporteur. Au-delà, les droits de douane habituels remplacent le forfait de 3 €.
Ces montants peuvent être intégrés au prix payé à la commande. Vérifiez les conditions du vendeur pour savoir si les droits et taxes sont compris et si des frais restent à régler à la livraison.$
Les produits fonctionnent-ils en France ?
Les mentions Global, EU ou HK demandent de regarder la référence exacte du produit. Pour un smartphone, vérifiez notamment les réseaux mobiles compatibles et les langues disponibles. Regardez aussi le format de la prise, les accessoires fournis et les conditions de garantie.

articles.title: Il n’a pas 12 ans et a conçu une appli de révision avec Claude pour CP jusqu'à Terminale, à partir d'un bout de papier
articles.text:
Liam, presque 12 ans, a conçu avec l'aide de son papa SoughIA, une application de révision qui veut couvrir le programme scolaire du CP à la Terminale. Le garçon l’a développée avec Claude Code, en vibe coding, à partir d’un simple brouillon.
Jeune garçon de pas encore 12 ans à la tête bien pleine, Liam a conçu SoughIA, une application de révision dont les leçons sont générées par l'intelligence artificielle, appli pensée pour accompagner les élèves du CP à la Terminale. Il l'a développée en vibe coding avec Claude Code, l'assistant de programmation d'Anthropic, à partir d'un brouillon manuscrit et sous l'œil bienveillant de son père, dirigeant d'un cabinet de conseil en IA à Strasbourg. Le prototype fonctionne déjà, mais il n'est pas encore ouvert au public et doit d'abord passer l'épreuve d'un test… dans la classe de Liam. Clubic raconte cette belle histoire.
Avec Claude Code, un enfant de 11 ans a créé sa propre appli de révision
Tout part d'une simple feuille de papier, remplie à la main par Liam, ratures et flèches comprises. En haut à droite, il hésite encore entre ChemaIA et SoughIA pour le futur nom. Au centre, Liam aligne quatre idées d'intelligence artificielle : l'une pour dessiner des BD, une autre pour concevoir des machines et des expériences de chimie, une troisième pour trier les mails. La dernière, une IA d'aide aux devoirs capable de s'adapter au niveau de l'élève, décroche la coche. Dans ses rêves de départ, elle devait même aider à réviser le permis de conduire et parler toutes les langues.
Et parce qu'il n'y a pas que des hasards dans la vie, son père, Yaniv Adjedj, dirige Reboot Conseil, une société de conseil en IT, IA et cybersécurité, installée à Strasbourg. Liam s'est d'abord initié à la programmation avec Scratch, un outil pensé pour les enfants avec lequel on assemble des blocs comme les pièces d'un puzzle. Il a ensuite suivi, une fois par semaine entre midi et deux, des cours de Python, un langage de programmation très répandu, dans les locaux de l'entreprise. Son papa lui a aussi appris à structurer une idée avant de la coder. « Je lui ai montré comment brainstormer, lister des idées, diverger, puis converger vers quelque chose qui l'intéresse », nous raconte-t-il. Autrement dit, ouvrir d'abord toutes les pistes, puis n'en garder qu'une, exactement ce que montre la feuille. Après s'être fait la main sur des projets plus simples, Liam a mis plusieurs semaines à imaginer et concevoir SoughIA.
Vient ensuite le vibe coding, cette manière qui fait des adeptes et qui consiste à programmer en décrivant à une IA ce que l'on veut obtenir. « Je lui ai donné un ordinateur et un accès à Claude Code et ensuite, il a itéré », résume le père. Le choix du modèle n'a rien d'un hasard. « Volontairement, je lui ai donné accès à un modèle assez faible », précise-t-il, en l'occurrence Claude Sonnet 4.6. Le garçon n'a eu droit au plus costaud Opus 5.5 qu'en fin de parcours, pour faire passer un cap à son projet.
« Je l'ai surtout encadré pour faire avancer son projet sans l'orienter, c'est ses choix et sa vie. » Yaniv Adjedj tient à le dire. Liam a nourri ses idées en discutant avec sa mère et avec des camarades de classe, et il a amélioré l'application au fil de ses propres envies, en s'en servant lui-même. Une leçon retenue en route, selon son père : « Il a très bien compris que c'est mieux quand on développe et qu'on est aussi utilisateur. »
Le projet a aussi appris à Liam à sortir de sa bulle. Comme il passait régulièrement dans les bureaux de son père, il en parlait de temps en temps aux personnes qui y travaillent, jusqu'à présenter son application devant l'équipe, à la manière d'un développeur qui montre son travail en réunion. « C'est un vrai apprentissage que de faire et de s'exposer », observe son père, pour qui le garçon a « bien surmonté la timidité de son âge pour parler avec passion ».
Une application de révision qui fait travailler avant de faire jouer
Sur le fond, SoughIA reprend la mécanique d'un cours bien mené, ramassée en une dizaine de minutes. L'élève suit une leçon de trois minutes, au rythme lent, moyen ou rapide, puis enchaîne deux exercices de compréhension et une évaluation notée sur 20. Sous la barre des 6/20, un rattrapage surprise l'attend le lendemain. Ça se termine à chaque fois par un résumé oral du cours précédent, en cinq phrases. Sur son brouillon, Liam avait même prévu des appréciations. Entre 13 et 16, l'élève pouvait encore s'améliorer, et au-delà de 16, la notion était considérée comme parfaitement acquise. Au premier lancement, un test de mémoire visuelle ou auditive ajuste la façon d'expliquer, et les chapitres suivent le calendrier scolaire de chaque classe.
Alors d'où viennent ces leçons ? SoughIA ne contient pas de manuels tout prêts, mais un immense sommaire de 3 510 chapitres répartis sur douze niveaux, chacun réduit à un titre et à une phrase qui fixe l'objectif. Quand l'élève ouvre un chapitre, c'est une IA qui rédige le cours en direct. Le travail est confié à gpt-oss, des modèles d'OpenAI que chacun peut télécharger et faire tourner librement, par l'intermédiaire de la Lamalo Engine, un aiguilleur qui envoie chaque demande vers le bon modèle et que le père présente comme « notre outil ». Une version plus grosse du même modèle se charge ensuite des vérifications. La quasi-totalité de ce que lit l'enfant est donc écrite par une machine, et l'application l'invite d'ailleurs à signaler les erreurs. L'objectif, à terme, est d'y associer les enseignants, pour que l'appli soit « pilotée finalement non par l'intelligence artificielle mais par les enseignants en utilisant l'IA comme un outil ».
Le garçon a eu le souci du détail, et de l'inclusivité. Des modes dédiés aux troubles dys et au TDAH ajustent l'affichage et les consignes, avec une police adaptée, des phrases courtes et lecture à voix haute pour la dyslexie, des leçons plafonnées à 300 mots pour le TDAH, et un temps doublé au calcul mental en cas de dyscalculie. « Liam y a pensé naturellement », assure son père, sans préciser si des spécialistes ont été consultés.
Pour souffler, la salle de jeux (échecs, dames, Motus, Géo-Explorer…) glisse des questions en pleine partie, et les pièces se gagnent surtout en apprenant. Les adultes ne sont pas oubliés, soyez rassurés. Un espace parents protégé par code affiche les notes par matière, le temps réellement passé à apprendre et les notions fragiles ou pas encore maîtrisées. Les parents peuvent aussi fixer les horaires et le temps de jeu. Quant aux enseignants, ils peuvent éditer un bilan PDF à partager avec les familles.
Pas de modèle économique, juste un premier test en classe
Pour l'heure, SoughIA reste un prototype. L'application web, qui s'installe comme une appli classique et fonctionne même sans connexion, n'est pas encore ouverte au public. Elle repose sur les briques de base du web (HTML, CSS et JavaScript), sans framework, ces boîtes à outils qui servent d'ordinaire à accélérer le développement. Leses prototypes de tennis, basket, football et autres ont été écrits en C# avec Blazor, une technologie de Microsoft, restent d'ailleurs à l'écart de la version actuelle. Quant aux tests, ils se limitent à « quelques copains » enthousiastes et à un directeur d'école séduit.
En matière de données, le projet part plutôt sur de bonnes bases. La progression reste sur l'appareil, aucun compte n'est exigé et la sauvegarde en ligne, facultative, est chiffrée. Ce chiffrement, basé sur l'algorithme standard AES-GCM, se fait directement dans le navigateur avec une clé tirée du code famille, avant que les données ne rejoignent les serveurs d'Upstash, le service d'hébergement de bases de données. Des comptes parents classiques, avec e-mail et mot de passe, sont en développement mais pas encore en service, nous confirme le papa de Liam. Chaque leçon générée transite toutefois par un serveur, et la conformité au RGPD, cruciale quand il s'agit d'enfants, reste à préciser, mais il est encore tôt. Yaniv Adjedj, qui s'occupe lui-même de cette sécurisation, promet de bons points de contrôle et « un harness digne de ce nom », autrement dit un cadre pour contrôler et tester l'application.
La prochaine étape sera un essai grandeur nature dans la classe de Liam, d'ici quinze jours à un mois. Aucun modèle économique n'est à l'ordre du jour. « Il n'y a pas de volonté de faire des bénéfices, c'est encore un enfant », sourit son père.
Pour lui, l'intérêt est ailleurs, à savoir « voir comment un enfant est capable d'exploiter des nouvelles méthodes d'apprentissages ». Sur ce terrain-là, la feuille griffonnée de Liam a déjà livré une belle démonstration. Et de très jolies promesses.

articles.title: CBN wants to know who's behind every crypto P2P transaction
articles.text:
Nigeria’s Central Bank has introduced new rules requiring cryptocurrency peer-to-peer (P2P) platforms to link every digital asset transaction to its corresponding bank payments, tightening oversight of how Nigerians trade cryptocurrencies outside traditional exchanges.
Under the regulations, P2P operators must route naira payments through banking or CBN-approved payment channels, verify traders’ identities, and keep records connecting each payment to the corresponding cryptocurrency transfer.
The requirements are part of the CBN’s new framework for non-security virtual assets, released on Thursday evening, which also requires stablecoin issuers to build the technical ability to freeze wallets, destroy tokens, and block transactions into their smart contracts.
“A provider shall not release or credit a Regulated Token in a P2P transaction unless it has verified that the name and the Bank Verification Number of the account from which the Naira payment was made, or to which it was made, match the verified customer on whose behalf the provider acts,” the CBN said. “The [Central Bank] may prescribe further requirements relating to payment-account verification, permitted customer categories, transaction and customer limits, and other controls.”
The new rules underscore the CBN’s push to tighten its grip on crypto trading, giving the regulator greater visibility into who moves money through P2P platforms. The regulator requires stablecoin issuers to build controls to freeze and block digital assets linked to suspicious activity.
P2P trading allows individuals to buy and sell cryptocurrencies directly with one another, often using bank transfers to settle payments while a trading platform facilitates the exchange. The model has let Nigerians access dollar-backed stablecoins such as USDT and USDC, including for cross-border transactions and foreign exchange (FX) purposes.
The scale of these transactions has grown sharply across Africa. Between 2022 and 2026, stablecoin transfers through P2P channels in Sub-Saharan Africa surged more than sixfold to $14.6 billion, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.
Nigeria has previously moved to restrict P2P cryptocurrency trading over concerns about its impact on the naira. In May 2024, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) announced plans to ban person-to-person crypto trading involving the local currency; the authorities blamed speculative activity in the cryptocurrency market for the naira’s depreciation.
The CBN’s new framework signals a shift toward regulating P2P transactions through licenced platforms, with stricter requirements to identify traders, trace payments, and monitor the movement of digital assets.
Under the new framework, operators must maintain records connecting each naira payment to its corresponding digital asset transfer, including wallet addresses, payment references, transaction values, and exchange rates.
The CBN will also require P2P providers to identify both parties to a transaction and monitor suspicious activity, including the use of third-party accounts, multiple wallets, and transactions split into smaller amounts to avoid regulatory scrutiny.
P2P transactions involving conversion between the naira and foreign-currency stablecoins will require separate CBN approval. Such transactions must also be settled through, or reported to, an authorised FX dealer and comply with applicable reporting and documentation requirements.
The regulations extend international anti-money-laundering (AML) standards to virtual asset transfers. Under the Financial Action Task Force’s (FATF) Travel Rule, regulated operators handling qualifying transfers of $1,000 or €1,000 and above, or their naira equivalent, must obtain information identifying the sender and recipient.
P2P platforms must also collect and retain sender and recipient information when both parties are their customers, regardless of the transaction amount. Transfers involving other virtual asset service providers (VASPs) are subject to the applicable Travel Rule information-sharing requirements.
“A provider of a P2P Service shall ensure that every customer using the service is subject to applicable customer identification, verification, customer due diligence and ongoing monitoring requirements before being permitted to transact,” the CBN said.
“The provider shall maintain sufficient information to identify each customer and counterparty participating in a P2P transaction and to attribute each transaction to the relevant customer accounts, wallets, payment accounts and settlement arrangements.”
Beyond transaction monitoring, the CBN requires licenced stablecoin issuers to embed enforcement capabilities directly into the software governing their tokens.
These include the ability to freeze wallet addresses or token balances following a lawful court order, regulatory directive, or instruction from the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU). Issuers must also be able to permanently destroy tokens held in frozen or confiscated addresses when legally authorised.
Smart contracts must support deny-listing, which blocks transactions involving wallets linked to suspected money laundering, terrorist financing, or sanctions violations, as well as a mechanism to suspend token transfers temporarily during major security incidents.
The powers will be subject to documented procedures, audit trails, access controls and legal authorisation requirements.
The framework also requires P2P operators to obtain explicit CBN approval before offering regulated services. The P2P provisions exclude private transfers between individuals, without an intermediary facilitating the transaction.
The measures deepen the CBN’s oversight of cryptocurrency payments, linking transactions on digital asset networks to identifiable customers, regulated financial institutions, and records that authorities can examine.
They also create a new compliance burden for P2P platforms and stablecoin issuers seeking to serve Nigerian customers, as the regulator moves to bring more of the country’s digital asset activity under formal supervision.

articles.title: La atracción más reciente de Japón te permite luchar con trajes de robot que cuentan con puntos de salud y movimientos especiales.
articles.text:
Los combates entre robots gigantes llevan décadas formando parte de los videojuegos y el anime japonés, pero ahora también es posible participar en uno sin ponerse delante de una pantalla. Desde el pasado 15 de octubre, Tokio cuenta con una nueva atracción llamada The Robot Park Odaiba en la que los visitantes pueden enfrentarse utilizando trajes robóticos equipados con sensores.
La experiencia (bautizada como Robot Fight) reproduce algunas mecánicas habituales de los juegos de lucha, incluidos los puntos de vida y los ataques especiales. Además, según explica la empresa responsable en su página oficial, los participantes se colocan los trajes y compiten por parejas en un espacio preparado para los enfrentamientos.
Los sensores detectan los golpes y descuentan puntos de salud al contrincante, mientras que una barra de energía permite ejecutar movimientos especiales capaces de cambiar el resultado. De hecho, incluso los que observan pueden intervenir mediante dispositivos de apoyo, y esto convierte cada combate en una experiencia que mezcla movimientos reales con elementos propios de un videojuego.
También es posible pilotar un robot de tres metros de altura
Lo sorprendente es que los combates no son la única propuesta de un recinto situado en la sexta planta del centro comercial Aqua City Odaiba. Así, otra de sus actividades permite controlar Skeletonics, un robot de unos tres metros de altura que reproduce y amplía los movimientos de los brazos del usuario a través de un sistema mecánico.
También se puede participar en Cyber KASSEN, una modalidad de lucha con espadas blandas y sensores, o asistir a un taller en el que se utilizan piezas de aluminio para construir pequeñas estructuras robóticas. En cuanto a los precios, la entrada de 30 minutos cuesta unos 11,31 euros y los pases de una hora y 90 minutos rondan los 16,97 y 22,62 euros respectivamente.
Al mismo tiempo, la empresa también ofrece descuentos para residentes en Tokio y permite acceder como acompañante por poco menos de 4 euros. Aunque no es necesario reservar con antelación, los combates de Robot Fight están limitados a mayores de siete años que midan al menos 1,10 metros. De esta forma, se trata de una oportunidad para quienes alguna vez han querido experimentar cómo sería participar en una batalla de robots fuera de la ficción.

articles.title: Grocery Giant Ahold Delhaize Estimates Financial Toll of October Cyberattack
articles.text:
Dutch-Belgian grocery giant Ahold Delhaize estimates that last month’s cyberattack, which disrupted operations in the US and the Benelux, will wipe €200 million to €250 million ($224 million to $280 million) off its fourth-quarter net sales.
The company, whose brands include Albert Heijn, Delhaize, Food Lion and Hannaford, published the estimate this week with its third-quarter results. The attack occurred after the quarter had closed.
The cybersecurity incident is also expected to cost Ahold Delhaize €75 million to €100 million ($84 million to $112 million) in fourth-quarter underlying and IFRS operating income. On top of that, the company faces incident response and remediation expenses, but believes these will have little effect on its IFRS operating income for 2026.
As a result, the retailer has revised its 2026 guidance downward. It now projects diluted underlying earnings per share, at constant exchange rates, to grow in the low single digits, rather than in the mid to high single digits it had previously forecast.
Free cash flow is now expected to reach around €2.1 billion ($2.36 billion), down from at least €2.3 billion ($2.58 billion). Ahold Delhaize attributes the reduction to the cyberattack and to newly introduced Serbian rules governing payments to suppliers.
The company first reported the incident in mid-October, announcing that it had disconnected some systems after detecting a security issue on its network. On October 19, it confirmed it had been hit by a cyberattack and said it had no evidence at the time that customer, associate or partner data had been stolen.
“As part of our protocols to assess and mitigate cybersecurity incidents, we took some systems offline to help protect our IT environment. To differing degrees, this mainly affected our online capabilities in the Benelux and the U.S., as well as our Benelux supply-chain operations,” Frans Muller, Ahold Delhaize’s president and CEO, said in a statement accompanying the latest financial report.
“While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations,” he said.
Ahold Delhaize has yet to disclose what type of attack it experienced.
“While the cybersecurity incident has, understandably, demanded significant attention, it is important that we keep it in perspective. Our response demonstrates the resilience of our business; the incident does not define our business,” Muller said.
This is not the first time the company’s systems have been targeted. In November 2024, a ransomware attack disrupted several of its US brands, including Hannaford supermarkets and Giant Food pharmacies. The INC Ransom group claimed responsibility, and Ahold Delhaize later disclosed that the personal information of more than 2.2 million people had been compromised.

articles.title: Amazon is now making a Melania Trump TV series
articles.text:
Following the Melania documentary movie that premiered earlier this year, Amazon is now planning to release a two-part Prime Video series focusing on the first lady. The show, Melania: The Series, is set to debut on November 20th.
Amazon is now making a Melania Trump TV series
Melania Trump is the focus of a new two-part Prime Video show debuting later this month.
“MELANIA, The Series reveals never-before-told stories, offering unprecedented insight into Melania Trump’s life, including the extraordinary days immediately following the 47th Presidential Inauguration,” according to a description in a press release.
Here’s what Amazon says the two episodes will be about:
I. Family & Trust:
Melania Trump sets priorities as she prepares to become America’s First Lady. But inside the White House, trust is tested, and the incoming First Lady must protect those closest to her while navigating the demands of power.
II. Pride & Honor:
The honor of serving as First Lady comes with an immediate call to action. Moments after the inauguration, First Lady Melania Trump sets her mission in motion for the American people.
Brett Ratner, who directed the Melania film, directed both episodes of the series.

articles.title: Gelsinger-backed Nagare Labs’ capacitorless Z2RAM promises SRAM speed with DRAM density — latest published cell retains data for over 300 seconds at 85°C, but further figures are projected
articles.text:
Gelsinger-backed Nagare Labs’ capacitorless Z2RAM promises SRAM speed with DRAM density — latest published cell retains data for over 300 seconds at 85°C, but further figures are projected
Its founders’ papers take hot retention from 0.1 to over 300 seconds, but stop at 85°C.
A Pat Gelsinger-backed Georgia Tech spinout, Nagare Labs, says its Z2RAM can put SRAM-speed memory, at DRAM density, directly on top of AI chips. The founders’ own papers show a fast-improving cell that, tested up to 85 degrees Celsius, holds data for over 300 seconds. Gen 1 is projected to have 5x SRAM density with six stacked layers, 14x DRAM speed, and 3x less read energy than SRAM.
AI chips require a lot of bandwidth, and it has been challenging to get sufficient yields of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to feed them. Even when manufacturers can get it, some reportedly plan to settle for fewer layers for yield reasons, and heat is another. Heat is also why Samsung’s zHBM, which stacks DRAM directly on the processor, is planned at only about four layers.
Alternatives include high-bandwidth flash, still in development, which stacks NAND like HBM and would sit beside the GPU, or SRAM stacked directly on the die, which is less dense and more expensive for the capacity, but also faster. DRAM, which is more capacious, can sit on top of the compute, but heat limits how hard the logic underneath can run.
That limit is already shaping chipmakers’ design path for stacked memory. Micron’s vHBM plans, for example, include heat-spreading structures. With HBM stacked on a logic die, and DRAM needing to be kept at or below 95 degrees Celsius, the logic’s heat output is capped at 220 W/cm², or 300 W/cm² with better thermal vias, according to a 2025 simulation by co-founder Shimeng Yu’s group. Nagare Labs says peak compute has grown 70% a year over the past three decades, against 20% for memory bandwidth.
The company describes its Z2RAM as “Two transistors and a shield. No capacitor,” where a write transistor places a charge on a storage node and the shield blocks noisy neighbors. The read transistor can sense without draining. In a gain cell like this, the read transistor’s gate capacitance holds the charge, so reads are non-destructive and the cell avoids DRAM’s write-back. Nagare aims for well under a picojoule per bit.
Nagare builds Z2RAM by depositing its layers on top of the accelerator and patterning them “together on one die,” much as 3D NAND flash scales by adding layers. There’s no interposer and no bonds between the memory layers, which is part of the secret sauce. One lithography exposure covers several layers at once, and standard 300 mm tools with DUV do the job, with no EUV required. The current roadmap is aiming at over 100 layers with “hundreds of thousands” of vertical connections.
Retaining data at higher temperatures is the challenge, and one the founders have probed repeatedly with their testing. A 2020 paper from co-founder Suman Datta’s group, on a tungsten-doped indium oxide two-transistor cell, had retention of 1 second at 25 degrees Celsius and just 300 milliseconds at 85°C. An update in 2025, which has Datta as a co-author, adds a third transistor and removes the gate overlap from its transistors, managing over 1,000 seconds at 25°C, up from 200 seconds with overlapped ones. It also simulated a GPU L2 at twice SRAM’s capacity but in the same area with 75–80% lower energy-delay-area product, a combined score that multiplies energy, delay and area.
Six months later, both founders showed a “folded asymmetric boosted” three-transistor cell that held data for over 300 seconds at 85°C, as compared to only 100 milliseconds for a conventional three-transistor design. That’s still below the roughly 95°C that Nagare says DRAM must stay under, so neither the founders’ published cells nor Z2RAM have shown retention above that line yet. The boosted cell is also “refresh-free,” which means data in the GPU’s last-level cache, profiled from AI workloads, doesn’t have time to decay before it is overwritten.
| What the founders’ papers measured and simulated, and what Nagare projects |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Figure | Value | Measured, simulated or projected | Conditions | Source | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2020 two-transistor cell, retention | 1 s; 300 ms | Measured | 25°C; 85°C | Datta’s group, IEDM 2020 | 
| 2025 three-transistor cell (self-aligned), retention | More than 1,000 s | Measured | 25°C | Georgia Tech, IEDM 2025 | 
| Conventional three-transistor cell, retention | 0.1 s | Measured | 85°C, to a 100 mV decay | Georgia Tech, VLSI 2026 | 
| Boosted three-transistor cell, retention | More than 300 s | Measured | 85°C, to a 100 mV decay | Georgia Tech, VLSI 2026 | 
| Write pulse | 10 ns | Measured | Two-transistor cell | Georgia Tech, IEDM 2025 | 
| Read delay | 2.6 ns | Simulated | 7nm design, 128×128 array | Georgia Tech, VLSI 2026 | 
| Cell area | 0.0168 µm² | Projected | 7nm design rules | Georgia Tech, VLSI 2026 | 
| Bit density | 5.7× that of 7nm SRAM | Simulated | Four tiers, 256MB, same area | Yu’s group, IEEE Trans. Computers 2026 | 
| GPU L2 energy-delay-area product | 75–80% lower than SRAM | Simulated | Twice the capacity in the same area | Georgia Tech, IEDM 2025 | 
| Logic power under stacked DRAM | 220 W/cm² (300 W/cm² with better thermal vias) | Simulated | DRAM kept at 95°C or below | Yu’s group, JxCDC 2025 | 
| Nagare Gen 1 density | 5× SRAM | Projected | Six layers, vs. 2nm HD SRAM | Nagare Labs | 
| Nagare Gen 1 speed | 14× faster than DRAM | Projected | Gen 1 | Nagare Labs | 
| Nagare Gen 1 read energy | 3× less than SRAM | Projected | Gen 1 | Nagare Labs | 
Physical space is also limited for this application, and the founders project their boosted cell at 0.0168 µm² at 7nm, compared with 0.0199 µm² for a high-density SRAM cell on TSMC’s 3nm (N3) process. A separate study from Yu’s group found that a four-tier, 256MB cache of two-transistor gain cells at 7nm could reach 5.7x the bit density of 7nm SRAM in the same area, in simulation. However, the return on investment falls off past seven or eight tiers because masks scale with layers. Nagare Labs’ claim of single lithography would potentially bypass this limitation.
That has not yet been proven, and nothing published yet shows it. “Where we are is literally lab prototypes,” Datta told The Register, adding that sampling of Z2RAM tiles is targeted within four years and production shipments, if they arrive, within the next decade. Yu told the outlet that no standard yet exists for integrating this kind of memory with an accelerator, which means Nagare might have to come up with the interface itself. Datta also mentioned reliability to the outlet, as single-electron effects can shift a cell’s threshold enough to upset the stored bit. It also remains to be seen if the tested three-transistor cells work sufficiently well as a two-transistor, single-shield product.
Even if Nagare clears those hurdles, a more important one lingers: It currently has no fab. The plan to scale depends on getting partners for fabrication as well as packaging. Nagare is reportedly looking for an R&D fab partner so it can scale beyond the university clean room. Perhaps the most similar type of memory-on-compute shipping today, and the one Datta cited to the outlet as a model for working with chipmakers, is AMD’s 3D V-Cache.
Z2RAM isn’t the first capacitorless memory to promise a 5x improvement over SRAM in density; it follows in the footsteps of Innovative Silicon’s Z-RAM from 20 years ago, a technology AMD licensed, though it was not pursued. A Georgia Tech paper due at IEDM in December covers a different device, a one-transistor, one-ferroelectric-transistor cell, aimed at the same gap between SRAM latency and DRAM density.
Gelsinger, previously CEO of Intel, which started as a memory company, phased out Optane, a low-latency non-volatile memory, in favor of CXL. Optane sought to bridge the gap between slower non-volatile storage, such as HDDs and standard SSDs, and DRAM. Now he sits on Nagare’s board, and Playground Global, where he is a general partner, led the startup’s $5 million round as Nagare searches for a solution to a different but related problem.
Nagare declined to share measured retention, latency, or energy figures. The founders’ boosted cell already holds data at 85°C longer than a cache needs, but until a fab-built, multi-layer Z2RAM stack is measured, retention above 95°C included, its headline numbers remain projections.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Taxbit is a digital-asset tax and accounting compliance platform. Founded in 2018, Taxbit helps enterprises such as exchanges, payment services, and brokers calculate gains and losses, collect tax documentation, and file information returns at scale. Now, a cited, permission-aware AI assistant helps compliance teams find answers right inside the product dashboard.
But the knowledge needed to use that dashboard well was scattered across the public website, API documentation, and help-center articles, and a meaningful share was never written down at all. When a customer asked “what does this form status mean?”, they either went digging or filed a support ticket. Today more than 55 percent of users who ask Assist a question return to ask another within 24 hours, according to Taxbit’s internal production analytics.
In this post, we share how we built Taxbit Assist, the AI assistant now embedded in the Taxbit dashboard, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. We cover the architecture, the retrieval work that made answers trustworthy enough to ship to regulated customers, how we handle safety and data residency, and how we continuously measure answer quality on live production traffic.
What the assistant had to get right
A generic chatbot was not an option in this domain. Four constraints shaped what we built:
- Grounded and cited – Our users make filing decisions. Every answer had to trace back to a source the user could open and read, and when the assistant didn’t know something, it had to say so.
- Role and organization awareness – The assistant shouldn’t walk a Support User through an admin-only workflow and send them to a page that they can’t open.
- No tax advice – Explaining how Taxbit computes cost basis (the accounting method used to compute a gain or loss) is product documentation. Telling a user which method to elect is tax advice. The line between the two is narrow.
- Regional data residency – Supported from a single codebase, with continuous quality measurement in production.
- Inside our compliance program – Taxbit Assist is developed and operated in line with ISO/IEC 42001, the international standard for AI management systems. Taxbit is also certified to ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27701 and holds a SOC 2 Type II report. Taxbit doesn’t train or fine-tune any model, and Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use prompts or completions to train models.
We are also a small team. Rather than build and operate the agent loop, conversation-state store, and session isolation ourselves, we chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for three reasons: its managed agent runtime removed infrastructure operations, built-in AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, eliminated a separate conversation-state store, and per-session isolation kept each user’s context contained. That let us put most of our effort into the retrieval and safety work that follows.
Solution overview
Taxbit Assist is a Strands Agents SDK application running on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram illustrates the solution architecture.
The workflow consists of the following steps:
- A user asks a question in the Taxbit dashboard. A streaming chat API forwards it to AgentCore runtime along with the user’s verified identity (email, organization ID, and dashboard roles).
- The runtime screens the incoming message with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Personally identifiable information (PII) is masked in place. If the message is blocked, the model is never invoked.
- The agent retrieves candidate passages from an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases knowledge base, and then reranks them server-side. The knowledge base uses the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability of Amazon Bedrock, backed by Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
- Amazon Bedrock models reason over the retrieved passages and verify that the user has access to the relevant feature and role before recommending any workflow. For model availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region.
- The answer streams back to the dashboard with source links. AgentCore memory carries the conversation across turns.
- Every request emits OpenTelemetry traces to Amazon CloudWatch, which feeds our evaluation tooling.
The agent runtime
The agent is a small Python application: a system prompt, a model, and eight tools. It ships as an ARM64 container image that AgentCore runtime pulls from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and scales on demand.
The tools are deliberately narrow:
- Knowledge base search, the primary tool.
- Two access checks, one for organization entitlement and one for the user’s dashboard role.
- Four support ticket tools to create, list, update, and close the caller’s own tickets.
- Current time, for the rare question that needs sub-day precision.
In this version, the agent has no read access to customer tax data. It answers from product knowledge, and the only writes it can perform are the caller’s own support tickets.
One security decision underpins all of them: the model never handles identity. The user’s email, organization ID, and roles come from the trusted calling service and are bound into each tool through a closure before the model sees it. The model can decide whether to check permissions but not whose permissions to check, because identity isn’t a parameter it can set. User input is sanitized at the boundary, so a prompt injection cannot imitate the trusted context line.
The agent runs a foundation model (FM) through Amazon Bedrock, invoked through cross-Region inference profiles.
Geography-aware inference handles data residency. The inference profile ID carries a geography prefix derived from the deployment Region, so EU deployments keep inference within the EU, and US deployments stay in the US. Beyond keeping inference in the right geography, we also support a bring your own key (BYOK) model. In BYOK accounts, conversation history and the other stores that hold client data are encrypted with the customer’s own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key.
Application inference profiles handle cost visibility. Each deployment wraps the system inference profile in a tagged application profile, so every model invocation carries cost-allocation tags and shows up in AWS Cost Explorer, broken down by workload.
Amazon Bedrock prompt caching cuts latency and token cost. The system prompt is byte-identical for every request and ends with a cache checkpoint, so the static prefix is cached across users. Per-request context travels on the user message instead.
Grounding answers in a curated knowledge base
Most of our engineering effort went into the knowledge base: an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base backed by Amazon S3 Vectors, with Cohere Embed English v3 for embeddings, producing 1,024-dimension float32 vectors compared by cosine distance. All of it is managed, so there is no vector database for us to operate.
Ingestion
Content flows in from three kinds of sources, each landing under its own prefix in a single Amazon S3 bucket.
The following diagram shows how content reaches the index.
Published content comes first: our public website, our API documentation, and our help-center articles, crawled by scheduled AWS Lambda functions. With sitemap lastmod timestamps and content hashes, a typical run only touches what changed since the previous one. Scoping mattered more than we anticipated. Our sitemap has roughly over 400 URLs, but only about over 70 belong in an answer-generating corpus, and /blogs/ alone accounts for more than 300 marketing pages. Left in, that campaign content competes with the help center to become the cited source for compliance questions. Excluding it was one of our highest-value retrieval changes, and it required no model work at all.
The second source is less conventional: Lambda functions read our product source code and generate Markdown documentation covering dashboard routes, permission gates, form eligibility logic, and reporting configuration. This captures product truth that exists nowhere else in prose, and it stays current because it’s regenerated from the code itself. The third source is curated content: hand-written articles and approved corrections that fill gaps the automated sources don’t cover.
Amazon EventBridge schedules the crawls on a staggered nightly and weekly cadence, and each scraper triggers an ingestion job only when something has changed. We group the nine scrapers into three umbrella data sources split by S3 sub-prefix (product-public/, product-internals/, curated/), which keeps related content together.
Contextual chunking
We chose semantic chunking, which splits documents at natural boundaries and outperformed fixed-size chunking on our retrieval tests. But a chunk pulled from the middle of a document loses track of what the document is about. In tax reporting, that context is often the whole answer: a passage that applies only to non-US filing regimes is actively misleading if it’s returned for a question about IRS Form 1099 (an information return for reporting payments).
To fix this, we used the knowledge base’s custom transformation hook to run a POST_CHUNKING Lambda function that prepends each chunk with its document’s H1 title and lead paragraph, which usually states where the content applies. The prefix is capped at roughly 128 tokens (80 characters of title and 300 of scope). Because Cohere Embed English v3 accepts up to 512 tokens per input, chunk bodies are capped at 384 so the header and body fit within that window together. A production probe found about 28 percent of our chunks sat in the 385–512 band and would have had their tails silently truncated.
This was the highest-impact retrieval change we made: chunks now carry their own scope into the vector index, instead of it living only in the document’s first chunk.
Two practical notes: First, Amazon Bedrock requires the transformation’s intermediate storage to be a separate bucket from the data source bucket. A distinct prefix on the same bucket is rejected. Second, enabling a custom transformation on an existing data source forces a replacement, so plan for a full re-ingestion rather than an in-place change.
Retrieval
At query time the pipeline over-fetches and then prunes:
The reranker runs inside Amazon Bedrock as part of the same Retrieve call, so there is no extra service hop. We keep the 75-candidate pool wide because authoritative articles routinely sit at vector rank 20–50 and only rerank to the top after they’re in the pool. The per-document cap keeps one heavily chunked page from filling every slot.
Citation eligibility is enforced by source type in code rather than by prompt instruction. Only the three published sources are citable, because only their URLs resolve to something a customer can open. Code-derived and curated content grounds answers, but doesn’t produce a link the customer can’t follow.
Safety and data handling
Three boundaries keep one tenant’s data out of another tenant’s session:
- The knowledge base holds no tenant-specific content: only published documentation, code-derived product reference, and curated articles.
- The entitlement and role-check tools take the caller’s organization and email from the service that already authenticated them, so the model can’t widen that scope.
- AgentCore runtime isolates each session, and conversation history is partitioned by memory, session, and actor ID. That actor ID must come from the calling service rather than from AWS caller identity, because the runtime executes under a single service role. An inferred identity would put every user’s history in one partition.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, which provides configurable safeguards based on your application requirements, screens every incoming message before the agent runs. We apply it as a standalone ApplyGuardrail call scoped to the current user turn, which avoids rescanning the entire conversation history on every turn.
The PII policy is tuned for tax data. Secrets that have no business flowing through a language model, such as passwords, card verification codes, and cloud access keys, are blocked outright. Numeric identifiers with narrow formats, including Social Security numbers, Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers (ITINs), bank account and routing numbers, and International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs), are anonymized in place. This lets the agent help with the workflow without ever seeing the value. Credentials for external integrations live in AWS Secrets Manager and are fetched at runtime, never baked into images or configuration.
Measuring quality on live traffic
The habit that has paid off most is measuring quality continuously in production, without ever blocking a response. The following diagram illustrates how the trace feed fans out to four independent consumers and how an expert’s correction finds its way back into retrieval.
AgentCore online evaluations sample 10 percent of live sessions from CloudWatch traces and score them with six built-in LLM-as-a-judge evaluators: helpfulness, harmfulness, coherence, instruction following, tool-selection accuracy, and tool-parameter accuracy. Results land in CloudWatch as metrics and per-session scores, so a quality regression shows up on a dashboard rather than in a customer complaint.
We layer our own judges on top, reading the same trace feed through a CloudWatch subscription filter. A Lambda function grades each sampled answer on faithfulness to the retrieved sources and relevance of the retrieved articles, and emits the results as CloudWatch metrics. We keep faithfulness and relevance separate because an answer can be faithful to sources that should never have been retrieved. When that happens, the problem is in the retrieval pipeline, not the model.
A foundation model classifier checks every response for tax-advice drift. The line between product documentation and tax advice is too fine for a topic filter: “Transferring between your own wallets isn’t a taxable event” is advice, while explaining how Taxbit applies FIFO (First In, First Out) is product documentation. A model prompted with instructions and examples reaches near-zero false positives, compared with roughly 25 percent for a topic filter. Neither classifier adds latency.
Humans close the loop. Sampled answers, with personal details scrubbed from each question and answer, go to an internal review channel where subject-matter experts can reply with a correction. Approved corrections are written into the knowledge base’s curated prefix and trigger an incremental ingestion job, so an expert’s fix reaches the next user’s answer within minutes, without a deployment.
Deployment and operations
The entire stack is defined in AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), so standing up a new environment, or a new Region with different residency requirements, is a configuration change. Every pull request runs an offline evaluation suite: a golden set of scenarios judged against expected tool paths and behavior, so prompt and retrieval changes get measured before they ship. The suite also runs nightly against production. Merges deploy to staging first, then to production behind a manual approval gate.
Results and impact
Taxbit Assist has been in production in the US and the EU since May 2026, with EU traffic served by in-geography inference. Answers are grounded in the curated knowledge base and cited to its sources, and the assistant checks feature availability and the user’s permissions before recommending a workflow. For an embedded support surface, repeat usage is the metric the team watches most closely.
One early example stands out. A new client integrating with Taxbit to collect tax documentation (W-8 and W-9 forms, the IRS tax withholding and identification forms) leaned on the assistant heavily during their build. Integration questions that would previously have landed in a shared channel with our team or a support ticket were answered on the spot. The client kept their integration moving without waiting on Taxbit’s support team, and the support team never saw the traffic.
Model cost averages under 20 cents per conversation. Prompt caching does much of that work: about three-quarters of input tokens are served from cache, which cuts model cost by more than half.
What we would do differently
- Scope the corpus before tuning prompts. After we narrowed the index to support and documentation content and gave every chunk its document’s scope, answers improved more than they had from any prompt revision.
- Measure guardrail filter strength against your own traffic. We measured the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails PII detectors against our own traffic and set the PIN and bank-routing detectors to detect-only, so numeric form identifiers such as 1099 pass through while the detectors still flag genuine sensitive values.
- Keep the system prompt byte-stable so prompt caching works across users.
- Bind identity in code from the first prototype. Our early test build had the model pass identity to the tools as an argument. We moved it to the calling service before launch so an injected prompt can’t widen its own access.
What’s next
Today, the assistant answers from product knowledge. The next step is an assistant that can answer questions like “How many of my payees are missing tax documentation?” by querying the customer’s own reporting data through the same identity-bound, permission-checked tool pattern. The user asks the question and the model decides which tool and filters to use, but the authenticated caller determines whose data that tool can read, so the model can’t change it.
Conclusion
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore let a small team ship a cited, permission-aware assistant to regulated enterprise customers in two geographies without operating our own infrastructure for orchestration, vector search, content safety, or evaluation. That freed us to spend our time where it mattered: the corpus, the retrieval pipeline, and what counts as a good answer in tax information reporting.
To learn more, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and the Strands Agents SDK on GitHub.
If you have questions or want to share how you are solving similar problems, leave a comment.

articles.title: Elektrisch ohne Batterie: Neue Zahnbürste aus chinesischem Labor bekämpft Karies mit Strom
articles.text:
Diese Zahnbürste erzeugt Strom: Wie das gegen Karies helfen soll
Archäologische Funde belegen: Seit mindestens 3000 Jahren versuchen Menschen, ihre Zähne mit eigens angefertigten Werkzeugen zu säubern, um Zahnkrankheiten zu vermeiden. Am Prinzip hat sich wenig geändert: Der tückische Belag auf den Zähnen, in dem sich Karies-Bakterien vermehren, wird durch mechanischen Druck beseitig.
Allerdings hält das meist nicht lange. Chinesische Forscher wollen das ändern: Ihre Zahnbürste erzeugt beim Putzen elektrische Ladungen und reaktive Sauerstoffmoleküle, die Bakterien schädigen.
Ladung durch Biegen
Yanhui Lu und Kollegen von der Peking University beschreiben in der Fachzeitschrift Science Advances eine Zahnbürste mit Borsten aus einem piezoelektrischen Material. Die Borsten bestehen aus Polyvinylidenfluorid, kurz PVDF, einem Kunststoff, der piezoelektrische Eigenschaften hat. Wird es mechanisch verformt, entstehen an seiner Oberfläche elektrische Ladungen. Beim Putzen biegen sich die Borsten. Dabei werden Ladungen frei, die mit Wassermolekülen reagieren. Es entstehen reaktive Moleküle, die die Membranen von Bakterien angreifen.
Nach drei Monaten simulierter Nutzung blieben die PVDF-Borsten weitgehend intakt. Der Zahnschmelz wurde nicht rauer. Oberflächenpotenzial und Spannung blieben auch nach drei Monaten realer Nutzung stabil. Die Bildung reaktiver Sauerstoffspezies ließ sich weiterhin nachweisen.
Erfolgreiche Tests
Im Labor testeten die Forscher die Borsten gegen zwei wichtige Krankheitserreger im Mund. Streptococcus mutans gilt als Hauptverursacher von Karies. Porphyromonas gingivalis ist mit Parodontitis verbunden, einer chronischen Entzündung des Zahnhalteapparats.
Die Unterschiede waren deutlich: Die elektrischen Borsten töteten 52,8 Prozent der Kariesbakterien ab. Das Putzen mit herkömmlichen Borsten aus Nylon nur 9,3 Prozent. Bei den Parodonditis-Bakterien lag die Rate bei 78 Prozent – mit Nylon bei acht Prozent.
In einem Alltagstest ließen die Forschenden zudem benutzte Zahnbürsten einen Monat in einer Umgebung liegen, die einem feuchten Badezimmer entsprach. Auf den PVDF-Bürsten siedelten sich deutlich weniger Bakterien an.
Außerdem führte das Team eine Studie mit 115 Freiwilligen durch. Alle Teilnehmenden hatten Zahnfleischentzündungen oder Karies. Sie putzten drei Monate lang mit einer von vier Bürsten: zwei PVDF-Varianten und zwei Nylon‑Varianten. Dazu gab es fluoridfreie Zahnpasta.
In beiden PVDF-Gruppen gingen Plaque, Zahnfleischentzündung und Zahnfleischbluten deutlich zurück. Der Rückgang des Belags setzte schnell ein, vor allem im ersten Monat. Das Zahnfleisch erholte sich langsamer.
Grenzen der Studie
Die Autoren benennen selbst mehrere Einschränkungen. Die Laborversuche liefen über längere Zeit am Stück. Neun Stunden entsprechen der gesamten Putzzeit einer Bürste über drei Monate. Echtes Putzen besteht aber aus kurzen Intervallen, gefolgt von Speichel, Essen und neuem Belag. Hier sollen künftige Modelle nachbessern.
Zudem wurde nur gegen herkömmliche Nylonbürsten verglichen. Vergleiche mit elektrischen, Schall- oder antimikrobiell beschichteten Zahnbürsten stehen noch aus. Ob und wann es die Piezo-Zahnbürsten zu kaufen gibt, ist also noch völlig offen.

articles.title: AI-powered cyberattacks put Indian fintechs on alert; Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
articles.text:
AI-powered cyberattacks put Indian fintechs on alert; Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
An advisory from the government body said the AI-assisted financial threat is still active and warns BFSI entities to treat it as an “immediate and continuing threat”.
Dear Reader,
Investor appetite for India’s B2C ecommerce sector appears to be cooling. Funding fell 33% to $1.6 billion across 356 rounds between January and November 3, 2026, compared with $2.4 billion across 621 rounds in the year-ago period, according to Tracxn. Late-stage and seed-stage funding declined 51% and 50%, respectively, while early-stage investments remained relatively stable, growing 3%.
While investors are becoming more cautious, the AI infrastructure boom is facing a different challenge: rising public concerns over its impact on local communities. OpenAI has pledged to pay the full electricity costs of data centres it owns and operates, while committing to greater transparency around construction plans and community consultations.
Meanwhile, India's cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has warned of AI-driven attacks targeting fintech firms and NBFCs, with hackers exploiting payment systems to siphon off funds.
Cybersecurity concerns are also surfacing across global financial services. Binance has revoked all API keys linked to third-party trading platform SignalPlus following a potential security issue reported by the company. The exchange said its own systems and user funds remain safe, and advised affected users to review their trading positions before reconnecting.
The risks extend beyond financial services. A cyberattack targeting refrigeration control systems at three sites operated by France's national blood service raised storage temperatures for plasma and other blood products. Monitoring systems detected the breach in time, allowing staff to move supplies before any products were compromised. Authorities are investigating the incident.
In today’s newsletter:
- CERT-In flags AI-driven attacks on NBFCs, fintech firms
- Saraniya Periasamy’s journey at Agnikul Cosmos
- Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
Here’s your trivia for today: What is a 'zero-day' vulnerability in cybersecurity? (Scroll down for the answer)
Artificial Intelligence
CERT-In flags AI-driven attacks on NBFCs, fintech firms
AI-powered cyberattacks targeting India’s financial services sector are escalating, prompting a fresh warning from CERT-In. The government cybersecurity agency has flagged a campaign called CRAFTY FALCON, which uses AI tools to target NBFCs, fintech companies and other financial institutions. The attacks have involved exploiting payment systems and stealing cryptocurrency assets.
Key takeaways:
- CERT-In has identified an active campaign called CRAFTY FALCON, which uses machine intelligence and AI-assisted tools to target financial institutions.
- Attackers have exploited merchant settlement APIs to move funds and stolen wallet keys to siphon cryptocurrency assets.
- The campaign has affected NBFCs, digital lending platforms, payment aggregators, fintech firms and crypto exchanges, with CERT-In warning that the threat remains active.
Inspiration
Saraniya Periasamy’s journey at Agnikul Cosmos
From joining a space-tech startup with no prior experience in the sector to leading the development of an orbital launch vehicle, Saraniya Periasamy’s journey has been anything but conventional. As Agnikul Cosmos’ fourth employee, she has played a key role in the company’s efforts to build indigenous rocket technology. Today, as Executive Vice President and Vehicle Director, she is helping steer the development of Agnibaan while encouraging more women to explore careers in space-tech.
Breaking barriers:
- Saraniya joined Agnikul Cosmos eight years ago as a Systems Engineer and went on to lead the development of its Agnibaan SOrTeD suborbital mission, which successfully flew in May 2024.
- She is now leading the development of Agnibaan, the company's orbital launch vehicle, with plans to demonstrate booster recovery and reuse, alongside exploring ways to repurpose its upper stage.
- Having transitioned from civil engineering and ocean technology into space, Saraniya believes self-doubt is often a bigger barrier for women than a lack of opportunities.
Ecommerce
Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
Shiprocket turned profitable in Q2 FY27, reporting a net profit of Rs 60 lakh against a loss of Rs 20.3 crore a year ago, while revenue grew 35% to Rs 673.6 crore. Its emerging business, led by Martech and omnichannel solutions, grew 61% during the quarter. The company also repaid Rs 242 crore in borrowings following its IPO, ending the first half debt-free.
News & updates
- Ambulance pricing: Blinkit Ambulance will charge Rs 2,500 for non-emergency transfers, while emergency services will continue to remain free. Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal said the move aims to discourage routine hospital visits and transfers from using emergency ambulances, keeping them available for critical cases.
- Ronaldo retires: Cristiano Ronaldo will retire from Portugal's national team after the November international break, ending a 23-year international career. He leaves as men's international football's record goalscorer with 146 goals in 234 appearances, having led Portugal to the Euro 2016 title and two Nations League victories.
What is a 'zero-day' vulnerability in cybersecurity?
Answer: A security flaw that attackers can exploit before a fix is available

articles.title: España ha elegido las aguas de Canarias para volar por los aires un buque de guerra que Marruecos tiene en su flota desde 1982
articles.text:
La Armada española acaba de realizar una demostración de fuerza en aguas del Atlántico. Un submarino de última generación, un buque de guerra con décadas de historia y un único torpedo han protagonizado unas maniobras que van mucho más allá de un simple ejercicio militar. Además, hay un detalle especialmente llamativo: la conexión del barco hundido con la flota de Marruecos.
Un torpedo al sur de Canarias. El submarino español S-81 Isaac Peral ha hundido al antiguo patrullero Infanta Elena durante el ejercicio de fuego real SINKEX 26, desarrollado en aguas del Atlántico, al sur de Canarias. Para enviar el buque al fondo del océano bastó el lanzamiento de un único torpedo, en una operación organizada para comprobar las capacidades de combate del primer submarino de la clase S-80.
El blanco no era una embarcación enemiga, sino un antiguo buque de la Armada retirado del servicio y preparado expresamente para ser hundido en condiciones controladas.
La conexión con Marruecos. El detalle más curioso está en la identidad del barco elegido. El Infanta Elena pertenecía a la clase Descubierta, una familia de corbetas construidas por la antigua Empresa Nacional Bazán, hoy Navantia, de la que también forma parte la Teniente Coronel Errahmani (F-501), fabricada en Ferrol para la Marina Real de Marruecos y entregada en 1982.
El buque marroquí entró en servicio en 1983, de modo que España ha utilizado como blanco una embarcación de la misma clase que exportó al país vecino hace más de cuatro décadas. Por supuesto, eso no significa que se haya atacado un barco marroquí ni que las maniobras estuvieran dirigidas contra Marruecos: el objetivo era un antiguo buque español, pero las coincidencias a la hora de elegir el blanco y el momento, no parecen baladí.
De patrullar los océanos a convertirse en blanco. El Infanta Elena acumulaba unos 46 años de trayectoria desde su incorporación a la Armada española. Concebido originalmente como corbeta y posteriormente reclasificado como patrullero, formó parte durante décadas de las capacidades de vigilancia y presencia naval del país.
Su destino final ha sido muy diferente al de sus antiguas misiones: servir como objetivo real para comprobar la eficacia del armamento submarino español. ¿La razón? La elección de un casco de estas características permite ensayar un ataque contra un blanco de dimensiones y resistencia propias de un buque militar.
Un solo disparo. Según la información publicada por Infodefensa, el Isaac Peral empleó un torpedo pesado filoguiado DM2A4, un arma de fabricación alemana y calibre de 533 milímetros. Este tipo de torpedo puede recibir instrucciones a través de un cable durante parte de su recorrido y está concebido para atacar tanto buques de superficie como submarinos.
Su capacidad destructiva reside en la potente carga explosiva y en los efectos de la detonación bajo el agua, capaces de provocar daños estructurales e inundaciones graves. La Armada ha confirmado el hundimiento con un único torpedo, aunque su comunicado no identifica expresamente el modelo empleado ni detalla cómo se produjo la explosión.
Mucho más que hundir un barco. El Isaac Peral, entregado a la Armada en 2023 y construido por Navantia, es el primer submarino español de la serie S-80. Lo hemos contado antes, su principal ventaja no es únicamente la potencia de sus torpedos, sino su capacidad para desplazarse discretamente bajo el agua y atacar sin revelar anticipadamente su posición.
El SINKEX 26 ha permitido demostrar esa capacidad con armamento real y comprobar la preparación de su tripulación. Como subraya la Armada, su valor disuasorio reside en la posibilidad de que un submarino esté patrullando sin ser detectado y pueda neutralizar una amenaza a distancia.
Un despliegue militar completo. Aunque el hundimiento ha concentrado toda la atención, la Armada ha informado que el ejercicio involucró a numerosas unidades. Participaron, por ejemplo, las fragatas Cristóbal Colón (F-105) y Navarra (F-85), el buque multipropósito Carnota (A-61), el buque de acción marítima Relámpago (P-43), tres aviones AV-8B Harrier, un helicóptero naval, un dron Scan Eagle y una aeronave de vigilancia marítima del Ejército del Aire y del Espacio.
Bajo la dirección del capitán de navío Rafael Mira Calvo, el objetivo fue comprobar cómo se coordinan los medios de superficie, submarinos y aéreos en un escenario próximo al combate real.
Un hundimiento preparado hasta el último detalle. Antes de utilizar el Infanta Elena como blanco, la Armada retiró sus combustibles, aceites y componentes contaminantes para reducir el impacto ambiental. También evaluó previamente las condiciones hidrográficas de la zona y activó protocolos de vigilancia de cetáceos y otras especies protegidas, además de medidas de seguridad para la navegación civil.
Dicho de otra forma, el casco del antiguo patrullero ha terminado en el fondo del Atlántico como resultado de un ejercicio planificado hasta el milímetro. Para España, el resultado representa una prueba de la capacidad ofensiva de su nuevo submarino. Para el Infanta Elena, el final de una trayectoria de décadas que comenzó como corbeta de una clase todavía vinculada a la historia naval de Marruecos.
Imagen | Armada, James C. Davis
